text: Elasticity of demand is a measure of how responsive the quantity demanded of a good or service is to changes in its price or other influential factors. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded in response to a percentage change in price or other variables. There are several types of elasticity of demand, including price elasticity of demand, income elasticity of demand, and cross-price elasticity of demand. Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in the good's own price, and is classified as elastic (greater than 1), inelastic (less than 1), or unit elastic (equal to 1). Income elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in consumer income, and is classified as positive (normal good) or negative (inferior good). Cross-price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in the price of a related good, and is classified as positive (substitutes) or negative (complements). Understanding the different types of elasticity of demand is crucial for businesses to develop effective pricing strategies, predict revenue changes, and make informed decisions about production and investment. For instance, a business with a product that has an elastic demand may benefit from reducing its price to increase sales, while a business with a product that has an inelastic demand may be able to increase its price without losing many customers. By analyzing elasticity of demand, businesses can gain valuable insights into consumer behavior and make data-driven decisions to drive growth and profitability.

text: Plate tectonics is a unifying concept in science that provides the framework for our understanding of the restless movements of the Earth and the phenomena that shape its surface. The outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) is divided into several large and small plates, which riding on the semi-fluid portion of the upper mantle (i.e., asthenosphere) can deform plastically under stress. These tectonic plates travel at a snail’s pace — about the rate at which your hair grows a few centimeters a year — pushed along by convection currents in the mantle, caused in turn by heat from earth’s core. While these plates shift, they bump into each other at borders, causing geologic signs of that activity such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, mountains forming and the semblance of ocean trenches and ridges. The idea of plate tectonics superseded previous theories (including continental drift, suggested by Alfred Wegener in the early 20th century), and the paradigm shift from continental drift to plate tectonics began in the mid-20th century, and was confirmed with the discovery of seafloor spreading, and the generation and validation of new geophysical and geochemical data and the development of geophysical and numerical models. Plate boundaries Most parts of the Earth's crust are on top of the plates, and there are essentially three kinds of plate boundaries: divergent (where plates spread apart), such as at mid-ocean ridges; convergent (where plates move toward each other), typically forming subduction zones or mountain ranges; or transform (where plates slip side by side horizontally), as happens at the San Andreas Fault. Different types of boundaries have different features and dangers. For instance, those at convergent boundaries generate strong earthquakes and volcanic arcs, whereas those at divergent boundaries divergent plate generate crust and are not usually as dangerous. It is because of plate tectonics that Earth’s crust gets recycled, continents and oceans are created, and we have resources like minerals and fossil fuels. It also is an important part of Earth’s carbon cycle and climate regulation, enabling phenomena such as volcanic outgassing and the burial of organic carbon. It has become a unifying theory in Earth science, explaining a diversity of surface features and phenomena. These are made possible in part by plate tectonics, which is therefore crucial not only to our understanding of the natural world but also to applications such as estimating hazards by tracking movements of plates and planning land use.

text: Endotoxins and exotoxins are the two primary types of bacterial toxins; however, they have different structures, sources, methods of action, and effects. Exotoxins are proteins produced by Gram positive and certain Gram negative bacteria as they grow and metabolize. They are extremely toxic, heat-labile (heat-inactivated), and it take very small quantities to produce severe effects. Examples are tetanus toxin from Clostridium tetani, botulinum toxin from Clostridium botulinum and diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Such toxins often attack certain cells or organs (nerve cells or intestinal lining, for example) and their effect is typically specific and precise. In contrast, endotoxins are LPS (lipopolysaccharides) found in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, such as E. coli, Salmonella and Pseudomonas. They are not released while the bacteria are alive but only when they die and the cell wall breaks apart. Endotoxins are heat-stable and less toxic than exotoxins, but they can induce systemic inflammation, including fever and shock that can cause death from such conditions as septic shock. In contrast to exotoxins, they are nonspecific in function and target. Endotoxins are determined in the pharmaceutical industry, in particular for injections drugs and medical equipment, for example in the LAL (Limulus Amebocyte Lysate) test. Exotoxins are a specific anti-host damaging and are secreted out by bacteria which are potent and active proteins whereas endotoxins are structural molecule of bacteria which comes out after the death of bacteria and are responsible for strong immune reaction.

text: Theories of intelligence attempt to explain the nature, structure, and components of human cognitive abilities, offering diverse perspectives on how intelligence is defined and measured. One of the earliest and most influential is Spearman’s Two-Factor Theory (1904), which posits a general intelligence (g factor) underlying all cognitive tasks, alongside specific abilities (s factors) tied to particular domains. In contrast, Thurstone’s Primary Mental Abilities (1938) identifies seven distinct factors, such as verbal comprehension, numerical ability, and spatial reasoning, rejecting a single g factor. Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Theory integrates these ideas, distinguishing between fluid intelligence (Gf)—the capacity to solve novel problems and adapt—and crystallized intelligence (Gc)—accumulated knowledge and skills, while also recognizing narrower abilities. Gardner’s Theory of Multiple Intelligences (1983) expands the concept beyond traditional IQ, proposing eight independent intelligences, including linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic, emphasizing cultural and contextual relevance. Sternberg’s Triarchic Theory (1985) focuses on three facets: analytical intelligence (problem-solving), creative intelligence (innovation), and practical intelligence (real-world adaptability), arguing that success depends on balancing these. Emotional Intelligence (EI), popularized by Goleman (1995), highlights the role of self-awareness, empathy, and social skills in effective functioning, separate from pure cognitive ability. PASS Theory (Das & Naglieri, 1994) links intelligence to four cognitive processes—Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, and Successive processing—rooted in brain function. More recently, dynamic theories emphasize intelligence as malleable and context-dependent, shaped by experiences and neuroplasticity. While psychometric approaches (e.g., IQ tests) dominate measurement, critics argue they may overlook creativity, wisdom, or cultural biases. These theories collectively illustrate intelligence as a multidimensional, evolving construct, encompassing logical, emotional, social, and practical dimensions, with ongoing debates about its universality versus diversity across individuals and cultures.

text: Self-concept refers to the collection of beliefs, perceptions, and evaluations that individuals hold about themselves, shaping their identity and influencing their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It encompasses multiple dimensions, including self-image (how one sees oneself physically, socially, and in terms of roles), self-esteem (the evaluative aspect, reflecting one’s sense of worth or competence), and ideal self (the person one aspires to be, often compared to the actual self, creating motivation or distress depending on alignment). Developed through experiences, social interactions, and cultural influences, self-concept begins forming in early childhood through feedback from caregivers, peers, and societal standards, evolving over time via introspection and life events. Theorists like Carl Rogers emphasized the importance of congruence between the real and ideal self for psychological well-being, while discrepancies can lead to anxiety or low self-esteem. Social psychologists highlight the role of social comparison (evaluating oneself against others) and reflected appraisal (internalizing others’ perceptions) in shaping self-concept. For instance, academic achievements, relationships, and societal stereotypes (e.g., gender roles) can reinforce or challenge one’s self-view. The self-concept is dynamic, adapting to new roles (e.g., becoming a parent) or crises (e.g., job loss), and is influenced by cognitive processes like self-schemas (mental frameworks about the self) and attributions (how one explains successes or failures). Cultural differences also play a role: individualistic cultures (e.g., Western societies) often foster an independent self-concept centered on personal traits, while collectivist cultures (e.g., East Asian societies) emphasize interdependent identities tied to group relationships. A well-defined self-concept provides stability and guides decision-making, but distortions (e.g., imposter syndrome or narcissism) can hinder functioning. In therapy, techniques like self-reflection and cognitive restructuring help individuals cultivate a healthier, more accurate self-concept. Ultimately, self-concept is foundational to human experience, bridging internal identity and external reality, and serving as a lens through which individuals navigate their world. Its study remains vital in psychology, education, and personal development, offering insights into motivation, resilience, and the pursuit of self-actualization.

text: In the IELTS Speaking section, band descriptors are used to assess a candidate's spoken English language proficiency and provide a clear understanding of the criteria used to evaluate their performance. Fluency and Coherence refers to the candidate's ability to speak fluently and coherently, without hesitation or repetition, and to link their ideas together logically. Lexical Resource assesses the candidate's vocabulary range, accuracy, and appropriacy, including their ability to use idiomatic language and collocations. Grammatical Range and Accuracy evaluates the candidate's ability to use a range of grammatical structures accurately, including verb tenses, sentence structures, and clause linking. Pronunciation assesses the candidate's ability to pronounce words and phrases clearly and accurately, including their intonation, stress, and rhythm. The band descriptors provide a detailed description of the characteristics of spoken English at each band level, from 0 to 9, and are used by examiners to assess a candidate's performance and award a band score. By understanding the band descriptors, candidates can gain insight into the criteria used to assess their speaking skills and identify areas for improvement, enabling them to prepare more effectively for the test and achieve their desired score. For example, a candidate who scores a Band 7 in Fluency and Coherence is able to "speak at length without noticeable effort or loss of coherence", while a candidate who scores a Band 5 is able to "keep going comprehensibly, even though pausing for grammatical and lexical planning and repair is very evident". By familiarizing themselves with the band descriptors, candidates can develop a clearer understanding of what is expected of them in the Speaking section and improve their overall performance.

text: Animals regulate their body temperature through a complex process that involves various physiological and behavioral mechanisms. Endotherms, such as mammals and birds, maintain a relatively constant body temperature by generating heat through metabolic processes, such as shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis, and by conserving heat through insulation, such as fur or feathers. They also use behavioral mechanisms, such as seeking shade or sun, to regulate their body temperature. Ectotherms, such as reptiles and amphibians, rely on external sources of heat, such as the sun or a warm rock, to regulate their body temperature, and often use behavioral mechanisms, such as basking or seeking shade, to control their temperature. Some animals, such as desert-dwelling lizards, can also use specialized physiological mechanisms, such as altering blood flow to the skin or using evaporative cooling, to regulate their body temperature. Additionally, some animals, such as hibernating mammals, can reduce their metabolic rate and body temperature during periods of inactivity or food scarcity, allowing them to conserve energy. Overall, the ability to regulate body temperature is crucial for an animal's survival, as it allows them to maintain optimal physiological function and respond to changes in their environment. By understanding how animals regulate their body temperature, we can gain insights into the complex interactions between an animal's physiology, behavior, and environment, and appreciate the remarkable diversity of thermoregulatory strategies that have evolved in different species.

text: Kepler's third law of planetary motion, also known as the Law of Harmonies, describes a mathematical relationship between the average distance of planets from the Sun and their orbital periods. It is the proposition that the square of the orbital period (T) of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (R) of its orbit. In formula form, T² ? R³. In other words, the farther a planet is from the Sun, the more time it takes to complete one orbit than its closer counterparts, and so on, in a known and predictable sequence. For example, Earth travels around the Sun in one year at a certain average distance, and Jupiter being farther away takes about twelve years. Kepler’s law was empirically formulated by Kepler himself, then theoretically explained by the law of universal gravitation in the Newtonian theory of gravitation. The proportionality constant is identical for all Planets of one and the same star, this implies a universal harmony with in Planetary systems. This law also enables astronomers and scientists to determine the period of any planet or moon if its distance from the central body is known, and vice versa. And as it turns out, it applies to moons around planets and man-made satellites around Earth, too. A cornerstone of astrophysics, planetary science, and space mission design, Kepler’s third law serves as the bridge between time and distance in orbital mechanics. It uncovers the beautiful mathematical structure of the motion of planets and is still considered the foundation of modern astronomy.

Pharmacological diversity offered by natural products provides unique chemical scaffolds and mechanisms of action that would be difficult to achieve through purely synthetic approaches, contributing to the discovery of novel drug targets and therapeutic pathways. Modern biotechnology applications utilize natural products in developing biosimilars, monoclonal antibodies, and recombinant proteins, while nanotechnology employs natural compounds as drug delivery vehicles and targeting agents. Complementary and integrative medicine increasingly incorporates standardized natural products alongside conventional treatments, with evidence-based herbal medicines gaining acceptance in mainstream healthcare systems. Pharmaceutical industry applications extend to using natural products as starting materials for semi-synthetic drug development, excipients in drug formulations, and quality control standards. Research and development continues to explore marine organisms, extremophiles, and previously unstudied plant species for new therapeutic compounds, while sustainable sourcing and biotechnological production methods ensure reliable supply chains. text: Public debt is a typical way for governments to pay for things, but it may have big effects on an economy depending on how much, why, and how it is managed. When used to pay for things that help the economy thrive, like infrastructure, education, and healthcare, public debt can be good in the short term. These things create jobs and enhance overall welfare. It lets governments keep spending even when their income is low, like during a recession or an emergency. This helps demand and keeps the economy stable. But the bad effects of public debt become clear when too much is borrowed, it is mishandled, or it is used to pay for things that don't help the economy. When the government has a lot of debt, it has to pay more in interest, which can take up a lot of its revenue and leave less for important services and growth. It could also lead to crowding out, which happens when the government borrows money and boosts interest rates, making people less likely to invest in private businesses. When debt is externally sourced, there is a risk of currency depreciation, especially if the country struggles to repay in foreign currencies. Over-reliance on borrowing can lead to debt traps and loss of investor confidence, ultimately resulting in lower credit ratings and increased borrowing costs. In extreme cases, countries may face sovereign debt crises, requiring austerity measures that hurt economic growth and social services. Despite these risks, public debt is not inherently bad; it depends on the debt-to-GDP ratio, the interest rate compared to growth rate, and how the borrowed funds are used. If managed wisely, with transparent governance and investment in productive sectors, public debt can support development without jeopardizing long-term fiscal sustainability.

text: An estimator is considered to be good if it gives the same kind of estimate on different data and if estimates on average do well in estimating the true value of a population parameter. There are a number of important properties 53 for a good estimator to possess. This is important for two reasons: first, it means the estimator is unbiased — its expectation is equal to the true value of the parameter — and therefore it does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the parameter. Two, the estimator should be consistent, ie., as your sample size n goes to infinity, your estimator should converge to the true value of the parameter being estimated in probability, hence accuracy improves with more observations. Third, a desirable estimator is efficient, that is, it has the smallest variance as among the unbiased estimators. Efficiency refers to how closely the estimator approaches the true value; the more efficient an estimator, the less the estimates it produces will tend to vary from the true value. Another one is the property of sufficiency, which ensures that the estimator contains all the information that the sample has on the parameter, and sufficient estimators make the most informative use of the data. Additionally, a desirable estimator is robust, that is, it does not heavily rely on small deviations or violations of the model assumptions, such as outliers, or non-normality. Even when some properties are courterintuitive (for instance, unbiasedness and minimum variance), statisticians want to balance the various properties of each estimator to have the best that suits the situation in hand. The estimator preference can also be data dependent, sample size dependent and computational well posed. It is of clear importance to understand these properties so that researchers can select estimators that enable meaningful and reliable conclusions, this is particularly important in disciplines such as medicine, economics, engineering and the social science. Last but not least, a good estimator leads to good statistical inference and decisions, such that our data analyses are valid and useful in practice.

text: An abstraction layer that conceals the intricacies of physical storage and offers a logical interface for data management, file systems are structured methods of organising, storing, and managing data on storage devices like hard drives, SSDs, or other media. They offer a hierarchical arrangement of files and directories that makes it possible for users and applications to locate, access, and manipulate data effectively.  Contiguous allocation, linked allocation, and indexed allocation are common file allocation techniques that file systems use to decide how to store files on storage media.  Contiguous allocation facilitates file access and provides good read/write speed, but it can also lead to fragmentation and make file expansion problematic. Linked allocation eliminates fragmentation and facilitates dynamic file growth by connecting file blocks by pointers, where each block carries a pointer to the next. However, it causes sequential access and longer seek times, which lowers performance for random access.  This is improved by index-based allocation, which keeps an index block with pointers to all of a file's blocks. This makes it possible to access any part of the file directly and minimises fragmentation, but it takes up more space for the index and may result in overhead when a file is created or deleted.  There are benefits and drawbacks to each approach: linked allocation is straightforward and adaptable but slower for random access; indexed allocation offers effective direct access at the cost of more space and complexity; contiguous allocation offers quick access but suffers from external fragmentation.  To improve dependability, speed, and fault tolerance, contemporary file systems frequently combine these techniques or add further features like journaling, caching, and metadata management.  Operating systems must choose suitable strategies based on workload requirements, hardware capabilities, and desired levels of performance and reliability because the choice of file allocation method has a significant impact on system performance, storage efficiency, and ease of file management.  System designers and users can maximise storage utilisation, minimise fragmentation, and enhance overall data access efficiency by being aware of these techniques.

text: The Boiling Water Reactor (BWR) is another type of nuclear reactor, which also uses water as both a coolant and moderator, but with a different design from the PWR. Here's how it works: The fuel, usually enriched uranium, is placed in fuel rods that are arranged in a reactor core. text: In political economy, socialism refers to a system in which the means of production are state or collectively owned and economic activity is controlled to achieve society's common good and the public's interest, rather than to generate profits for private owners. The basic premise of socialism is a desire to mitigate inequality and make sure that wealth and resources are more equally distributed to everyone in society. Under socialism, the government directs major parts of the economy – including health care, education, transportation and energy. It might also guarantee that necessities, and certain goods and services, be made available for free, or for a symbolic fee, so that these may be available for everyone, so that no one be deprived of them for lack of money. It’s a matter of focus: Socialism favors cooperation over competition, and holds that wealth is generated for the common good, rather than shunted to a few hands at the top. There are types of socialism which can and has existed — mostly as opposed to democratic political systems — with partial or mixed private ownership and more centralized or authoritarian socialist systems of some past communist states. In political economy, socialism is much more than a simple counterweight to capitalism that criticizes the inequalities or market failures of the capitalist system. Proponents of socialism contend that capitalism results in exploitation, poverty and unemployment, and thus should be superseded by more equitable systems of social organisation. Critics, however, argue that socialism can erode individual economic incentives, stifle innovation and result in inefficiency because of over-reliance on government control of the economy. Though countries such as the Soviet Union, Cuba and China have implemented socialist systems over the years, with mixed results. Many countries have adopted similar models to social democratic ones, which combine free-market dynamics with generous social safety nets, in the past few decades. Roughly speaking, socialism in political economy is a view that economic resources should be more evenly shared in society and that the state should guarantee the satisfaction of all citizens’ basic needs so that poverty and social exclusion are reduced.

text: The refugee crisis represents a significant humanitarian challenge that intersects deeply with international politics, as millions of individuals are forced to flee their home countries due to conflict, persecution, violence, and human rights violations. This crisis has been exacerbated by ongoing wars, such as those in Syria and Afghanistan, as well as by political instability in regions like Africa and Central America, leading to unprecedented levels of displacement. As refugees seek safety and asylum, they often encounter complex political landscapes that influence their ability to find refuge. Countries receiving large numbers of refugees face a range of pressures, including economic strain, social integration challenges, and political backlash from segments of their populations that may oppose immigration. This has led to varying responses from governments, with some nations adopting open-door policies while others implement strict border controls and restrictive asylum laws. International organizations, such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), play a crucial role in coordinating humanitarian assistance and advocating for the rights of refugees, yet their efforts are often hampered by geopolitical interests and the reluctance of some states to share the burden of refugee resettlement. The refugee crisis also influences international relations, as countries may leverage their positions on refugee policies to gain political favor or negotiate other diplomatic agreements. Furthermore, the rise of nationalism and populism in various parts of the world has led to increased anti-refugee sentiment, complicating international cooperation and humanitarian efforts. Ultimately, the refugee crisis is not merely a humanitarian issue but a complex interplay of international politics, where the responses of states and the global community reflect broader themes of security, human rights, and the challenges of globalization, necessitating a coordinated and compassionate approach to address the needs of displaced populations while balancing national interests.

text: Consumer protection in hospitality refers to the comprehensive legal framework designed to safeguard guests' rights and ensure fair treatment when accessing accommodation, dining, and related services within the hospitality industry. This protection encompasses several key areas, beginning with truthful advertising and marketing practices that require hotels, restaurants, and other hospitality businesses to accurately represent their facilities, services, amenities, and pricing without misleading or deceptive claims about room quality, availability, or additional charges. Price transparency regulations mandate clear disclosure of all fees, taxes, and surcharges upfront, preventing hidden costs that might only be revealed at check-in or checkout, while also requiring accurate representation of promotional rates and package deals. Booking and reservation protections establish consumers' rights regarding cancellation policies, modification procedures, and refund processes, with many jurisdictions requiring reasonable cancellation terms and clear communication of any penalties or restrictions. Health and safety standards form a critical component, with regulations ensuring that hospitality establishments maintain proper sanitation, fire safety measures, structural integrity, and compliance with disability access requirements to protect guest welfare. text: The American Revolution, which erupted in 1775, was the culmination of a series of political, economic, and social factors that fueled colonial discontent with British rule. One of the primary catalysts was the imposition of taxes and tariffs by the British government following the costly French and Indian War (1754-1763). To recoup war debts and finance the maintenance of British troops in North America, Parliament enacted several measures, including the Stamp Act of 1765 and the Townshend Acts of 1767, which levied taxes on everyday items and legal documents. These taxes were met with fierce opposition from the colonists, who argued that they were being taxed without representation in Parliament, leading to the rallying cry of "no taxation without representation."In addition to economic grievances, the British government's increasing attempts to assert control over colonial governance further alienated the colonists. The Intolerable Acts of 1774, enacted in response to the Boston Tea Party, restricted colonial self-governance and closed Boston Harbor, igniting widespread outrage and unity among the colonies. The First Continental Congress convened in 1774 to address these issues, marking a significant step toward collective action against British authority.The ideological underpinnings of the revolution were also crucial, as Enlightenment ideas about individual rights, liberty, and self-governance gained traction among colonial leaders. Thinkers like John Locke influenced revolutionary leaders, who began to articulate a vision of a society based on democratic principles and the consent of the governed. Pamphlets such as Thomas Paine's "Common Sense" galvanized public support for independence by arguing for the colonies' right to self-determination and the rejection of monarchical rule.The situation escalated into armed conflict with the Battles of Lexington and Concord in April 1775, marking the beginning of the Revolutionary War. As the conflict progressed, the colonies united in their struggle for independence, culminating in the Declaration of Independence in 1776, which formally asserted their break from British rule. The American Revolution was thus driven by a combination of economic grievances, political oppression, and Enlightenment ideals, leading to the establishment of a new nation founded on principles of liberty and democracy. The revolution not only transformed the American colonies but also inspired other movements for independence and democratic governance around the world.

text: Residuals in regression are the differences between the observed values of the dependent variable and the predicted values based on the regression model. Residuals can also be used to evaluate the goodness of fit of the model, with smaller residuals indicating a better fit. For example, if the residuals are randomly distributed around zero, it suggests that the model is a good fit to the data. On the other hand, if the residuals exhibit a pattern, such as a curve or a non-random distribution, it may indicate that the model is not adequate or that there are other factors that are not accounted for. By analyzing the residuals, researchers can refine the model and improve its accuracy. Additionally, residuals can be used to identify observations that are not well-predicted by the model, which can be useful for identifying outliers or influential observations. text: Cache memory is a small, fast type of volatile memory located close to the CPU that stores copies of frequently accessed data and instructions to reduce the average time to access memory. Because main memory (RAM) is slower than CPU registers, the CPU uses cache to bridge this speed gap, improving processing efficiency. When the CPU needs data, it first checks the cache (cache hit). If the data is found, it is accessed quickly; if not (cache miss), the data is fetched from the slower main memory and also loaded into the cache for future access. Cache is organized in multiple levels: L1 (smallest and fastest, inside the CPU core), L2 (larger but slower), and sometimes L3 (shared across cores). The cache uses algorithms like Least Recently Used (LRU) to decide which data to evict when new data needs space. By keeping frequently used data close, cache significantly speeds up execution of repetitive tasks and loops. It can store instructions, data, or both, depending on architecture. Cache coherence mechanisms ensure data consistency in multi-core processors. Overall, cache memory optimizes CPU performance by minimizing time-consuming accesses to slower main memory.

text: Most stars, both in the solar neighborhood and in young clusters, are members of binary or multiple systems. Yet the formation and early evolution of binary and multiple stars is poorly constrained observationally, and not well understood theoretically. For instance, the fraction of wide binaries in dense star-forming regions such as the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC) and IC 348 are comparable to that of field stars (Duchêne et al. 1999; Köhler et al. 2006) whereas the frequency of binaries is much higher among young stars in dispersed T associations like Taurus-Auriga (e.g., Simon et al. 1995; Ghez et al. 1997a; Brandeker et al. 2003); for reviews see Mathieu et al. (2000) and Duchêne et al. (2007). Furthermore, high-order multiples are more common in nearby star-forming regions than for solar-type main-sequence stars in the solar neighborhood (Correia et al. 2006). Some simulations suggest that stars usually form in triples and higher-order multiple systems only to be dispersed later, with the fraction of stars in multiple systems decreasing from 80% down to 40% by about 10 Myr (Delgado-Donate et al. 2004). Predictions are that the binary fraction is higher among higher mass stars, and that brown dwarfs are never close companions to stars (Goodwin et al. 2004). While past multiplicity surveys, using speckle imaging and adaptive optics (AO) on 4 m class telescopes, have drawn attention to the ubiquity of binaries in star-forming regions (e.g., Ghez et al. 1993; Leinert et al. 1993), their limited contrast and angular resolution have left many key questions unanswered or only partially answered. For instance, the frequency of higher-order multiples is uncertain, and so is the frequency of very low mass stellar and substellar companions (Ahmic et al. 2007). Multiple systems are probably common.

text: The origin of the Evershed flow is not completely understood (Borrero 2009; Scharmer 2009; Schlichenmaier 2009; Bellot Rubio 2010; Nordlund & Scharmer 2010). Models based on moving flux tubes explain the flow in terms of a pressure gradient that builds up along the tubes as they rise from the sunspot magnetopause (Schlichenmaier et al. 1998; Schlichenmaier 2002). Siphon flow models, on the other hand, invoke pressure gradients resulting from different field strengths at the footpoints of elevated magnetic arches (e.g., Meyer & Schmidt 1968; Degenhardt 1989; Montesinos & Thomas 1997). In both cases, mass conservation is secured by downflows that occur in the mid and outer penumbra as the field lines return to the solar surface. Another possibility is that the Evershed flow is caused by convection in the presence of the sunspot magnetic field, which induces an anisotropy in the radial direction. The idea was put forward by Scharmer et al. (2008) and seems to be supported by radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations (Heinemann et al. 2007; Rempel et al. 2009a, 2009b). According to the simulations, hot weakly magnetized material ascends in the penumbra and becomes nearly horizontal after being deflected outward by the inclined sunspot field. This results in a penumbral filament—an elongated overturning flow pattern with an upward component at the center (the Evershed flow) and lateral downflows at the edges. The process is similar to granular convection in the quiet Sun, except for the existence of a preferred horizontal direction.

text: Safety interlocks in nuclear plants are automated safety devices designed to prevent unsafe operations and ensure that the plant operates within prescribed safety limits. They are critical components of the plant’s safety systems, functioning as safeguards to protect personnel, the environment, and the reactor itself from accidents. Safety interlocks are typically hardware or software-based controls that disable or restrict certain actions unless specific safety conditions are met. For example, a common safety interlock prevents the startup of the reactor unless the containment is sealed, the emergency core cooling system is operational, or the safety systems are fully engaged. They also restrict movement of control rods, prevent opening of high-pressure systems, or inhibit power changes if safety parameters are not within limits. Interlocks are designed with redundancy and fail-safe features, meaning that failure of an interlock results in a conservative safety response, such as automatic shutdown. They are activated by sensors measuring parameters like pressure, temperature, neutron flux, or radiation levels. If any parameter exceeds safe limits, the interlock system triggers alarms, disables unsafe equipment, or initiates automatic shutdown sequences. The purpose of safety interlocks is to eliminate human error or oversight in critical safety operations, providing a reliable barrier to prevent accidents or mitigate their severity. They are an essential part of the plant’s defense-in-depth strategy, working alongside other safety systems such as alarms, emergency shutdown systems, and containment barriers. Regular testing, maintenance, and calibration of interlocks are necessary to ensure their proper functioning over the plant’s lifespan. Well-designed interlocks also aid plant operators by providing clear, immediate feedback if unsafe conditions arise, enabling swift corrective actions. In sum, safety interlocks are fundamental safety devices that prevent hazardous operations, enforce safe operating conditions, and provide an essential layer of protection against potential accidents in nuclear power plants.

text: Treaties and conventions A treaty or convention is a formal written agreement between states or international actors that sets out and obliges in international law each party to do, or refrain from doing, certain things. Though the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, there is a nuance: Treaties are large, flexible instruments, used for things as varied as peace settlements, trade deals and arms control; conventions are multilateral treaties negotiated under the auspices of international organizations — like the United Nations — and their goal is often to standardize laws or pursue common goals among many countries. Both need the approval of the parties by signature and ratification before they have force in law. Treaties serve as the foundation of international relations, establishing clear rules about the rights, responsibilities and agencies of states as well as provide predictability, cooperation and peaceful coexistence. Examples are the Treaty of Versailles, Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and Geneva Conventions that cover humanitarian considerations in wartime. Treaties such as the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) establish international norms for certain issues, with monitoring and enforcement provisions. These treaties often contain dispute resolution procedures, reporting requirements, and provisions on how to amend or terminate a treaty. Enforcement is difficult but theoretically possible, because of the principle of state sovereignty and lack of a centralized global authority. Compliance is often driven by diplomatic pressure, reputational concerns, shared interests and, in some scenarios, sanctions or interventions endorsed by international institutions. Treaties and conventions play a major role in the international system by facilitating the harmonisation of law and the protection of human rights, the regulation of trade and environment and by reducing conflict. There is also the evolution of global norms and values, including regarding sustainable development and disarmament, that allow for collective responses to global challenges no one state can deal with alone.

text: Guardianship in Muslim law, known as "wilayah," is a legal institution designed to protect and manage the affairs of individuals lacking legal capacity, primarily minors and those with mental incapacity. The concept encompasses several categories including guardianship of marriage (wilayah al-nikah), property (wilayah al-mal), and person (wilayah al-nafs). Islamic jurisprudence establishes a hierarchy of guardians, typically beginning with the father, followed by the paternal grandfather, then other male relatives according to proximity of kinship. Guardians are entrusted with significant responsibilities including protecting the ward's interests, managing their property prudently, arranging marriages (particularly for female wards in traditional interpretations), and ensuring proper education and maintenance. The law imposes strict conditions on guardians, requiring them to be Muslim, sane, mature, and to act solely in the ward's best interests without any conflict of interest. Guardianship typically terminates when the minor reaches the age of majority, upon the death of the ward, if the guardian is deemed unfit by a court, or when an incapacitated person regains their legal capacity. Contemporary applications of Muslim guardianship principles vary significantly across different Muslim-majority countries, with some jurisdictions maintaining traditional interpretations while others have implemented reforms to enhance protections for wards, particularly women and children.

text: The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix is a strategic tool used by organizations to evaluate their product portfolio based on market growth rate and relative market share. It helps managers decide where to invest, develop, or divest by classifying products into four categories: Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks (or Problem Children), and Dogs. Stars represent products with high market share in high-growth markets; they often require substantial investment to maintain growth but have the potential to become cash cows. Cash Cows have a high market share in low-growth markets and generate more cash than they consume, providing funds for other business units. Question Marks are products with low market share in high-growth markets and need significant resources to improve their position; management must decide whether to invest in them or withdraw. Dogs have low market share in low-growth markets and usually generate low or negative cash flow; they may be candidates for divestiture. The BCG matrix provides a visual framework for analyzing the balance of a company’s product mix and prioritizing resource allocation to maximize profitability and growth. It encourages strategic thinking about market conditions and competitive positioning. However, the matrix simplifies complex market dynamics by focusing only on two dimensions and does not consider factors like profitability, competition, or synergies. Despite its limitations, the BCG matrix remains a popular and useful tool for portfolio management, helping firms identify which products to nurture and which to phase out. In practical use, companies combine BCG analysis with other strategic assessments to formulate well-rounded investment decisions. In summary, the BCG matrix aids in optimizing product strategies by categorizing products according to growth potential and market strength, supporting better resource management and long-term planning.

text: The Least Squares Method (formally known as Ordinary Least Squares or OLS) is the standard technique used in simple and multiple linear regression to estimate the regression coefficients (the slope and intercept) that define the best-fitting line for the data. The objective of OLS is to minimize the sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed data points and the regression line. These vertical distances are the residuals (the prediction errors). By squaring the errors, the method ensures that all deviations are treated as positive values and that larger errors are penalized more heavily, resulting in a unique line that is optimally close to all the data points simultaneously. This minimization process yields the coefficient estimates that make the calculated line the "line of best fit," providing the most reliable linear model for predicting the dependent variable from the independent variables, assuming the underlying statistical assumptions are met.

text: Government forms can be categorized across multiple dimensions, creating a rich tapestry of political systems that reflect different approaches to organizing power, authority, and decision-making within societies. The most fundamental distinction lies between democratic and authoritarian systems, where democratic governments derive legitimacy from popular consent and maintain accountability through regular elections, while authoritarian regimes concentrate power in the hands of a few leaders or a single party with limited popular input. Within democratic systems, we find parliamentary governments where the executive emerges from and remains accountable to the legislature, presidential systems where executive and legislative branches are separately elected and maintain independence, and hybrid semi-presidential systems that combine elements of both. Monarchies represent another major category, ranging from absolute monarchies where the sovereign holds unlimited power, to constitutional monarchies where royal authority is constrained by democratic institutions and the monarch serves primarily as a ceremonial figurehead. Federal systems distribute power between national and subnational governments, with each level having constitutionally protected spheres of authority, while unitary systems concentrate power in a central government that delegates administrative functions to lower levels. Totalitarian governments seek to control all aspects of society through extensive surveillance, propaganda, and repression, while authoritarian systems typically focus on maintaining political control while allowing some social and economic autonomy. Military governments emerge when armed forces seize power, often during periods of crisis or instability, while theocratic systems base their authority on religious principles and leadership by religious officials. Single-party states maintain political control through a dominant party that suppresses opposition, and confederations create loose associations of independent states that retain most of their sovereignty while cooperating on specific issues. Each governmental form reflects different philosophical assumptions about human nature, the source of political legitimacy, and the proper relationship between rulers and the ruled.

System calls are frequently used to allocate memory, read or write files, start or stop processes, and communicate over networks. The OS verifies the request, completes the required actions, and then sends the result back to the program. Usually, when a program makes a system call, it sets off a software interrupt or trap that moves the CPU from user mode to kernel mode. System calls enable standardised and secure resource management procedures by providing an abstraction layer that conceals low-level details and hardware complexity. System calls vary throughout operating systems, although they typically cover comparable functions including memory management (mmap, brk), process management (exec, wait), file management (open, close, read, write), and inter-process communication (pipe, socket). System calls are necessary to preserve security and dependability by imposing access control and making sure that applications don't interact with the system or one another. Additionally, they act as a basis for more complex libraries and APIs, which make programming easier by offering functions that are easy to use and internally call these system calls. In conclusion, system calls serve as the entry point for programs to communicate with the operating system and carry out privileged tasks effectively and safely.

Indeed, an impetus for the early development of plasma wave theory was the serendipitous detection of falling tones by a 22-km telephone line in Austria in 1886, and later by German soldiers using amplifiers for tapping enemy phone conversations during World War I [1], [2]. These classic whistlers are short bursts of audio frequency radio noise that exhibit a decreasing pitch. The whistler pitch decreases with time because the higher frequency components of the burst have higher group velocities within the magnetized ionosphere medium [3]. These whistler waves are generated by broadband radio noise from atmospheric lightning strikes and plasma instabilities in the magnetosphere and are ducted from hemisphere to hemisphere along the geomagnetic field within density irregularities (see [4] for a comprehensive history of whistler measurements and theory).

text: Self-reports of offending and victimization permit researchers to gain insight into offenses that are not reported to the authorities, but they face a number of limitations that may impact on the validity and reliability of estimates. However, there are also several important constraints, such as: honesty bias and social desirability bias, that impact the quality of the data, which can lead to under or over-estimation both in the level of crime participation, either to not look like trying to judge, or for hiding the seriousness of the offences, or for wanting to look in a certain way. Remembering problems can also be the cause of errors, especially concerning distant or stressful events. Sampling bias: there may be a bias in the level of participation of some groups, with those who offend more frequently (e.g., active offenders, deprived communities) being less likely to participate. In addition, to some types of crime being delicate and complex, disclosing such offenses may be confused or not disclosed truthfully, thereby data quality. And there are methodological issues, around how questions are framed and worded on questionnaires, or about being as anonymous as possible to encourage honesty. Despite some shortcomings, self-report research remains indispensable in criminology for bringing to light hidden criminal phenomenon, but the findings derived from this method are required to be triangulated with other data sources and be read through a critical lens within its methodological limitations; more triangulation from qualitative studies and other statistical data is needed to know to what extent MAR is a reliable measure to use for sensitive data that we would like to know without either overreporting or underreporting.

text: The Christian Church, primarily the Roman Catholic Church in Western Europe, played an omnipresent and profoundly influential role in medieval society, serving as the dominant institution that shaped nearly every aspect of life from the fall of the Roman Empire to the dawn of the Renaissance. Spiritually, it was the central authority, providing a unified belief system, moral guidance, and the promise of salvation. The Church administered the sacraments, which were deemed essential for spiritual well-being, and its teachings permeated daily life, from birth to death. Politically, the Church wielded immense power, often rivaling or even surpassing that of secular rulers. The Pope, as the head of the Church, held significant moral and political authority, able to excommunicate kings, issue interdicts (forbidding sacraments in a region), and even sanction crusades. Bishops and abbots, often drawn from noble families, held vast lands and commanded considerable wealth and influence. The Church maintained its own legal system, canon law, and ecclesiastical courts, which often had jurisdiction over a wide range of matters, including marriage, wills, and moral offenses. Economically, the Church was a massive landowner, accumulating vast wealth through tithes (a tenth of produce or earnings paid to the Church), donations, and the profits from its extensive estates. Monasteries, in particular, were significant economic centers, engaging in agriculture, brewing, and scholarship. Socially, the Church provided essential services that the state often could not, including education through cathedral schools and monastic scriptoria (which preserved classical and religious texts), healthcare through monastic infirmaries, and charity for the poor and sick. It also offered a path for social mobility for individuals from humbler backgrounds, as entering the clergy could provide opportunities for advancement. The Church's cathedrals and monasteries were not just religious sites but also centers of community life, art, and architectural innovation, fostering a shared cultural identity across diverse regions. Despite its spiritual mission, the Church was a complex institution, occasionally marked by corruption and internal power struggles, but its overarching influence on medieval thought, art, law, and daily life was unparalleled, shaping the very fabric of European civilization.

text: Modus ponens is a fundamental rule of inference in logic that allows one to derive a conclusion from a conditional statement and its antecedent. It follows the structure: If P, then Q; P is true; therefore, Q is true. This logical form is one of the most basic and widely used rules of deduction in formal logic and everyday reasoning. The first premise is a conditional statement that establishes a relationship between two propositions, where P is the antecedent and Q is the consequent. The second premise asserts that the antecedent P is true. From these two premises, one can validly conclude that Q must also be true. For example, if we know that "If it is raining, then the ground is wet" and we observe that "It is raining," we can validly conclude that "The ground is wet." Modus ponens is essential in various fields including mathematics, computer science, philosophy, and artificial intelligence, as it provides a reliable method for drawing conclusions based on given information. Its validity stems from the meaning of the conditional connective "if...then," which guarantees that whenever the antecedent is true, the consequent must also be true. This logical rule forms the foundation of many deductive arguments and is often contrasted with other forms of reasoning such as modus tollens, affirming the consequent, and denying the antecedent. Understanding modus ponens is crucial for developing critical thinking skills and for constructing sound arguments in both formal and informal contexts.

text: Developing countries face numerous challenges in establishing and maintaining effective media systems, which impact their ability to inform, educate, and empower their populations. One major obstacle is limited financial resources, which hinder investments in infrastructure, technology, and skilled personnel needed for modern media operations. Many developing countries lack widespread access to digital platforms and reliable internet, restricting the dissemination of information and limiting the reach of independent journalism. Another challenge is government censorship, control, or influence over media outlets, which can suppress critical voices, restrict press freedom, and promote state propaganda. This limits the media’s role as a watchdog and hampers transparency and accountability. Weak legal frameworks and lack of professional standards also contribute to media fragility, making it difficult to ensure ethical journalism and protect journalists from violence, harassment, or imprisonment. Cultural and linguistic diversity in many developing nations adds complexity to media operations, requiring content in multiple languages and culturally sensitive programming. Moreover, low literacy levels and limited media literacy skills hamper the ability of the population to critically evaluate information, making communities vulnerable to misinformation and propaganda. Economic instability and political unrest further destabilize media systems, leading to closures or restrictions of media outlets and a lack of consistent, credible information flow. In addition, the dominance of foreign media companies can overshadow local content, reducing indigenous voices and cultural expression. All these challenges create a cycle of media dependency, limited diversity, and restricted access to reliable information, which ultimately impairs development efforts. Addressing these issues requires investment in infrastructure, legal reforms promoting press freedom, capacity building, and fostering local content creation. Strengthening media systems in developing countries is crucial for promoting democracy, human rights, social progress, and sustainable development.

text: System order within the context of control systems refers to the number of energy storage elements (e.g. capacitors, inductors or integrators) apparent from a set of ordinary differential equations in a model for the system. A basic property of a system that dictates how it behaves and responds to the input. The order of a system is important because it indicates the dynamic behaviour of the system as a higher order corresponds to higher powers in the denominator which in turn means, higher system dynamics, and hence influence stability, transient-response time and steady-state response. The order of a system is identified by the largest power of Laplace variable(s) in its transfer function. In example, a first-order system has one energy storage element (usually represented by a first-degree polynomial in the transfer function), and its response is characterized only by an exponential term. Some examples would be simple RC circuits or those first-order filters. A second-order system, on the other hand, involves two energy storage elements, and its transfer function contains a second-degree polynomial. Second-order systems often exhibit more complex behavior, including oscillations or damping effects, which are crucial in the analysis of mechanical systems, such as mass-spring-damper systems or electrical circuits with inductance and capacitance. Higher-order systems (third-order, fourth-order, etc.) become increasingly complex, often requiring numerical methods to analyze their behavior. The system order affects the system’s transient response, including the rise time, peak time, settling time, and overshoot. Lower-order systems tend to have simpler and faster responses, while higher-order systems may experience more complicated transients and slower settling. Understanding the system order is essential for designing control systems that meet desired performance criteria, ensuring stability, and achieving an appropriate balance between responsiveness and accuracy.

text: The Bechdel test is a simple metric used to evaluate the representation of women in fiction. To pass the test, a work must feature at least two named female characters who talk to each other about something other than a man. Despite its simplicity, many popular films fail the test, highlighting the lack of substantial female interaction and storylines. It’s not a measure of feminist quality, but rather a quick indicator of whether women are present as fully realized characters with their own agency and interests.

text: A transfer function is a mathematical representation that defines the dynamic relationship between the input and output of a linear time-invariant (LTI) system in the frequency domain, typically expressed as the ratio of the Laplace transform of the output to the Laplace transform of the input, assuming zero initial conditions. It encapsulates the system’s behavior—including gain, poles, zeros, and transient response—while abstracting away internal complexities, making it a cornerstone of control theory and signal processing. For example, in an electrical circuit, the transfer function might relate voltage input to current output, or in a mechanical system, force input to displacement output. The poles of the transfer function indicate system stability (right-half plane poles imply instability), while zeros influence transient performance. Transfer functions simplify the analysis of systems in series (multiplication of individual transfer functions) or feedback loops (using block diagram algebra), enabling engineers to design controllers (e.g., PID) that meet desired specifications like rise time, overshoot, or steady-state error. They are pivotal in modeling diverse systems—from RC filters and DC motors to aerospace autopilots—and are used with tools like Bode plots, Nyquist criteria, or root locus for frequency-domain analysis. While limited to LTI systems, extensions (state-space models) handle nonlinearities and time-varying parameters. By providing a compact, algebraic framework, transfer functions bridge theoretical design and practical implementation, optimizing performance in automation, robotics, and communication systems.

text: Radiation plays a crucial role in various high-energy density plasmas, such as those found in the cores of solar-like stars. Essential quantities that describe the interaction between radiation and matter include spectral opacity and emissivity. In hot, dense stellar interiors where matter and radiation are in thermal equilibrium, Kirchhoff's law enables the derivation of emissivity from opacity. Opacity, which characterizes a medium's resistance to the transport of radiative energy, is a fundamental parameter in the modeling of stellar structure and evolution. Although metallic elements (those with atomic numbers greater than 2) are present at only a few percent in stellar mixtures, they significantly impact opacity. In stellar interiors and envelopes, these elements are variably ionized depending on their atomic number, temperature, and density. The bound-bound and bound-free absorption processes of partially ionized elements can thus become major contributors to opacity.

text: In 2006, Takahashi and Yamanaka [1] demonstrated that differentiated cells can be converted into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by the expression of four transcription factors - Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc - which have been termed Yamanaka factors. From the perspective of basic cell biology, somatic cell reprogramming has radically altered our thinking on the plasticity of cell states. In addition, the derivation of iPSCs from numerous normal and diseased cell sources has enabled the generation of patient-specific stem cells for eventual use in cell therapy and regenerative medicine. A number of alternatives and refinements to the original four-factor reprogramming method have been devised over the years. These have included ectopic expression of alternative reprogramming factors, such as Nanog and Lin28, manipulation of pathways that act as barriers to reprogramming, such as p53 and p21, transient expression of reprogramming proteins to avoid stable genetic modification, and inclusion of chemical inhibitors that increase the efficiency of the reprogramming process [2]. However, reprogramming largely remains dependent on the delivery and exogenous expression of one or more of the original Yamanaka factors.

text: Entrepreneurship refers to the process of designing, launching, and running a new business or venture, often involving innovation, risk-taking, and creativity. Entrepreneurs identify opportunities, gather resources, and take calculated risks to create value and achieve success. There are several types of entrepreneurship, including small business entrepreneurship, which involves starting and running a small business, often with limited resources and a local focus. Scalable entrepreneurship, on the other hand, involves creating a business with high growth potential, often with a innovative product or service and a plan to expand rapidly. Social entrepreneurship involves creating businesses that address social or environmental problems, while corporate entrepreneurship involves the creation of new businesses or innovations within an existing organization. Other types of entrepreneurship include serial entrepreneurship, where an individual starts multiple businesses, and lifestyle entrepreneurship, where an individual creates a business that allows them to pursue their passions and maintain a desired lifestyle. Understanding the different types of entrepreneurship can help individuals and organizations to identify opportunities, develop effective strategies, and create successful ventures.

text: A non-coding RNA (ncRNA) is a functional RNA molecule that is not translated into a protein. Members of this class of molecule are involved in many cellular processes and include highly abundant and functionally important RNAs, such as transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), as well as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), PIWI-associated RNAs (piRNAs), small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), promoter-associated RNAs (PARs) and the recently identified telomere specific small RNAs (tel-sRNAs). Moreover, the recent demonstration that other ncRNAs, the ultraconserved genes or transcribed ultraconserved regions (T-UCRs) [1], are involved in human carcinogenesis suggests that the broad family of ncRNAs contributes to molecular alterations in several pathological conditions. miRNAs are a conserved class of non-coding RNAs that regulate the translation of mRNAs (messenger RNAs) by inhibiting ribosome function, decapping the 5' cap structure, deadenylating the poly(A) tail and degrading target mRNAs [2]. miRNAs are involved in mechanisms of gene regulation in both normal and diseased conditions and have a role during development, regulation of cell proliferation and apoptosis. The first miRNAs were identified in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as small RNAs that interacted with the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of the lin-14 mRNA to inhibit its expression [3].

text: World poverty is a complex issue with multiple causes including factors that affect the economy, politics, climate, social and the culture and thus the poor in the global south cannot afford to meet their basic needs. Poverty is, mostly, a matter of an economically unfair distribution of wealth and natural resources, restricted access to markets and low level of industrialization in many developing countries. Sturctural problems such as: inadequate infrastructure, poor educational systems, and a lack of accessible healthcare, serve to perpetuate poverty by keeping social mobility relatively low. Political instability, corruption, poor governance and conflict inhibit economic growth and the development of institutions which could help reduce poverty. In the past colonialism and the extraction of resources by outside powers has left legacies which still stifle the economic progress of many areas. Poor communities, heavily reliant on agriculture, are disproportionately affected by environmental degradation such as soil erosion, deforestation and climate change, making them less resilient to shocks such as drought and climate. Global structures of economy – trade policy, debt holdings, etc. – may also put a developing country at a competitive disadvantage in terms of access to global markets. Besides this, increase in population in certain areas create stress on the insufficient resources and public facility. Gender, ethnic and caste based social stratification can further exclude some groups and hinder their escape from poverty. Aid dependence, although charitable in nature, can generate cycles of dependence, rather than self-sustaining growth. The remedy for global poverty is to address these basic causes with policies promoting economic inclusiveness, good governance, investment in human capital, protection of environmental sustainability, and international fairness in trade and finance. Millions continue to live in chronic deprivation if the structural and systemic nature of poverty is not effectively addressed, with serious implications for global stability, health and development.

text: Overview in his 1920 deathbed letter to Hardy, Ramanujan gave examples of 17 curious q-series he referred to as ‘mock theta functions’ [11]. In the decades following Ramanujan’s death, mathematicians were unable to determine how these functions ?t into the theory of modular forms, despite their rather ubiquitous nature. Finally, the 2002 Ph.D. thesis of Zwegers [45] showed that while the mock theta functions were not modular, they could be ‘completed’ to produce real analytic vector-valued modular forms. Zwegers’s breakthrough catalyzed the development of the overarching theory of ‘weak Maass forms’ by Bringmann, Ono, and collaborators [15,16,35,42]. Ramanujan’s mock theta functions, it turns out, are examples of ‘holomorphic parts’ of weak Maass forms, originally de?ned by Bruinier and Funke [18].

text: Epigenetics is key to animal development because it controls gene expression without changing the DNA sequence, enabling the organism to dictate when, where and how certain genes are activated, suppressed or modified as it grows and differentiates. This regulation is crucial to instruct one fertilised egg to give origin to highly complex multicellular organisms made up of a great variety of cell types with specific jobs, all with identical genetic material. Epigenetic factors include DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA action, all of which modify the structure of chromatin (the complex of DNA and protein in which it is packaged within a nucleus), resulting in the activation or silencing of genes. Methyl groups added to DNA, usually on cytosine bases, can, for instance, silence genes by keeping transcription factors from finding them, and changes to the chemical nature of histone proteins—such as the addition or subtraction of acetyl or methyl chemical groups—can pack or loosen chromatin so that genes are either activated or turned off. Epigenetic regulation during morphogenesis in the embryo Epigenetic control of when and where genes are expressed governs embryonic development, including the formation of tissues, organs, and body structures. These changes help to set cell identity by making sure that liver cells, nerve cells and muscle cells switch on only the genes they need to work properly even though they all have the same genome as their colleagues do. Epigenetically regulated mechanisms also include genomic imprinting, where genes are expressed from only one of the two parental alleles, depending on the sex of the parent and the gamete. What's more, epigenetic reactions help animals process environmental cues -- like nutrition, stress or toxins -- that can then trigger gene expression changes impacting development, growth, and in some cases, behavior. Some epigenetic modifications are reversible, whereas others are stable over cell divisions, and in few cases (three proven cases, L1 transposed elements, prions, and reporter gene silencing) they are stable over generations, and also transmitted to the offspring, and therefore they is could affect traits that are not in accordance with Mendelian rules. This flexibility is what makes epigenetics a critical mediator between the genome and the environment – with functions that extend beyond normal development to disease processes, such as cancer, metabolic disorders or developmental defects that arise when regulation goes off course. In conclusion, epigenetics is essential for animal development, because it controls gene expression independently of DNA sequence, permitting precise control in the coordination of a cell differentiation, tissue formation, and a response to environmental cues, which in time determines for the next several decades of life what the genetic information will "look like" and do.

text: Television, as a combination of audio and visual elements, can be used to communicate sophisticated information to a heterogeneous audience. As an effective medium, it has the ability to tell nuanced stories with immediacy and move audiences with emotional force, and is proven to be a powerful tool for the dissemination of news, education, cultural content and entertainment. According to both domestic and international news coverage, television informs the public about social issues and can influence public opinion, whose analysis can also become a topic of political discussion. It is also a mirror of society and what people may accept until it does make them challenge prevailing norms and beliefs. Dramas, reality shows, talk shows, or sports broadcasts keep audiences entertained while discreetly incorporating cultural narratives, ideologies and commercial messages. The use of television is the defining factor that makes it more persuasive than print or radio — because it can contain body language, facial expressions, scenery, and storytelling. TV is also an effective advertising medium, as it has an extensive audience coupled with strong audio-visual impact, which are essential elements in publicity. The medium also serves an important educational function, from childrens programmes to science documentaries to television ‘‘university’’ courses that address educational disparities. Television still remains a powerful medium even in the age of the internet – more so in emerging markets where penetration of smartphones and high-speed internet lags behind. Over the years, the shape has changed as digital broadcasting, smart TVs, and streaming services have given viewers more to interact with and choose from. That said, the discipline of structured programming, high TV production values, and government regulation of traditional TV channels, television remains an ear to the ground part of the mass comm mix.

text: The partition of India and Pakistan was a traumatic event that occurred in 1947, as British India was divided into two separate nations, India and Pakistan, along communal lines. The partition was the result of a complex and contentious process, driven by the Muslim League's demand for a separate homeland for Muslims, and the Indian National Congress's opposition to the idea of partition. The British government, led by Lord Louis Mountbatten, ultimately agreed to the partition plan, which was formalized in the Indian Independence Act of 1947. The partition led to one of the largest mass migrations in history, as millions of Hindus and Muslims crossed the newly created borders, resulting in widespread violence, displacement, and trauma. The partition also led to the creation of two separate nations, India and Pakistan, with distinct governments, economies, and cultures. The legacy of the partition continues to be felt today, with ongoing tensions between India and Pakistan, particularly over the disputed region of Kashmir. The partition also had a profound impact on the people of the region, with many families being divided, and communities being torn apart. The trauma of the partition continues to be felt today, with many people still bearing the scars of the violence and displacement that occurred during that time. The partition of India and Pakistan remains a significant and contested event in modern history, with ongoing debates about its causes, consequences, and legacy. The event continues to be studied and remembered, serving as a reminder of the importance of understanding the complexities of history and the need for ongoing dialogue and reconciliation.

text: For several decades, the interplay between heavy tails and serial dependence in a strictly stationary sequence (Xt) of random variables with common distribution F has attracted a lot of attention. One of the main goals of this research is to investigate the distributional behavior of suitable functions acting on (Xt) and to compare it with the corresponding behavior of an iid sequence with the same marginal distribution F. In a dependent sequence (Xt), high/low level exceedances typically appear in clusters and significantly determine the distributional behavior of functions of (Xt). Not surprisingly, linear processes (such as ARMA) with heavy-tailed innovations were the first objects of interest: they constitute a major class of stationary processes in time series analysis. The extremes of such processes were studied first by Rootzén [35] in the case of infinite variance stable innovations and later by Davis et al. [11] for general innovation processes with regularly varying tails. Another class of a heavy-tailed stationary processes constitute solutions to stochastic recurrence equations. Pioneering work by Kesten [23] and Goldie [16] showed that the marginal distributions of such a process have power law tails. The extreme value theory of such processes was studied in detail in [18].

text: Secondary growth is the increase in the thickness of stems and roots due to the activity of lateral meristems, the vascular cambium, and the cork cambium. This process is typical of woody plants and is essential for their structural support, transport of water and nutrients, and storage of food. The vascular cambium is a layer of meristematic cells located between the xylem and phloem, producing secondary xylem (wood) towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside. The secondary xylem provides structural support and facilitates the transport of water and minerals, while the secondary phloem transports the products of photosynthesis. The cork cambium, or phellogen, is a layer of meristematic cells located in the outer cortex, producing cork cells (phellem) towards the outside and phelloderm towards the inside. The cork cells provide a protective layer that reduces water loss and prevents pathogen entry, while the phelloderm provides additional structural support and storage. The process of secondary growth allows the plant to increase in girth, ensuring its structural integrity, transport efficiency, and adaptation to various environmental conditions. This process is essential for the plant's growth, development, and survival in diverse ecosystems, reflecting its evolutionary adaptations and ecological strategies.
