Travel agencies not only simplify the complex process of travel planning but also contribute to the tourism economy by promoting destinations and supporting service providers. Their expertise, customer service, and logistical support make them indispensable for travelers seeking convenience, reliability, and expert guidance, ultimately enhancing the overall travel experience.

text: Liberalism in international relations is a theoretical perspective that focuses on the ability of cooperation among actors of different states in the world of politics which has derived from the development of universal principles of law, economics, and international organizations which is also a key foundation of the international society. Unlike realists who tend to regard the international system as naturally anarchic and conflictual, liberalism advocates think that anarchy can be under control by the reason of men, democracy, trade and also, by international law, and that a peaceful solution is possible. The liberal tradition of thought found its most eloquent expression in the work of Immanuel Kant, who proposed a world in which republics, bound by legal rules and economic interdependence, would be less likely to wage war against one another — what would later be known him as the “Democratic Peace Theory.” The liberal institutionalism, which is a sub-school of liberalism emphasizes how international organization such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Trade organization can reduce transaction cost, build trust and can also enforce agreement between states. Liberals also emphasize increasing importance of transnational actors ––NGOs, corporations, and advocacy networks ––in setting the global agenda and in the effort to promote human rights, environmental standards, and development objectives. Economic liberals maintain that free markets and free trade create common interests that discourage conflict and promote shared prosperity. The target of realists who argue it is naïve about power politics and constructivists who argue it fails to appreciate identity and norms, liberalism nevertheless offers important lessons for the study of diplomacy, global governance, peace-building and multilateralism. It still affects foreign policy, particularly in democracies dedicated to rule of law, human rights, collective security and international entanglements.

text: Social media has revolutionized diplomacy by transforming how states, diplomats, and international organizations communicate, engage with publics, and shape narratives in real-time. Platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram provide instant channels for governments to directly reach global audiences, bypassing traditional media filters. This immediacy allows for rapid crisis communication, public diplomacy campaigns, and diplomatic signaling that can influence both domestic and international perceptions. Social media also facilitates people-to-people diplomacy by connecting citizens across borders, enhancing cultural exchange and grassroots dialogue. However, the rise of social media has introduced challenges such as misinformation, propaganda, and cyber manipulation, which can escalate conflicts, distort facts, and undermine trust in official communications. Diplomats now must navigate a complex environment where public opinion is shaped online and diplomatic actions are scrutinized globally within seconds. Social media also increases transparency and accountability but can pressure policymakers with rapid public reactions and viral controversies. As a result, digital diplomacy has become an essential tool in modern international relations, requiring new skills, strategies, and policies to harness its benefits while mitigating risks. The impact of social media extends beyond communication—it reshapes power dynamics by empowering non-state actors and amplifying voices that were once marginalized, thus broadening the scope and complexity of diplomacy in the 21st century.

text: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) are the two main Monetary Policy Tools used by Reserve Bank of India(rbi), to control the Stability, Inflation, money flowing in and out of the country. CRR is the minimum amount of cash a commercial bank must have, as a proportion of its net demand and time liabilities, or the money that it can lend. Bank’s don’t have the authority to lend or invest this money but it does control how much (There is some discussion on whether they still do via Fractional-Reserve Banking practices) credit (this is purely my opinion, so I could be totally wrong) is available within the economy! Theoretically, using CRR the RBI can either increase or decrease money flow - for example, increasing CRR would mean banks have less to lend which reins in inflationary trends and conversely reducing CRR allows more money in the market economy to fire economic growth. On the other hand, SLR is that percentage of net demand and time liabilities which banks are required to keep as liquid assets in the form of cash, gold or approved securities before extending credit to the customers. This is ensured by requiring banks to hold an adequate amount of safe, liquid assets, which in turn ensures the soundness and solvency of the financial system. SLR is also an instrument that the RBI uses for managing inflation and to fuel growth: Whenever the RBI wants to curtail lending by banks, it raises SLR and when it wants the banks to lend more, it does the opposite. CRR and SLR are the regulatory guardrails that regulate credit availability, liquidity & inflation in a economy. They are a component of the RBI’s monetary policy framework and have widespread significance for banking operations, interest rates and overall economic activity.

text: A Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) is a three-layer semiconductor device (either NPN or PNP) that amplifies or switches electronic signals using both electrons and holes as charge carriers. It consists of three terminals: emitter (heavily doped, emits charge carriers), base (thin and lightly doped, controls carrier flow), and collector (moderately doped, collects carriers). In an NPN transistor, when a small forward bias is applied to the base-emitter junction (V<sub>BE</sub> > 0.7V for silicon), electrons from the emitter diffuse into the base and are swept across the reverse-biased base-collector junction, creating a larger collector current (I<sub>C</sub> = ?I<sub>B</sub>, where ? is the current gain). A PNP transistor operates similarly but with opposite voltage polarities and hole-dominated conduction. BJTs work in three modes: active (amplification, where I<sub>C</sub> is proportional to I<sub>B</sub>), saturation (fully on, behaving as a closed switch), and cutoff (fully off, open switch). Key applications include analog amplifiers (audio, RF), digital logic circuits, and power regulation. While BJTs offer high gain and fast response, they suffer from thermal runaway (due to positive temperature coefficient) and higher power loss compared to MOSFETs. Modern variants like Darlington pairs (for very high gain) and heterojunction BJTs (HBTs) (for high-frequency use in telecom) address specific needs. Despite being overshadowed by MOSFETs in switching applications, BJTs remain vital in precision analog circuits and high-frequency systems due to their linearity and reliability.

text: The objective of this paper was to combine the Lagrangian approach in robot dynamics with qualitative reasoning and its potential applications, while developing closed-form equations of motion for robots, particularly robots having multiple degrees of freedom and the presence of coupled joints. Newton-Euler Newton-Euler deals with forces and torques, the lagrangian method deals with scalar energy functions (T - V, the lagrangian L = T - V). This method uses generalized vitual coordinates (joint angles or displacement) to represent the configuration of the system and it reduces the modeling of system composed by connected rigid bodies. Applying the Euler-Lagrange equation to each generalized coordinate yields a set of second-order differential equations expressing the dynamics of the robot, i.e., how torques or forces at the joints cause the robot to move. The approach is especially useful for systems with constraints, as well as when working with generalized coordinates, and is widely used for the dynamic modeling of robotic arms, manipulators, and other articulated robots. It also accelerates control design and simulation, because it presents a rigorous basis to study implications of mechanical structure, and energy distribution for motion and stability.

text: Depth of field (DOF) is a critical concept in photography and cinematography that refers to the range of distance within a scene that appears acceptably sharp in the image. It is influenced by three main factors: aperture, focal length, and the distance between the camera and the subject. Aperture, measured in f-stops, plays a significant role in determining the depth of field. A larger aperture (smaller f-stop number) results in a shallow depth of field, where only a narrow plane of the scene is in focus, and the background and foreground are blurred. This effect is often used to isolate the subject and create a sense of depth and dimension in the image. Conversely, a smaller aperture (larger f-stop number) increases the depth of field, keeping more of the scene in focus from the foreground to the background. Focal length, which is the distance between the camera's lens and the image sensor, also affects the depth of field. A longer focal length (telephoto lens) compresses the scene and results in a shallower depth of field, while a shorter focal length (wide-angle lens) expands the scene and increases the depth of field. The distance between the camera and the subject further influences the depth of field, with closer subjects resulting in a shallower depth of field and distant subjects increasing the depth of field. Mastering depth of field is essential for controlling the visual focus and composition of an image, allowing photographers and cinematographers to guide the viewer's attention and convey the desired narrative and emotional impact.

text: The International English Language Testing System (IELTS) is structured into four main components that comprehensively assess English language proficiency across all essential skills. The examination begins with the Listening section, which lasts approximately 30 minutes and consists of four recordings featuring different English accents and situations, ranging from everyday social conversations to academic lectures, with candidates answering 40 questions that test their ability to understand main ideas, specific information, speaker opinions, and attitudes. Following this, the Reading section spans 60 minutes and presents three long texts with a total of 40 questions, where the Academic version includes texts from books, journals, magazines, and newspapers suitable for university-level study, while the General Training version focuses on everyday English usage with materials from advertisements, company handbooks, and general interest publications. The Writing component, also allocated 60 minutes, requires candidates to complete two tasks: Task 1 involves describing visual information such as graphs, charts, or diagrams in the Academic test or writing a letter in the General Training test, while Task 2 demands a 250-word essay responding to an argument, problem, or point of view. Finally, the Speaking section lasts 11-14 minutes and consists of three parts conducted as a face-to-face interview with a certified examiner, beginning with general questions about familiar topics, progressing to a short presentation on a given topic, and concluding with a discussion of more abstract ideas related to the presentation topic, allowing assessors to evaluate fluency, coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range, accuracy, and pronunciation across all four language skills.

text: Predicting threat from environmental events is a fundamental ability of humans and many nonhuman species, and engages species-specific defensive responses to facilitate survival. To investigate such fear memory, classical (Pavlovian) fear conditioning paradigms are commonly used, in which an initially neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) predicts an upcoming aversive unconditioned stimulus (US). Besides addressing a basic associative learning mechanism, such paradigms are also thought to model psychiatric conditions in humans such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other anxiety disorders (Lissek et al., 2005; VanElzakker, Dahlgren, Davis, Dubois, & Shin, 2014). Consequently, fear conditioning is used to develop interventions for the prevention or erasure of pathological fear (Carmichael & Lockhart, 2012; Grillon, Cordova, Morgan, Charney, & Davis, 2004; Reist, Duffy, Fujimoto, & Cahill, 2001; Schiller et al., 2010). Such investigations require an ability to detect subtle differences in fear memory strength. In rodent species, fear conditioning with unescapable foot shock results in freezing behavior that is easy to quantify (LeDoux, 1998). In contrast, humans do not exhibit overt freezing. Instead, human fear memory is often assessed via activity of the autonomic nervous system as measured with skin conductance response (SCR; Bach, Daunizeau, Friston, & Dolan, 2010; Staib, Castegnetti, & Bach, 2015), heart period response (HPR; Castegnetti et al., 2016), or pupil size (Kluge et al., 2011; Korn, Staib, Tzovara, Castegnetti, & Bach, 2016; Reinhard, Lachnit, & König, 2006). Yet, SCR are susceptible to internal emotional, cognitive, and motor processes unrelated to fear memory and typically require long intertrial intervals (ITIs) because of slowness of the peripheral signal (Boucsein, 2012; Hamm & Vaitl, 1996). Similarly, HPR may reflect motor preparation independent of stimulus valence (Hamm & Vaitl, 1996).

text: Sexual violence is a critical area of study within gender studies, approached through an interdisciplinary lens that examines its roots in gender inequality, power imbalances, and social norms. Research consistently shows that sexual violence disproportionately affects women, sexual minorities, and gender minorities, with perpetrators predominantly being men, reflecting broader patterns of patriarchal dominance and control. For example, surveys like the SAFEDUC 2024 report reveal that over half of female students experience sexual harassment, and significant percentages report physical or sexual assault, highlighting the widespread nature of this violence in educational settings. Gender studies analyze how cultural beliefs about masculinity, femininity, and heteronormativity contribute to the normalization of violence and the silencing of victims. Intersectional approaches emphasize that experiences of sexual violence vary depending on the interplay of gender with race, sexuality, and other identities, which can increase vulnerability and complicate access to justice and support. Scholars also investigate the “Nordic paradox,” where countries with high gender equality still report high rates of sexual violence, suggesting complex societal dynamics and potential backlash effects as traditional gender roles are challenged. Gender studies promote prevention and intervention strategies informed by evidence, advocating for policies that address structural inequalities and support survivors. Organizations like the Sexual Violence Research Initiative (SVRI) work globally to build research capacity, advance knowledge, and influence policy to end violence against women and children, especially in low- and middle-income countries. Overall, gender studies frame sexual violence not only as individual acts of harm but as systemic issues rooted in gendered power relations, aiming to transform social attitudes and institutions to create safer, more equitable societies.

text: The collapse of the Soviet Union resulted from a complex convergence of internal structural weaknesses, economic failures, political reforms, and external pressures that ultimately overwhelmed the communist system's capacity to maintain control over its vast territories and diverse populations. The fundamental economic contradictions within the centrally planned economy became increasingly apparent during the 1980s, as the Soviet system struggled to compete with Western technological advancement, consumer goods production, and economic efficiency while devoting enormous resources to military spending and subsidizing client states worldwide. The arms race with the United States, particularly the Strategic Defense Initiative, placed unsustainable financial burdens on an already strained economy, while the costly war in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989 further depleted resources and undermined popular support for the regime. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, including glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), were intended to revitalize the Soviet system but instead unleashed forces that ultimately destroyed it by encouraging political dissent, weakening central control, and exposing the depth of systemic problems. The policy of glasnost allowed previously suppressed nationalist movements and political opposition to emerge, while perestroika disrupted established economic relationships without creating effective alternatives, leading to shortages, inflation, and social unrest. External factors including the democratic revolutions in Eastern Europe, the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the loss of satellite states demonstrated the weakness of Soviet power while inspiring independence movements within Soviet republics. The Chernobyl nuclear disaster in 1986 symbolized the system's technological backwardness and lack of transparency, while growing awareness of living standards in the West through improved communication undermined the legitimacy of communist ideology. The failed coup attempt in August 1991 by hardline communists paradoxically accelerated the dissolution process by weakening central authority and empowering Boris Yeltsin and other reformers who ultimately presided over the Soviet Union's peaceful dissolution.

text: "Informally, a hash table is a structure that can map keys to values, and provides a fast way to do so, using what's called a hash function" x = self.hashCode(key) "x is an index to the table's internal array" When keys are inserted into the hash function it returns an index where the value is to be stored, providing constant time (O(1)) average case complexity for access, insertion and deletion. Because different keys can be mapped into the same index, we get a collision. Different methods are used by hash tables to deal with collisions. One such approach is chaining: each array entry contains a linked list (or other dynamic structure) of all elements that hash to the same index; new entries are added to the list at that index. Another approach is open addressing, in which in case of collisions the algorithm searches for the next free place in the array (using probe sequences), and inserts the item in that place. Both approaches have their compromises in speed and memory used and the choice depends on how much data the method expects and required performance. Hash tables are used for example in a variety of applications dictionaries, caches and symbol tables, where quick access to the data is the priority. Although they are fast on average, performance can be in the worst case if frequent collisions happen, or if load factor (the number of keys divided by the number of slots) is too high, for which reason we use rehashing or resizing.

text: A constitutional amendment is a formal change or addition to a constitution, typically aimed at updating or clarifying its provisions to reflect changing societal values, needs, or circumstances. In Bangladesh, the process of amending the constitution is outlined in Article 142 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. To amend the constitution, a bill must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the total number of members of the Jatiya Sangsad (National Parliament). This means that at least two-thirds of the members present and voting, and not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the Sangsad, must approve the bill. Once the bill is passed by the required majority, it is sent to the President for assent. The President must give assent to the bill within seven days of its presentation, and the amendment becomes effective upon the President's assent. Certain provisions of the constitution, such as those related to the basic structure or fundamental rights, may require a more rigorous amendment process or may be considered immune to amendment. The process of constitutional amendment in Bangladesh is designed to ensure that changes to the constitution are made with broad consensus and reflect the will of the people, while also protecting the core principles and values of the constitution.

text: Kepler’s second law, also known as the law of equal areas, states that a line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. This means that a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun (at perihelion) and slower when it is farther away (at aphelion), ensuring that the area swept by its orbital radius remains constant over time. Published in 1609 as part of Kepler's Astronomia Nova, this law arose from his analysis of Tycho Brahe’s precise observations of Mars’s orbit, which revealed that planets do not move at uniform speeds—a departure from the ancient belief in perfectly circular, constant-velocity orbits. Mathematically, the law reflects the conservation of angular momentum, as the gravitational force exerted by the Sun (a central force) ensures no torque acts on the planet, keeping its angular momentum constant. For example, Earth travels about 30 km/s at perihelion (early January) compared to 29 km/s at aphelion (early July), yet the triangular area swept per day remains identical. This principle applies not only to planets but also to moons, comets, and artificial satellites, illustrating the universal nature of orbital mechanics. Kepler’s second law was later explained by Newton’s laws of motion and gravitation, which showed that the varying speed results from the interplay between inertia and the Sun’s gravitational pull. The law has practical implications in space mission planning, such as timing satellite maneuvers or calculating transfer orbits between planets. It also underpins modern astrophysics, helping scientists model binary star systems and the accretion disks around black holes. By demonstrating that planetary motion is governed by precise, predictable rules rather than arbitrary celestial perfection, Kepler’s second law was a cornerstone in the transition from geocentric to heliocentric cosmology, reinforcing the idea that nature’s laws are both measurable and mathematically elegant. Its legacy endures in orbital dynamics, where the balance between kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy continues to shape our understanding of the cosmos.

text: The evolution of tourism from its inception to its mature, sustainable industry operation is outlined by the stages of tourism development.  Small groups of daring or inquisitive tourists visit a place during the first stage of exploration, which is frequently prompted by natural or cultural features.  In this stage, the region is largely undeveloped, tourism is typically unstructured, and services and infrastructure are scarce.  The second stage is engagement, in which stakeholders and local communities begin actively promoting tourism, investing in basic utilities, and recognising the industry's potential.  Local companies start serving tourists, and infrastructure like roads, lodging, and amenities start to take shape.  The third stage, known as development, is characterised by a rapid expansion of facilities and services, formalised marketing, and significant external investment.  At this point, large-scale hotels and attractions start to appear, and tourism frequently becomes more commercialised, which might raise worries about overdevelopment.  Consolidation is the fourth stage, during which the destination's primary attractions are well-established and growth levels out.  The sector gets increasingly structured with standardised services and marketing tactics when visitor numbers reach their peak.  Controlling the quantity of visitors and preserving quality are essential during this stage to stop resource degradation.  The fifth stage, known as stagnation, occurs when market saturation, competition, or environmental deterioration cause visitor growth to stall or even drop.  The location can see a drop in both economic returns and guest satisfaction.  Rejuvenation or decline, depending on how problems are handled, is the last stage.  While decline may result in abandonment or a decrease in tourism, rejuvenation entails reviving the location through marketing, innovation, and sustainable practices.  In order to ensure long-term viability, the stages of tourism development emphasise the significance of meticulous planning, resource management, and sustainable practices.  Understanding these phases aids in the implementation of initiatives by industry stakeholders and policymakers to prolong the growth phase, reduce adverse effects, and promote a resilient and sustainable tourist sector that supports local populations and protects natural and cultural resources.

text: A servo motor is an advanced indirect drive motor usually used in robotics and automation applications where precise control of angular or linear position, velocity and acceleration is required. It operates in a closed loop system, in the motor responds to a command and moves and then corrects the move via feedback (typically from an encoder or potentiometer) to preserve accuracy. Solid motor An ordinary servo motor comprises of a motor, a feedback sensor, a control circuit and, if it uses a mechanism, a gearbox for torque. In particular, servo motors are noted for their precise control and ability to hold a position, and to accelerate and decelerate very quickly, for example to the required position as rapidly as possible, then hold that position. There are two primary types of motors: AC servos and DC servos, although DC servos are more prominent in smaller scale robotics since they are cheaper and easier to manufacture. Unlike a standard motor, the servo motor can change its position from one angle to another by sending a single pulse of varying width (0-180 or 360 degrees) so depending on what the shaft is required to do the control signal necessary varies. Thanks to the precision, reliability and responsiveness of servo motors, they are a preferred choice in applications requiring precise motion control.

text: Testing the significance of regression coefficients involves determining whether the observed relationship between an independent variable and the dependent variable is statistically meaningful or could have occurred by chance alone. This process typically employs hypothesis testing procedures that evaluate whether each regression coefficient is significantly different from zero, which would indicate that the corresponding independent variable has a genuine effect on the outcome variable. The most common approach uses a t-test for each individual coefficient, where the null hypothesis states that the true population coefficient equals zero, meaning the variable has no linear relationship with the dependent variable, while the alternative hypothesis suggests the coefficient is not zero, indicating a meaningful relationship exists. The test statistic is calculated by dividing the estimated coefficient by its standard error, producing a t-value that follows a t-distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the sample size minus the number of parameters estimated in the model. This t-value is then compared to critical values from the t-distribution table or converted to a p-value that represents the probability of observing such an extreme result if the null hypothesis were true. When the p-value falls below a predetermined significance level, typically 0.05, researchers reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the coefficient is statistically significant. The standard error of each coefficient reflects the precision of the estimate and is influenced by factors such as sample size, variability in the data, and multicollinearity among predictors. Confidence intervals provide additional insight by showing the range of plausible values for the true population coefficient, with intervals that exclude zero indicating statistical significance. It's important to note that statistical significance doesn't necessarily imply practical significance, as very small effects can be statistically significant with large sample sizes, while meaningful effects might not reach significance with small samples. Additionally, when testing multiple coefficients simultaneously, researchers should consider adjusting significance levels to account for multiple comparisons and reduce the risk of Type I errors.

text: Social disorganization theory is a criminological perspective that explains crime and delinquency as a result of the breakdown of social institutions and communal relationships in certain neighborhoods or communities. Developed by Clifford Shaw and Henry McKay in the 1920s and 1930s through their work in Chicago, the theory posits that environmental factors—rather than individual traits—are key drivers of criminal behavior. Specifically, it argues that neighborhoods characterized by poverty, high residential mobility, ethnic diversity, and family disruption lack the social cohesion and informal social controls necessary to prevent crime. In such areas, institutions like schools, families, and community organizations fail to function effectively, leading to weakened social bonds, low collective efficacy, and a diminished ability to enforce norms or regulate behavior. As a result, criminal activity becomes more prevalent and even normalized among residents, especially youth, who may lack positive role models or supervision. Social disorganization theory has significantly influenced crime prevention strategies, emphasizing the importance of community-based interventions, such as neighborhood watch programs, youth mentorship, improved urban planning, and investments in local institutions to rebuild social capital. It has also encouraged law enforcement to focus not just on policing but on community engagement and building trust. One key strength of the theory is its ability to explain the spatial distribution of crime—why certain neighborhoods consistently experience higher crime rates despite changes in population. Critics, however, argue that the theory can be too deterministic and may overlook individual agency, cultural factors, or systemic inequalities like racism. Nonetheless, social disorganization theory remains a foundational concept in urban criminology and sociology, highlighting how environmental instability and the erosion of social structures can foster conditions conducive to crime.

text: Dijkstra's Algorithm is a greedy algorithm used to find the shortest path between a single source node and all other nodes in a graph where edge weights are non-negative. It operates by maintaining a set of nodes for which the shortest path from the source has been definitively found, and a distance array storing the current shortest known distance to every other node. The process starts by setting the source distance to zero and all others to infinity.It iteratively selects the unvisited node with the currently smallest known distance, marks it as visited, and then relaxes all of its unvisited neighbors. Relaxation involves checking if the path to a neighbor through the current node is shorter than the neighbor's current recorded distance; if so, the neighbor's distance is updated. By continuously selecting the closest unvisited node, the algorithm systematically expands the shortest path tree until all reachable nodes have been included. Its typical time complexity is O((V+E)logV) when implemented with a Min-Priority Queue.

text: The levels of organization in animal bodies represent a systematic hierarchy that defines the complexity and functional integration of living organisms, starting from the simplest units to highly complex systems that sustain life. At the most basic level are cells, the fundamental units of life, each specialized to perform particular functions such as muscle contraction, nerve transmission, or secretion; animals are multicellular, meaning their bodies are composed of many different types of cells working together. These cells are grouped into tissues, which are collections of similar cells that carry out a specific activity. There are four primary types of animal tissues: epithelial tissue, which covers body surfaces and lines cavities providing protection and absorption; connective tissue, which supports, binds, and connects other tissues and organs, including bone, cartilage, and blood; muscle tissue, responsible for movement and locomotion; and nervous tissue, which transmits electrical impulses for communication and coordination. Tissues combine to form organs, distinct structures that perform specialized functions necessary for survival, such as the heart pumping blood, lungs facilitating gas exchange, or kidneys filtering waste. Organs work together in organ systems, which are groups of organs coordinating to carry out broader physiological tasks; for example, the digestive system includes the mouth, stomach, intestines, and accessory glands working together to process food and absorb nutrients, while the circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, and waste products throughout the body. At the highest level is the organism itself, representing the complete living animal, whose integrated organ systems maintain homeostasis and enable reproduction, movement, response to stimuli, and growth. These levels of organization demonstrate increasing complexity, with each level depending on the proper functioning and coordination of the lower levels, emphasizing the interdependence within an animal’s body. This hierarchical structure allows animals to perform complex life processes efficiently and adapt to changing environments. Moreover, understanding these levels is fundamental in fields like physiology, medicine, and developmental biology, as disruptions at any level—from cellular defects to organ failure—can affect the health of the entire organism. In summary, the levels of organization in animal bodies—from cells to tissues, organs, organ systems, and ultimately the whole organism—reflect a carefully structured arrangement that underpins the biological complexity and functional harmony essential for life.

text: The mind-body problem is a central issue in philosophy that explores the relationship between the mental and physical aspects of existence, addressing questions about the nature of consciousness, identity, and the interaction between mind and body. It arises from the apparent distinction between subjective experiences, thoughts, and emotions, which constitute the mind, and the objective, material processes of the body, such as neural activity and physiological functions. Philosophers have proposed various theories to explain this relationship, ranging from dualism, which posits that mind and body are fundamentally separate substances, to physicalism, which asserts that mental states are entirely reducible to physical processes. René Descartes famously argued for substance dualism, suggesting that the mind is a non-material entity distinct from the physical body, connected through the pineal gland. In contrast, materialists like Gilbert Ryle and Daniel Dennett reject dualism, advocating for a monistic view where mental phenomena emerge from or are identical to brain activity. Other approaches include idealism, which holds that reality is fundamentally mental, and panpsychism, which suggests that consciousness is a universal property of matter. The mind-body problem also involves questions about causation, such as how mental intentions can influence physical actions and how physical stimuli can produce subjective experiences. Advances in neuroscience and cognitive science have provided insights into the biological basis of consciousness, yet the subjective nature of experience, often referred to as the "hard problem" of consciousness, remains a profound mystery. The mind-body problem has implications for ethics, psychology, artificial intelligence, and medicine, influencing debates about free will, personal identity, and the nature of mental health. By examining the mind-body relationship, philosophers seek to understand the complexities of human existence and the interplay between subjective and objective realities.

text: Non-parametric tests are statistical methods used when data do not meet the assumptions required for parametric tests, such as normal distribution, equal variances, or interval-level measurement. These tests are especially useful for analyzing ordinal data, ranked data, categorical data, or data with outliers and skewed distributions, as they do not rely on specific probability distributions. Unlike parametric tests, which use parameters like the mean and standard deviation, non-parametric tests are distribution-free and often focus on medians or the ranks of data rather than raw values. They are broadly applied when the sample size is small or the data cannot support more robust parametric methods. Typical statistics calculations include the Mann-Whitney U-test for two independent groups, paired sample Wilcoxon rank sum test, Kruskal-Wallis testing for more than two groups and Chi-square testing to evaluate the association between categorical variables. Non-parametric tests versus parametric tests While non-parametric tests are typically less powerful than parametric tests when respective assumptions are met, these methods provide more robust and precise results in the presence of violated assumptions and are thus indispensable approaches in the practical research of fields such as medicine, psychology, or social sciences where data can be distorted away from theoretical distributions.

text: Shutter speed is a fundamental setting in photography that determines the length of time the camera's shutter remains open, allowing light to reach the sensor. It is measured in seconds or fractions of a second, such as 1/1000, 1/500, 1/250, 1/125, 1/60, 1/30, 1/15, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, and 1 second or longer. Shutter speed plays a crucial role in controlling the exposure of an image, as well as the way motion is captured. A faster shutter speed, such as 1/1000 or 1/500 of a second, allows less light to reach the sensor and is ideal for freezing fast-moving subjects, such as sports, wildlife, or action scenes. Faster shutter speeds are also useful in bright lighting conditions, where a shorter exposure time helps prevent overexposure. Conversely, a slower shutter speed, such as 1/30 or 1/15 of a second, allows more light to reach the sensor and is suitable for capturing motion blur, such as the smooth flow of water, the streaks of car lights, or the movement of people. Slower shutter speeds are also useful in low-light conditions, where a longer exposure time helps capture more light and produce a brighter image. However, using a slow shutter speed requires careful handling to avoid camera shake, which can result in blurry images. To mitigate this, photographers often use a tripod or other stabilizing devices to keep the camera steady during long exposures. Shutter speed is one of the three key elements of the exposure triangle, along with aperture and ISO, and it plays a crucial role in determining the overall exposure and creative effect of an image. Understanding and mastering shutter speed is essential for achieving the desired exposure and capturing motion effectively in various photographic situations.

text: Stagflation is an economic condition characterized by the unusual and challenging combination of stagnant or very slow economic growth, high unemployment, and rising inflation occurring simultaneously. This phenomenon defies traditional economic theories, such as the Phillips Curve, which suggests an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment. Stagflation typically arises from negative supply shocks, like sudden increases in the prices of essential commodities such as oil, which raise production costs across the economy and lead to higher consumer prices while simultaneously slowing down economic output and job creation. It presents a policy dilemma because measures to control inflation, such as tightening monetary policy by raising interest rates, can further suppress economic growth and increase unemployment, whereas policies aimed at stimulating growth, like increasing government spending, may exacerbate inflation. The term gained prominence during the 1970s when the oil embargo led to soaring inflation and unemployment in the United States and other countries, challenging Keynesian economic models and prompting the development of alternative theories like monetarism. Recent global disruptions, including the COVID-19 pandemic and geopolitical tensions, have raised concerns about a potential return of stagflation in the mid-2020s. Stagflation is particularly troublesome because it combines the worst aspects of inflation and recession, making it difficult for policymakers to address without worsening one of the problems. In summary, stagflation is a rare but severe economic condition marked by slow or negative growth, rising unemployment, and persistent inflation, often triggered by supply shocks and complicated by conflicting policy responses.

text: Avoidance of threats and discovery of food are crucial for organisms’ survival, as is the reliable prediction of both threat and food sources. Classical conditioning (Pavlov, 1927) is a simple learning model that explains how organisms make associations between events in order to predict threats or food. In other words, biologically salient events (unconditioned stimuli, US) become associated with initially irrelevant stimuli if such stimuli occur contiguous and contingent to the US (Rescorla, 1988). Through their association with the US, the irrelevant stimuli (now labeled conditioned stimuli, CS) acquire affective and predictive properties and are able to elicit specific responses (conditioned responses, CR) such as fear in the case of a threatening US (Andreatta & Pauli, 2015; Lipp, Sheridan, & Siddle, 1994; Sjouwerman, Niehaus, Kuhn, & Lonsdorf, 2016) or appetitive responses in the case of a rewarding US (Andreatta & Pauli, 2015; Blechert, Testa, Georgii, Klimesch, & Wilhelm, 2016; Kim, Shimojo, & O'Doherty, 2011; Klucken et al., 2015; Kruse, Leon, Stark, & Klucken, 2017; Myers et al., 2017; van den Akker, Nederkoorn, & Jansen, 2017). Following such learning processes, survival is further optimized by generalization toward other stimuli that have never been associated with the US but which share properties with the CS (Hearst, 1960; Pearce, 1987). Notably, the similarity of the so-called generalization stimuli (GS) to the CS can be perceptual but also conceptual (Dunsmoor & Murphy, 2015; Dymond, Dunsmoor, Vervliet, Roche, & Hermans, 2015). Specifically, human studies found strong fear responses such as startle potentiation (Lissek et al., 2008, 2010) or a greater skin conductance response (SCR, Ahrens et al., 2016; Onat & Buchel, 2015; Schiele et al., 2016) to both the CS predictive of an aversive US (e.g., an electric shock or a desperate female scream) and GS that were perceptually similar to the CS.

text: Punishment in psychology is a consequence that is used to decrease the likelihood of a behavior recurring in the future. It is a fundamental principle in B.F. Skinner's theory of operant conditioning and is sometimes referred to as the ""pleasure and pain principle"" or the ""punch line principle."" It can de divided into two main types, positive punishment and negative punishment. Positive punishment is adding something unpleasant following a behavior, for example, reprimanding a child for behaving badly in order to prevent said behavior. Negative punishment, which removes a desirable stimulus, acts to decrease behavior, as when a teen’s phone is taken away when he or she breaks the rules. This strategy can teach your dog to fear you, and if you use treats or punishment, can create negative associations in the long term, e.g. if you use treats with punishment, your dog will start to fear treats or your dog may become anxious or aggressive if not trained correctly. Punishment is most effective when it is close in time to the behavior, is consistent, and corresponds in intensity to the behavior. It is an entirely different process to reinforcement whose goal is to cause an increase in behaviour, while punishment’s purpose is directly aimed at suppressing behaviour. Successful behavior modification frequently depends more on using reinforcement to make good behavior more frequent than on using punishment to deter from bad behavior – punishment may even accomplish the opposite by not showing a person what to do instead and damage relationships or self-esteem.Punishment and reinforcement operate in the opposite manner: Reinforcement increases a behavior that was done willingly, and punishment decreases a behavior that was done willingly.

text: Cardinal and Ordinal utility are the two alternative methods that are being used in the consumer theory to demonstrate how an individual get satisfaction by consuming different good and services. Restaurant utility posits that utility is a quantifiable benefit, that it can be quantified in real numbers, and that there are actual quantities of the real “thing” called “utility”. For instance, a consumer might state that an apple gives them 10 utils of satisfaction and a banana 5, which means that the apple provides exactly twice as much satisfaction as the banana. This concept actually gives us a way to compare utility numbers with each other and perform some arithmetic on the utility numbers which economists can't do with degrees of utility. Ordinal utility, on the other hand, does not try to quantify utility in exact amount. On the contrary, it orders preferences by satisfying. One can say that one prefers an apple to a banana, but one cannot say how much. Ordinal utility is what underlies modern consumer theory, through such tools as indifference curves—when we have the full range of indifference curves, we don’t need to know what the actual level of utility is, only the rankings of bundles of goods. Cardinal utility was common in economic work before it was rejected (for example in the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility), but came under attack for its lack of realism - for assuming that utility can be measured like weight or distance. Ordinal utility is a more realistic and feasible representation that emphasizes consumer preferences with no need for quantified satisfaction indicators. Thus the primary distinction between them is that cardinal utility gives a numerical value for utility to the degree that individual actually expect to consume a good, while ordinal utility only carries information about the purchasing ability of the consumer and is accordingly more broadly used in modern economics since it is conceptually coherent and relatively easy to graph and measure.

text: Balance of power is a fundamental concept in International Relations that describes the distribution of power among states and the mechanisms used to prevent any single state from achieving dominance over others. This principle suggests that states naturally seek to maintain equilibrium in the international system by forming alliances, building up their own capabilities, or working to constrain potential hegemons that threaten the existing order. The concept operates on the assumption that states are primarily concerned with their security and survival, leading them to oppose any actor that becomes too powerful and could potentially threaten their independence. Balance of power can manifest in different forms, including a simple balance between two major powers, a complex balance involving multiple states, or a balance maintained through alliance systems where smaller states align with one major power to counterbalance another. Historical examples include the European balance of power system that operated from the Treaty of Westphalia through World War I, where major powers like Britain, France, Austria, and Russia continuously adjusted their relationships to prevent any single state from dominating the continent. The concept also encompasses balancing behaviors such as internal balancing, where states increase their own military and economic capabilities, and external balancing, where states form alliances to aggregate power against a common threat. Critics argue that balance of power thinking can lead to arms races, alliance rigidity, and ultimately conflict when the balance breaks down. Despite these criticisms, the concept remains relevant in analyzing contemporary international relations, including discussions about rising powers like China and how existing powers like the United States respond to maintain global stability and their own security interests.

text: ADR (Automated Dialogue Replacement), also known as looping, is a post-production process in filmmaking where actors re-record their dialogue in a controlled studio environment to replace unclear, distorted, or otherwise unusable audio captured during on-set filming. During ADR sessions, actors watch the filmed scene repeatedly, synchronizing their new delivery with their lip movements on screen, often guided by a series of beeps or visual cues to ensure precise timing. The re-recorded dialogue is then meticulously edited and mixed into the soundtrack, with engineers matching ambient tones, reverb, and pitch to blend seamlessly with the original audio. ADR isn’t just for fixing errors—it’s also used creatively to enhance performances (e.g., intensifying whispers in a thriller) or alter dialogue for clarity or censorship. While ADR demands significant time and skill to avoid unnatural or "canned" results, advancements in AI and voice-matching technology are streamlining the process. From blockbusters (where action scenes often require ADR due to loud set conditions) to animated films (where voice acting is entirely studio-recorded), ADR ensures that every word resonates with crisp, intentional impact, proving that what audiences hear is often as carefully crafted as what they see.

text: The scientific method in psychology is a systematic, step-by-step process used by researchers to investigate human behavior and mental processes in an objective and replicable way. It begins with observing a phenomenon or behavior of interest, followed by formulating a clear research question or problem based on those observations. Next, psychologists develop a hypothesis, which is a testable prediction that proposes a relationship between two or more variables. The hypothesis is then tested through carefully designed experiments or studies, where data is collected and analyzed to determine whether the hypothesis is supported or refuted. After analyzing the results, researchers draw conclusions and interpret the findings in the context of existing theories and knowledge. Finally, the results are published and shared with the scientific community, allowing others to review, replicate, or challenge the findings. This process is cyclical, as new questions often arise from previous research, leading to further investigation. The scientific method emphasizes empiricism, relying on observable and measurable evidence rather than subjective opinions, and requires that hypotheses be falsifiable, meaning they can be tested and potentially disproven. Ethical considerations, such as obtaining informed consent and ensuring participant confidentiality, are integral to the process. By applying the scientific method, psychology distinguishes itself from philosophy and speculation, providing a rigorous framework to better understand complex human behaviors and mental functions. This approach allows psychologists to build reliable knowledge, develop effective interventions, and contribute to fields like mental health, education, and social policy. In summary, the scientific method in psychology is a structured approach to inquiry that involves observation, hypothesis formation, experimentation, analysis, and dissemination, all aimed at producing objective and verifiable knowledge about human behavior and mental processes.

text: Definition and implementation Fertilization is a multistep biological event resulting in the union of a male (sperm) and female (egg or ovum) gamete, giving rise to a zygote through the fusion of their nuclei (Fig. This event normally takes place in the fallopian tube of mammals, such as humans. It starts with ovulation, when the ovary releases a mature egg into the fallopian tube. Millions of sperm are ejaculated during intercourse with the female but only a few hundred make it to the neighborhood of the egg. In this case, sperm must break through the protective layers surrounding the egg, such as the corona radiata and zona pellucida of humans, before fertilization can occur. It is made possible by enzymes the sperm releases from an acrosome, a caplike structure on the sperm’s head. After a sperm eventually binds to the egg’s plasma membrane, several chemical events take place which make sure no more sperms enter, called the cortical reaction. The sperm nucleus and egg nucleus fuse together in a phenomenon we call syngamy, and a diploid zygote is formed with a full complement of chromosomes (from both Mom and Dad!). This single-celled zygote remains still and contains the genetic instructions required to grow a new organism. Once fertilized, the zygote will start to undergo a series of extremely rapid mitotic divisions known as cleavage as it passes down the fallopian tube to the uterus. These divisions result in the development of a multicellular structure known as a blastocyst, which attaches to the lining of the uterus, establishing pregnancy. Fertilization not only returns the diploid number of chromosomes but also establishes the genetic sex of the embryo, based on whether the sperm contains an X or Y chromosome. The process provides genetic diversity by way of the combination of parental genes and is necessary for the continuation of most sexually reproducing organisms. In summary, fertilization is a gesture and a dance highly coordinated and properly timed in the course of interactions between the male and the female gametes that include communication, recognition and fusion mechanisms which lead to the generation of new life.

text: Fill light is a secondary light source used in photography, videography, and cinematography to reduce the contrast created by the key light and illuminate the shadow areas of a subject without overpowering the primary illumination. While the key light establishes the main exposure and creates the fundamental shadows that give dimension to the subject, the fill light works to soften these shadows and reveal detail in the darker areas that might otherwise be lost or appear too harsh. The fill light is typically positioned on the opposite side of the key light, often at a lower intensity to maintain the natural hierarchy of lighting while preventing the shadows from becoming completely black or overly dramatic. The ratio between the key light and fill light, known as the lighting ratio, determines the overall contrast and mood of the image or scene. A higher ratio with minimal fill light creates dramatic, high-contrast lighting suitable for film noir or intense dramatic scenes, while a lower ratio with stronger fill light produces softer, more even illumination often preferred for beauty photography or commercial work. Fill light can be achieved through various methods, including additional artificial lights, reflectors that bounce the key light back onto the subject, or natural sources like windows or ambient room lighting. The quality of fill light is usually softer and more diffused than the key light to avoid creating competing shadows or conflicting light directions. Professional photographers and cinematographers carefully balance the fill light intensity to maintain the three-dimensional quality established by the key light while ensuring adequate detail visibility in shadow areas, creating a polished and professional-looking result that serves the artistic vision of the project.

text: Many of the readers are certainly familiar with linked lists, as they are one of the fundamental data structures at the core of computer science curricula. A box represents a node; it is divided in two parts, one representing the information fields, the other representing the pointer to the next node. text: Macro photography is a genre of photography that focuses on extreme close-ups of small subjects, and usually the term refers to the art of taking close up photos of things. Another is the use of tripods, soft lighting from more than one direction and focus stacking (combining multiple shots with differing focus points) are techniques frequently used to get sharp, well lit results. text: The concept of intelligence has been a subject of extensive debate, leading to several prominent theories attempting to define and explain its nature. Early theories focused on intelligence as a single, general ability, while later theories proposed multiple, distinct abilities. 1. Spearman's Two-Factor Theory (g and s factors): Charles Spearman (1904) proposed that intelligence consists of a general intelligence factor (g), which underlies all intellectual abilities, and specific factors (s factors), which are unique to particular tasks. The 'g' factor explains why individuals tend to perform consistently across various cognitive tests. 2. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities: Louis Thurstone (1938) challenged the 'g' factor, proposing that intelligence is composed of seven distinct primary mental abilities: verbal comprehension, word fluency, number facility, spatial visualization, associative memory, perceptual speed, and inductive reasoning. He argued that these operate somewhat independently. 3. Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) Theory: This is one of the most comprehensive and empirically supported theories, integrating earlier work. It posits a hierarchical model with 'g' at the top, followed by broad abilities (e.g., fluid intelligence, crystallized intelligence, quantitative reasoning, visual processing, auditory processing, short-term memory, long-term retrieval, processing speed, reaction time), and then narrow abilities at the bottom. Fluid intelligence (Gf) is the ability to reason and solve novel problems independently of acquired knowledge, while Crystallized intelligence (Gc) is the ability to use learned knowledge and experience. 4. Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences: Howard Gardner (1983) proposed that intelligence is not a single entity but comprises at least eight (and possibly more) distinct intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic. Each intelligence is relatively independent and may be expressed in different ways, challenging traditional measures that focus primarily on linguistic and logical-mathematical abilities. 5. Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence: Robert Sternberg (1985) proposed three distinct forms of intelligence: analytical intelligence (problem-solving, typically measured by IQ tests), creative intelligence (ability to deal with novel situations and generate new ideas), and practical intelligence (ability to adapt to real-world contexts and solve everyday problems, often called "street smarts"). These diverse theories highlight the complexity of intelligence, moving beyond a singular construct to recognize a broader range of cognitive capacities and forms of human cleverness, while also sparking ongoing debates about how intelligence should be defined, measured, and cultivated.

text: Price discrimination arises when a monopolist sets different prices to different people for the same good, not because costs of production are different, but because consumers’ willingness or ability to pay is different. This tactics helps the monopolist take the consumers surplus and makes more money from it. Price discrimination will apply if three conditions are met: the firm is selling a product that cannot be resold at the same price between customers, the firm has limited ability to differentiate between customers according to demand elasticity and is able to segment the market without restriction. Price discrimination occurs in three degrees. Perfect price discrimination (or first degree) involves charging consumers exactly what they are willing to pay. Under this mechanism all consumer surplus is harvested but is hard to implement because of a lack of information. Second degree price discrimination means several pricing for quantity or package such as bulk rate and food plan. (Partial) price discrimination Tier price Share Eligible consumers endogenously self-select into multiple pricing tiers depending on their preferences. 3rd degree price discrimination is a situation in which market is segregate in different section like for students or senior citizens or for different geographic areas charging them a different rate according to their elastic which means how responsive they are to the rate. For instance, tickets for flights, movies and costs incorporated towards consumed electricity are commonly third-degree price discriminator. Price discrimination can be efficient and make it possible for more consumers to drink (especially in places like public transportation, where seats would otherwise go unsold), but can raise concerns about fairness if some consumers get asked to pay much higher prices than others. In practice, price discrimination allows a monopolist to sell more units to price-sensitive customers without cutting the price for everyone. It is a standard practice in many industries that are dominated by firms having pricing powers.

text: Fishes are aquatic vertebrates characterized by several distinctive features that enable them to live efficiently in water. Their body is typically divided into three main parts: the head, trunk, and tail, although these divisions may not always be externally obvious. They possess a backbone made of either cartilage (in cartilaginous fishes like sharks) or bone (in bony fishes), providing structural support and flexibility. Fishes breathe through gills, specialized respiratory organs located on either side of the head, covered by a bony flap called the operculum; gills extract dissolved oxygen from water, allowing fishes to survive underwater. Their bodies are usually covered with scales that protect against injury and parasites, and these scales can be of different types such as ganoid, cycloid, or ctenoid. For movement and stability, fishes have several fins: paired pectoral and pelvic fins for steering and balance, and unpaired fins including the dorsal, anal, and caudal (tail) fins, which provide propulsion and help maintain equilibrium. Many bony fishes possess a swim bladder, an internal gas-filled organ that controls buoyancy, enabling them to maintain depth without constant swimming. Fishes are ectothermic (cold-blooded), meaning their body temperature varies with the surrounding water temperature. They have a lateral line system, a sensory organ running along the sides of their body that detects vibrations and water pressure changes, aiding in navigation, predator avoidance, and prey detection. Their eyes are adapted for underwater vision, and they have internal ears with otoliths to sense sound and balance. Fishes reproduce mostly by laying eggs, and their streamlined bodies and muscular systems allow efficient swimming. These combined anatomical and physiological traits make fishes well adapted to diverse aquatic habitats, from freshwater rivers and lakes to deep marine environments.

text: If no outside force acts on a closed and isolated system, the law of conservation of momentum says that the total momentum of that system stays the same.  This means that the overall momentum before an event (like a collision) is the same as the total momentum after the event.  This law comes from Newton's third law of motion. It may be written mathematically as m?u? + m?u? = m?v? + m?v?, where m? and m? are the masses of the two bodies that hit each other, u? and u? are their initial speeds, and v? and v? are their ultimate speeds.  This idea is true for both elastic and inelastic collisions, although only elastic collisions keep kinetic energy.  The law of conservation of momentum is a very helpful tool for figuring out and solving problems that have to do with collisions, explosions, and propulsion.  When you shoot a gun, for example, the bullet goes forward and the gun goes back.  The bullet moves far faster than the pistol, even though it is much lighter.  The bullet gains momentum that is equal in size and opposite in direction to the gun's lost momentum, which keeps the system's overall momentum the same.  In space, where there is no air resistance, astronauts utilize this same idea to shift direction by pushing things away. The object's velocity is balanced by the astronaut's opposing movement.  This concept also regulates interactions at the atomic and subatomic levels, like in particle accelerators, where collisions between particles are studied based on the idea that momentum is conserved. Moreover, this law is used by engineers when designing automobiles, safety devices, and mechanical systems. In theoretical ideal cases, no external forces (for example friction or air resistance) are present, and the momentum does not change. This universal law lays the foundation for classical mechanics and it still dominates the way we perceive movement and interaction in every sector of physics.

text: The basic function of irony is to communicate the opposite of what is said (Grice, 1975). This indirectness can make ironic language harder to understand than literal language and increases the chances of misinterpretation. However, the benefit of using irony comes from its various subtle and complex effects, serving additional communicative functions that would be absent in the literal equivalent. For example, if Paddy does something particularly clumsy, Sara may respond with “Nicely done!” in which case Sara may intend to elicit a certain emotional response, such as amusement or anger. Here, we will examine immediate emotional reactions to ironic and literal comments in written communication. One controversial issue is whether using irony increases or decreases the positive or negative impact of a message. Brown and Levinson (1987) argued that one function of irony is to reduce threat. In line with this, Dews and Winner (1995) present evidence that irony reduces the strength of a statement: criticism becomes less negative, and praise becomes less positive (see also Harris & Pexman, 2003). Based on such findings, Dews and Winner proposed the tinge hypothesis, according to which the meaning of an ironic comment is automatically affected by the literal meaning. In ironic criticism, the intended disapproval of “Nicely done!” is automatically “tinged” with the positive literal reading of the phrase, and vice versa for ironic praise. The implication of the tinge hypothesis is that an ironic comment provokes a weaker emotional response in the recipient than its literal equivalent, and thus may have less impact on the relationship between speaker and recipient.

text: A sympathetic solar event is defined as consecutive eruptions occurring in different locations but having a certain physical connection, the existence of which is evidenced by previous statistical studies (Pearce & Harrison 1990; Moon et al. 2002; Wheatland & Craig 2006) and observations of individual sympathetic flares (Shi et al. 1997; Bagala et al. 2000; Gopalswamy et al. 1999). The key point of the sympathy of successive eruptions is to determine their causal linkage. Some studies have suggested that a direct magnetic interaction between different magnetic structures or a traveling disturbance indicated by surges/jets can link two eruptions as a sympathetic pair (Wang et al. 2001; Jiang et al. 2008, 2009a). Schrijver & Title (2011) showed that all eruptions in the 2010 August 1–2 global sympathetic event were connected by a system of separatrices, separators, and quasi-separatrix layers at the topological divisions of coronal magnetic force lines. However, an alternative driving mechanism for the sympathetic event is that an eruptive magnetic structure can easily weaken or remove the magnetic fields overlying other magnetic structures and thus can trigger another interrelated eruption (Gary & Moore 2004; Ding et al. 2006; Wang et al. 2006; Peng & Hu 2007; Zuccarello et al. 2009). A multiple-arcade helmet streamer might be a potential candidate for such a configuration. It is well known that coronal helmet streamers are quite common structures in the Sun and are generally associated with coronal mass ejections (CMEs; Illing & Hundhausen 1986; Sime 1989). While some CMEs are due to the symmetrical eruptions of concentric filaments in single-arcade streamers with a simple overlying bipolar field (Low 1996), a common magnetic configuration of the source fields for many CMEs should be large-scale complex magnetic systems with multiple arcades (Webb et al. 1997). Therefore, the multiple-arcade helmet-streamer configuration is crucial for the understanding of many CMEs. There are two kinds of helmet streamers, i.e., unipolar and bipolar streamers, which correspond to large-scale closed magnetic field regions containing an even or odd number of arcades sandwiched between like- or opposite-polarity open fields, respectively (Hundhausen 1972; Neugebauer et al. 2002; Wang et al. 2007).

text: In the evaluation of information retrieval systems, precision and recall are two core measures: precision is the ratio of the number of documents retrieved by the system, that are relevant with respect to the query (i.e., the number of useful documents returned by the system among all the returned documents), whereas recall is the ratio of relevant documents retrieved by the system (i.e., the number of relevant documents in the collection found by the system). High precision requires that the results list is nearly all correct, but possibly incomplete, which corresponds to the ideal scenario that the user seeks very high quality answers without sifting through noise (e.g., for expert legal or medical users). High recall guarantees a high coverage which is vital if not finding an important document could be expansive (e.g. in law for a literature review). Yet precision and recall are generally mutually exclusive; broadening to increase recall can decrease precision by introducing unrelated items, and focusing to increase precision can discard related documents, at the cost of recall. To trade off this precision-recall frontier, composite evaluations such as the F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) or precision-recall curves can be used to assess system performance across thresholds. In practice, system designers optimize according to the use-case—news investigation systems may optimize for recall, web search engines may optimize for precision, and user satisfaction. More advanced systems attempt to mitigate this trade-off via query expansion, relevance feedback, faceted browsing, and personalized ranking. The analysis of these metrics is key because they are some of the key tools for assessing the effectiveness of an IR, testing its relevance in terms of algorithmic parameters and guaranteeing that the information retrieval system returns to the user only adequate and even relevant results.

text: Cancer is one of the most feared and aggressive diseases in the world and is responsible for more than 9 million deaths universally. Staging cancer early increases the chances of recovery. The selection of the augmentations techniques was based achieving the least impact on manipulating the features of the images. This phase helps to overcome the overfitting problem and trains the model to achieve better accuracy. The third phase is deep CNN architecture. In this phase, an architecture of two main convolutional layers for featured extraction and two fully connected layers is introduced to classify the 5 different types of cancer according to the availability of images on the dataset. The results and the performance metrics such as recall, precision and F1 score show that the proposed approach achieved an overall testing accuracy of 96.90%. text: Symbiosis is a close and long-term biological interaction between two different biological organisms, which can be beneficial, harmful, or neutral for one or both of the participants. These interactions are essential for the survival, reproduction, and ecological success of many species, and they play a crucial role in shaping the structure and function of ecosystems. Symbiosis can be categorized into several types based on the nature and outcomes of the interaction:Mutualism: Mutualism is a type of symbiosis in which both participants benefit from the interaction. These relationships are often obligate, meaning that the organisms are dependent on each other for their survival and reproduction. Examples of mutualism include the relationship between corals and zooxanthellae, which are photosynthetic algae that live within the coral's tissues. The zooxanthellae provide the coral with nutrients and energy through photosynthesis, while the coral provides the algae with protection and access to sunlight. Another example of mutualism is the relationship between ruminant mammals, such as cows and sheep, and the microorganisms that inhabit their digestive tracts. The microorganisms break down complex plant materials, such as cellulose, into simpler compounds that the mammal can absorb and utilize, while the microorganisms benefit from the stable and nutrient-rich environment of the digestive tract.Commensalism: Commensalism is a type of symbiosis in which one participant benefits from the interaction, while the other is neither helped nor harmed. These relationships are often facultative, meaning that the organisms can survive and reproduce independently of each other. Examples of commensalism include the relationship between barnacles and whales, in which the barnacles attach to the whale's skin and benefit from the protection and transportation provided by the whale, while the whale is unaffected by the presence of the barnacles. Another example of commensalism is the relationship between epiphytic plants, such as orchids and bromeliads, and the trees on which they grow. The epiphytes benefit from the access to sunlight and the elevated position provided by the tree, while the tree is unaffected by the presence of the epiphytes.Parasitism: Parasitism is a type of symbiosis in which one participant, the parasite, benefits from the interaction, while the other, the host, is harmed. These relationships are often obligate for the parasite, meaning that it is dependent on the host for its survival and reproduction, while the host can often survive and reproduce independently of the parasite. Examples of parasitism include the relationship between tapeworms and their mammalian hosts, in which the tapeworm lives within the host's digestive tract and absorbs nutrients from the host's ingested food, while the host is harmed by the loss of nutrients and the potential for disease and infection. Another example of parasitism is the relationship between mistletoe and the trees on which it grows, in which the mistletoe extracts water and nutrients from the tree's vascular system, while the tree is harmed by the loss of resources and the potential for reduced growth and reproduction.Symbiosis is a fascinating and essential aspect of ecology and evolution, and it reflects the dynamic and interconnected nature of the natural world. By studying the diverse and remarkable symbiotic interactions of organisms, scientists can gain insights into the processes and mechanisms that shape the relationships and interactions of species and the incredible diversity of life on Earth.

text: Standard error is a measure of the variability or dispersion of a sample statistic, such as the mean, when multiple samples are drawn from a population. It quantifies how much the sample statistic is expected to fluctuate from one sample to another due to random sampling variability. Specifically, the standard error provides an estimate of the precision of the sample statistic as an approximation of the corresponding population parameter. For example, the standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size (n). This reflects that larger samples tend to produce more precise estimates of the population mean, resulting in smaller standard errors. The standard error is crucial in constructing confidence intervals, conducting hypothesis tests, and assessing the reliability of sample estimates. It helps researchers understand the degree of uncertainty associated with their sample statistics and whether observed differences or relationships are likely to be genuine or due to sampling variability. The smaller the standard error, the more precise the estimate; conversely, larger standard errors indicate greater variability and less confidence in the estimate. Standard error also plays a key role in the application of the Central Limit Theorem, which states that the distribution of the sample mean approaches normality as the sample size increases, with the spread of this distribution determined by the standard error. In practical terms, it is an essential concept for interpreting statistical results, understanding the accuracy of estimates, and making informed decisions based on sample data. Overall, standard error provides a standardized way to measure the uncertainty inherent in sampling, facilitating more accurate and meaningful statistical inference.
