text: Natural circulation is a component of passive heat removal systems in nuclear plants and is based on natural buoyancy forces serving to move coolant through the reactor and heat removal systems down to a heat sink. It results from the hot coolant expanding and becoming less dense as it becomes heated in the reactor core, and thus it will rise (float) towards the top of the reactor vessel or loop. As it gives up heat (usually to a steam generator or heat exchanger), it cools and becomes denser, sinking back to the bottom of the core to start the cycle again. This coolant circulation is induced by the density contrast between the hot and cold portion of the coolant and it strongly depends on the vertical distance between heat source and heat sink, system configuration and coolant characteristics as viscosity and thermal expansion. Natural circulation is also essential in passive safety systems, and, especially, in modern or innovative reactor concepts such as Advanced Passive (AP1000) PWRs, Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and Integral Pressurized Water Reactors (iPWRs). Without any power, it provides core cooling which is critically important during plant shutdowns, power failure, or in case of an accident such as a station blackout (SBO). Natural circulation in old reactor designs is a phenomenon that prevails during low power modes or to remove decay heat after the power plant has been shutdown, with forced cooling being the dominant mode during normal operation. The key benefit of natural circulation is simplicity and reliability by minimizing the amount of active parts and failure points. Yet it has a number of design problems such of low flow rate, flow instability possibilities and the necessity to vent, and our pipe and elevation configuration becomes more critical for the loop to be stable. These considerations involve the need for engineers to evaluate potential thermal-hydraulic transient such as steam voiding, in order to assure the stability of the system. Altogether, PC is a fundamental feature of passive and inherent safety concepts, and the latter are a serious option for future reactor systems.

text: The Ottoman Empire emerged in the late 13th century as a small Turkish principality founded by Osman I in northwestern Anatolia, gradually expanding through strategic military campaigns, political alliances, and administrative innovations to become one of history's largest and most enduring empires. The empire's early expansion was facilitated by the declining Byzantine Empire and fragmented political landscape of Anatolia, allowing Ottoman forces to consolidate control over Turkish beyliks while simultaneously launching campaigns into the Balkans, capitalizing on European disunity and Byzantine weakness. The conquest of Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II marked a pivotal moment in Ottoman expansion, as the capture of this strategic city not only eliminated the Byzantine Empire but also provided the Ottomans with a crucial gateway between Europe and Asia, establishing them as a major power capable of challenging both Christian Europe and Islamic rivals. Ottoman military superiority was built on several innovations, including the elite Janissary corps composed of Christian-born soldiers converted to Islam, advanced artillery and siege techniques, and a disciplined military structure that combined traditional Turkish cavalry with modern firearms and engineering capabilities. The empire's administrative system, known as the millet system, allowed religious and ethnic minorities to maintain their customs and laws under Ottoman sovereignty, creating a relatively stable multi-ethnic empire that facilitated expansion by reducing local resistance and encouraging cooperation from conquered populations. Under Suleiman the Magnificent in the 16th century, the empire reached its territorial zenith, stretching from the gates of Vienna to the Indian Ocean, encompassing southeastern Europe, western Asia, and North Africa, while simultaneously developing a sophisticated legal system, architectural marvels, and cultural achievements that demonstrated imperial power and sophistication. The Ottoman expansion was driven by a combination of religious zeal, economic opportunity, and strategic necessity, as control of trade routes between Europe and Asia provided enormous wealth, while the concept of ghazi warfare legitimized territorial expansion as a religious duty, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of conquest and consolidation that sustained imperial growth for centuries.

text: The solar EUV and X-ray radiation plays a double role in the physics of the solar upper atmosphere: by representing an important term in the energy equation, and by bearing the signatures of the most important physical phenomena that occur during solar activity, namely, flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). It is also one of the primary energy inputs to Earth's upper atmosphere: it heats the thermosphere, creates the ionosphere, and drives a number of dynamical motions and photochemical reactions at different heights. By its own nature, the EUV and X-ray emission of the Sun is highly variable on all time scales, from a factor two to several orders of magnitude (Woods et al. 2004). The largest variations occur at the shortest wavelengths. In recent years, the 10–170?Å range has attracted considerable attention because of several instruments, both already launched and being developed, that can observe astrophysical objects in this spectral interval. EUVE, Chandra, and XMM-Newton obtained high-resolution spectra from all kinds of astrophysical objects, while the Thermosphere Ionosphere Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics and Solar EUV Experiment (SEE) and the recently launched Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) include instrumentation aimed at studying the solar corona, the solar irradiance, and their variability using this range. In particular, the Extreme-Ultraviolet Variability Experiment (EVE; Woods et al. 2010) and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA; Lemen et al. 2011; Boerner et al. 2011) on board SDO include spectral windows in the 10–170?Å range aimed at studying the energy input, storage, and release mechanisms that rule coronal heating and the variability of the solar spectrum.

Symbolically, for a random variable X, CDF is defined as F(x) = P(X ? x). It is a complete characterization of the probability distribution of a random variable, either continuous or discrete. For discrete distributions, the CDF is a staircase function that jumps up by the probability at each possible value of X showing the cumulative probabilities up to that point. Smooth CDFs In a continuous distribution the CDF will be a nice, smooth function, which is its integral over the PDF. One of the simplest but most crucial uses to which the CDF is put is in calculating probabilities over intervals; for instance, the probability that X lies between a and b is P(a ? X ? b) = F(b) - F(a). The CDF also plays an important role in statistical hypothesis testing, where it is used to calculate quantiles, percentiles, and p-values. It is a tool that helps statisticians to find the probability of values occurring below or above a particular value which is very useful in hypothesis testing. In addition, the CDF allows comparison of distributions, such as empirical data and theoretical models. In simulation and the generation of random variables, inverse transform sampling use involves taking the inverse of the CDF to generate values for a specific distribution. Another attribute of a CDF is that it is a nondecreasing function which ranges between 0 and 1, the cdf starting at 0 as x approaches negative in?nity and rising to one as x approaches positive in?nity. This makes the CDF a flexible and fundamental object in theoretical and applied probability, making it possible to accurately quantify and model uncertainty in many applications.

text: SQL, or Structured Query Language, is a standardized programming language used for managing and manipulating relational databases. It provides a means for users to create, read, update, and delete (often referred to as CRUD operations) data stored in a database. SQL is widely used due to its powerful capabilities for querying and managing data, making it an essential tool for database administrators, developers, and data analysts.The SELECT statement is used to retrieve data from one or more tables in a database. Users can specify which columns to retrieve and apply conditions to filter the results. For example, one might select the names and ages of all employees from a table where the age is greater than 30. The UPDATE statement is used to modify existing records in a table. Users can specify which columns to update and apply conditions to determine which records to change. For instance, one might update the salary of an employee with a specific ID to a new value. The DELETE statement is used to remove records from a table. Users can specify conditions to determine which records to delete. For example, one might delete an employee record from a table based on the employee's ID. These basic SQL operations form the foundation for interacting with relational databases, allowing users to efficiently manage and manipulate data according to their needs. SQL's versatility and ease of use make it a fundamental skill for anyone working with databases.

text: Wolof, like most natural languages, has pervasive ambiguity, that is, a word or sentence can be analyzed in more than one way. The language is rich in ambiguities of many kinds, including morphological, lexical, syntactic and semantic ambiguities. The ambiguity phenomenon is perhaps the most serious problem faced by natural language processing (NLP) systems, and this is true for many reasons. First, ambiguity typically pertains to all levels of sentence analysis. As MacDonaldetal.(1994)noted, theoretically, linguistic information can be ambiguous at any given point in a sentence. Furthermore, many sentences that do not seem ambiguous to humans, due to extensive world knowledge, may present ambiguities to automatic parsers(and to other NLP systems as well in general). Accordingly, large-scale, linguistically motivated grammars tend to be massively ambiguous. Ambiguities can arise, for example, via alternative definitions of morphological and lexical entries, from syntactic or semantic ambiguities, and the interaction of the different ambiguities.

text: A wind turbine captures kinetic energy from moving air and converts it into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electricity through a generator. The process begins with the wind blowing across the turbine blades, causing them to rotate. The blades are aerodynamically designed to maximize energy capture from the wind, which causes the rotor to spin around a central hub connected to a shaft. This shaft is coupled to a generator, often via a gearbox that increases rotational speed to optimize electricity production. The generator uses electromagnetic induction to produce electrical current, which is then transmitted through power lines. Wind turbines are typically installed in open areas with consistent wind flow, such as coastal regions, plains, or hilltops. They come in various sizes, from small turbines for individual use to large, utility-scale turbines capable of powering thousands of homes. The efficiency of a wind turbine depends on factors such as wind speed, blade design, and turbine height; higher elevations generally experience stronger and steadier winds. Modern turbines incorporate advanced control systems to optimize performance, protect against extreme weather, and prolong operational life. They are a clean energy source because they generate electricity without emitting greenhouse gases or other pollutants. In addition to environmental benefits, wind turbines help diversify energy supplies, reduce reliance on fossil fuels, and support local economies through job creation and land lease payments. Challenges include intermittency, as wind does not blow constantly, and the variability in wind speeds, which can affect power output. Storage solutions like batteries or grid management strategies are essential to maintain a stable power supply. Offshore wind farms are increasingly popular due to higher wind speeds at sea and less land use conflicts. The development of wind technology continues to improve efficiency and reduce costs, making it a vital component of sustainable energy strategies worldwide. Overall, wind turbines are powerful tools for harnessing natural kinetic energy, contributing significantly to global efforts to transition to renewable and clean energy sources for a sustainable future.

text: Photosynthesis is the fundamental biological process by which green plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert light energy, typically from sunlight, into chemical energy in the form of glucose, using carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and water from the soil, while simultaneously releasing oxygen as a byproduct, making it essential for life on Earth as it provides food for most organisms and maintains atmospheric oxygen levels. The light-dependent reactions, also known as the photo reactions or Hill reactions, occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts and represent the first stage of photosynthesis where light energy is captured and converted into chemical energy in the form of ATP and NADPH. These reactions begin when chlorophyll and other photosynthetic pigments in photosystem II absorb light photons, exciting electrons to higher energy levels and initiating a series of electron transfer reactions along the electron transport chain. Water molecules are split through photolysis, releasing electrons to replace those lost by chlorophyll, protons that contribute to the proton gradient, and oxygen as a waste product. The excited electrons move through cytochrome complexes to photosystem I, where they are re-energized by additional light absorption and ultimately transferred to NADP+ to form NADPH. Simultaneously, the movement of protons across the thylakoid membrane creates an electrochemical gradient that drives ATP synthesis through chemiosmosis via ATP synthase enzymes. The light-dependent reactions thus produce the ATP and NADPH required for the subsequent light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) while generating oxygen that sustains aerobic life on Earth.

text: Operating on the fundamental tenet of transforming thermal energy into mechanical effort, a heat engine is an incredibly inventive apparatus that forms a vital component of contemporary technology.  By taking advantage of a temperature differential, it achieves this through a continuous, cyclic process: it absorbs a significant amount of thermal energy (Q_h) from a high-temperature source, like burning fuel or a nuclear reaction, converts some of this energy into mechanical output that is useful, like turning a shaft or moving a piston, and then inevitably discards the remaining waste heat (Q_c) to a colder reservoir, such as the surrounding atmosphere or a body of water.  A theoretical maximum efficiency, known as the Carnot efficiency, is set by the profound second law, which states that no engine can be completely efficient because some energy must always be expelled as waste. The first law, which guarantees energy conservation, states that the net work output equals the heat input minus the heat rejected.  By converting thermal potential into the kinetic energy that propels our world forward, everyday wonders like internal combustion engines in cars, steam turbines in power plants that produce electricity, and even jet engines are all useful examples of the heat engine concept. As such, they are essential for industry, transportation, and power generation.

text: Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), also known as anticonvulsants or antiseizure medications, represent a diverse group of pharmacological agents primarily utilized to prevent or reduce the frequency and severity of epileptic seizures, which characterize epilepsy, a neurological disorder marked by recurrent, unprovoked abnormal neuronal activity in the brain; AEDs do not cure epilepsy but rather manage its symptoms by stabilizing neuronal excitability and preventing the propagation of abnormal electrical discharges. The selection of an appropriate AED is highly individualized, depending on the specific seizure type (e.g., focal or generalized onset), the patient's age, co-existing medical conditions, potential drug interactions, and the drug's side effect profile. AEDs primarily exert their therapeutic effects through several key mechanisms, often involving the modulation of critical neurotransmitter systems or ion channels. Many AEDs act by enhancing GABAergic (inhibitory) neurotransmission, as GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter, thereby dampening neuronal excitability; examples include barbiturates (e.g., phenobarbital), benzodiazepines (e.g., clonazepam), and valproic acid, which also has multiple other mechanisms. Another major mechanism involves blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, thereby stabilizing neuronal membranes and preventing the rapid, repetitive firing of action potentials that underlie seizures; drugs in this category include phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and topiramate. Some AEDs work by blocking voltage-gated calcium channels, particularly T-type channels, which are implicated in absence seizures, with ethosuximide being a prime example for this seizure type, while gabapentin and pregabalin bind to specific calcium channel subunits. Additionally, newer AEDs like levetiracetam modulate synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), influencing neurotransmitter release, and offering a broad spectrum of activity with a generally favorable side effect profile. Other AEDs may utilize varied or multiple mechanisms, such as felbamate acting as an NMDA receptor antagonist and GABA-A receptor potentiator, though its use is restricted due to serious side effects. Ultimately, the goal of AED therapy is to achieve seizure freedom with minimal adverse effects, often necessitating careful dose titration and ongoing patient monitoring to optimize outcomes.

text: Geological disposal is a method for permanently isolating high-level and intermediate-level radioactive waste in deep underground repositories to prevent environmental or human exposure. Waste, like spent fuel or reprocessing byproducts, is sealed in corrosion-resistant canisters (e.g., copper or steel) and buried 500-1000 meters deep in stable geological formations, such as granite or clay, chosen for low permeability and seismic stability. For example, Finland’s Onkalo repository targets 2025 operation. The process ensures isolation for thousands of years, matching isotopes’ half-lives (e.g., plutonium-239, 24,110 years). Multiple barriers—canisters, backfill (bentonite), and host rock—prevent radionuclide migration. Ethical challenges include ensuring intergenerational safety and avoiding disproportionate impacts on local communities, often rural or indigenous. Technical challenges involve site characterization, predicting long-term geological stability, and engineering durable containers. Public opposition, as with Yucca Mountain, delays projects due to safety concerns. Cost, often billions, and long-term monitoring add complexity. Alternatives like reprocessing reduce waste volume but increase proliferation risks. Geological disposal supports nuclear power’s sustainability, enabling ~10% of global electricity, but requires IAEA oversight, transparent public engagement, and advanced engineering to ensure environmental safety and ethical responsibility, balancing energy benefits with long-term risk mitigation.

text: Television has played a pivotal role in mass communication since its widespread adoption in the mid-20th century, revolutionizing how information and entertainment are delivered to mass audiences. As a broadcast medium, television possesses unparalleled reach, simultaneously transmitting content to millions of households across geographical boundaries, making it a powerful tool for disseminating news, educational programming, and cultural content. Through visual and auditory stimulation, television creates immersive experiences that print media cannot match, allowing viewers to witness historical events as they unfold and fostering shared cultural experiences that shape collective memory. The medium's influence extends beyond information delivery to shaping public opinion, social norms, and consumer behavior through carefully crafted programming and advertising. Television has served as a cultural unifier, creating common reference points across diverse populations while also reflecting and sometimes reinforcing societal values and divisions. Despite the rise of digital media and streaming platforms, television continues to evolve, adapting to new technologies while maintaining its position as a cornerstone of mass communication, capable of reaching audiences of all ages and backgrounds with content ranging from local news to global events, thereby remaining a vital channel for information dissemination, cultural exchange, and entertainment in contemporary society.

text: Strategic management is the comprehensive process of defining an organization’s direction, setting long-term objectives, formulating policies and plans, implementing actions, and evaluating outcomes to achieve sustainable competitive advantage and organizational success. It involves assessing both the internal environment (such as resources, capabilities, and culture) and the external environment (including market trends, competitors, and regulatory forces) to develop a strategy that aligns with the organization's mission and vision. The strategic management process typically consists of four key stages: environmental scanning, strategy formulation, strategy implementation, and strategy evaluation and control. This process helps businesses adapt to changing market conditions, capitalize on opportunities, mitigate threats, and allocate resources effectively. Strategic management is critical in today’s volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) business world, where organizations must be proactive rather than reactive. It involves stakeholders at all levels—from top executives setting corporate strategy to departmental managers aligning operations with strategic goals. Tools such as SWOT analysis, PESTEL analysis, Porter’s Five Forces, and the BCG Matrix are commonly used in strategic decision-making. Moreover, strategic management emphasizes continuous learning and adaptation, encouraging organizations to innovate, monitor performance, and make necessary adjustments. A well-executed strategic management process enhances organizational performance, fosters long-term growth, and builds resilience. It also helps companies maintain alignment between their goals, activities, and external challenges. For example, a company facing intense competition may develop a differentiation strategy to stand out through innovation or customer service. In summary, strategic management is not a one-time event but an ongoing, dynamic process that enables organizations to navigate complexity, seize opportunities, and remain competitive in their industries over time.

text: Sexuality is policed through a combination of laws, customs, religious beliefs and institutional standards that determine what is acceptable behaviour, what is moral, and what is criminal. An age of consent law may govern such factors as the age at which a person can consent, and the type of sexual activity (maximum and minimum) for which they are legally permitted to consent. Consensual same-sex activity remains a crime in much of the world, and the rights of L.G.B.T.Q.+ people are not protected or are legally discriminated against. Religious institutions, as well as traditional cultural mores, frequently have rules around sexuality — often advocating for abstinence waiting for heterosexual marriage that is monogamous and bashing premarital sex, queer sexualities or sex education. These norms are perpetuated in media and education by either supporting traditional values, or in some cases, subverting these norms (Douglass 1999). Regulation of sexuality contributes to social control, reproduction of gender inequality, and moral constraint. The feminist and queer movements challenge unfair laws and social norms by defending our ability to make decisions about our own bodies, our sexual expression, the quality of our sexual relationships, and our ability to freely love and publicly live out that love across sexualities and identities.

text: Although mangrove forests are high in economical values than other ecosystems [20], mangrove forests suffer from accumulated marine litter pollution [21] and still perceived as the most convenient dumping sites. Some mangrove estuaries are suppressed by the impact of leachate and overflow garbage from the nearby illegal landfills [22]. In addition, oil spills [23], and chemical waste are also affecting the mangroves and other coastal marine habitats. The mangrove ecosystem is increasingly threatened by anthropogenic human activities such as land use conversion for agriculture and aquaculture, deforestation, greenhouse gas emission, waste dumping and overpopulation. This problem worsens with the increasing of industrial, plantation and mining activities carried out along estuary rivers. These activities not only affect the mangrove ecosystem but also alter soil quality by releasing harmful contaminants such as organic compounds, oils and heavy metals which eventually leach into the aquifer and thus affecting the water quality [24], [25]. Stressors such as land, water and air pollution are straining the ecosystem as these resources are the necessities for all living things. The disturbances of water, soil and air pollution defined for the mangrove ecosystem are evident. In the mangrove ecosystem, the accumulation of heavy metals in the roots poses deleterious effects on the leaf number, stem basal diameter, biomass production and is also toxic to soil microbial communities. The interactive effects of trace metals even decrease the photosynthetic rate, and create osmotic stress toxicity to the mangrove seedlings [28]. Moreover, studies covered by Sobhanardakani, et al. text: Consciousness is a complex and widely debated concept, often defined as the state or quality of being aware of an external object or something within oneself. It encompasses three main aspects: sentience, which is the capacity to feel, perceive, or experience subjectivity; wakefulness, referring to the state of being awake rather than asleep or in a coma; and awareness, which is the ability to perceive and know what is happening internally and externally. Philosophically and scientifically, it represents the "hard problem" of how physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective, first-person experience. It is the very essence of what it is like to be you, comprising all your perceptions, sensations, feelings, and thoughts at any given moment.

text: Reliability in mechatronic systems, which integrate mechanical, electronic, and software components, is ensured through a combination of design, testing, and maintenance practices. During the design phase, engineers employ robust design principles to anticipate and mitigate potential failures. This includes using high-quality components, implementing redundancy where critical, and conducting thorough risk assessments. Simulation and modeling tools are utilized to predict system behavior under various conditions, allowing for the identification and resolution of potential issues before physical prototypes are built. Testing is a critical component of ensuring reliability, involving rigorous stress testing, environmental testing, and performance testing to verify that the system operates as intended under real-world conditions. This may include accelerated life testing to simulate long-term use and identify wear-out mechanisms. Additionally, fault detection and diagnosis systems are integrated into mechatronic systems to monitor performance in real-time and predict potential failures, enabling proactive maintenance. Regular maintenance and updates are essential to sustain reliability over the system's lifespan. This includes scheduled inspections, component replacements, and software updates to address emerging issues and improve performance. Finally, feedback from users and operators is invaluable for identifying unforeseen issues and making continuous improvements to the system. By combining these practices, engineers can design and maintain mechatronic systems that are reliable, durable, and capable of performing their intended functions with minimal downtime.

text: The presentation and testing of word lists has been a fundamental source of empirical data in the study of the psychology of memory (e.g., Anderson et al., 1998, Baddeley, 1986, Baddeley et al., 2014, Crowder, 1976, Greene, 1992, Kahana, 2012, Murdock, 1974, Neath and Surprenant, 2003). Using word lists, the experimenter can exercise near complete control over the selection and ordering of the experimental stimulus set, and can exert close control over the timing and procedure used at study and test. This method has been widely used to study memory in tasks such as free recall (e.g., Murdock, 1962), serial recall (e.g., Drewnowski & Murdock, 1980), recognition memory (e.g., Ratcliff, Clark, & Shiffrin, 1990), and tests of implicit memory (e.g., Hayman & Tulving, 1989). In the free recall task, participants are presented with a list of words, one at a time, and at the end of the list, they must try to recall as many of the list items as they can, in any order that they like. Theories of free recall have sought to explain the characteristic serial position curves and the regularities in the output order in the task. The serial position curve refers to the graph relating the probability of recall with the position on the experimenter’s list. Specifically, results from laboratory studies have shown that participants tend to recall more words from early list positions (the primacy effect) and later list positions (the recency effect) than the middle of the list (sometimes known as the asymptote) such that there is a U-shaped serial position curve (e.g., Deese, 1957, Jahnke, 1965, Murdock, 1962).

text: Consideration is a fundamental element of a valid contract, referring to something of value exchanged between the parties, such as money, goods, or services. It is essential for the contract to be enforceable, as it demonstrates that both parties have incurred a legal detriment or provided a benefit, creating a mutual obligation. Without consideration, a promise is generally not binding, and the contract may be deemed void or voidable. Consideration can be either executory (a promise to do something in the future) or executed (an act already performed). For example, in a contract for the sale of goods, the consideration is the price paid by the buyer and the goods provided by the seller. In the case of Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893), the consideration was the buyer's use of the product as directed and the seller's promise to pay £100 if the buyer contracted influenza. Consideration is necessary for a valid contract because it ensures that both parties have a stake in the agreement and are legally bound to fulfill their obligations. However, there are exceptions to the requirement of consideration, such as contracts under seal, promissory estoppel, and certain charitable subscriptions, where the courts may enforce a promise even in the absence of consideration.

Washimi and Taniuti [1] were first to show that the evolution of ion acoustic solitary waves (solitons) in a plasma could be described with the Korteweg-deVries (K-dV) equation. After this pioneering work, researchers have attempted to investigate the soliton propagation using the K-dV equation in nonrelativistic [2]–?[5] as well as in relativistic plasmas [6]–?[10]. Taking relativistic speed of ions and zero electron inertia, it was shown that the phase velocity and amplitude of ion acoustic soliton are greatly influenced by the ion temperature and relativistic effect [6].

text: In this contribution, we will take in consideration the case of a reaction wheel system with the aim to reduce the risk for human population during uncontrolled re-entry. We will perform a detailed analysis aiming to the substitution of critical materials with more demisable ones. The majority of current risk analysis tools and D4D techniques are mainly oriented on the evaluation of demisability for different components of a spacecraft and the associated casualty risk. Although extremely effective under a demisability point-of-view, this approach does not usually consider performance as a parameter for the analysis (see Fig. 1). For this reason, the substitution of critical materials with others easier to ablate may reduce the overall performance of the component, potentially compromising the main function of the whole system. In this contribution, instead, the selection process is based on demisability and performance as concurrent objectives to optimize.

text: The role of women in the labor market has changed dramatically throughout history, as societal conventions and gender equality have shifted. In traditional (and largely pre-industrial) societies, domestic work is often not counted as part of the economy but nonetheless it can account for significant value. But in the 19th century, with the industrial revolution, more women started working outside the home — particularly in factories and textile mills where they often labored for long hours and less pay than their male counterparts. Women became more visible in the work force in the early part of the 20th century, particularly during periods of war — both World War I and II — when thousands of men went off to war and women took over what had been their jobs, whether at offices or hospitals or factories.These contributions played a pivotal role in challenging the traditional gender norms that confined women to the domestic sphere. That this would represent, both symbolically and materially, a huge game-changer as well also looked to be the case when women’s liberation groups began to spring up in the mid-20th century — they were mobilized around demands for equal pay in work places and professions that had excluded them (euconmomically as well) from many occupations. And more women began enrolling in college and pursuing graduate degrees (especially law, medicine and business), which had traditionally been the domain of men. Women’s increased entry into the labor market also occurred at a time when family composition was changing with growing numbers of women working while raising children. While in recent years women have been able to obtain significant leadership and managerial positions, there are still wage and ratio imbalances between genders. The rise of the digital age has further transformed women’s roles in the workforce, offering more flexible work arrangements and opportunities for women in tech, entrepreneurship, and remote work. Today, while challenges remain—such as gender-based discrimination and the gender pay gap—women continue to push for greater equality, striving to break down remaining barriers and expand their influence in all sectors of the economy. Women’s roles in the workforce have undeniably changed from their traditional positions, reflecting broader movements toward gender equality and socio-economic progress.

text: Correctional institutions play a vital role within the criminal justice system by incarcerating individuals convicted of crimes, providing opportunities for punishment, rehabilitation, and societal protection. These institutions include prisons, jails, detention centers, and correctional facilities designed to hold offenders for varying periods based on the severity of their crimes and legal sentences. Their primary functions are to punish offenders, deter future criminal behavior, incapacitate dangerous individuals, and serve as a means of social control. Correctional institutions also aim to rehabilitate offenders through various programs that address substance abuse, mental health issues, education, and vocational training, with the ultimate goal of reducing recidivism. They operate under legal and procedural standards that ensure prisoners' rights are protected, including access to healthcare, legal counsel, and humane treatment. Security is a central concern; facilities are designed with multiple layers of control, surveillance, and personnel to prevent escapes, violence, and contraband entry. Correctional institutions also serve a societal function by demonstrating that criminal behavior has consequences, reinforcing social norms and laws. Many correctional systems are increasingly focused on rehabilitation and reintegration, recognizing that long-term societal safety depends on helping offenders become productive citizens post-release. This involves preparing inmates for life outside the prison through skill development and behavioral programs. Correctional institutions often work in tandem with parole and probation systems to monitor offenders after release, providing ongoing supervision and support. Challenges faced by correctional institutions include overcrowding, violence, mental health issues among inmates, and the high costs associated with incarceration. There is also ongoing debate about the effectiveness of incarceration in reducing crime and whether alternative sanctions might be more appropriate for certain offenders. The correctional system's effectiveness depends on proper management, adequate resources, and policies that balance punishment with opportunities for reform. The overarching aim is to protect society from criminal activity while offering offenders pathways for change and reintegration. As society evolves, correctional institutions are increasingly emphasizing humane treatment, evidence-based rehabilitation programs, and community-based alternatives to incarceration when appropriate, striving to improve outcomes for individuals and the community as a whole.

text: Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology aimed at improving the quality of processes by identifying and removing defects and minimizing variability in manufacturing and business processes. Developed by Motorola in the 1980s, Six Sigma seeks to achieve near-perfection in operations by setting a goal of no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities. The methodology is based on a structured approach known as DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control), which guides practitioners through a systematic process of problem-solving and continuous improvement. Six Sigma utilizes statistical tools and techniques to analyze process data, identify root causes of defects, and implement solutions that enhance efficiency and reduce variation. It involves a hierarchy of belts—Yellow, Green, Black, and Master Black Belts—each representing different levels of training and expertise in Six Sigma methodologies. By applying Six Sigma, organizations can achieve significant improvements in product quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, leading to cost savings and increased profitability. The approach fosters a culture of data-driven decision-making, collaboration, and ongoing improvement across all levels of the organization.

text: An overwhelming amount of observational data provides clear and compelling evidence for the presence of dark matter (DM) on a wide range of scales. This component, believed to be responsible for the "missing" mass in our universe, is the main ingredient for all the structures we have in our universe. This is one of the oldest unsolved problems in cosmology, dating back to the 1930s (Zwicky, 1933; Bertone and Hooper, 2018) and is also one of the best-measured ones. The evidence for dark matter was initially observed from the study of the rotation curves of galaxies. Nowadays, the evidence for dark matter comes from precise measurements on a wide range of scales. From sub-galactic and galactic scales to clusters, going up to the large-scale structure (LSS). On cosmological scales, the observed anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) (Ade et al., 2016), together with data from Type Ia Supernovae, determine the total energy density of matter with high precision. This, together with the bounds on the abundance of the light chemical elements from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, which constrains the amount of baryonic matter in the universe, strongly shows the need for a clustering component of non-baryonic origin that does not interact (strongly) with photons, and that dominates the matter content of the universe, accounting for approximately 85% of all matter. The same non-luminous and clustering component is necessary to explain the structures we see in our universe today, as is evident in observations of the large-scale structure of our universe (Anderson et al., 2014; Tegmark et al., 2004).

text: Digital theatre is a form of theatre that integrates technology with live performance or creates performance specifically for digital platforms, blending traditional theatrical elements with modern digital tools to reach wider or virtual audiences. This can include live-streamed performances, interactive online experiences, or multimedia productions that use video, animation, virtual reality, and other digital effects to enhance storytelling. Digital theatre allows for new possibilities in how stories are told, offering innovative ways to engage audiences through digital mediums such as social media, websites, and streaming services. It can also involve creating performances that exist entirely online, where actors and audiences interact through virtual spaces, breaking the geographical and physical barriers traditionally associated with theatre. During the COVID-19 pandemic, digital theatre gained significant popularity as many live performances moved online, and companies adapted by producing content that could be accessed remotely, keeping the art form alive during periods of social distancing. A prime example of digital theatre is the National Theatre's NT Live initiative, which streams live recordings of performances to cinemas worldwide, enabling audiences to experience the production remotely. Additionally, digital theatre can experiment with immersive technologies, allowing audiences to engage with the performance in novel ways, such as through virtual or augmented reality, where the audience becomes part of the action or interacts with the environment in real-time. Somewhere on the plus side of digital theatre is its disregard for the certainties of stage and its potential for more experimental and global collaboration. Digital theatre has a lot in common with old-fashioned theatre, but it embraces the versatility of modern technology – which makes it an exciting and developing art form. From virtual performances, to immersive storytelling, to mixed media live theatre production, digital theatre offers new artistic horizons and opportunities for audience participation as well as the cultural sharing of theatrical heritage worldwide. In essence, it is a way of bringing the theatre to an entirely new audience and giving platforms for exciting ways of experiencing performance – from anywhere in the world during these unpredictable times for audiences– making them part of that digital age we live in.

text: The Age of Exploration, which unfolded between the 15th and 17th centuries, was driven by a complex interplay of economic, technological, political, and religious motivations. European powers, particularly Spain and Portugal, sought new trade routes to access the lucrative markets of Asia, circumventing the Ottoman-controlled land routes. The desire for spices, gold, and other valuable commodities fueled maritime ambitions, while technological advancements in navigation—such as the compass, astrolabe, and improved cartography—enabled longer, more precise voyages. Monarchs supported expeditions to expand their empires, gain prestige, and access new sources of wealth, often granting explorers royal sponsorship. Religious motives also played a crucial role, with Christian missionaries accompanying explorers to spread Christianity to non-European lands. The Portuguese pioneered oceanic exploration under Prince Henry the Navigator, leading to the rounding of Africa and discovery of a sea route to India by Vasco da Gama. Spain followed with Christopher Columbus's voyage in 1492, initiating European contact with the Americas. The consequences of the Age of Exploration were profound and far-reaching: it marked the beginning of global interconnectedness and colonial expansion. Indigenous populations in the Americas and elsewhere faced devastating consequences, including the spread of diseases like smallpox, violent conquest, and exploitation. The transatlantic slave trade emerged, forcibly relocating millions of Africans to the New World. European powers established vast overseas empires, altering global political and economic dynamics and initiating centuries of imperial competition. New products, ideas, and cultures flowed across continents, reshaping diets, economies, and societies worldwide. Scientific and geographic knowledge expanded, challenging old worldviews and laying groundwork for the Enlightenment. Trade networks became increasingly global, fostering the rise of mercantilism and capitalism. Despite its contributions to exploration and knowledge, the Age of Exploration also ushered in extensive suffering through colonization, forced labor, and cultural erasure. It redefined international relations and territorial boundaries, leading to enduring legacies of inequality and cultural transformation. Ultimately, this era transformed the world by linking previously isolated continents into a web of exchange, conquest, and cultural interaction, marking the onset of modern globalization and shifting the balance of power toward European dominance.

text: The media plays a significant role in shaping public perception of crime, often influencing how people understand the prevalence, nature, and severity of criminal activities. Through news reports, television shows, movies, and social media, the media frames crime stories in ways that can heighten fear and anxiety, sometimes disproportionately to actual crime rates. Sensationalized coverage tends to focus on violent and dramatic crimes, such as homicides, sexual assaults, and serial offenses, which captures public attention but may create a distorted view that crime is more widespread or dangerous than statistics indicate. This phenomenon, known as the “mean world syndrome,” leads individuals to perceive their communities as less safe, affecting their behavior and attitudes toward law enforcement and social policies. Moreover, media often emphasizes certain types of offenders or victims based on race, gender, or socioeconomic status, reinforcing stereotypes and biases that can influence public opinion and criminal justice responses. For example, minority groups are frequently overrepresented as criminals in media portrayals, which can contribute to racial profiling and discrimination. The media also plays a role in setting the public agenda by highlighting particular crimes or issues, prompting political and legislative action that may not always align with actual crime trends. However, media can also have positive effects by raising awareness about crime prevention, victim support, and social justice issues. The rise of social media has further amplified the speed and reach of crime-related information, sometimes leading to misinformation or moral panics. In summary, the media profoundly affects public perception of crime by shaping narratives, influencing fear levels, reinforcing stereotypes, and impacting policy debates, underscoring the need for responsible and balanced reporting to foster informed and rational public discourse.

text: Sexual reproduction in plants is a biological process involving the fusion of male and female gametes (sperm and egg cells) to form a zygote, which then develops into a new individual. This mode of reproduction is fundamental to the life cycle of most plants, especially flowering plants (angiosperms) and conifers (gymnosperms), and is crucial for generating genetic variation within a species, thereby enhancing adaptability and evolutionary fitness. The process typically begins with the formation of specialized reproductive structures that produce the gametes. In flowering plants, these structures are the flowers, which contain male reproductive organs (stamens) and/or female reproductive organs (carpels/pistil). Stamens produce pollen grains, which contain the male gametes (sperm nuclei), while the ovules within the ovary of the carpel contain the female gamete (egg cell). The first key step is pollination, the transfer of pollen from the anther (part of the stamen) to the stigma (receptive tip of the carpel). Pollination can occur through various agents like wind, water, or animals (e.g., insects, birds), or even through self-pollination within the same flower or plant. Upon successful landing on a compatible stigma, the pollen grain germinates and grows a pollen tube down through the style towards the ovule within the ovary. The pollen tube serves as a conduit for the male gametes. The second critical step is fertilization, where the male gametes (typically two sperm nuclei in flowering plants) are delivered to the ovule. In angiosperms, this involves a unique process called double fertilization, where one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote, which will develop into the embryo, and the other sperm nucleus fuses with the central cell (containing two polar nuclei) to form a triploid endosperm, a nutritive tissue that provides food for the developing embryo. Following fertilization, the ovule develops into a seed, which contains the embryo and its food reserve, and the ovary matures into a fruit, which protects the developing seeds and often aids in their dispersal. The seed, upon finding suitable conditions, will germinate and grow into a new plant. The immense significance of sexual reproduction in plants lies in the genetic recombination that occurs during meiosis (gamete formation) and the fusion of genetically distinct gametes. This recombination shuffles alleles, creating new combinations of traits in the offspring, which increases genetic diversity within the population. This diversity is vital for a species' ability to adapt to changing environments, resist diseases, and evolve, ensuring long-term survival and providing the raw material for natural selection and plant breeding programs.

text: Animals have evolved a diverse array of sensory systems that allow them to perceive and respond to their environment, ensuring their survival and reproductive success. These sensory systems detect various types of stimuli, such as light, sound, chemicals, temperature, and mechanical pressure, and convert them into electrical signals that can be processed by the nervous system. Vision is a common sensory modality, with animals using specialized photoreceptor cells in their eyes to detect light and form images. Auditory systems, found in many animals, detect sound waves and convert them into neural signals, allowing animals to hear and communicate. Chemical senses, such as olfaction (smell) and gustation (taste), enable animals to detect and identify chemicals in their environment, which can provide information about food, predators, or potential mates. Mechanoreception, the ability to detect mechanical stimuli, is crucial for sensing touch, pressure, and vibrations, and is mediated by specialized sensory cells or organs. Thermoreception allows animals to detect temperature changes, which can be important for regulating body temperature and finding suitable habitats. Additionally, some animals possess unique sensory adaptations, such as electroreception in certain fish and amphibians, which allows them to detect electric fields, or magnetoreception in birds and other animals, which enables them to sense the Earth's magnetic field for navigation. These diverse sensory systems work together to provide animals with a comprehensive understanding of their environment, allowing them to navigate, find food, avoid predators, and interact with conspecifics. The complexity and sensitivity of these sensory systems reflect the evolutionary pressures that have shaped animal behavior and ecology, highlighting the remarkable adaptability of animals to their environments.

text: The multiplication law of probability is one of the elementary rules used to calculate the probability of the simultaneous occurrence of two or more events. The rule is based on whether the events are independent or dependent. When the events are independent— the happening of one event does not change the probability of the other—the rule is simple: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For instance, if you toss a fair coin and roll a fair die, the probability of a head and a 6 is P(Head) × P(6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. Since the die is not affected by the outcome of the coin, we multiply their separate probabilities. But for dependent events, where the occurrence of the first event affects the occurrence of the second event, we modify the formula by incorporating the conditional probability: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A), where P(B|A) is the probability B occurs when it is known that A has already occurred. For instance in a 52 card deck, the probability of getting two aces in a row with output is P(Ace on 1st draw) × P(Ace on 2nd draw | Ace on 1st) = 4/52 × 3/51 = 1/221. Since the number of cards and the number of aces have changed, the probability of of a second draw from the same deck has also changed. The multiplication rule is important in studying combinations of events as in statistics, genetics, quality control, decision trees etc. It is also employed in the computing joint probabilities in statistical modelling and risk analysis. Incorrect interpretation of the rule, such as mistaking independence for dependence, can cause large quantitative errors in inferences. In other words, correctly recognizing the relationship between events is an important consideration of the multiplication rule in all instances.

text: Price leadership is a pricing strategy commonly observed in oligopolistic markets, where a single dominant firm, known as the price leader, sets the price of a product or service, and the other firms in the industry follow that pricing decision rather than competing aggressively on price. This practice arises because firms in oligopoly are highly interdependent, and frequent price changes can lead to instability or destructive price wars. The price leader is usually the largest, most efficient, or most influential firm in the market, capable of setting a price that maximizes its own profits while being acceptable to smaller competitors. There are several forms of price leadership. In dominant firm leadership, the largest firm with cost advantages sets the price, and smaller firms act as price takers. In barometric price leadership, a firm recognized for its accurate judgment of market conditions adjusts prices, and others follow because they trust its foresight. In collusive price leadership, firms, either formally or informally, agree to let one firm announce prices on behalf of the group, which helps maintain stability without explicit cartel arrangements. The main features of price leadership include the existence of a few large firms, high barriers to entry, homogeneous or slightly differentiated products, and the need to avoid uncertainty in pricing decisions. The advantages of price leadership are that it reduces the risk of price wars, ensures relative stability in the market, and allows firms to focus on non-price competition such as advertising, branding, and product quality. However, it can also lead to higher prices for consumers, reduced competition, and potential exploitation if the leader sets prices significantly above costs. Despite these drawbacks, price leadership is widely observed in industries like steel, cement, oil, airlines, and automobiles, where a few large firms dominate and prefer stability over aggressive rivalry. In essence, price leadership reflects the balance between competition and cooperation in oligopolistic markets, where firms recognize their mutual dependence and follow the leader’s pricing strategy to maintain profitability and market order.

text: Mean, median, and mode are three commonly used measures of central tendency in statistics, each providing a different way to represent the center or typical value of a dataset. Mean is the arithmetic average of all values in a dataset, calculated by summing all the values and then dividing by the total number of values. It is sensitive to extreme values (outliers), which can skew the result. Median, on the other hand, is the middle value when the data points are arranged in ascending or descending order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values. The median is less affected by outliers compared to the mean, making it a better measure for skewed distributions. Mode refers to the value or values that appear most frequently in a dataset. A dataset can have no mode, one mode (unimodal), or multiple modes (bimodal or multimodal) if multiple values share the highest frequency. While the mean is most useful for symmetric distributions, the median is often preferred for skewed data, and the mode is useful for identifying the most common value or trend in categorical data. Together, these measures offer different perspectives on the distribution of data.

text: Vahanian’s theological saeculum gives rise to a radical secular theology that begins in an iconoclasm of the self, includes an iconoclasm of the culture in which one finds oneself, and continually seeks a way to restate the biblical tradition into a post-Christian world. As Vahanian (1966) emphasizes, this means “any speech about God is also an iconoclastic speech about man, about his secularism as well as his religiosity. Indeed, human speech calls for just that iconoclastic understanding of the human experience” (34). For in speaking about God we expose our self-idolatry as humans, a self-idolatry in turn shattered by the iconoclasm of speech concerning God who is radical other. What we are left with is an iconoclastic faith that “has no other proper sphere of action other than secularity” (Vahanian, 1966: 47). This secularity is the world we exist within, and what is this world? “The world is what takes place in and through the word” (Vahanian, 1966: 56) which occurs via the word expressing the verbal nature of the reality of the world. It is the word that enables the world to be, that enables us to be humans in the world. And so what is God? “God is a word, the word that our words do not speak of unless they are shocked both out of their literal and out of their symbolic meaning” (Vahanian, 1966: 61).

text: Maxwell's equations are a set of four fundamental partial differential equations that form the cornerstone of classical electromagnetism. Developed by James Clerk Maxwell in the 19th century, these equations elegantly describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated and how they interact with each other and with electric charges and currents. Their significance is immense as they unified what were previously disparate phenomena—electricity, magnetism, and light—into a single, coherent theory. The four equations are: Gauss's Law for Electricity: Relates the electric field to the distribution of electric charges, stating that electric field lines originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges, and the electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the total electric charge enclosed within that surface. Gauss's Law for Magnetism: States that magnetic monopoles do not exist; magnetic field lines are continuous loops, always forming closed paths, meaning the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero. Faraday's Law of Induction: Describes how a changing magnetic field creates (induces) an electric field, which is the principle behind electromagnetic induction, leading to generators and transformers.Ampère's Law with Maxwell's Addition: States that magnetic fields are generated by electric currents and by changing electric fields (Maxwell's displacement current term). This crucial addition by Maxwell predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves. The most profound implication of Maxwell's equations was the prediction that oscillating electric and magnetic fields could propagate through empty space as self-sustaining electromagnetic waves, and that these waves would travel at a constant speed, which Maxwell calculated to be the speed of light (c). This unified light, radio waves, X-rays, and other forms of radiation as different manifestations of the same electromagnetic wave phenomenon. This prediction was later confirmed experimentally by Heinrich Hertz. Maxwell's equations not only consolidated earlier laws (Coulomb's Law, Ampere's Law, Faraday's Law) but also opened up entirely new fields of physics and engineering, leading to the development of radio communication, television, radar, and countless other technologies. They are considered one of the most elegant and powerful sets of equations in physics, laying the foundation for modern electrical engineering, optics, and ultimately, inspiring Einstein's theory of special relativity by showing that the speed of light is a universal constant.

text: A z-test is a statistical test used to determine whether there is a significant difference between the sample mean and the population mean, or between two sample means, when the population standard deviation is known. It is commonly used when the sample size is large (typically n > 30), as the Central Limit Theorem ensures that the sampling distribution of the sample mean will approach a normal distribution. The test is based on the z-score, which measures how many standard deviations the sample mean is away from the population mean. The formula for the z-score is Z=(X??)?/nZ = \frac{(X - \mu)}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}Z=?/n(X??), where XXX is the sample mean, ?\mu? is the population mean, ?\sigma? is the population standard deviation, and nnn is the sample size. A larger z-score indicates a greater difference between the sample mean and the population mean. Once the z-score is calculated, it is compared to a critical value from the standard normal distribution, which is typically set at 1.96 for a 95% confidence level. If the z-score exceeds the critical value, the null hypothesis is rejected, indicating that the sample mean is significantly different from the population mean. Z-tests are commonly used in hypothesis testing for large datasets, such as testing the effectiveness of a new treatment or comparing the performance of two groups. However, the z-test assumes that the data are normally distributed and that the population standard deviation is known, which can limit its applicability in certain situations. In cases where the population standard deviation is unknown, a t-test is typically used instead. Despite these limitations, the z-test remains a powerful tool for statistical inference when its assumptions are met.

text: The role of human rights in criminal justice is absolutely fundamental, serving as a critical framework that guides, constrains, and legitimizes the entire system, from policing and investigation through to trial, sentencing, and incarceration. Human rights principles, enshrined in international instruments like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, ensure that individuals within the criminal justice process are treated with dignity, fairness, and respect, even when accused of serious crimes. At the investigative stage, human rights demand protections against arbitrary arrest and detention, ensuring individuals are informed of charges, have access to legal counsel, and are free from torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. During trial, core human rights principles guarantee the right to a fair trial, including the presumption of innocence, the right to a public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal, the right to confront witnesses, and the right not to be compelled to testify against oneself. These rights aim to prevent wrongful convictions and ensure due process. Furthermore, human rights set limits on sentencing and punishment, prohibiting disproportionate penalties, cruel and unusual punishment, and ensuring that any deprivation of liberty is justifiable and respects the inherent dignity of the person. This extends to conditions of detention, where human rights dictate standards for humane treatment, access to healthcare, and protection from violence, aiming for rehabilitation rather than mere retribution. The integration of human rights principles into criminal justice systems seeks to balance the state's legitimate interest in maintaining public order and prosecuting offenders with the imperative to protect individual liberties and prevent abuses of power. By establishing universal standards for justice, human rights promote accountability for state actors, provide avenues for redress for victims of state abuses, and foster public trust in the legal system. They act as a vital check on state authority, ensuring that the pursuit of justice does not compromise the fundamental rights and freedoms that define a just and civilized society, thereby upholding the rule of law and promoting a more humane and equitable approach to crime and punishment.

text: Strain theory, developed by sociologist Robert K. Merton in 1938 and later expanded by others like Albert Cohen and Robert Agnew, explains crime as a result of societal pressures and the inability to achieve culturally emphasized goals through legitimate means. Merton argued that when individuals face a disconnect between societal expectations (e.g., wealth, success) and the limited opportunities to attain them (due to poverty, discrimination, or lack of education), they experience strain or frustration, which may lead to deviant behavior. Merton identified five adaptations to this strain: conformity (accepting goals and means), innovation (using illegal means to achieve goals, like theft), ritualism (abandoning goals but following rules), retreatism (rejecting both goals and means, e.g., substance abuse), and rebellion (seeking to replace societal goals with new ones). Agnew expanded the theory beyond economic goals, highlighting that strain can also arise from negative relationships (e.g., abuse, bullying) or the loss of positive stimuli (e.g., job loss), which provoke emotions like anger or despair, further pushing individuals toward crime. Strain theory helps explain why crime rates are higher in disadvantaged communities, where the gap between aspirations and opportunities is widest. Critics argue it overlooks individual agency and cultural variations in goal-setting, but its insights have influenced policies aimed at reducing inequality, such as job programs, educational access, and community support initiatives. By framing crime as a social rather than purely individual failure, strain theory underscores the need for structural solutions to alleviate pressure and provide lawful pathways to success, reinforcing the idea that crime prevention requires addressing root causes of societal discontent.

text: Devised theatre is a collaborative, innovative form of performance where the script, staging, and overall production are created collectively by a group of performers, directors, and sometimes designers, rather than relying on a pre-existing play or a single playwright’s vision. Unlike traditional theatre, which typically begins with a fixed text, devised theatre starts with a concept, theme, or source material—such as personal stories, social issues, or historical events—and evolves through improvisation, experimentation, and group discussion. This process-driven approach emphasizes the ensemble’s creativity, allowing diverse voices, perspectives, and skills to shape the final work, often resulting in performances that are highly original and responsive to contemporary concerns. Companies like Complicité or The Wooster Group exemplify this, crafting works that blend movement, multimedia, and fragmented narratives to explore themes like migration or identity. Devised theatre often incorporates non-traditional elements, such as physical theatre, found objects, or site-specific settings, to challenge conventional storytelling, as seen in productions like Tectonic Theater Project’s The Laramie Project, which used community interviews to address homophobia. It is particularly effective in community and activist settings, empowering participants—often non-professionals—to share personal or cultural narratives, as in youth theatre projects tackling issues like racial justice. The process fosters inclusivity, allowing marginalized voices to shape the narrative, and can adapt to local contexts, using regional languages or cultural motifs. However, devised theatre requires strong collaboration and trust, as the lack of a fixed script demands flexibility and consensus among participants. Its performances are often fluid, evolving with each iteration, and may prioritize emotional impact or thematic resonance over polished aesthetics. By breaking from hierarchical production models, devised theatre democratizes the creative process, making it a powerful tool for cultural expression, social commentary, and community-building. Its adaptability ensures relevance across contexts, from experimental urban stages to rural community centers, celebrating collective creativity while challenging audiences to engage with fresh, provocative perspectives on the human experience.

text: Trajectory planning in robotics corresponds to finding a time-parametrized path that should follow the end effector or the joints of a robot to go from a given starting position to a goal with desired properties. It guarantees that the robot kinematically moves in a smooth, efficient and safe manner, considering physical limits, such as joint limits, velocity, acceleration, jerk (rate of change of acceleration), and obstacle avoidance. A trajectory is more than a geometric path; it includes how the robot moves along the path through time. In joint-space trajectory planning, the trajectory is provided as a function of time of each joint angle, which is suitable for tasks such as pick and place. Cartesian-space motions are defined by position and orientation in 3D space, allowing an easy to understand processes of moving of the end-effector in complex environment. Such techniques as polynomial interpolation (e.g., cubic or quintic splines), trapezoidal velocity profiles, and B-splines are employed to create smooth trajectories. Advanced widgets could use optimization-based or artificial intelligence (such as genetic algorithms or neural networks) for manipulation of dynamic obstacles or live changes. Motion planning is important for many robotic applications such as industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and even humanoid robots to make sure their movements are accurate as well as within the capabilities of the system. text: Interfaces and abstract classes are tools for obtaining abstraction in oop, but they serve different purposes and they have different usages and capabilities. An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated, and may contain both abstract methods (i.e., method declarations without implementation) and concrete methods (i.e., methods that have full implementation). Here are examples of how to do this: Base Class as a base and be derived from by other classes which the base class will share code and partially implement. An Abstract class may also contain variable members, constructors and access specifier ofstring class as private or protected e.t.c. An interface on the other hand is a pure abstraction, a contract that a class must fulfill. It usually is composed of abstract methods (in some modern languages, default methods also) and constants. The class that implements an interface is forced to implement all of its methods. Interfaces support multiple inheritance, a class can implement more than one interface, this is important in languages like Java that doesn’t allow multiple class inheritance. Another important consideration when deciding whether to use an abstract class or an interface is whether or not you need to share implementation between classes, if so use an abstract class, if not use an interface. For instance, in an abstract class Vehicle, you would provide a method startEngine(), and an implementation of fuelCapacity(); an interface Drivable would only declare drive() and would not specify how it is done. A class Car could use Vehicle as a base and implement Drivable, mixing common behavior with a common contract. So in the end, the abstract class is about partial code reuse and inheritance, and the interface is a way of defining capabilities while allowing the implementation to accomplished in any way you see fit. The decision is based on design considerations, code sharing and requirement of multiple inheritance.

text: In contract law, an offer is a definite promise to be bound by specific terms, communicated to another party (the offeree), demonstrating an intention to create a legally binding agreement. It must be clear, complete, and leave no room for negotiation. For example, “I offer to sell you my car for $5,000” is a valid offer. However, an advertisement is generally considered an invitation to treat, not an offer. Acceptance is the unqualified and unequivocal agreement to all terms of the offer, communicated by the offeree to the offeror. It must mirror the offer exactly – any alteration constitutes a counter-offer, which rejects the original offer. For instance, if someone responds to the car offer with “I accept, but will pay $4,500,” this is a counter-offer, not acceptance. A legal example illustrating offer and acceptance is Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893), where the company advertised a reward for anyone who contracted influenza after using their smoke ball. Mrs. Carlill’s use and subsequent illness constituted acceptance of the unilateral offer, establishing a binding contract. Without a valid offer and unqualified acceptance, a legally enforceable contract doesn’t exist; these are the foundational elements for contractual agreement.

text: Media accountability refers to the mechanisms, processes, and norms through which media organizations and individual journalists are held responsible for their actions, ethical conduct, and the quality and impact of their content on society. It is the expectation that media, given its powerful role in shaping public discourse and informing citizens, should operate responsibly and transparently, answering to the public interest. Media accountability is crucial for maintaining public trust, promoting journalistic credibility, and ensuring that the media fulfills its democratic functions effectively. These mechanisms can be broadly categorized into internal and external forms. Internal accountability refers to self-regulatory measures adopted by media organizations themselves, such as robust editorial policies, codes of conduct, internal ombudsmen or public editors who handle complaints, fact-checking departments, and internal review processes to ensure accuracy and fairness. These mechanisms reflect a commitment to professional standards within the media institution. External accountability encompasses mechanisms originating outside the direct control of media organizations. This includes legal frameworks, such as defamation laws, privacy laws, and freedom of information acts, which provide legal recourse for those harmed by media actions. It also involves self-regulatory bodies like Press Councils or Media Councils, which receive public complaints and issue non-binding but morally significant adjudications. text: Singularities in Robot Kinematics Singularities in robot kinematics are particular configurations in which a robot’s Jacobian matrix becomes singular and thus the robot loses a degree of freedom or control manipulability. Some directions are no longer reachable at a singularity, and the robot might have to undergo unpredictable or endless joint velocities to achieve motion in the Cartesian space. For the control, the force generation and for planning of the trajectories these arrangements are disadvantageous. For example, on a standard 6-DOF robot, at a singularity, some of the axes of rotation of the wrist joint align so that two or more become parallel, a condition referred to as a "wrist singularity." Other known configurations are shoulder singularities where a robot can no longer move because the arm is completely extended. On singular points, the Jacobian determinant vanishes, thus loosing invertibility and resulting in a system for inverse kinematics or velocity solutions which is ill-conditioned. This can lead to instability or in extreme cases even physical damage when the controller tries to perform impossible motions. For singularity avoidance, path planners and control laws generally use detection and avoidance algorithms (e.g., damped least squares or null-space optimization). Awareness and avoidance of singularities is important for the successful operation of a robot to be smooth and safe, particularly in high precision or constrained environments such as surgical or space robotics. In general, the control of singularities is very challenging in robot design and real-time control algorithm execution.
