text: There are several merits of PID controllers that lead them to be the most dominant type in the industry and engineering applications. What you very much get is precise, steady, and responsive control as three classes of operations (which address various behavior of the system) get mixed up—proportional, derivative, and integral. The proportional part is used to provide correction and helps in reducing the present error, the integral part is used to eliminate residual steady state error generally caused at the quintessence of the final control element, due to accumulated errors, and the derivative component helps in improving system stability and response by forecasting future trends in error. This middle-of-the-road combination enables PID controllers to reach the desired setpoint very quickly, while keeping overshoot and steady state error in check. A further advantage is that they are simple and can be easily implemented in either analog or digital. Although PID controllers are very powerful and do not need to know any specific mathematical model for the system, they are widely used in many applications, including the regulation of temperature, the control of motors, robotics and process automation. PID controllers are also versatile, as their Kp, Ki, and Kd tuning parameters can be set to resist to different kind of systems (underdamped, overdamped etc.), or even those having non-linear characteristics. Moreover, contemporary PID algorithms can incorporate integral anti-windup, setpoint weighting and filtering for improved robustness and responsiveness. Given their capabilities in dealing with dynamics, disturbances and changes in the technology, if the control system goes up or down Manual select the desired output from your system. The widespread use and acceptance of PID means that PID controllers form part of the control system in almost all control engineering course and control engineers design or tune them sooner or later. In general, PID controllers are practical and relatively simple, but offer moderate control performance.

text: There is considerable evidence at this time that internal secular evolution is an important physical process in disk galaxies. Kormendy & Kennicutt (2004) have argued that such evolution accounts for the disklike "pseudobulges" seen in late-type galaxies, and evidence of bulges built through secular evolution has been found to be present across the entire Hubble–de Vaucouleurs sequence (Laurikainen et al. 2007). text: A file system is the way an operating system organizes, names, stores, and retrieves files on a storage device, including a hard disk or SSD; it also provides a way to keep track of the physical location of stored information on the device. Manage metadata about files, including names, permissions, time stamps and disk file locations. File systems have to perform a few other duties, such as those to allocate space, manage directories, and maintain data integrity. Various aspects of file allocation schemes are how files are laid out on disk to optimize space utilisation and access speed. The contiguous allocation keeps all information in one place in a single (continuous) block of disk space, but is so inflexible that external fragmentation can occur. Linked allocation organizes files in linked lists of disk blocks dispersed here and there on the disk, supporting flexible file sizes and not contributing to external fragmentation, but access time is slower due to the sequential search of links in order to obtain the disk blocks. An indexed allocation is when an index block has every block of the file as its children, allowing for direct access to any part of the file, and reduced file traversal time, as opposed to (linked) list and (contiguous) bitmap allocation schemes, however, it requires overhead for the indexing, and may in turn be restricted in its size by the disk block. Some filesystems use a combination of these approaches, and variations thereof, in order to optimize performance and minimize fragmentation. The approach for allocation influences performance, storage usage and the amount of file access overhead. Contemporary file systems also utilize journaling, cacheing, and metadata optimization for better reliability and performance. Similarly, file systems and their allocation policies are also key for organizing data throughout storage devices, which affect to what extent that data can be accessed easily, reliably and securely by both users and applications.

text: The field of bioinformatics has been enabled by massively-parallel DNA sequencing technologies that make it feasible to collect terabases (Tbp) of DNA sequence in just days (Illumina, Inc., 2019). Coupled with ever-increasing computing performance and storage capacity, this data has grown at rates which have outpaced Moore’s Law (Gauthier et al., 2019; Schatz et al., 2010). When viewed in the context of development and commercialization of a GM product, bioinformatics is used to 1) facilitate the discovery phase by identifying exogenous sequences that confer a desirable plant phenotype, such as herbicide tolerance, insect resistance, or an improved nutrient profile, and 2) assess potential hazard as a component of a multifaceted product safety assessment in the regulatory/product commercialization phase. These two applications for bioinformatics have remained constant since the first commercialization of a GM product in the mid 1990?s, when the challenge faced by bioinformaticians was the relative scarcity and inaccessibility of primary sequence data. The vast expansion of database size brought on by modern sequencing technologies have shifted the challenges faced by bioinformaticians. The issue at hand is now lies in the filtration and interpretation of mass quantities of rapidly generated data, attributing meaning or function to these influxes of data, the appropriate incorporation and integration of that data into existing repositories, an finally and how predefined models/regulations from an era of data scarcity are interpolated in an era of excess (Endel and Piringer, 2015; Marx, 2013). The development of a GM product can be divided into a number of phases that typically span 11–13 years (Prado et al., 2014). The Discovery phase involves the identification of gene(s)/protein(s) that yield a commercially-viable trait(s). The first and second phases involve the testing of those gene(s)/proteins(s) under diverse real-world field conditions to confirm trait efficacy and stability (Prado et al., 2014). The third regulatory phase prior to commercialization involves assessment of potential hazards and risks, that underpin the conclusion of safety for the introduced gene(s)/proteins(s) (Prado et al., 2014). In each of these phases bioinformatics play an important role.

text: Constructivism in International Relations (IR) is a theory emphasizing the role of ideas, norms, and identities in shaping global politics. Unlike realism or liberalism, which focus on material power or institutions, constructivism, articulated by scholars like Alexander Wendt, argues that social constructs—beliefs, values, and identities—define state behavior and international outcomes. States act based on shared understandings, not just power or interests. For example, sovereignty is a norm constructed through historical practices like the Treaty of Westphalia. Constructivists see the international system as socially constructed “‘anarchy is what states make of it’” shaped by interactions and perceptions. Key concepts include identity, where a state’s self-perception (e.g., as a democracy) influences its actions; norms, like human rights, guiding behavior; and socialization, where states adopt global norms through diplomacy or institutions. Constructivism explains change, such as the rise of environmental norms or shifts in state alliances. It highlights non-state actors, like NGOs, in shaping global agendas. Critics argue it lacks predictive power or overemphasizes intangibles. Constructivism complements realism and liberalism by explaining cultural or ideological shifts, like post-Cold War cooperation. It informs IR policies on diplomacy, norm-building, and conflict resolution, emphasizing dialogue and shared values to foster stability and mutual understanding in a dynamic global system.

text: International organizations play a pivotal role in disaster rehabilitation by mobilizing global expertise, resources, and coordination to support affected nations in transitioning from crisis to sustainable recovery. Agencies like the United Nations (UN), World Bank, and Red Cross provide immediate humanitarian aid—including food, medical supplies, and temporary shelters—while also addressing long-term rebuilding needs through funding, technical assistance, and policy guidance. They facilitate multilateral cooperation, ensuring fragmented efforts are harmonized, and advocate for inclusive approaches that prioritize vulnerable groups, such as women, children, and displaced populations. Financial mechanisms like the World Bank’s Disaster Risk Management loans or the UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) offer rapid financing for reconstruction, while platforms like the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR) help governments integrate resilience into infrastructure and urban planning. Specialized programs restore livelihoods by supporting small businesses, agriculture, and vocational training, and they promote environmental rehabilitation, such as reforestation or wetland restoration, to mitigate future risks. Knowledge-sharing is another critical function; organizations like UNDRR (UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction) disseminate best practices, from earthquake-resistant construction to community-based early warning systems. They also hold stakeholders accountable, monitoring aid distribution to prevent corruption and ensuring compliance with international standards like the Sendai Framework. In conflict-affected regions, groups like the International Organization for Migration (IOM) address displacement challenges, providing housing solutions and psychosocial support. However, challenges persist, including bureaucratic delays, cultural mismatches, and donor-driven agendas that may not align with local priorities. Despite these hurdles, international organizations amplify recovery efforts by bridging gaps in capacity and resources, fostering innovation, and advocating for policies that turn devastation into opportunity. Their role extends beyond material aid—they are catalysts for transformative resilience, ensuring communities not only recover but emerge stronger, more equitable, and better prepared for future disasters.

text: Over the past decades, search engines have become one of the main ways for us to acquire information (Croft et al., 2010). In the research and development of search engines, evaluation has always been a major force, which became central to such an extent that new designs and proposals and their evaluation became one (Saracevic, 1995). Offline evaluation (Sanderson, 2010) (also called test collection evaluation or batch evaluation) and online evaluation (Hofmann et al., 2016) are two main kinds of approaches for Web search evaluation. Different from online evaluation approaches (e.g. A/B testing (Kohavi et al., 2009) and interleaved comparisons (Joachims, 2002), as well as their variants (Li et al., 2015; Schuth et al., 2015)), which are usually based on implicit measurement of realistic users’ experience of systems in a production environment, offline evaluation approaches usually compare different search systems based on test collections. The genesis of test collection evaluation of information retrieval systems can be traced back to the work of Cleverdon (1959), which is well known as the Cranfield paradigm and has been widely used in some IR benchmark workshops (e.g. TREC ,1 CLEF ,2 and NTCIR 3) for many years. In the Cranfield framework, a test collection, which consists of a corpus, representative topics (also referred to as queries), and relevance judgments for query-document pairs, is constructed to access effectiveness of different search systems with official evaluation metrics.

text: The criminal justice system faces numerous challenges in preventing wrongful convictions, many of which stem from systemic flaws, human error, and structural inequalities. One major issue is eyewitness misidentification, as memory can be unreliable and influenced by stress, bias, or suggestive police procedures. Similarly, false confessions—often resulting from coercive interrogations, psychological pressure, or the vulnerability of juveniles and individuals with mental impairments—pose a serious risk. Another challenge lies in the misuse or misinterpretation of forensic evidence, where flawed methods, contamination, or overstated expert testimony can mislead juries. Prosecutorial misconduct, such as withholding exculpatory evidence or overzealous pursuit of convictions, further undermines fairness, while ineffective defense representation, often due to underfunded public defenders, leaves defendants without adequate protection of their rights. Systemic issues like racial bias, socioeconomic disparities, and jury prejudice also contribute to unequal treatment and increase the likelihood of wrongful outcomes. Additionally, reliance on jailhouse informants or unreliable witnesses can introduce false testimony into trials. The appeals process, while designed to correct errors, is often slow, limited, and resistant to revisiting convictions, making it difficult to overturn wrongful verdicts once they occur. Preventing wrongful convictions requires addressing these challenges through reforms such as improved forensic standards, mandatory recording of interrogations, better training for law enforcement, stronger defense resources, and greater transparency in prosecutorial practices. Ultimately, the greatest challenge lies in balancing the pursuit of justice with the protection of individual rights, ensuring that the innocent are not punished while the guilty are held accountable.

text: Here, we expand the aforementioned work by taking information from other ions into consideration. Specifically, we propose a new Bayesian hierarchical model to quantify LC-MS peak intensities. As our approach does not depend on the perfect alignment of the peaks at scan-level, it can handle peaks with different width in retention time. It can also handle missing peaks or scans by including a an indicator in the model. Finally, we include the variation of the instrument across the runs in the model to address the drift across the queue. The model includes two main layers. The first layer models the observed intensities based on the original unknown ion abundance, a missing rate for scans, and a peak shape function with several parameters. It also includes the error terms to represent noise in instrument measurements. In the second layer, the parameters of the peak shape function are modeled as a linear combination of several fixed and random effects related to each ion. In addition, a noise term is considered to model the variation of the peak shape across different runs. To learn the parameters of the Bayesian model, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is used.

text: The effects of climate change on the storage of medicines include raised temperatures, variable moisture and extreme weather, which may impact upon the stability, efficacy and safety of medicines. text: The Jacobian matrix in robotics is a fundamental mathematical tool that establishes the relationship between joint velocities and the resulting end-effector velocities in both linear and angular dimensions, serving as a crucial bridge between joint space and Cartesian space motion analysis. This matrix represents the partial derivatives of the end-effector position and orientation with respect to each joint variable, effectively capturing how small changes in joint angles or displacements translate into corresponding changes in the end-effector's spatial velocity. The Jacobian is typically a 6×n matrix where n represents the number of joints in the robotic manipulator, with the first three rows corresponding to linear velocity components and the last three rows representing angular velocity components of the end-effector. Each column of the Jacobian represents the contribution of a specific joint to the overall end-effector motion, providing insight into how individual joint movements affect the robot's performance. The Jacobian matrix is essential for solving inverse kinematics problems, particularly when determining joint velocities required to achieve desired end-effector velocities, which is crucial for smooth trajectory execution and real-time control applications. It plays a vital role in identifying singular configurations where the robot loses degrees of freedom or becomes unable to move in certain directions, as these singularities correspond to configurations where the Jacobian becomes rank-deficient or non-invertible. The matrix is instrumental in force control applications, where it relates joint torques to end-effector forces and moments through the transpose relationship, enabling robots to perform delicate manipulation tasks requiring precise force regulation. Advanced robotic applications utilize the Jacobian for optimization-based control strategies, redundancy resolution in over-actuated systems, and dynamic analysis where it helps relate joint space dynamics to task space requirements, making it indispensable for sophisticated robotic systems requiring precise motion control and force interaction capabilities.

text: Pollination is the act of moving pollen from the male part of a flower (anther) to the female part (stigma), allowing fertilization. There are two main types of pollination: self-pollination and cross-pollination. Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same flower or of another flower of the same plant. It is called self pollination, a method which ensures genetic purity, is high in accuracy, but low in genetic diversity. On the other hand, cross-pollination refers to the action by which pollen is taken from the anther to the stigma of a flower in another plant of the same kind. It is an important driver for genetic diversity, with the offspring of interbred gene pools exhibiting better health and survival. Pollination may be carried out by pollinators including the wind (anemophily), insects (entomophily), birds (ornithophily), and mammals. For instance, plants that rely on the wind for pollination usually have small, light pollen and feathery stigmas and insect-pollinated flowers are often large and brightly coloured and secrete nectar to attract the visitors. Certain plants have developed particular mechanisms for ensuring that it is not just the sweet whisper of a summer breeze that causes them to be only self- or cross-pollinating: from the timing of pollen release to physical barriers. The manner in which organisms are pollinated contributes substantially to reproductive success and evolutionary fate of plant species. Pollination results into fertilization followed by seed formation that is very important in the life of a plant.

text: The question of whether knowledge can be certain is a deeply philosophical one, often debated in epistemology. Many philosophers argue that absolute certainty in knowledge is difficult, if not impossible, to achieve due to the fallibility of human perception and reasoning. Skeptics maintain that since our beliefs and perceptions can be influenced by biases, errors, and limitations, we can never be entirely certain about what we know. For instance, the problem of induction raises doubts about our ability to predict future events based solely on past experiences, suggesting that even well-supported scientific claims may lack absolute certainty. Conversely, some rationalists and foundationalists argue that certain types of knowledge, particularly in mathematics and logic, can be known with certainty, as they are derived from clear definitions and deductive reasoning. Descartes' famous "Cogito, ergo sum" ("I think, therefore I am") exemplifies a claim he believed to be indubitable. However, even in these domains, questions arise about the assumptions underlying our reasoning processes. Ultimately, the pursuit of knowledge often involves navigating a spectrum of certainty, where some beliefs may be more justifiably certain than others. This ongoing inquiry emphasizes the complexity of knowledge and the importance of critical examination in our understanding of certainty, belief, and truth.

text: Self-report studies, widely used in various fields such as psychology, sociology, and criminology, offer valuable insights into individuals' thoughts, feelings, and behaviors through direct responses from participants. However, these studies are not without limitations, which can significantly impact the validity and reliability of the findings. One major limitation is the potential for bias in participants' responses, as individuals may not accurately report their behaviors or experiences due to social desirability, fear of judgment, or a desire to present themselves in a favorable light. This can lead to underreporting of negative behaviors, such as criminal activity or substance abuse, and overreporting of positive traits, skewing the data and rendering it less reliable. Additionally, self-report studies often rely on participants' memory, which can be faulty or influenced by various factors such as time, context, and emotional state. Memories can be reconstructed or altered, leading to inaccuracies in the reported information. Furthermore, self-report measures may not capture the complexity of certain behaviors or experiences, as individuals might lack the self-awareness or insight necessary to provide an accurate account of their thoughts or actions. This is particularly relevant in studies involving sensitive topics, where participants might feel uncomfortable disclosing personal information or may not fully understand the implications of their responses. Moreover, self-report studies typically rely on convenience sampling, which can limit the generalizability of the findings. If the sample is not representative of the broader population, the results may not be applicable to other groups, thereby compromising the external validity of the study. The subjective nature of self-reports also raises concerns about the comparability of data across different individuals, as personal interpretations of questions can vary widely. Another limitation is the potential for response biases, such as acquiescence bias, where participants tend to agree with statements regardless of their true beliefs, or extreme response bias, where individuals may choose only the most extreme options on a scale. These biases can further distort the findings and lead to erroneous conclusions. In addition, self-report studies often lack the ability to establish causal relationships, as they primarily provide correlational data rather than experimental evidence. This limitation makes it difficult to determine whether reported behaviors are a result of specific influences or merely coincidental. Although self-report studies can be a useful tool for gathering subjective data, researchers must remain cognizant of these limitations and consider complementing self-report methods with objective measures or triangulating data from multiple sources to enhance the robustness and credibility of their findings. By acknowledging these challenges, researchers can better interpret the results and contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the phenomena under investigation.

text: The phylum Echinodermata comprises marine invertebrates characterized by unique features such as a calcareous endoskeleton, a water vascular system, and pentaradial symmetry in adults. These organisms, including sea stars, sea urchins, sand dollars, brittle stars, and sea cucumbers, are exclusively marine and occupy diverse habitats from shallow waters to deep-sea environments. A defining trait of echinoderms is their deuterostome development, placing them evolutionarily closer to chordates than other invertebrates. The water vascular system, a network of hydraulic canals, powers their tube feet, which are used for locomotion, feeding, and gas exchange. Another key feature is their endoskeleton made of ossicles (small calcium carbonate plates), often covered by a thin epidermis, giving many species a spiny texture—hence the name "Echinodermata" (meaning "spiny skin"). While adult echinoderms exhibit five-part radial symmetry, their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical, suggesting an evolutionary adaptation to a sedentary or slow-moving lifestyle. Echinoderms also possess remarkable regenerative abilities, with some species capable of regrowing lost arms or even entire bodies from a single limb. Their feeding strategies vary widely; sea stars are often predators, sea urchins graze on algae, and sea cucumbers are detritivores. Additionally, echinoderms play crucial ecological roles, such as maintaining coral reef health (e.g., sea urchins controlling algal growth) and serving as bioindicators for marine ecosystems. Their unique combination of anatomical, developmental, and physiological traits distinguishes them from other animal phyla, making them a fascinating group in evolutionary and ecological studies.

text: Hearing is a system through which sound waves are collected by the ear and are then sent to the brain, which allows for the perception of different sounds in our environment, whether they are voices, music or noise, and for distinguishing one from the other. It begins when the sound waves enter the outer ear and travel through the auditory canal, causing the eardrum to vibrate. Those vibrations are transmitted by the 3 small middle ear bones (malleus, incus, and stapes) to the cochlea in the inner ear. The cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled structure containing hair-cells that break down sound frequency. These hair cells convert mechanical movement into an electrical signal. The signals are then dispatched by the auditory nerve to the brainstem and then to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe, where the brain makes sense of things like pitch, volume, direction and rhythm. Human auditory perception is an integration of both bottom-up sensory input and top-down cognitive processing, such as attention, memory and language comprehension. It allows us to locate where sound is coming from, to understand speech, and to enjoy complex sound environments such as music. Disruptions, at any stage of this neurophysiological cascade such as hearing loss (HL) or auditory processing disorders (APDs), have profound, negative effects on speech understanding and on quality of life. In general, the ability to process auditory information is crucial to the participant’s ability to function in the world, be it in terms of social interaction or environmental awareness.

text: A good estimator in statistics is one that provides reliable and accurate estimates of unknown population parameters based on sample data. There are several key properties that characterize a good estimator. First, it should be unbiased, meaning the expected value of the estimator equals the true parameter value; this ensures that the estimator does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the parameter. Second, the estimator should be consistent, which means that as the sample size increases indefinitely, the estimator converges in probability to the true parameter value, guaranteeing improved accuracy with more data. Third, a good estimator should be efficient, meaning it has the smallest possible variance among all unbiased estimators. Efficiency relates to the precision of the estimator; a more efficient estimator produces estimates that are more tightly clustered around the true value. Another important property is sufficiency, which indicates that the estimator captures all the information in the sample relevant to the parameter; sufficient estimators allow for maximum data utilization. Furthermore, a good estimator should be robust, meaning it is not unduly affected by small deviations or violations of model assumptions, such as outliers or non-normality. While some properties might conflict (for example, unbiasedness and minimum variance), statisticians aim to balance these to select the most appropriate estimator for a given context. The choice of estimator also depends on the data structure, sample size, and computational feasibility. Understanding these properties helps researchers choose estimators that provide meaningful and reliable conclusions, which is critical in fields like medicine, economics, engineering, and social sciences. Ultimately, a good estimator facilitates sound statistical inference and decision-making, ensuring that analyses are both valid and practical.

text: Random sampling holds a fundamental importance in research and statistical analysis because it ensures that every individual or element within a population has an equal chance of being selected, which significantly enhances the representativeness and generalizability of the findings. By employing random sampling techniques, researchers minimize selection bias, which occurs when certain members of a population are more likely to be chosen than others, thus skewing the results and compromising the validity of the study. This method allows for a more accurate reflection of the entire population’s characteristics, enabling researchers to draw valid inferences and make reliable predictions about the population based on the sample data. Additionally, random sampling supports the application of probability theory, which is essential for conducting statistical tests and estimating the precision of the results, such as calculating confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests with known levels of error. It also facilitates the use of randomized controlled trials, which are considered the gold standard in experimental research because they help establish causality by controlling for confounding variables through random assignment. Furthermore, random sampling reduces the risk of systematic bias that can occur in non-random sampling methods, such as convenience sampling, which may over-represent certain groups and under-represent others, leading to distorted findings. This randomness increases the likelihood that the sample will encompass the diversity of the population, including variations in demographic, socioeconomic, and behavioral factors, which is crucial for comprehensive analysis and decision-making. In practical terms, random sampling improves the efficiency of data collection processes and enhances the credibility and replicability of research results, since other researchers can replicate the sampling process and verify findings. Overall, the importance of random sampling lies in its ability to produce unbiased, representative samples that underpin sound statistical analysis, support valid conclusions, and ultimately inform evidence-based decisions across various fields such as social sciences, medicine, marketing, and public policy. Without it, research risks being biased, unreliable, and less applicable to the broader population, which underscores its critical role in scientific inquiry and data-driven decision-making.

text: The so-called corona loss is that the air around the conductors is ionized due to the strong electric field, leading to the loss of power in high-voltage transmission lines. When the voltage drop in the vicinity of a conductor becomes to high, the air molecules are ionized, and a visible discharge called the corona effect is produced. This ionization is accompanied by a weak blue flash of light, a hissing sound due to creation of ozone and audible ticks due to generation of gaseous ions. Corona loss leads to continuous discharge of electrical energy to the atmosphere which decreases efficiency of power transmission. It also induces radio interference and noise, which may be an issue in urban areas. Corona loss is influenced by the surface shape and condition of the conductor, its size and shape, the spacing of the conductor, operating voltage, atmosphere condition such as humidity, air pressure, and altitude. Corona loss is minimized for conductors of bigger diameters and with perfectly smooth surfaces while it is maximised for conductors with rough or damaged surfaces. The electric field intensity reduces and share of corona loss in total loss decreases in both cases. Though generally corona loss is a small fraction of total loss of transmission, at very high voltage such as extra-high voltage (EHV) and ultra-high voltage (UHV) lines is more and more distinct. Consequently, the understanding and avoiding of corona loss is important in high-voltage power transmission system design and operation in order to achieve efficient, reliable and environmentally-friendly system operation.

text: Definitions Crime: An act of, or failure to act that violates a law." [1] [in] An act or the commission of an act that is forbidden or the omission of a duty that is commanded by a public law and that makes the offender liable to punishment by that law; especially: a gross violation of law. It is behaviour that is considered to be undesirable, particularly on the grounds of morality, and is generally prohibited by criminal law. Crime Definitions of crime can vary by culture and sometimes by legal system, although these differences are not so great that because of this the crime's character becomes unrecognizable. First, crime is a breach of normative rules, and only an act of which the latter has already made a manifestation in its official prescription as crime, has an orientation to be recognized as crime. Second, with crime comes punishment, and an actor that commits a crime must be subject to the legal punishment as prescribed by law. Third, crime is a social construct, as what is criminal varies over time and between societies based on moral values, politics and cultural norms. Fourth, crime is often based on culpability or mens rea, the condition of mind of perpetrators and distinguishing their actions as being accidental or deliberate. Fifth, crimes are mostly committed on the basis that there are victims (persons, thing or the society at large) who will suffer damages or losses as a result of the commission of the crime. Furthermore, a crime may either be public or private: a public crime is one in which the state arraigns the wrongdoer, whereas a private crime is one that is prosecuted by another private individual. Some offenses are mala in se (wrong in themselves, such as murder), while others are mala prohibita (wrong because they are prohibited, such as parking violations). Crimes are also classified as felonies, misdemeanors, or infractions, depending on the nature of the crime and the punishment. Knowledge of crime and its features is crucial for the purposes of policing, policy perspectives and responses to criminal conduct.

text: Bioavailability is defined as the extent and rate at which the active drug ingredient or its active moiety enters the systemic circulation, thereby becoming available at the site of action to exert its therapeutic effect. When a drug is administered intravenously, its bioavailability is considered 100% because it directly enters the bloodstream without any barriers. However, for other routes such as oral administration, bioavailability is often less than 100% due to factors like incomplete absorption through the intestinal lining and first-pass metabolism in the liver, which reduces the amount of active drug reaching systemic circulation. Bioavailability is quantitatively measured by comparing the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) of the drug after non-intravenous administration to the AUC after intravenous administration, with adjustments for dose differences. Key parameters used in this measurement include C_max (the maximum plasma concentration) and T_max (the time to reach C_max), which provide insights into the rate and extent of absorption. Understanding bioavailability is crucial for determining appropriate drug dosages, ensuring therapeutic efficacy, and assessing bioequivalence between different formulations. Drugs with narrow therapeutic indices require careful bioavailability evaluation to avoid sub-therapeutic effects or toxicity. Overall, bioavailability helps in optimizing drug formulation and delivery methods to maximize clinical benefits while minimizing adverse effects.

text: The diffuse, low surface brightness regions at the outskirts of galaxies provide critical insights into the processes driving galaxy evolution. Galaxies are generally thought to grow in an "inside-out" manner, where the central regions form first and the outer regions develop subsequently. Therefore, the most recent indicators of galaxy assembly are expected to be found in these faint outer regions. Interactions and accretion events leave behind enduring tidal tails and stellar streams (Arp, 1966; Toomre & Toomre, 1972; Bullock & Johnston, 2005; Martínez-Delgado et al., 2010). Additionally, star formation in the outer disks of galaxies offers clues about star formation mechanisms at low gas densities (Kennicutt et al., 1989; Martin & Kennicutt, 2001; Bigiel et al., 2008). Dynamical models suggest significant radial migration of stars, whereby stars formed in the inner disk can migrate outward, thereby populating the outer disk regions (Sellwood & Binney, 2002; Debattista et al., 2006; Roskar et al., 2008a, 2008b). The nearby spiral galaxy M101 (NGC 5457) offers an excellent opportunity to study the outer disk of a large Sc galaxy in detail. M101, the dominant member of a small galaxy group (Geller & Huchra, 1983; Tully, 1988), exhibits notable asymmetry indicative of recent or ongoing interactions with its companions (Beale & Davies, 1969; Rownd et al., 1994; Waller et al., 1997). Given that small group environments are typical for galaxies, the processes influencing M101 likely reflect those affecting the broader galaxy population. Moreover, M101 has been extensively studied across various wavelengths, providing a comprehensive view of its baryonic components' structure and kinematics. Its proximity allows for deep space-based imaging, enabling direct observation of its stellar populations and offering valuable information about the distribution of stellar age and metallicity in its disk (see, e.g., de Mello et al., 2008; Dalcanton et al., 2009, 2012; Radburn-Smith et al., 2011, 2012).

text: Resonance is a strong physical process that takes place when an oscillatory system is driven by an external force at the same, or close to the same, frequency that the system itself prefers to oscillate at. Any oscillating system (like a pendulum, a bridge, even a musical instrument or an electrical circut) has one or more natural frequencies at which it likes to oscillate if slightly disturbed. The system will oscillate around this natural frequency, and any external force with the same frequency as the natural frequency, will create resonance -a large increase in the amplitude of the system's oscillations. This occurs because the system more effectively draws energy from the external force – each successive push provides just the right amount of energy in time with the system’s motion. For small concentrations of energy loss, one can very quickly achieve a very large amplitude, which can sometime result in structural damage. One of the most well-known incidents in history was the collapse in 1940 of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, which led to self-excited vibrations that destroyed it at its own natural frequency. Resonance has its uses, though; it is used in musical instruments to make sound louder, in radio receivers to pick out one frequency from among the others, as well as in medical devices such as MRI machines that excite atomic nuclei at resonance frequencies. Engineers design systems carefully so as to prevent resonances or to damp them out. The analysis of resonance deals with forced oscillation, resonance curves, and Q-factors, which tell us how “sharp or broad” the resonance peak is. Resonance is an important phenomenon in mechanics and civil engineering, and in the study of acoustics, electronics and even quantum physics, where resonant absorption of energy is a key process involved in atomic and molecular transition.

text: The Black Death, a devastating pandemic that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1351, had profound and far-reaching impacts on the continent. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, the plague resulted in the deaths of an estimated 25-30 million people, roughly one-third of Europe's population at the time. The immediate impact was a dramatic reduction in the labor force, leading to labor shortages and a significant increase in wages for surviving workers. This shift in the economic landscape contributed to the decline of the feudal system and the rise of a more market-oriented economy. Socially, the Black Death led to widespread fear and uncertainty, with many people turning to religion for solace, while others blamed minority groups, such as Jews, for the outbreak, leading to increased persecution. The plague also had a profound effect on art and literature, inspiring a wave of morbid and reflective themes as people grappled with the reality of death and the fleeting nature of life. In the long term, the Black Death accelerated changes in European society, contributing to the decline of the medieval order and paving the way for the Renaissance and the modern era. It also prompted improvements in public health and sanitation practices as communities sought to prevent future outbreaks.

text: Performance appraisal is a formal and systematic process through which an organization evaluates an employee’s job performance over a specific period, comparing actual outcomes with predetermined standards to assess efficiency, productivity, and potential for growth. It serves multiple purposes, including providing feedback, identifying training needs, determining promotions or salary adjustments, and fostering employee development. Various methods of performance appraisal are used, broadly categorized into traditional and modern approaches. Traditional methods include the ranking method, where employees are ranked against each other; the paired comparison method, which evaluates employees in pairs; the grading method, assigning categories like excellent or poor; the checklist method, using yes/no questions to assess traits; and the critical incident method, which records specific instances of effective or ineffective behavior. Modern methods focus more on results and development, such as Management by Objectives (MBO), where performance is measured against mutually agreed goals; the Behaviorally Anchored Rating Scale (BARS), which uses specific behavioral examples to rate performance; the 360-degree feedback system, which gathers input from supervisors, peers, subordinates, and even clients; and the assessment center method, which evaluates employees through simulations, role plays, and case studies. In practice, organizations often combine multiple methods to ensure fairness, accuracy, and developmental value. Thus, performance appraisal is not merely about evaluation but also about motivating employees, aligning individual performance with organizational goals, and fostering continuous improvement.

text: Chromosomal mosaicism is defined as the presence of two or more karyotypically different cell lines in the same individual. Somatic mosaicism mostly results from post-zygotic errors in recombination or replication. Whole chromosomal aneuploidies (in which there are more than or fewer than two copies of one or more chromosomes) can arise by non-disjunction or anaphase lagging. Imbalances of chromosomal segments can originate from unrepaired breakages. Chromosome instability is common in human cleavage-stage embryos that have been fertilized in vitro. This has become more apparent through the application of new techniques for the analysis of the chromosome content of single blastomeres. Recent array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) analysis [1] of normally developing, good quality preimplantation embryos confirmed the presence of a high percentage of chromosomal abnormalities at cleavage stage. In addition, this analysis [1] showed that all abnormal embryos were mosaic for the aberrations found and that not only could whole chromosome aneuploidies be detected, but also a significant number of segmental aberrations. Most of these embryos are selected against during the first days and weeks of gestation. As a consequence mosaicism is observed in just 5% of aneuploid spontaneous miscarriages between 6 and 20 weeks [2] and in only 1 to 2% of viable pregnancies screened by chorionic villus sampling [3, 4].

text: However, a main goal in Mars exploration is still unsolved: the possibility of past life on Mars has been suggested from the evidence of liquid water 3.5 Gy ago, a period during which life emerged on Earth. As on Earth, ancient sediments may have recorded any possible biological activity in this period. The Curiosity rover has provided evidence for aqueous conditions, past habitability (Grotzinger et al. 2014, 2015; McLennan et al. 2014), and the presence of organics (Fressinet et al. 2015), but the question of the emergence of life remains unsolved. In contrast, the preservation of life until present time is a more tenuous possibility, given cold temperatures, lack of liquid water, and exposure to UV radiation. However, recent findings (methane detection, putative liquid flows on seasonally warm slopes) re-opened the debate. While exobiology is a central objective of most martian missions, our review does not develop this topic, but aims to set up the context for future exobiological studies by presenting the state-of-the-art of geological, geochemical, geophysical, and atmospheric observations and modeling.

text: Capitalism is an economic system based on the private ownership of the means of production and their operation for profit according to market principles of supply and demand. Beginning in Europe in the early modern period and expanding with the European conquest of the Americas, it grew so strongly that its effects can now be seen in the neoliberal globalization, globalised capitalism across the world. Overarching principles include the defense of private property, the protection of free competition and limited intervention of the state in the marketplace ("laissez-faire" economics). Capitalism promotes an entrepreneurial and investment environment,skilled in driving efficiency and innovation through rewarding those that best-fills consumer needs. But capitalism isn’t without its flaws, either: It can leave behind large wealth disparities, encourage volatile economic swings (think: recessions), and a tendency to exploit workers and the environment. In reaction, most capitalist nations have developed formal social nets and regulations, to balance free markets and government interventions in order to keep the public safe and free of abject poverty. There are many types of capitalism now, ranging from the highly regulated welfare state to the more freewheeling, deregulated and globalised neoliberal order. For all its flaws, capitalism has been the world’s most prevalent economic system, delivering wealth to most people in most places in ways that have fuelled popular hopes and aspirations while engendering endless disputes about sustainability, fair sharing and the social responsibilities of markets and corporations.

text: There are four connected spheres on Earth which allow humans and animals to survive on Earth: lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. The lithosphere is the solid, outer part of the Earth, which includes Earth's crust (the outer layer of the Earth), as well as the underlying cool, dense, and rigid upper part of the upper mantle. It is divided into several plate that ride on a more ductile relative asthenosphere and is responsible for plate tectonics including mountain-building, volcanism, and earthquakes. The lithosphere is the solid surface on which terrestrial ecologies are based and human civilizations build. Above that is the atmosphere—Earth’s thin envelope of nitrogen (about 78 percent) and oxygen (about 21 percent), with traces of argon, carbon dioxide and water—and finally the shell of gases around Earth. This gaseous blanket covers the Earth and reaches beyond 500 km above it and consists of zones—troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere—that have different properties. The atmosphere also serves as a protective shield against ultraviolet solar radiation, which can otherwise harm life on Earth. All of Earth’s water in liquid, solid, and gas form is its hydrosphere. This water body comprises approximately 71% of the Earth’s surface and includes oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, glaciers, ground water and atmospheric water vapour. The hydrosphere can also be thought of in terms of human influences, such as management and use, and is common to the Earth at all times and not restricted to the atmosphere. Finally, the biosphere encompasses all living organisms and their habitats from deep soil to high in the atmosphere and through oceans and continents. It consists of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans, all of which interact with one another and with other spheres of the environment to constitute ecosystems. These interactions are animated--the biosphere (plants) need the hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (soil), and atmosphere (air) to grow; humans can draw on resources and alter conditions in all these spheres. The four are interdependent and interact in many ways, affecting Earth’s complex and fragile environmental balance, and that’s why studying them is so crucial.

text: Graphic design is the visual backbone of brand recognition, transforming abstract brand values into tangible, memorable experiences that foster instant identification and emotional connection. text: There is a highly compact cluster of blue stars (Lauer et al. 1998; Brown et al. 1998) at the heart of the M31 double nuclear cluster of old stars. Kormendy & Bender (1999) showed that this blue cluster in turn hosts the ?108?M? supermassive black hole also known to reside in the nucleus (Dressler 1984; Dressler & Richstone 1988; Kormendy 1988; Richstone et al. 1990). Bender et al. (2005) argue that the integrated spectrum and spectral energy distribution (SED) of the stars are consistent with their formation in a burst 200 Myr ago. Young stars are also closely bound to the nuclear black hole in our Galaxy (Forrest et al. 1987; Allen et al. 1990; Krabbe et al. 1995), suggesting that this may not be a rare phenomenon. Understanding how apparently young stars were formed deeply interior to the tidal field of a supermassive black hole probes several issues of how stars and gas interact within such an extreme environment (see Alexander 2006 for a review). Study of the blue cluster in M31 provides an additional context in which to test theories for the formation of the unusual population surrounding the Milky Way black hole. There is a diversity of ideas for explaining the origin of the M31 blue cluster. Chang et al. (2007), for example, argue that the cluster is the expected consequence of the non-axisymmetric structure of the surrounding M31 nucleus funneling gas from stellar mass loss into orbit around the black hole, where it periodically reaches surface densities sufficient to induce collapse and star formation. Likewise, Levin & Beloborodov (2003), Bonnell & Rice (2008), and Wardle & Yusef-Zadeh (2012) have advanced idea of the formation of compact disks of young stars around the Milky Way black hole by massive central accretion of gas. In contrast, Demarque & Virani (2007) argue that the blue stars in M31 result from stellar collisions and tidal stripping acting on an old population of stars interacting within the high-velocity orbits and strong tidal field associated with the black hole.

text: Understanding counterfactuals, such as, "If the moon were made of cheese, I could have eaten a slice of the moon for lunch," requires readers to momentarily accept false information as true (e.g., that the moon is made of cheese) and then adjust subsequent events according to that hypothetical scenario (e.g., I ate a slice of the moon for lunch). However, readers must also incorporate the conditional framework to suppress the explicit content of the sentence and infer the implied facts (e.g., that the moon is not made of cheese) in order to grasp the sentence's intended meaning (e.g., I did not eat a slice of the moon for lunch). Counterfactual thinking thus relies on individuals' imaginative capacities to entertain a fictionalized version of reality, engaging many of the same specialized cognitive processes as Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning (Perner, 2000; Riggs et al., 1998; Van Hoeck et al., 2014) and implicating a common set of executive functions, including working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility (Drayton et al., 2011; Van Hoeck et al., 2014).

text: The ‘multi-task learning’ [16] makes the joint training and inference for correlated tasks possible. The basic idea of this learning approach is that if two tasks are correlated, then part of their model structures can be shared. This structure sharing allows the two tasks to share the data statistics, leading to more robust models. A typical multi-task learning strategy in the deep learning framework is to share the low-level layers of neural nets, while keeping the higher-level layers task-dependent. This is essentially a feature sharing strategy [17]. This multi-task learning approach based on structure sharing has been widely used in multilingual speech recognition, where the ASR tasks on different languages are treated as correlated, and the feature extraction component can be shared, due to the commonality of human languages [18] –?[20]. This approach has been found to be especially useful for low-resource languages for which only limited training data are available [21] , [22]. As another example, Chen and colleagues [23] found that phone recognition and grapheme recognition can be treated as two correlated tasks, and a DNN model trained with the two tasks as objectives outperforms the ones trained only with phone targets. Other multi-task learning research work has been reviewed in [17].

text: SQL, or Structured Query Language, is a standardized programming language specifically designed for managing and manipulating relational databases. It enables users to perform various operations on the data stored in a database, including retrieving, updating, inserting, and deleting data. SQL is essential for database administrators, developers, and data analysts as it provides a powerful and flexible way to interact with databases. One of the fundamental SQL commands is the SELECT statement, which is used to retrieve data from one or more tables. For example, the query SELECT * FROM customers; retrieves all columns and rows from the "customers" table, while SELECT first_name, last_name FROM customers WHERE city = 'New York'; retrieves only the first and last names of customers residing in New York. The UPDATE statement is used to modify existing records in a table. For instance, to change the email address of a customer with a specific ID, you might use UPDATE customers SET email = 'newemail@example.com' WHERE customer_id = 1;, which updates the email field for the customer whose ID is 1. This command allows for targeted updates, ensuring that only the intended records are modified. The DELETE statement is used to remove records from a table. For example, DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1; deletes the customer record with the ID of 1 from the "customers" table. It is crucial to use the WHERE clause with DELETE to avoid removing all records unintentionally. Additionally, SQL supports various clauses and functions that enhance its functionality, such as JOINs for combining data from multiple tables, GROUP BY for aggregating data, and ORDER BY for sorting results. SQL also allows for the creation and management of database structures through commands like CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, and DROP TABLE. Overall, SQL is a powerful tool for data manipulation and management, providing a wide range of capabilities that allow users to work efficiently with relational databases. Its versatility and robustness make it an essential skill for anyone involved in data management or analysis, enabling effective data retrieval, manipulation, and reporting in various applications and industries.

There are different hardware components such as sensors, actuators, and embedded systems. There are also different collections of software products, proprietary and commercial, for control and monitoring. As a result, every component, as well as their integration, can be a contributing factor to a CPS attack. Understanding the current CPS security vulnerabilities, attacks and protection mechanisms will provide us a better understanding of the security posture of CPS. text: The collective attitudes, beliefs, values, and conventions that influence how people behave politically both individually and in groups within a community are referred to as political culture. For instance, a society that prioritizes conformity and deference to authority may tend toward authoritarianism or less democratic governance, whereas a society that values individual liberties, the rule of law, and democratic participation is more likely to establish a stable democracy. It reinforces particular ideas and behaviors by being passed down through the generations via institutions, media, and socialization processes.  Scholars frequently make a distinction between three categories of political culture: participant (active engagement and involvement in politics), subject (passive acceptance of authority), and parochial (limited understanding or involvement).  Active involvement, political tolerance, and civic duty are all encouraged by a thriving political culture and are necessary for maintaining democratic institutions.  On the other hand, instability, corruption, or public indifference might result from a weak or fragmented political culture.  Because political culture affects the creation of policies, political campaigns, and governance tactics, it is essential for leaders, political scientists, and policymakers to understand it.  It also aids in the explanation of regional and national differences in political behavior.  Stakeholders can address social differences, find obstacles to political involvement, and encourage the growth of a more knowledgeable, involved, and inclusive populace by examining the current political culture.  In the end, political culture shapes a society's political climate and level of governance by serving as the social glue that binds political institutions and practices together.

Expression of these risk alleles is probably influenced by the presence of other diabetes risk factors, such as lifestyle, viral exposures and perhaps other genetic variants. In addition to the susceptibility genes identified through conventional association studies, a small number of diabetes-associated genes has been discovered whose effects are mediated through imprinting. Imprinting is a type of genetic effect characterized by parent-to-offspring transmission whereby the expression of the phenotype in the offspring depends on whether the transmission originated from the mother or father. In imprinting, one allele of a specific gene is silenced (through epigenetic mechanisms such as methylation) when inherited from one parent but expressed when inherited from the other. Thus, phenotype expression of imprinted genes is a consequence not only of sequence variation per se, but also of methylation and histone modifications that silence one allele, allowing a normal state of monoallelic gene expression without altering DNA sequence. The consequence of the imprinting phenomenon for association studies is that sequence variation in only the expressed allele will influence phenotype, manifesting in a seemingly non-classical transmission or inheritance pattern that may obscure any genotype-phenotype association.

text: Greenhouse gases are gases in the atmosphere of Earth that can trap heat. These gases have the property of absorbing infrared radiation emitted from the Earth's surface (and causing the greenhouse effect), then reradiating that radiation back toward the surface. The principle greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and fluorinated gases. The most prevalent anthropogenic gas is carbon dioxide (CO2), which is largely the by-product of the combustion of fossil fuels (e.g., coal, oil, and natural gas) for electricity generation, transportation, and industrial sectors. Deforestation and changes in land use also result in huge emissions of CO2 because the trees that would've otherwise have sucked that gas out of the atmosphere via photosynthesis are chopped or burned down. Methane is a far more powerful greenhouse gas than CO2 molecule-for-molecule, with 25-30 times the warming potential over a 100-year period, but with a relatively short atmospheric lifetime. Most methane emissions come from livestock digestion (enteric fermentation), landfills, rice paddies and fossil fuel extraction processes such as natural gas leaks. Nitrous oxide is released through agricultural (primarily the use of nitrogen-containing fertilizers), industrial, and some microbial processes in soil and the ocean, and it has about 300 times the warming potential of CO2 on a 100-year timescale. Fluorinated gases (hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulfur hexafluoride) are nonnatural gases created in refrigeration and manufacturing processes that, in smaller amounts, are many times more effective at trapping heat in the atmosphere and can remain in the atmosphere for thousands of years. Water vapor is another natural greenhouse gas and its concentration is dependent on temperature; it serves as a feedback that amplifies warming but is not directly augmented by human emissions. The build-up of these greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is the top cause of anthropogenic climate change, leading to global warming, changes in precipitation, and effects on all life on Earth, including human life. As such, monitoring and reducing emissions of these gases through international agreements, technological advances, and sustainable policy is necessary in order to limit climate change induced damages.

text: Most stars, both in the solar neighborhood and in young clusters, are members of binary or multiple systems. Yet the formation and early evolution of binary and multiple stars is poorly constrained observationally, and not well understood theoretically. For instance, the fraction of wide binaries in dense star-forming regions such as the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC) and IC 348 are comparable to that of field stars (Duchêne et al. 1999; Köhler et al. 2006) whereas the frequency of binaries is much higher among young stars in dispersed T associations like Taurus-Auriga (e.g., Simon et al. 1995; Ghez et al. 1997a; Brandeker et al. 2003); for reviews see Mathieu et al. (2000) and Duchêne et al. (2007). Furthermore, high-order multiples are more common in nearby star-forming regions than for solar-type main-sequence stars in the solar neighborhood (Correia et al. 2006). Some simulations suggest that stars usually form in triples and higher-order multiple systems only to be dispersed later, with the fraction of stars in multiple systems decreasing from 80% down to 40% by about 10 Myr (Delgado-Donate et al. 2004). Predictions are that the binary fraction is higher among higher mass stars, and that brown dwarfs are never close companions to stars (Goodwin et al. 2004). While past multiplicity surveys, using speckle imaging and adaptive optics (AO) on 4 m class telescopes, have drawn attention to the ubiquity of binaries in star-forming regions (e.g., Ghez et al. 1993; Leinert et al. 1993), their limited contrast and angular resolution have left many key questions unanswered or only partially answered. For instance, the frequency of higher-order multiples is uncertain, and so is the frequency of very low mass stellar and substellar companions (Ahmic et al. 2007). text: Data clustering, a fundamental data mining technique, involves the unsupervised partitioning of a dataset into clusters based on the similarity between its elements [1], [2]. The primary objective of data clustering is to ensure that objects within a cluster are more similar to each other than to objects in other clusters, emphasizing higher intra-cluster similarity compared to inter-cluster similarity. Earlier research in data clustering predominantly focused on static data, which refers to data with features that remain unchanged or change negligibly over time [3], [4]. However, advancements in data storage capabilities have enabled the collection and storage of time series data from various domains, including sales data, stock prices, biomedical measurements, and electrical power system measurements, for extended periods. Consequently, there is a growing need to efficiently analyze these datasets, leading to increased interest in time series clustering techniques. Time series clustering can be performed using two main approaches: raw data-based and feature-/model-based representations of temporal sequences [3]. In the raw data-based approach, standard clustering algorithms are combined with distance measures suitable for temporal sequences. On the other hand, feature-based time series clustering involves transforming time series data into static data through feature extraction methods, while model-based clustering methods represent temporal sequences using mathematical models. The transformed or modeled time series data can then be subjected to standard clustering methods with distance measures suitable for static data. The most commonly used clustering algorithms for time series data include partitioning methods (such as k-means and k-medoids) and hierarchical methods, although various other algorithms like density-based, model-based, grid-based, and neural network-based methods have emerged to address diverse clustering tasks [2], [5].

text: Intersectionality is a concept and analytic framework to understand how aspects of social identity, such as gender, race, class, sexuality, disability, age, and other similar conditions of difference, as they mutually constitute systems of discrimination and classification. Intersectionality: Intersectionality highlights the many different ways that people can be oppressed, and discourages us from thinking of social injustice in a one-size-fits-all fashion – because inequalities don’t affect all people in the same way and therefore cannot be ended using the same methods that work for one group as for another. text: The distinction between primary and secondary sources is fundamental to historical research and analysis, defining the nature of the evidence historians use to reconstruct and interpret the past. Primary sources are direct, firsthand accounts or original materials from the time period being studied. They are created by individuals who experienced or witnessed the events they describe, or who were directly involved in the creation of a particular artifact or document. Examples include letters, diaries, speeches, government documents (e.g., treaties, laws, census records), photographs, artifacts (e.g., pottery, tools, buildings), oral testimonies, autobiographies, and original works of art or literature. The value of primary sources lies in their immediacy and authenticity; they offer unfiltered insights into the thoughts, experiences, and perspectives of people from the past, allowing historians to get as close as possible to the historical event itself. However, primary sources are not without their limitations; they can be biased, incomplete, or difficult to interpret without sufficient context. On the other hand, secondary sources are accounts or interpretations of historical events created by individuals who did not directly experience or witness those events. Instead, secondary sources analyze, interpret, and synthesize information from primary sources (and often other secondary sources) to offer a broader perspective or a specific argument about the past. Examples include textbooks, academic articles, biographies written long after the subject's death, documentaries, and historical monographs. The purpose of secondary sources is to provide analysis, context, and new interpretations, building upon existing scholarship. They are crucial for understanding the prevailing interpretations of a historical period or event and for identifying areas of academic debate. While secondary sources offer valuable analytical frameworks and comprehensive overviews, their reliability depends heavily on the accuracy and objectivity of the primary sources they draw upon, as well as the historian's own biases and methodology. Historians typically use both primary and secondary sources in conjunction, with primary sources providing the raw data and secondary sources offering crucial analytical and interpretive frameworks to construct a nuanced understanding of history.

text: Mens rea and actus reus are the two basic requirements for criminal responsibility. The term “mens rea,” which means guilty mind in Latin, refers to a state of mind or intention of the person who is committing the crime. It serves to demonstrate that the accused was in the appropriate state of mind, i.e., intention or knowledge or recklessness or negligence when the offence was committed. The element of mens rea determines the degree of punishment. "The law doesn't concern itself with motive in that sense," Shapiro says, "it concerns itself with the actions, and specifically foreseeability or the intent." Actus reus on the other hand denotes “guilty act” and refers to the external act or behaviour which is a crime. That can be a voluntary act (say, punching someone), a voluntary omission (like failing to feed a child) or a state of affairs (such as possessing illegal drugs). Traditionally mens rea and actus reus have to be established at the same time for an individual to be criminally responsible – the so called “concurrence” of them. One example is theft: the actus reus is taking another person’s property, the mens rea is the desire to permanently deprive the owner of such property. Some crimes are, however, crimes of strict liability (i.e., liability without intent), and this is true of some traffic offenses. These are the exceptions, and for most serious crimes, both elements are necessary. “Mens rea” is judged taking into account evidence of the facts, conduct and circumstances of the actions of the accused. Therefore, the combination of actus reus and mens rea means that a criminal law punishes only people who knowingly or recklessly harm others ? not those absolutely ignorant of harmful actions, or who harms others without being aware they’re doing so.

text: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to disassemble a nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons, or conversely, the energy released when these nucleons come together to form a nucleus. It is a measure of the stability of a nucleus: the higher the binding energy per nucleon, the more stable the nucleus. The concept is rooted in Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle, which explains that a small amount of mass is converted into a significant amount of energy during nuclear formation or decay. When nucleons bind together to form a nucleus, some of their mass is lost, appearing as energy that holds the nucleus together. This energy is called binding energy because it must be supplied to break the nucleus apart, overcoming the nuclear forces that keep it intact. The binding energy varies among different nuclei, generally peaking around iron and nickel, which are the most stable elements. This variation explains why energy can be released in nuclear reactions: when lighter nuclei fuse or heavier nuclei undergo fission, the resulting nuclei have higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy in the process. Conversely, if a nucleus has lower binding energy, it tends to decay or split to reach a more stable state with higher binding energy. The calculation of nuclear binding energy is fundamental to understanding nuclear reactions, energy production, and nuclear stability. In nuclear power plants, the energy released during fission is directly related to the difference in binding energies between the original nucleus and the fission products. The concept of binding energy also underpins nuclear astrophysics, explaining phenomena such as stellar nucleosynthesis and the lifecycle of elements in the universe. Overall, nuclear binding energy is a crucial concept that explains the stability of atomic nuclei and the energy dynamics involved in nuclear reactions, highlighting the profound connection between mass and energy at the atomic level.

text: Intentionality was a concept coined by philosopher Franz Brentano and later adopted and developed by phenomenologists such as Edmund Husserl, and refers to the property of mental states or acts of being directed towards an object or away from an object. In other words, mental states, such as beliefs, desires, perceptions, and memories, are by their very nature "about" things in the world (events, objects, states of affairs), and that they have this "aboutness" is a feature of what it is to be in a mental state. So if we have a mental state, it doesn’t exist all alone, but it’s always pointing at something: something that exists outside ourselves (for example, a chair or my friend JP), something that could exist (for example, an imaginary situation), or even something abstract (like justice or freedom). When a man, for example, believes that it is raining, his belief refers not to the concept of rain in his mind, but to the idea of rain in the world, though there is no such thing in the world. This intentionality of mental states distinguishes them from non-mental phenomena, like physical objects, which do not have the inherent property of being "about" something. Intentionality also relates to the way our mental states can accurately or inaccurately represent the world, as in the case of false beliefs or misperceptions. The theory of intentionality helps bridge the gap between subjective experience and objective reality by showing how mental states reference or correspond to external states of affairs, whether accurately or not. It highlights the complexity of human cognition, wherein our thoughts and emotions not only exist within our minds but are also fundamentally structured by their relationship to the world around us.

text: Within-group variance and between-group variance are fundamental concepts in ANOVA, used to compare means across multiple groups. Within-group variance measures the variability of data points within each group, reflecting how much individual observations deviate from their respective group mean. It captures random variation or noise, such as differences in test scores among students within the same teaching method group, and is calculated as the average of the squared differences between each observation and its group mean. Between-group variance, on the other hand, measures the variability among the group means themselves, indicating how much the group means differ from the overall mean across all groups. It is calculated as the variance of the group means, weighted by sample size, relative to the grand mean. In ANOVA, the F-statistic is the ratio of between-group variance to within-group variance. A high F-value suggests that the between-group variance is large compared to the within-group variance, indicating significant differences among group means, likely due to the effect of the independent variable (e.g., different treatments). Conversely, a low F-value suggests that group means are similar, and differences may be due to random variation. Within-group variance is assumed to be similar across groups (homogeneity of variances), and both variances assume normality and independence of observations. These variances are critical because they allow ANOVA to partition total variability into components attributable to the treatment effect (between-group) and random error (within-group), enabling researchers to test hypotheses about group differences in fields like psychology, biology, and social sciences. Understanding these variances helps interpret whether observed differences are meaningful or due to chance.

text: PID is a feedback control strategy extensively used in control systems and robotics that integrated the continuous error, and manipulating the proportional, integral and derivative terms. All three of these parts serve different purposes: the P part (proportional) produces an output value that is proportional to the current error value and gives immediate corrective action; the I part (integral) eliminates the residual error by adding this term to the proportional term to reach a desired setpoint; the D part (derivative) predicts the system behavior and thus improves the system stability, since it smooths the output response, thus affecting any process variable changes. These are combined in a single control signal by the PID controller, and then transmitted to the actuator of the system to drive the error towards zero. The outcome is a consistent, high-performance and versatile control algorithm well suited for a wide variety of systems, varying from industrial applications and robotics to thermostat control and motor drives. PID controllers are widely used because of its simplicity, robustness, and ease of tuning, however bad tuning could induce instability or poor performance. Tuning involves the adjustment of the 3 gains: Kp - proportional gain; Ki - integral gain; and Kd - derivative gains to achieve the desired balance between system response, stability, and error correction. For a few applications the PI- or PD-control is known to be sufficient and advanced optional such as PI or PD controller controls the system without one component, can be applied. In general, PID control is a fundamental control strategy to achieve the ideal operating conditions for systems in dynamic environments.
