text: A drug is any substance that, when absorbed into the body of a living organism, alters normal bodily function. Drugs can be therapeutic agents used to prevent, diagnose, or treat diseases, or they can be substances of abuse that produce psychoactive effects. Therapeutic drugs are designed to interact with specific molecular targets, such as receptors, enzymes, or ion channels, to produce beneficial physiological or biochemical effects. The effects of drugs can vary widely depending on factors such as dose, route of administration, individual variability, and the presence of other substances. A poison, on the other hand, is any substance that causes harm or death to a living organism when absorbed, inhaled, or ingested. Poisons can be chemicals, plants, animals, or other substances that disrupt normal biological processes, leading to toxic effects. The toxicity of a substance depends on various factors, including the dose, duration of exposure, route of entry, and individual susceptibility. Poisons can cause a range of adverse effects, from mild irritation to severe organ damage or death. An antidote is a substance that counteracts the effects of a poison or drug overdose, providing a specific treatment to mitigate toxic effects. Antidotes work through various mechanisms, such as binding to the poison to form a non-toxic complex, inhibiting the poison's action at its target site, or enhancing the body's ability to eliminate the poison. Examples of antidotes include naloxone, which reverses the effects of opioid overdose, and atropine, which counteracts the toxic effects of organophosphate poisoning. The development and use of antidotes are critical in the management of poisoning and drug overdose, providing life-saving interventions and improving patient outcomes.

text: The basic difference between invertebrates and vertebrates is with or without spine/skeketon, that is only feature of vertebrates. Vertebrates are the members of the phylum Chordata that have a relatively well-developed internal skeleton, a backbone or spine (either bony or cartilagenous), and a "closed" circulatory system. It is constituted by bony fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals; these animals are characterized by a highly developed nervous system and highly developed organ systems (e.g., a closed circulatory system or complex respiratory organs). Vertebrates generally, are also larger and more complicated in body-plan, also have greater mobility and freedom of action as well as specialization. They are also usually very cephalized (dominated by a head) and this will allow for more advanced forms of behavior and the complexity in response to environmental details. Invertebrates, in contrast, are animals without a backbone: they are the huge amount and majority of all animal species — 95% or more by some counts. They occur in all of the major phyla, from Mollusca (snails, clams and octopuses) to Arthropoda (insects, spiders and crustaceans), Annelida (segmented worms) and beyond. Invertebrates come in a stunning variety of body forms and levels of complexity, ranging from an amoeba to a squid. A hard, shell-like exterior is present in Arthropodes as well in this case for protective and motor end purposes, but various underclasses of the Invertebrates only have a diminished or more stiff exoskeleton for protection. While there isn't a cephalic support, some relatively complex invertebrates (like cephalopods) do have an elaborate central system and some can perform much more complicated behaviors and problem-solve. Since invertebrates are characterised by a rapid reproductive turnover, and can occupy multiple disparate ecological niches, they are important as pollinators, decomposers or as prey/hosts for other types of animal groups that might be conservation targets as well significant contributors to their ecosystems. Whilst vertebrates and invertebrates both contribute to life on earth there are differences between them, however it is this great diversity that embodies the animal kingdom. Separating these two populations (in the range of species 'times') can allow us to classify animals, their rates and paces of evolution and potentially give glimpses as to how they have adapted physiologically and anatomically, which has permitted them to live in different environments. While distinct from one another, both are examples of the remarkable adaptability and diversity of animal life that contribute to an intricate tapestry of biodiversity which supports ecosystems across the globe.

text: Experimental findings of the last decade shed new light on the physics of the magnetotail plasma system, e.g. investigation of very thin current sheets, and motivated a number of theoretical studies. An example of such theoretical investigations is the analytical 1D collisionless self-consistent model of thin current sheet [Zelenyi L.M., Malova, H.V., Popov, V.Yu., Delcourt, D., Sharma, A.S. 2004. Nonlinear equilibrium structure of thin currents sheets: influence of electron pressure anisotropy. Nonlinear Processes in Geophysics 11, 1–9]. The principal characteristic of this model is its anisotropy (typical features of thin current sheet). Because anisotropic current sheets have larger free energy than Harris’ ones, we decided to revisit the classical problem of their stability. The linear tearing instability, as the most natural mechanism for the spontaneous reconnection of magnetic field lines, is investigated in the frame of our anisotropic model. We search for regions in the parameter space of the current sheet where the system could become unstable. The main region of instability is concentrated near Bn?0.1B0 and its width depends on the parameters of the system. This result conforms with an earlier work by Galeev and Zeleny [1976. Tearing instability in plasma configurations. Zhurnal Eksperimental’noi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki, 70(6), 2133–2151(in Russian)], which suggested that tearing mode could develop in a limited region of Bn values (however, these gaps were erroneously ascribed to Harris equilibrium). Therefore, the current investigation of the stability of anisotropic current sheets in the magnetotail could help to extend the previous results about the stability of Harris-like current sheets with magnetized electrons, and have implications for the physics of substorm initiation.

text: The nitrogen cycle is a crucial biogeochemical process that transforms nitrogen between its various chemical forms, allowing it to be used by living organisms. Atmospheric nitrogen (N?) is abundant but unusable by most plants and animals. The cycle begins with nitrogen fixation, where bacteria convert N? into ammonia (NH?), a form plants can absorb. This can occur in the soil, in plant roots (with symbiotic bacteria), or in aquatic environments. Ammonia is then converted into ammonium (NH??) and subsequently into nitrites (NO??) and nitrates (NO??) through nitrification, a process carried out by different types of bacteria. Plants absorb nitrates from the soil and use them to build proteins and nucleic acids. Animals obtain nitrogen by consuming plants or other animals. When organisms die or produce waste, decomposers break down organic matter, releasing ammonia back into the soil through ammonification. Finally, denitrification occurs when bacteria convert nitrates back into atmospheric nitrogen, completing the cycle. Human activities, such as the use of synthetic fertilizers, have significantly altered the nitrogen cycle, leading to environmental problems like water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Understanding the nitrogen cycle is vital for sustainable agriculture and environmental management.

text: This method of growing plants without soil is called hydroponics. Hydroponics is a type of soilless farming that involves growing plants in a water-and-nutrient solution or on inert mediums like perlite, coconut coir or rock wool, rather than in soil. This technique offers precise controls over nutrient composition, pH, and water endowment, which often results in faster growth rates and higher yields compared with traditional soil-based agriculture. There are different types of hydroponic system, from the nutrient film technique (NFT) to the deep water culture (DWC), aeroponic (where roots are misted with nutrients) and ebb and flow, to fit various types of crops and sizes of production. Example of the benefits of the hydroponic system: Using water in a hydroponic system is very economical: The water is re-circulated and is returned to the system without loss (except for evaporation). This renders it highly UNsupported, especially in semi-arid or urban areas where land and water are limited. What’s more, because hydroponics doesn’t involve soil, it’s less susceptible to soil-borne diseases and pests, so you don’t need to rely as heavily on pesticides. Hydroponic farming however can be done either inside or in a greenhouse and does not rely on weather or climate to make the spears grow. Most hydroponic crops are salad greens, herbs, tomatoes and strawberries that prefer tightly managed spaces. It is a good system but requires close attention and can be a very technical with regards to the nutrients, pH and oxygen delivery to the roots. The set-up cost is high so it’s best suited for commercial and urban farming projects. As the world’s population increases and land available for food production decreases, hydroponics offer a sustainable solution to create high quality foods that will help feed the world’s population, but hydroponics can complement and strengthen the coming future of conventional agriculture and assures food security.

text: The duties of a director of a company are varied and are essential in maintaining proper corporate governance, transparency and accountability in the company’s business. A director has a fiduciary duty to the corporation, which is a legal responsibility to act in the company’s best interest, rather than in their own personal interest. They also have 3 fiduciary duties, these are the duty of care, diligence and skill, namely that they must make decisions prudently, attend board meetings and be informed about what is happening at the company. The directors also owe a duty of loyalty and must not have conflicts of interests and not make secret profits and not have any interest in transaction of the company. According to statutory law – the Companies Act in Bangladesh, India and UK – they are also responsible to see that the financial statements are true, that books of accounts are correct and that statutory filing (such as annual return) are filed on time. They should not "fraud" people or trade while in an insolvent position. Directors may be held personally responsible, civilly or criminally, if they are found to have committed a breach of their duty, especially if their action or failure to act causes such loss to the company’s or stakeholders’ interests. The company also has a number of tasks to perform, such as to hire auditors, to make dividends, providing shares and controlling large decisions, for instance mergers or liquidation. In today’s corporate environment, directors are increasingly required to pay attention to environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, particularly in listed companies. For independent directors specifically, they have extra duties related to monitoring the conduct of the executive management board. Directors have to see to compliance with both the company’s articles of association and the specific sectoral laws, so their role is not just one of management, but is also very much a regulatory one.” Therefore, it is imperative that a director of a charity have integrity, dedication, and high ethical standards.

text: Mycorrhiza refers to a mutualistic association between the roots of most terrestrial plants and specialized soil fungi, which plays a critical role in plant nutrition, growth, and ecosystem functioning. In this symbiotic relationship, the fungal partner colonizes the root system and extends its hyphae into the surrounding soil, increasing the effective surface area for water and nutrient absorption, particularly phosphorus, nitrogen, and micronutrients, which are often limited in soil. In return, the plant supplies the fungus with carbohydrates (like glucose and sucrose) derived from photosynthesis, which the fungus cannot produce on its own. Mycorrhizae are broadly categorized into ectomycorrhizae, which form a sheath around root surfaces and penetrate the root cortex extracellularly, and endomycorrhizae (particularly arbuscular mycorrhizae, or AM), which invade root cells and form structures like arbuscules and vesicles for nutrient exchange. Mycorrhizal associations enhance plant drought tolerance, disease resistance, and stress adaptation, by improving water uptake, producing antimicrobial compounds, and modifying root architecture. In nutrient-poor or degraded soils, mycorrhizae significantly improve plant establishment and biomass. In addition, they contribute to soil stabilization and improve the gaseous cycle by promoting decomposition of organic materials or carbon sequestration as well as biodiversity conservation through more intimate relationship with multiple plant species through mycorrhizal network(i.e. wood wide web), which is an informative & ecosystem function network operating underground between plants for exchanging nutrients, information and communication etc. The use of mycorrhizal inoculants is popularly touted as sustainable practice to reduce the dependence on chemical fertilizers and enhance crop yield in agriculture and forestry ecosystems. These are ancient associations, more than 400 million years old presumably having offered a template for the colonisation of land by plants. Therefore, mycorrhizae are essential partners to plants, required for nutrient provisioning and assisting in maintaining a healthy ecosystem and increasing long term plant productivity.

text: Urban planning plays a transformative role in climate resilience by shaping cities to withstand and adapt to climate impacts while mitigating future risks through strategic design, policy, and infrastructure. Well-planned cities incorporate climate-resilient zoning, steering development away from floodplains, coastal erosion zones, or wildfire-prone areas, while preserving natural buffers like wetlands and urban forests that absorb stormwater and cool microclimates. Green infrastructure—such as bioswales, rain gardens, and permeable pavements—reduces urban flooding by enhancing water absorption, while expansive tree canopies and green roofs combat heat islands, lowering temperatures in vulnerable neighborhoods. Mixed-use, transit-oriented development minimizes urban sprawl, cutting emissions and reducing reliance on carbon-intensive transport, while compact, walkable designs improve emergency evacuation efficiency. Building codes that mandate energy-efficient, flood-resistant, or earthquake-proof structures ensure long-term durability against escalating climate extremes. Equitable access to resources—like cooling centers, clean water, and emergency shelters—is prioritized to protect marginalized communities disproportionately affected by climate shocks. Urban planners integrate renewable energy systems, district cooling, and microgrids to maintain power during disasters, while circular waste and water systems enhance resource efficiency. Participatory planning engages communities in resilience-building, ensuring solutions reflect local needs and Indigenous knowledge, particularly in informal settlements. Early warning systems and resilient critical infrastructure—such as elevated roads or floodproof hospitals—ensure continuity of essential services. By linking land-use policies with climate adaptation strategies—like Rotterdam’s water squares or Singapore’s sponge city model—urban planning turns vulnerabilities into opportunities for innovation. However, fragmented governance or short-term economic priorities can undermine resilience, emphasizing the need for cross-sector collaboration and long-term investment. Ultimately, proactive urban planning doesn’t just react to climate threats; it reimagines cities as adaptive, inclusive, and low-carbon ecosystems capable of thriving amid uncertainty

text: Carbohydrates are organic compounds that contain carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) atoms in a particular ratio (Cm(H2O)n), where m ? 1 and n ? 3 (as in water), with n a whole number that is different for each molecule. They are major metabolic fuels for all animals, adlements of body structure and storage compounds for some animals. Based on their structure, carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides. The monosaccharide is the simplest carbohydrate and the simplest form of sugar. They include glucose, fructose and galactose, and are sometimes called "simple sugars." They serve as rapid energy and substrates of complex carbohydrates. Oligosaccharides are made up of 2–10 monosaccharide units connected by glycosidic bonds. One of the common oligosaccharides is disaccharide (e.g. sucrose-glucose + fructose, lactose-glucose + galactose, maltose-glucose – glucose). These are found in everyday foods like sugar, milk and cereals. Polysaccharides are formed of many tens or hundreds — even in some cases many thousands — of monosaccharides. Those are starch (stored power for plants), glycogen (stored power for animals) and cellulose (structure in plants). Carbohydrates are not just energy suppliers, but act in cell-surface recognition, in immune reactions and as components of DNA/RNA (as sugar side chains). Nutritionally they are classified as simple or complex carbohydrates, and eating too many of them, including refined sugars, is associated with obesity and diabetes. Finally, carbohydrates are one of the most general biomolecules, classified by molecular complexity into mono-, oligo-, and polysaccharides, and are essential tools for life and metabolism in every living organism.

text: Reactor trip systems represent the most critical safety mechanisms in nuclear power plant design, functioning as automatic shutdown systems that rapidly terminate the nuclear chain reaction when predetermined safety limits are exceeded or potentially dangerous conditions are detected throughout the reactor facility. These sophisticated systems continuously monitor multiple reactor parameters including neutron flux levels, reactor coolant temperature and pressure, steam generator water levels, containment pressure, and seismic activity, using redundant sensor networks and logic circuits to ensure reliable detection of abnormal conditions that could threaten reactor safety. The trip system operates through rapid insertion of control rods into the reactor core within seconds of receiving a trip signal, utilizing either gravity-assisted drop mechanisms or spring-loaded insertion systems that can function even during loss of electrical power, effectively absorbing neutrons and immediately halting the fission process. Multiple independent trip channels provide defense-in-depth protection, with typical designs incorporating at least two out of three or two out of four logic systems that must agree before initiating a reactor trip, preventing spurious shutdowns from single component failures while maintaining the ability to trip the reactor if any channel detects genuine safety concerns. The trip system encompasses both reactor protection system functions that respond to nuclear steam supply system parameters and engineered safety feature actuation systems that activate emergency core cooling, containment isolation, and other safety systems as needed. Common trip conditions include high neutron flux indicating excessive power levels, low reactor coolant flow that could lead to inadequate heat removal, high reactor coolant temperature suggesting loss of heat sink capability, and seismic disturbances that could damage reactor components. Advanced trip systems incorporate digital technology with sophisticated algorithms that can distinguish between normal operational transients and genuine safety threats, reducing unnecessary trips while maintaining conservative safety margins. The system's design philosophy emphasizes fail-safe operation, meaning that any component failure or loss of power will result in a reactor trip rather than continued operation, ensuring that reactor safety is never compromised by instrumentation or control system malfunctions.

text: An adiabatic process is a thermodynamic transformation in which a system undergoes changes in its state variables without any heat exchange with its surroundings, meaning that no thermal energy flows into or out of the system during the process. This occurs either when the system is perfectly insulated from its environment, preventing any heat transfer, or when the process happens so rapidly that there is insufficient time for significant heat exchange to occur. During an adiabatic process, any change in the system's internal energy must result entirely from work done on or by the system, since the first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy equals the heat added minus the work done by the system, and with zero heat transfer, the internal energy change equals the negative of the work done by the system. For an ideal gas undergoing an adiabatic process, the relationship between pressure and volume follows the adiabatic equation PV to the power of gamma equals constant, where gamma is the heat capacity ratio, creating a steeper curve on a pressure-volume diagram compared to an isothermal process. During adiabatic compression, work done on the gas increases its internal energy and temperature since no heat can escape, while during adiabatic expansion, the gas does work against external pressure, decreasing its internal energy and temperature. Common examples of adiabatic processes include the rapid compression and expansion of gases in internal combustion engines, where the piston moves too quickly for significant heat transfer, the expansion of gases through turbines in power plants, and atmospheric processes where air masses rise or fall rapidly, such as in cloud formation and weather systems. Sound waves in gases also propagate through adiabatic compression and expansion cycles, as the rapid pressure changes occur too quickly for heat exchange. Understanding adiabatic processes is essential for analyzing engines, compressors, turbines, and atmospheric phenomena, as they represent one of the fundamental idealized processes used in constructing theoretical thermodynamic cycles.

text: Mechanical and chemical weathering are two fundamental processes that contribute to the breakdown and alteration of rocks and minerals at or near the Earth's surface, but they operate through different mechanisms and result in distinct changes to the materials involved. Mechanical weathering, also known as physical weathering, involves the physical disintegration of rocks into smaller fragments without altering their chemical composition. This process can occur through various mechanisms, including freeze-thaw cycles, thermal expansion, and abrasion. For instance, when water seeps into cracks in rocks and freezes, it expands, exerting pressure on the surrounding rock and causing it to fracture. Similarly, temperature fluctuations can cause rocks to expand and contract, leading to the development of cracks and eventual fragmentation. Mechanical weathering is particularly effective in environments with significant temperature variations or where physical forces, such as wind or water, are prevalent.In contrast, chemical weathering involves the alteration of the chemical composition of rocks and minerals through chemical reactions. This process can lead to the dissolution of minerals, the formation of new minerals, and the release of ions into the surrounding environment. Chemical weathering is driven by factors such as water, acids, and biological activity. For example, when rainwater, which is slightly acidic due to dissolved carbon dioxide, comes into contact with limestone, it can dissolve the calcium carbonate in the rock, leading to the gradual erosion of the limestone. Other common forms of chemical weathering include hydrolysis, where minerals react with water to form new minerals, and oxidation, where minerals react with oxygen, often resulting in the rusting of iron-bearing minerals.The key difference between mechanical and chemical weathering lies in the nature of the changes they induce: mechanical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical structure, while chemical weathering alters the minerals themselves, often resulting in the formation of new substances. Both processes are essential in shaping the Earth's landscape, contributing to soil formation, and influencing ecosystems. They often work in tandem, as mechanical weathering can increase the surface area of rocks, making them more susceptible to chemical weathering. Understanding the differences between these two weathering processes is crucial for geologists, environmental scientists, and land managers, as they play significant roles in soil development, nutrient cycling, and the overall health of terrestrial ecosystems.

text: A photograph histogram is a visualisation of the tonal values in an image, where the various shades of gray throughout the image are shown, ranging from black (left) to white (right). It offers a fast, objective method for photographers to evaluate exposure, contrast and dynamic range, without the risk of relying on the display appearance. The pixels at the vertical axis are quantified by brightness, from dark tones through midtones to white, on the horizontal. A moderately well-distributed histogram may at first glance contain a spread of tones without too much clipping at either end (loss of shadow detail, clipping to the left) or the other (loss of highlight detail, clipping to the right). Histograms are especially handy in difficult lighting situations where the image on the camera’s LCD screen might not be reliable due to bright light or the screen brightness. Photographers can change exposure, ISO, shutter speed or aperture to eliminate underexposure or overexposure by reading the histogram. Specialized histograms can also display individual color channels (red, green, blue), which can help in color balancing and correction. Some are live-histogram during shooting, which can give an idea for how you're exposing on screen, but not for the ND filter which only cuts down light entering the lens. In post-production, histograms are similarly useful among editors, who can quickly determine where adjustments are required, like regarding the recovery of shadow detail or reduction of blown highlights. Being able to read a histogram allows photographers to create technically strong images with retained detail, enhancing print or display quality. Historgams do not hold any compositional or emotional value, however they are a vitally important technical tool for handling light and tone. The ability to understand histograms is a must known to photographers who strive for perfect exposure: it is especially critical in genres like landscape or studio photography, in which only precise lighting can reflect a perfect lighting balance.

text: Singularities in Robot Kinematics Singularities in robot kinematics are particular configurations in which a robot’s Jacobian matrix becomes singular and thus the robot loses a degree of freedom or control manipulability. Some directions are no longer reachable at a singularity, and the robot might have to undergo unpredictable or endless joint velocities to achieve motion in the Cartesian space. For the control, the force generation and for planning of the trajectories these arrangements are disadvantageous. For example, on a standard 6-DOF robot, at a singularity, some of the axes of rotation of the wrist joint align so that two or more become parallel, a condition referred to as a "wrist singularity." Other known configurations are shoulder singularities where a robot can no longer move because the arm is completely extended. On singular points, the Jacobian determinant vanishes, thus loosing invertibility and resulting in a system for inverse kinematics or velocity solutions which is ill-conditioned. This can lead to instability or in extreme cases even physical damage when the controller tries to perform impossible motions. For singularity avoidance, path planners and control laws generally use detection and avoidance algorithms (e.g., damped least squares or null-space optimization). Awareness and avoidance of singularities is important for the successful operation of a robot to be smooth and safe, particularly in high precision or constrained environments such as surgical or space robotics. In general, the control of singularities is very challenging in robot design and real-time control algorithm execution.

text: The safety features of nuclear reactors are designed to prevent accidents, contain radioactive materials, and protect personnel and the environment. They include multiple layers of defense, passive safety systems, and engineered safeguards that operate automatically or manually. One of the fundamental safety features is the containment structure, usually a thick, reinforced concrete and steel vessel that encloses the reactor core to contain any accidental release of radioactive materials. Control rods are used to manage the chain reaction, allowing operators to shut down the reactor quickly in emergencies or to control power levels during normal operation. Emergency core cooling systems provide backup cooling in case of loss of coolant accidents, preventing overheating and potential core damage. Passive safety systems rely on natural physical principles such as gravity, natural convection, and pressure differentials to maintain safety without active intervention, reducing reliance on external power or human operators. These include gravity-fed water tanks, natural circulation cooling, and pressure relief valves designed to automatically activate during abnormal conditions. Redundant safety systems are incorporated to ensure multiple layers of protection, so if one system fails, others can still prevent an accident. Modern reactors also feature fail-safe shutdown mechanisms, where the reactor automatically shuts down if certain parameters exceed safe limits. Additionally, reactors are equipped with sophisticated monitoring and control systems that continuously assess parameters like temperature, pressure, neutron flux, and radiation levels, enabling prompt detection of anomalies. Safety culture and rigorous regulatory oversight further enhance reactor safety, with regular inspections, safety drills, and strict adherence to operational protocols. The design of nuclear reactors emphasizes inherent safety features, such as negative temperature coefficients, where the reaction slows down as temperature increases, preventing runaway reactions. Overall, safety features are integral to nuclear reactor design, ensuring that the risks associated with nuclear power are minimized. These measures have been developed and refined over decades of experience, making nuclear energy a safe and reliable source of electricity when properly operated and maintained. The continuous improvement of safety features remains a priority in the nuclear industry to address emerging challenges and to promote public confidence in nuclear technology.

text: In film, continuity is the degree to which the details, style, characters, and other attributes of a scene, episode, or film adhere to or to lead to a logical sequence and aesthetic structure. It’s a matter of preserving coherence in everything that is visible in the frame — actors’ spatial positions, their costumes, makeup, the objects in the set, lighting, weather, dialogue — so that one shot joins undetectably to the next, even if scenes are shot out of order. Effective continuity helps keep audiences in the story, rather than noticing the clumsy jolts of discontinuity — when an actor’s drink, for example, is suddenly full after they’ve picked it up and taken half the contents away, or an actor’s haircut has changed between shots. There are different types of continuity, with visual continuity maintaining consistency of the places, props and costumes among takes; spatial continuity prevents confusing the directions of subjects and objects; and interframe continuity, the decisión of the result of the sequence and the sequence of time, they must be linear with a peculiarity: when shooting at different times, the lateness can cause apparent solapamientos. Continuity of dialogue and action also comes into play, ensuring that lines and movements remain in perfect sync across takes. The job of making sure everything fits together belongs mostly to the script supervisor, the person who keeps track of everything that happens on the set, and who absolutely must know what’s been filmed at any given time. Editors contribute during post, though, piecing together matching takes and using invisible cuts to maintain the illusion of nonstop action. This becomes even more of a problem when we are dealing with a complex scene, with multiple camera angles, stunts, those long shooting hours, and then even the slightest mistake becomes obvious. Here and there, filmmakers might even want to break or resist continuity for aesthetic or narrative reasons (think of surreal or avant-garde works), but in general, if we are to remain immersed in watching a movie (its own little world), continuity is everything. When these goofs happen, they distract audience members and detract from the overall quality of the movie, no matter how small they may be. So a true attention to detail is necessary from pre-production planning (storyboarding shots) through on-set supervision and post production editing in order for there to be a consistent visual language. Continuity is like the ticker tape of the cinema; it’s what makes watching a movie seem effortless, it forms that unmistakably seamless cinematic feel which prevents the viewer from having to rethink or re-emotion their way through a film because an image or performance just doesn’t connect with what they’ve seen before.

text: Wilting is a common and often alarming symptom in plants, characterized by the loss of turgidity in non-woody tissues, causing leaves, stems, and sometimes flowers to droop, sag, or shrivel. This visual cue indicates a disruption in the plant's water balance, specifically when the rate of water loss through transpiration exceeds the rate of water absorption by the roots, or when water transport through the vascular system is impeded. The underlying cause of wilting can be either physiological (abiotic) or pathological (biotic). Physiologically, wilting commonly occurs due to insufficient soil moisture, where the roots cannot absorb enough water to replace what is lost by the leaves, leading to a temporary or permanent decline in cell turgor. Excessive heat, low humidity, or strong winds can also exacerbate water loss, resulting in wilting even if soil moisture is adequate. Pathologically, wilting is a classic symptom of various plant diseases, particularly those caused by vascular pathogens. Fungi (e.g., Fusarium, Verticillium) and bacteria (e.g., Ralstonia) can invade and multiply within the xylem vessels, physically blocking the water-conducting tissues or producing toxins that interfere with water movement. This blockage prevents water from reaching the upper parts of the plant, even if water is abundant in the soil, leading to the characteristic drooping. Symptoms of wilting can range from temporary wilting during the hottest part of the day, with recovery at night (often a sign of water stress), to persistent wilting that affects entire branches or the whole plant, eventually leading to chlorosis (yellowing), necrosis (tissue death), and plant death. Wilting may begin on lower leaves and progress upwards, or it might affect one side of the plant first. Observing the pattern and persistence of wilting, along with other associated symptoms like stem discoloration or lesions, is crucial for diagnosing the underlying cause and implementing appropriate corrective measures, whether it involves irrigation, shading, or disease management strategies.

text: Maxwell's equations are a group of four basic equations that explain how electric and magnetic fields act and interact with each other and with matter. James Clerk Maxwell came up with these equations in the 1800s. They brought together the formerly independent disciplines of electricity and magnetism into a single, clear theory termed electromagnetism. There are four equations: Gauss's law for electricity, which connects electric fields to electric charges; Gauss's law for magnetism, which says that magnetic monopoles don't exist and that magnetic field lines are closed loops; Faraday's law of induction, which shows how a changing magnetic field makes an electric field; and Ampère's law with Maxwell's correction, which says that electric currents and changing electric fields make magnetic fields. The most revolutionary idea that came from Maxwell's equations was that electromagnetic waves, like light, radio waves, X-rays, and gamma rays, move across space at a constant speed, which he figured out to be the speed of light. This discovery made it clear that light is an electromagnetic wave. Maxwell's equations were the basis for many technological advances, including as wireless communication, electrical circuits, radar systems, and MRI machines. They are also important for developing and evaluating electric motors, generators, antennas, and waveguides. They are also very important to the development of special relativity, since Einstein's theory was based on the idea that the speed of light is always the same, which came from Maxwell's work. Maxwell's equations are thought to be some of the most beautiful and powerful equations in modern physics. They describe how the classical electromagnetic field behaves in both vacuum and matter. They also help us comprehend quantum electrodynamics (QED), which goes even deeper into how electromagnetic interactions work at the quantum level. Maxwell's equations are very important because they not only describe how electric and magnetic fields work, but they also bring them together into one basic force that controls a lot of the physical universe and is the basis of contemporary society.

text: International cooperation is of paramount importance in environmental conservation because environmental issues inherently transcend national borders, demanding collective action to address their complex and interconnected nature. Many critical environmental challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, ocean pollution, and transboundary air pollution, are global in scope; emissions from one country affect the entire planet, species migrate across continents, and pollutants travel through atmospheric and oceanic currents. No single nation, regardless of its economic or political power, can effectively tackle these problems in isolation. International agreements, conventions, and treaties, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Montreal Protocol, and the Paris Agreement, provide essential frameworks for countries to coordinate efforts, set common goals, and establish binding commitments. These platforms facilitate the sharing of scientific knowledge, best practices, and technological innovations, accelerating the development and implementation of effective conservation strategies worldwide. Furthermore, international cooperation enables the pooling of resources – financial, technical, and human – which is particularly crucial for developing countries that often bear a disproportionate burden of environmental degradation but lack the capacity to address it alone. It fosters a sense of shared responsibility and can help resolve disputes over shared natural resources, such as transboundary rivers or migratory species. Collaboration also allows for the establishment of international protected areas or corridors that are vital for the survival of wide-ranging species. Without international cooperation, there is a risk of "free-riding," where some nations benefit from the conservation efforts of others without contributing their fair share, or a "race to the bottom," where countries relax environmental regulations to gain economic advantage, leading to further degradation. Ultimately, effective international cooperation is indispensable for building consensus, mobilizing global action, and creating a just and sustainable future where global environmental commons are protected for the benefit of all humanity and future generations.

text: The law of large numbers is a foundational theorem in probability and statistics stating that as the size of a sample increases, the sample mean will converge to the expected value or population mean. This principle formalizes the intuitive understanding that aggregating more observations leads to more stable and accurate estimates of underlying parameters. There are two versions of the law: the weak law, which guarantees convergence in probability, and the strong law, which ensures almost sure convergence. Mathematically, for a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables X?, X?, ..., X? with mean ?, the sample average X? = (X? + X? + ... + X?) / n approaches ? as n tends to infinity. The law of large numbers underscores the importance of sufficient data in statistical inference and justifies empirical approaches to estimating probabilities, means, and other parameters. In practical terms, this law implies that results obtained from larger samples are more likely to reflect the true characteristics of the population, reducing the effects of random variability. For example, in environmental health studies evaluating average pollutant levels, increasing the number of monitoring stations or observations enhances the accuracy of the population-level estimates. The law also explains the reliability of repeated measurements in experimental settings, where averaging over trials reduces noise and leads to more consistent outcomes. While the law does not specify the rate of convergence or the sample size required, it provides a theoretical assurance that long-run averages stabilize with increasing data. Importantly, the law of large numbers should not be confused with the gambler’s fallacy, which falsely assumes that past outcomes influence future probabilities in random processes. By reinforcing the value of large and representative samples, the law of large numbers serves as a cornerstone for statistical reasoning, risk assessment, and decision-making across scientific disciplines and practical applications.

text: Pharmaceutical items are routinely produced and controlled to quality levels suitable for their intended purpose thanks to a set of globally accepted standards known as Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP).  GMP emphasizes methodical processes, sanitation, and quality control across the whole production process, from sourcing raw materials to packing and delivery.  The fundamental tenets of GMP include rigorous adherence to procedural documentation, proven manufacturing methods, sufficient facilities, and appropriate employee training.  To avoid contamination, cross-contamination, and adulteration of medications, producers must keep their workspaces clean and hygienic.  In order to confirm the quality, potency, and safety of raw materials, materials used during processing, and final products, GMP also requires extensive testing.  In order to provide accountability and traceability for every batch produced and to facilitate investigations in the event of quality issues, documentation and record-keeping are essential components.  Compliance with GMP standards is ensured by routine inspections by regulatory bodies; violations may result in fines, product recalls, or the suspension of manufacturing licenses.  Risks include microbiological contamination, inaccurate labeling, inconsistent dosing, and impurity presence are reduced when GMP is followed.  Additionally, it encourages ongoing enhancements to manufacturing procedures, guaranteeing that pharmaceuticals fulfill the necessary standards and are safe for patients.  In order to promote uniformity and safety in global markets, agencies like as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States, the European Union, and the World Health Organization have unified GMP standards.  Following GMP is crucial for pharmaceutical firms to preserve their reputation and consumer trust in addition to receiving regulatory approval.  In conclusion, GMP offers a framework to ensure the efficacy, safety, and quality of medications, safeguarding the public's health and guaranteeing that pharmaceutical goods consistently achieve their intended therapeutic goals.

Even after the Sun's polarity reversal the build-up of the polar fields was slow (Dikpati et al. 2004), resulting in unusually weak polar fields at the end of cycle 23 compared to those in cycles 21 and 22. In order to understand the cause of such a weak polar field at the end of cycle 23 and its consequences for the solar–terrestrial environment, many scientists have extensively employed simulations from flux-transport dynamo models (Dikpati & Charbonneau 1999; Dikpati et al. 2008, 2010a) and surface-transport models (Wang et al. 2005; Schrijver et al. 2002; Schrijver & Liu 2008). In both these classes of models the polar fields originate from the decay of tilted, bipolar active regions, namely, the so-called Babcock–Leighton mechanism (Babcock 1959; Leighton 1964). The ingredients (advection and diffusion) that directly influence the latitudinal transport of the radial fields in the two classes of models are the same. However, one of the differences in the evolutionary patterns of the polar fields is that, in flux-transport dynamo models, poloidal fields produced at the surface by the Babcock–Leighton effect are axisymmetric (i.e., in the r–? plane) and they evolve due to advection and diffusion by the action of both the latitudinal and radial components of the meridional flow as well as by the action of a depth-dependent turbulent diffusivity.

text: The 20th and 21st centuries have witnessed an unprecedented acceleration of environmental degradation, presenting humanity with a series of interconnected and existential challenges driven primarily by rapid industrialization, population growth, and unsustainable consumption patterns. The most pressing issue is climate change, caused largely by the emission of greenhouse gases from the burning of fossil fuels. This leads to rising global temperatures, more frequent and intense extreme weather events (heatwaves, droughts, floods, storms), sea-level rise threatening coastal communities, and disruptions to ecosystems and agriculture. Closely related is biodiversity loss, with species extinction rates dramatically increasing due to habitat destruction (deforestation, urbanization, agriculture), pollution, climate change, and invasive species. This erosion of biodiversity undermines ecosystem stability and the essential services they provide, such as pollination and water purification. Pollution, in its various forms, remains a critical challenge. Air pollution from industrial emissions and vehicles contributes to respiratory diseases and acid rain. Water pollution from industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, and plastic waste contaminates freshwater sources and oceans, harming marine life and human health. Plastic pollution, in particular, has become a global crisis, with microplastics now found ubiquitously. Resource depletion, especially of finite resources like fossil fuels, minerals, and fresh water, poses a long-term threat to global stability and economic growth. Unsustainable land use practices, including deforestation, desertification, and soil degradation, reduce arable land and exacerbate climate impacts. Furthermore, the issue of waste management has escalated, with ever-growing amounts of solid waste, hazardous waste, and electronic waste posing disposal challenges and contaminating environments. These challenges are often interconnected, forming a complex web that requires global cooperation and systemic changes in energy production, consumption habits, economic models, and governance to transition towards more sustainable and equitable human-environment interactions.

text: The ALARA principle—"As Low As Reasonably Achievable"—is a cornerstone of radiation protection philosophy and operational practice, emphasizing that exposures to ionizing radiation should be minimized to the lowest possible levels while considering economic, social, and practical constraints. It arises from the understanding that no amount of radiation is entirely risk-free, and therefore, all reasonable efforts must be made to reduce both occupational and public exposures. The ALARA concept is embedded in regulatory frameworks and is applied across various industries, including nuclear energy, medicine, research, and industrial radiography. Its implementation relies on three key strategies: time, distance, and shielding. Limiting time spent near radiation sources reduces exposure linearly, increasing distance from the source decreases intensity exponentially (per the inverse square law), and applying appropriate shielding materials attenuates radiation before it reaches the individual. The principle also encourages the use of advanced technological solutions—such as remote handling tools, automation, and optimized imaging techniques—to reduce direct human interaction with radioactive sources. Organizational commitment to ALARA is demonstrated through radiation safety programs, training, routine exposure monitoring using dosimeters, safety audits, and continual improvement initiatives. Regulatory bodies like the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and national authorities mandate that facilities design protocols, equipment, and infrastructure with ALARA in mind—from the layout of radiation work areas to maintenance schedules and protective gear standards. Furthermore, the principle supports ethical obligations toward both employees and the public, reinforcing the need for transparency and accountability in risk communication and emergency preparedness. In medical contexts, ALARA governs diagnostic imaging, ensuring that procedures use the minimum necessary dose while achieving diagnostic value, especially critical for vulnerable populations such as children. The evolution of radiation standards and technologies continues to reflect the dynamic application of ALARA, pushing industries to achieve better safety outcomes, improved public trust, and responsible stewardship of ionizing radiation in an increasingly complex and interconnected world.

text: Mammals are a diverse, highly evolved vertebrate class that have a number of characteristic traits which differentiate them from other groups of animals and has allowed for their successful colonisation of such a wide variety of habitats, from terrestrial to aquatic life. The one of the dead giveaways about mammals are the mammary glands, the specialized glands that produce milk to feed their young, giving them important nutrients and antibodies to protect against disease. Mammals have quite a few hairy or furry body part that enables them to be useful in a variety of ways, including heating (keeping body warm) Provides help to blend in with the surrounding, The sensory system Reduces communication They are endothermic, that is, warm-blooded, so have the ability to keep their internal body temperature constant, independent of external temperature, thanks to metabolic heat generation and physiological mechanisms such as sweating or shivering. Mammals are gifted with a well developed and intricate brain, including an extensive cerebral cortex, where highly evolved behaviors, learning, memory and complex social interactions occur. Their skeleton features a characteristic mandible (dentary) as well as three middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) for amplified auditory response. Most mammals have specialized teeth (incisors, canines, premolars, and molars) tailored to meet the diverse nature of their diets, which can include herbivory, carnivory, and omnivory. Mammals are viviparous — with the exceptions of monotremes, which lay eggs — and are characterized by internal fertilisation of the eggs and the live birth of the young. The offspring of most mammals are born relatively developed and receive care from their parents, including nourishment, grooming and in some groups protection, ensuring that more individuals survive to adulthood. The diaphragm, a sheet of smooth muscle that the toad uses to force air into its lungs, allows for a high metabolic rate, despite the energy cost of jumping and burrowing. Mammals have lungs and a four-chambered heart to facilitate gas exchange and maximize the flow of oxygenated blood. They are most commonly characterized by their limbs being specialized for different types of locomotion, including walking, running, climbing, swimming, and/or flying, as well as their development of distinctly acute senses of vision, hearing, smell or touch. Social structures and forms of communication in other species are far more highly developed, such as in species that use vocalizations, body languages, or chemical cues. In general, the synergy of mammals’ physiological, anatomical and behavioural adaptations enable them to exploit a wide variety of habitats and ecological circumstances, rendering them one of the most successful and plastic animal group on the planet.

text: For almost a century, drug discovery was driven by the quest for magic bullets, which act by targeting one critical step in a disease process and elicit a cure with few other consequences. However, this concept is far from biological reality, and even the most successful rationally designed drugs (such as Gleevec®) show a quite promiscuous binding behavior, which has opened novel therapeutic possibilities [1]. Today, the emerging picture is that drugs rarely bind specifically to a single target, and this challenges the concept of a magic bullet. Indeed, recent analyses of drug and drug-target networks show a rich pattern of interactions among drugs and their targets, where drugs acting on a single target seem to be the exception. Likewise, many proteins are targeted by several drugs with quite distinct chemical structures [2]. Drug-repositioning strategies seek to exploit the notion of polypharmacology [3], together with the high connectivity among apparently unrelated cellular processes, to identify new therapeutic uses for already approved drugs. The main advantage of this approach is that, since it starts from approved compounds with well-characterized pharmacology and safety profiles, it should drastically reduce the risk of attrition in clinical phases. There are several successful examples of drug repositioning (for example, thalidomide to treat leprosy or finasteride for the prevention of baldness), although they were all found by serendipity and are not the result of well-thought strategies.

text: The Denavit–Hartenberg (D-H) parameters are a widely used mathematical convention in robotics and kinematic modeling that provides a systematic and standardized method for describing the geometry, position, and orientation of robotic manipulators. Introduced by Jacques Denavit and Richard Hartenberg in 1955, the D-H convention simplifies the complex spatial relationships between adjacent robot links by assigning coordinate frames to each link and defining their transformations using only four parameters. These parameters are: link length (a?), link twist (??), link offset (d?), and joint angle (??). The link length (a?) represents the distance between the axes of two consecutive joints, measured along the common normal. The link twist (??) is the angle between the two joint axes, measured about the common normal (x-axis). The link offset (d?) is the distance between two coordinate frames measured along the joint axis (z-axis), and the joint angle (??) is the rotation about the z-axis that aligns one link coordinate frame with the next. For revolute joints, ?? is the variable parameter, while for prismatic joints, d? varies depending on the joint’s movement. Using these four parameters, the D-H convention defines the homogeneous transformation matrix, which expresses the position and orientation of one link with respect to the previous one. By multiplying these matrices sequentially from the base to the end effector, one can determine the overall forward kinematics of a robotic manipulator—essentially calculating the end effector’s position and orientation in three-dimensional space given the known joint variables. This method provides a clear and structured way to model both serial and parallel robotic arms, significantly reducing the complexity of kinematic equations and avoiding redundant calculations. The D-H parameter model is fundamental in robotic control, simulation, and design, as it allows engineers to analyze and predict robot motion accurately. However, the traditional D-H convention has certain limitations, especially for robots with complex or offset joint configurations, leading to the development of modified D-H parameters that provide more flexibility. Despite this, the original D-H method remains one of the most popular and practical tools in robotics due to its simplicity, efficiency, and consistency. In summary, the Denavit–Hartenberg parameters form the mathematical foundation for representing robotic linkages and movements, enabling efficient computation of robot kinematics and motion control in modern robotic systems.

text: The Great Depression (1929–1939) was a global economic crisis triggered by multiple causes, profoundly impacting societies and reshaping governance. The primary cause was the U.S. stock market crash of October 1929, driven by speculative overinvestment, excessive borrowing, and inflated stock prices, wiping out wealth and consumer confidence. Overproduction in agriculture and industry led to falling prices and unsold goods, causing layoffs and farm bankruptcies. Unequal wealth distribution concentrated money among elites, reducing consumer spending. Weak banking systems, lacking regulation, collapsed as panicked withdrawals drained reserves, with over 9,000 U.S. banks failing by 1933. International factors, like World War I reparations and trade imbalances, strained economies, exacerbated by protectionist policies like the U.S. Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930), which crippled global trade. Consequences were devastating: global GDP fell, unemployment soared (25% in the U.S.), and poverty surged, with shantytowns called “Hoovervilles” symbolizing hardship. Socially, families faced homelessness and hunger, prompting migration, as in the U.S. Dust Bowl. Politically, it discredited laissez-faire economics, leading to government intervention; Roosevelt’s New Deal introduced welfare, public works, and banking reforms, shaping modern social safety nets. Globally, economic distress fueled extremist movements, with Hitler and Mussolini exploiting unrest to gain power. Trade collapsed, and colonial economies suffered, spurring independence movements. The Depression spurred economic theories, like Keynesianism, advocating government spending to stimulate growth. Recovery began with New Deal policies and World War II’s economic boost, but the crisis left lasting legacies: stronger state roles, labor protections, and international financial institutions like the IMF (1944). The Great Depression reshaped economies, politics, and social structures, highlighting vulnerabilities in global capitalism and influencing modern economic policy.

text: Translating natural navigation instruction to a sequence of behaviors can be implemented by using a typical attentional encoderdecoder model [3] with a single soft attention layer fusing the graph and instruction information [1]. The attentional encoder-decoder model uses two bidirectional Gated Recurrent Units (bi-GRUs) [4] to encode the instruction and graph independently and one unidirectional GRU as a decoder to generate the navigation behaviors. The attention mechanism computes the attention distribution based on the encoder states and decoder state to determine which part of the input information to focus in the translation process. However, the attention distribution is generated based only on the current decoder state and is discarded in each decoding step after the calculation of the context vector, which may ignore useful patterns in attention history. And the graph is the topological map of the whole environment, while navigation instruction has local information about the route of the interest. A single soft-attention layer fusing the instruction and the environment is not enough to cover the route information. The fusion information and attention distribution play a big role in generating behavior during decoding process. This inspired us to improve model performance by getting better fusion information and generating more accurate attention distribution

text: Socialism is a political and economic ideology advocating for collective or governmental ownership and control of the means of production and distribution of goods and services. It emphasizes reducing economic inequality, promoting social justice, and ensuring that wealth and resources are distributed more equitably among all members of society. Unlike capitalism, which relies on private ownership and free markets, socialism seeks to diminish the influence of private capital and profit-driven motives, favoring instead planning, cooperation, and public ownership. Socialists argue that economic resources should serve the interests of the community rather than individual profit, and that wealth disparities can lead to social injustice, exploitation, and inequality. Various forms of socialism exist, ranging from democratic socialism, which advocates for social ownership within a democratic political framework, to more radical forms like Marxism, which aim for a classless society. Many socialist policies include universal healthcare, free education, workers’ rights, and social safety nets, all designed to promote equality and reduce poverty. Historically, socialism has been implemented in different ways, from the welfare states of Western Europe to the centrally planned economies of the Soviet Union and other communist states. While socialism has faced criticism for potentially reducing incentives for innovation and economic efficiency, it remains influential in shaping social policies and political debates worldwide. Modern socialists often seek reforms within existing democratic systems, advocating for increased social welfare, regulation of markets, and public ownership of key industries. The core goal of socialism is to create a more just and egalitarian society by addressing economic inequality and prioritizing collective well-being over individual profit. Despite diverse interpretations and implementations, socialism continues to inspire political movements aimed at reforming or transforming capitalist societies toward greater social justice.

text: Library management operates on several core principles designed to optimize resource accessibility, service quality, and operational efficiency. Central to these principles is collection development and management, which involves the systematic selection, acquisition, and maintenance of materials that align with the library's mission and user needs. Equally important is the organization of information through standardized classification systems and cataloging practices that enable users to locate resources efficiently. Access management forms another critical principle, encompassing circulation policies, loan periods, and equitable service delivery to all patrons. User-centered service delivery drives modern library management, emphasizing community engagement, information literacy programs, and responsive reference services. Effective resource allocation and budget management ensure financial sustainability while balancing print, digital, and human resource investments. Staff development and management principles focus on cultivating knowledgeable professionals capable of adapting to evolving information landscapes. Technology integration has become indispensable, requiring libraries to maintain digital infrastructures, online databases, and automated systems that enhance accessibility. Preservation and conservation practices safeguard both physical and digital collections for future generations. Finally, continuous assessment through data-driven evaluation methods allows libraries to measure performance, identify areas for improvement, and demonstrate value to stakeholders, creating a feedback loop that informs strategic planning and service refinement. These interconnected principles form the foundation of contemporary library management, guiding institutions as they evolve to meet changing community needs in an increasingly digital information environment.

text: Reference service in libraries is a fundamental function that involves providing assistance, guidance, and instruction to help users locate, access, and use information resources effectively. The primary goal of reference service is to support the informational, educational, and research needs of library users, enhancing their ability to find, evaluate, and utilize information. Reference service encompasses several key activities and practices, including reference interviews, reference consultations, reference instruction, and reference resources. Reference interviews involve the initial interaction between a reference librarian and a user to determine the user's information needs, preferences, and context. This includes the use of communication and questioning techniques to gather and clarify information about the user's topic, purpose, and requirements, as well as the establishment of a rapport and understanding between the reference librarian and the user. Reference consultations involve the provision of personalized and in-depth assistance, guidance, and support to help users locate, access, and use information resources. This includes the provision of one-on-one reference consultations, group reference sessions, and other reference activities and programs to engage and assist library users, as well as the use of reference tools, techniques, and strategies to identify and retrieve relevant information. Reference instruction involves the provision of instruction, training, and support to help users develop and enhance their information literacy skills and competencies. This includes the provision of reference instruction sessions, workshops, and other learning activities and resources to teach and guide library users, as well as the use of instructional methods, materials, and technologies to facilitate and enhance the learning and application of information literacy skills. Reference resources involve the provision of access to and support for the use of reference collections, tools, and materials. This includes the development and maintenance of reference collections, such as encyclopedias, dictionaries, handbooks, bibliographies, and other reference works, as well as the provision of access to and support for the use of reference databases, websites, and other reference tools and resources. By providing reference service, libraries enhance their ability to support the information needs and goals of their users, contributing to the advancement of knowledge, learning, and research.

text: Psychophysiological alterations are a core diagnostic feature of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD; Langeland & Olff, 2008). With respect to cardiac changes in PTSD patients, meta-analyses have reported that adults with PTSD have a higher heart rate at rest when compared to control groups with or without a history of trauma exposure. In addition to a higher baseline heart rate, PTSD patients show larger cardiac responses to startling sounds and to idiosyncratic trauma reminders (Buckley & Kaloupek, 2001; Pole, 2007). Likewise, PTSD patients react more strongly to standardized trauma cues than controls with or without a history of trauma exposure (Pole, 2007). Ehlers et al. (2010) demonstrated that trauma survivors with PTSD exhibit differential heart rate responses to standardized trauma-related pictures as early as 1 month after the trauma. Moreover, the increased cardiac reactivity of PTSD patients is not restricted to trauma reminders but generalizes to nontrauma-related emotional cues such as standardized affective pictures (Adenauer, Catani, Keil, Aichinger, & Neuner, 2010). Additionally, the importance of the relationship between heart rate responses and PTSD has been emphasized by findings that heart rate levels early after trauma exposure prospectively predict PTSD (Bryant, Harvey, Guthrie, & Moulds, 2000; Shalev et al., 1998). Here, an elevated heart rate was indicative of increased PTSD symptoms. To sum up, besides higher baseline heart rates and its predictive value for PTSD symptoms, enhanced heart rate reactivity in PTSD patients has been shown to include both greater heart rate deceleration in response to threatening stimuli as well as greater subsequent heart rate acceleration when threat was perceived as imminent (Adenauer et al., 2010; Cuthbert et al., 2003; McTeague et al., 2010). Here, depending on the nature of tasks and stimuli used, prior studies were able to detect either deceleration or acceleration of heart rates (Pole, 2007).

text: Bacterial adhesion to mammalian tissue constitutes the first step in host colonization, through specific structures known as fimbriae and pili. F17 and F18 fimbriae are wire-like structures expressed on the surface of enterotoxigenic and septicemic Escherichia coli (ETEC) strains that secrete toxins causing diarrhea in infantile livestock [1]. The long and flexible F17 and F18 have an overall morphology and carbohydrate specificity clearly distinguishable from the rigid, rod-shaped type-1 and P pili from uropathogenic E. coli strains, and easily reach in between the digiform brush border microvilli of intestinal epithelia [2,3]. F17, F18 and type-1 fimbriae are assembled by the chaperone/usher biogenesis pathway [4] and comprise a few thousand copies of a major pilin (F17A [5], FedA and FimA respectively), several minor pilin proteins and a single two-domain adhesin (TDA) at the tip (F17G [6], FedF [7] and FimH, respectively). The N-terminal domain of TDAs is a lectin domain, also called receptor-binding domain, because it mediates adherence of fimbriated bacteria to glycoconjugate receptors on host epithelial linings [8]. Indeed, the key information for the unique interaction between the fimbrial adhesin and the host cell lies in the recognition of distinct glycan receptors on the host cell itself and is highly specific [9,10]. For example, FimH is the TDA of type-1 pili and interacts with glycoproteins on the bladder wall [8]. The optimal receptor epitope, recognized by FimH with the highest affinity, is the exposed Man?1, 3Man?1, 4GlcNAc?1, 4GlcNAc structure of N-linked high-mannose type glycans [11].

text: Non-traditional security threats significantly affect international relations by expanding the concept of security beyond military concerns to include issues like climate change, pandemics, organized crime, resource scarcity, and forced migration, thereby altering the priorities, actors, and mechanisms of global governance. Unlike traditional threats that stem from inter-state conflicts, non-traditional threats are transnational in nature, crossing borders and impacting multiple countries simultaneously, which necessitates cooperative, multidimensional responses. These threats challenge the state-centric focus of traditional security paradigms, demanding engagement from non-state actors, international institutions, and civil society to develop comprehensive strategies. For instance, climate change poses existential risks through rising sea levels, extreme weather, and biodiversity loss, influencing geopolitical stability, economic development, and migration patterns. Similarly, pandemics like COVID-19 have exposed vulnerabilities in health systems, disrupted global supply chains, and reshaped diplomatic agendas, illustrating how non-traditional threats can rival or surpass military threats in scale and impact. Organized crime and drug trafficking undermine rule of law, fuel corruption, and contribute to state fragility, while cyberattacks threaten critical infrastructure, economic assets, and democratic institutions. These evolving risks compel states to redefine their security doctrines, prioritize resilience, and invest in early warning systems, adaptive governance, and multilateral collaboration. Regional organizations and global platforms such as the United Nations, World Health Organization, and INTERPOL play crucial roles in coordinating responses, facilitating information sharing, and setting norms to address non-traditional threats. The influence of such threats also extends to international aid, diplomacy, and trade, as states integrate development, humanitarian assistance, and environmental sustainability into their foreign policy agendas. Moreover, non-traditional security concerns highlight disparities in capacity and vulnerability, prompting discussions around equity, justice, and global solidarity. They encourage a shift toward preventive diplomacy and holistic approaches that encompass social, economic, and environmental dimensions of security. Critics argue that the expansive definition of security may dilute focus and resources, but proponents assert that the interconnected nature of modern threats necessitates broad, inclusive frameworks. Ultimately, non-traditional security threats reshape international relations by emphasizing interdependence, collective responsibility, and the need for innovative governance models capable of addressing complex, cross-cutting challenges in a rapidly changing global landscape.

text: One of the more remarkable features of developmental systems is their robustness to perturbation [7]. At the species level, this is seen as the general tendency for organisms to develop normally despite the insults, environmental or genetic, that may arise during ontogeny. Somehow genetic systems are able to produce healthy individuals with symmetric, well-coordinated organ systems even across wide ranges of temperature, nutrition, or when new genetic material is introduced by admixture or mutation [8]. Runting in domestic animals, minute flies that are half the normal size, and miniaturization of many plants demonstrate the ability of developmental systems to adjust to circumstances. Above the species level, robustness is seen in the persistence of developmental genetic mechanisms across taxa [9]. Wherever we look, conserved molecular pathways underpin the development of homologous traits: vertebrate body patterning, organogenesis, and neuronal pathfinding all trace back hundreds of millions of years, in many cases also being clearly identifiable in invertebrates [10]. Kaufman [11] has argued that this robustness is often embedded in the logic of regulatory pathways that, once evolved, entrench development, although ongoing stabilizing selection may help to ensure robustness.

text: A cash crop is an agricultural crop cultivated primarily for sale and profit rather than for subsistence or local consumption. These crops are grown on a commercial scale and are typically sold in domestic or international markets, contributing significantly to the economic development of farming communities and national economies. Unlike staple crops, which are grown to meet the basic food needs of the population, cash crops are often non-essential food items or industrial raw materials. Examples include cotton, coffee, tea, tobacco, sugarcane, cocoa, and oilseeds such as soybeans and sunflower. The cultivation of cash crops is influenced by factors such as climate, soil type, market demand, and access to infrastructure. In many developing countries, cash crops are grown for export, generating foreign exchange earnings and supporting rural livelihoods. However, reliance on cash crops can pose risks, including market volatility, environmental degradation, and reduced food security if subsistence farming is neglected. The global pricing of cash crops is often determined by commodity markets, making farmers vulnerable to fluctuations caused by overproduction, trade policies, or geopolitical tensions. Sustainable cash crop farming involves practices such as crop rotation, integrated pest management, and fair trade certification to ensure environmental stewardship and equitable economic benefits. Governments and agricultural organizations support cash crop production through subsidies, research, and extension services. Technological advancements, including precision agriculture and biotechnology, have improved yields and resilience, enabling farmers to meet growing demand while minimizing resource use. Despite their economic importance, cash crops have been associated with social and ethical concerns, such as labor exploitation, land grabbing, and monoculture practices that threaten biodiversity. Addressing these challenges requires a balanced approach that integrates economic goals with social responsibility and ecological sustainability. In summary, cash crops are vital components of global agriculture, offering income opportunities and industrial inputs, but their cultivation must be managed carefully to ensure long-term viability and equitable development.

text: Shape is an important feature for characterizing objects in several branches of science, including computer vision, medical diagnostics, bioinformatics, and biometrics. The variability exhibited by shapes within and across classes is often quite structured and there is a need to capture these variations statistically. One of the earliest works in statistical analysis and modeling of shapes of objects came from Kendall and colleagues [6], [12]. While this formulation took major strides in shape analysis, its limitation was the use of landmarks in defining shapes. Since the choice of landmarks is often subjective and also because objects in images or in imaged scenes are more naturally viewed as having continuous boundaries, there has been a recent focus on shape analysis of curves and surfaces, albeit in the same spirit as Kendall's formulation. Consequently, there is now significant literature on shapes of continuous curves as elements of infinite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds called shape spaces.
