text: Theatre addresses race and ethnicity by serving as a powerful medium for exploring, challenging, and reimagining the social constructs, historical legacies, and lived experiences associated with racial and ethnic identities. Through performance, theatre can illuminate systemic injustices, celebrate cultural heritage, and foster dialogue across diverse communities. It provides a space for marginalized voices to be heard, often confronting stereotypes, discrimination, and exclusion within both society and the theatrical industry itself. Playwrights such as August Wilson, Lorraine Hansberry, David Henry Hwang, and Suzan-Lori Parks have created works that center the experiences of African American, Asian American, Latinx, and Indigenous communities, using drama to interrogate issues of identity, power, and representation. Theatre also engages with intersectionality, recognizing how race and ethnicity intersect with gender, class, sexuality, and other axes of identity. Productions may incorporate culturally specific aesthetics, languages, and performance traditions, challenging Eurocentric norms and expanding the theatrical canon. The genre includes both mainstream and ethnic-specific theatres, with companies like the National Black Theatre, Teatro Campesino, and Native Earth Performing Arts leading efforts to produce culturally resonant work. Theatre education and community engagement initiatives further address race and ethnicity by involving diverse participants in storytelling, fostering empathy, and promoting equity. The practice of color-conscious casting, as opposed to color-blind casting, acknowledges the significance of racial identity in character portrayal and narrative context. Theatre also critiques its own history of exclusion and appropriation, including practices like blackface and yellowface, advocating for ethical representation and inclusive production models. In academic and critical discourse, theatre intersects with critical race theory, postcolonial studies, and performance studies, offering tools to analyze how race is performed, constructed, and contested on stage. Contemporary movements such as Black Lives Matter have influenced theatrical content and practices, prompting institutions to examine their policies and programming. Theatre festivals, panels, and workshops dedicated to racial equity further amplify these efforts. Ultimately, theatre’s ability to embody complex narratives and evoke emotional resonance makes it a potent vehicle for addressing race and ethnicity, fostering understanding, and inspiring social change. Its continued evolution reflects the ongoing struggle for justice, inclusion, and the affirmation of diverse cultural identities within the performing arts and beyond.

text: Fruits, botanically speaking, are the mature ovaries of flowering plants, containing seeds. They develop after fertilization and serve to protect the developing seeds and aid in their dispersal. While we often associate fruits with sweet, fleshy edibles, the botanical definition encompasses a much wider range of structures. Fruits are broadly classified into three main categories: simple fruits, aggregate fruits, and multiple fruits. Simple fruits develop from a single ovary in a single flower, further divided into fleshy fruits like berries (tomatoes, grapes), drupes (peaches, cherries), and pomes (apples, pears), and dry fruits like dehiscent fruits (pods, capsules) that split open to release seeds, and indehiscent fruits (grains, nuts) that don’t. Aggregate fruits develop from multiple ovaries within a single flower, like raspberries and strawberries. Multiple fruits form from the fused ovaries of multiple flowers clustered together, such as pineapples and figs. Beyond these classifications, fruits can also be categorized based on their dispersal mechanisms – wind-dispersed (maple seeds with wings), water-dispersed (coconuts), or animal-dispersed (fleshy fruits eaten by animals). The diversity of fruit types reflects adaptations to various environments and dispersal strategies, playing a crucial role in plant reproduction and ecosystem dynamics.

text: Streptococcus suis is a Gram-positive bacterium, which is an emerging cause of serious infections, such as meningitis, septicemia, endocarditis and pneumonia in pigs and zoonotic meningitis in humans [1,2,3,4]. There are currently 35 known capsular serotypes in S. suis, of which the serotype 2 capsule (SS2) is the most virulent. Recently, multilocus sequencing has been used to more accurately identify the relatedness of virulent strains. Based on this, S. suis sequence type 1 and 7 (ST1 and ST7) have been found to be associated with the most severe infections [5]. Host- and tissue-specific adhesion of both the Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria is a prerequisite for infection and invasive disease [6,7]. Bacteria interact with host mucosal cells in order to colonize their ecological niche. Adhesion is important for avoiding the cleaning mechanisms of the host mucociliary system. Bacteria have evolved multiple adhesins to specifically recognize host cell surface carbohydrate and protein receptors [8]. S. suis has rapidly evolved drug resistance against antibiotics by horizontal transfer [9]. Therefore, novel means to prevent and treat infections are needed. Anti-adhesion therapy is based on the inhibition of bacterial attachment to a specific receptor structure [10,11]. Once the structures of the receptors are known, more potent high-affinity receptor analogs can be designed. An advantage of the prevention of infections by receptor analogs could be that bacteria do not develop resistance, in contrast to the traditional bactericidal drugs. Since anti-adhesive compounds target adhesins, which are required for a specific colonization of the host, the mutant phenotypes of bacteria deficient in adhesion would be eliminated by the host.

text: Types of criminal offenses are outlined in the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) and the Penal Code, although in the majority of the cases, they are quite ad-hoc in the sense that they require to be found out on the facts of a case. One of the important classification is that of cognizable and non-cognizable offences. Cognizable offences are more serious crimes such as murder, rape, robbery, and kidnapping, in which police can make arrests without a warrant and begin an investigation without the approval of a court beforehand. Less grave non-cognizable crimes including defamation, public nuisance and simple hurt also need a magistrate's nod to investigate. A bailable offence is one where a person arrested or detained has a right to apply for bail. In bailable offences, an accused has the right to bail out; in non-bailable offences, bail is obtained by discretion of court as it’s a question of severity of crime. There are compoundable offences and non-compoundable offences too. Compoundable offences Compounding of offences means that the complainant enters into a compromise with the accused, and is available in offences where compromise has been made between the parties, such as criminal trespass and simple hurt. Non-compoundable offence Unlike compoundable offences, non-compoundable offences cannot be withdrawn even if the parties agree, such as in case of murder and rape. You also have summons cases and warrant cases. Summons cases are the ones which are of less serious nature and are governed by a Summary procedure whereas the warrant ones are the more serious ones and are governed by Detailed procedure. The category is crucial because it dictates the law to be observed, the appropriate level of the court, police powers to investigate and the rights of the accused parties. This state-facilitated system has ensured the smooth working of the criminal justice system with graduated levels of formality depending on the seriousness of the offense. text: Fundamental ideas known as the laws of reflection explain how light reacts to reflective surfaces.  According to the first law, the normal to the surface at the point of incidence, the incident ray, and the reflected ray are all in the same plane.  This implies that the incoming ray, the reflected ray, and the line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the light impacts (referred to as the normal) all exist within a single plane when a light beam strikes a mirror or other reflecting surface.  The angle of incidence, or the angle formed by the incident ray and the normal, is equal to the angle of reflection, or the angle formed by the reflected ray and the normal, according to the second law.  The normal, an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact, is used to quantify both angles.  Whether on rough, diffuse surfaces or smooth, polished surfaces, these rules apply universally to all forms of reflection.  They describe how light routes in optical systems are predictable, how images are created in mirrors, and how reflection affects how light behaves in different settings.  Since it guarantees that light beams follow a predictable route, the rule of reflection is essential to the construction of optical instruments like telescopes, microscopes, and laser systems.  It also serves as the foundation for the laws of image formation in plane mirrors, which ensure that the image behind the mirror is oriented correctly and appears at the same distance as the item in front of it.  Simple yet effective, the principles of reflection offer a precise guideline for comprehending how light interacts with surfaces.  They also form the basis for more complex optical phenomena and technologies, such as total internal reflection and fiber optic transmission.Essentially, from common mirror reflections to sophisticated scientific instruments, these laws aid in our comprehension and prediction of how light will behave in a wide range of real-world applications.  They are essential to the study of how light interacts with surfaces and interfaces in both natural and artificial systems since they constitute the fundamental ideas of geometrical optics.

text: Earthquakes are measured using two primary scales: the Richter scale and the Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw). The Richter scale, developed in 1935, measures the magnitude of an earthquake based on the amplitude of the largest seismic wave recorded on a seismograph. It’s a logarithmic scale, meaning each whole number increase represents a tenfold increase in amplitude and roughly a 32-fold increase in energy released. However, the Richter scale is less accurate for large earthquakes and doesn’t accurately reflect the total energy released. The Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) is now the most commonly used scale by seismologists. It’s also logarithmic but is based on the seismic moment – a measure of the physical size of the rupture area, the amount of slip along the fault, and the rigidity of the rocks. Mw provides a more accurate and comprehensive measure of earthquake size, especially for large events. Both scales are logarithmic, so a magnitude 6 earthquake is ten times larger in amplitude than a magnitude 5 earthquake, and releases approximately 32 times more energy. Earthquakes are generally categorized as minor (less than 4.0), light (4.0-4.9), moderate (5.0-5.9), strong (6.0-6.9), major (7.0-7.9), and great (8.0 or greater).

text: State is a supreme political organization and has a complete power over a definite territory and population, where it governs with a clear organized political system. It is the most elementary level of political organization, framing laws and institutions for those involved in the broad areas of law enforcement, defense, foreign policy, and the regulation of the economy. Population, territory, government, and sovereignty are the four indispensable attributes of a modern state. The population is the people living within the borders of the state, and their number and variety do not matter. The territory means the well-defined geographic area (land, water and air space) the sovereignty of which belongs to the state. The government is the arm or agency of the state that carries out and enforces the laws, collects taxes, and supplies public services, such as roads, schools, welfare, and so forth. It is normally composed of three branches: executive, legislative, and judiciary. What’s most important in all this is sovereignty, by which I mean the exclusive and ultimate authority of the state to govern itself without outside influence. Inward and outward sovereignty are in turn related to internal and external autonomy. Without sovereignty, no state is capable of operating as an independent actor. States are unlike governments: states are permanent and abstract, governments are temporary and specific. The State has several functions: protecting citizens, ensuring justice, organizing the economy, and representing the nation in international affairs. It must also maintain national security and welfare through institutions and policies. Are there theories of state formation? There are many. Today, state remains the dominant actor in domestic governance and international relations, the embodiment of legal authority and institutional continuity. Analysis of elements of the state helps students comprehend systems of politics, conflicts over sovereignty, and interactions between citizens and authority institutions.

text: Objectivity Objectivity is a professional norm of journalism (journalistic professional standard) that states that above all, the journalist should strive for accuracy, and not include their own opinion or bias in the news report. It also demonstrates the need to present the truth as it is, rather than always having a story or an agenda to back up an editorial one’s perspective. At bottom, objectivity means that the journalist is to be a disinterested party, reporting factually about what has occurred without introducing his own views or advancing the cause of one side over the other. That comes through careful sourcing, fact-checking and presenting multiple views within one story. A political scandal provides a prime illustration of this: when reporting on a political dispute, an impartial journalist cannot simply pass on the statements of one disputant, but must also give space to statements, counter-arguments, and qualifications from the other side. The intent is to enable readers (and viewers) to make up their informed minds, not be led to one side of the argument or the other. Being objective also means staying away from emotionally loaded or biased language and sticking with factual reporting. Absolute objectivity may be impossible for humans to achieve, but the pursuit of objectivity is a discipline that can reduce and minimize human bias and foster journalistic integrity. Disbelievers in objectivity say that pretending to be neutral somehow covers for unconscious bias or gets you off the hook for speaking out on messy moral topics like racism or injustice. But most news organizations solve this problem by distinguishing between news (even when it’s somewhat biased) and opinion sections like columns or editorials. While debates continue to shift and develop, objectivity continues to be important as it creates a trust among journalists and the public. But in the current media environment, which has been criticized for its partisanship and sensationalism, objectivity is what enables the audience to trust that the journalist’s first allegiance is to truth and transparency, and that their ultimate purpose is service. Thus, objectivity not only characterizes good journalism, but also is what keeps the press credible and relevant in democratic cultures.

text: Unawareness of one's own motor deficits is usually referred to as anosognosia for hemiplegia. It commonly occurs following brain damage, and patients may have anosognosia even when their motor deficits severely restrict daily life. Different theories have been proposed to account for anosognosia, but no theoretical interpretation appears to account for all of the different aspects of anosognosia that have been reported in the literature (see Vallar & Ronchi, Citation2006, and Vuilleumier, Citation2004, for recent reviews). There is now a growing consensus to consider anosognosia a heterogeneous syndrome, whereby varied signs and symptoms can be differently associated with different types of denial of motor deficits (Cocchini, Beschin, & Della Sala, Citation2002; Davies, Davies, & Coltheart, Citation2005; Marcel, Tegnér, & Nimmo-Smith, Citation2004; Vuilleumier, Citation2004). Despite the general consensus in considering anosognosia in these terms, the debate on anosognosia is complicated by diagnostic discrepancies (Orfei et al., Citation2007). text: Galaxy clusters represent the largest class of self-gravitating systems formed in the universe, with typical masses of M?1014?15h?1M?. In the context of the standard structure formation scenario, cluster halos correspond to rare massive local peaks in the primordial density perturbations (e.g., Tinker et al. 2010). Galaxy clusters act as powerful cosmic lenses, producing a variety of detectable lensing effects from strong to weak lensing (Kneib and Natarajan 2011), including deflection, shearing, and magnifying of the images of background sources (e.g., Umetsu et al. 2016). The critical advantage of cluster gravitational lensing is its ability to study the mass distribution of individual and ensemble systems independent of assumptions about their physical and dynamical state (e.g., Clowe et al. 2006). Weak gravitational lensing is responsible for the weak shape distortion, or shear, and magnification of the images of background sources due to the gravitational field of intervening massive objects and large-scale structure (Bartelmann et al. 2001; Schneider 2005; Umetsu 2010; Hoekstra 2013; Mandelbaum 2018). Weak shear lensing by galaxy clusters gives rise to levels of up to a few 10% of elliptical distortions in images of background sources. Thus, the weak shear lensing signal, as measured from small but coherent image distortions in galaxy shapes, can provide a direct measure of the projected mass distribution of galaxy clusters (e.g., Kaiser and Squires 1993; Fahlman et al. 1994; Okabe and Umetsu 2008). On the other hand, lensing magnification can influence the observed surface number density of background galaxies seen behind clusters, by enhancing their apparent fluxes and expanding the area of sky (e.g., Broadhurst et al. 1995, 2005b; Taylor et al. 1998; Umetsu et al. 2011b; Chiu et al. 2020). The former effect increases the source counts above the limiting flux, whereas the latter reduces the effective observing area in the source plane, thus decreasing the observed number of sources per unit solid angle. The net effect, known as magnification bias, depends on the intrinsic faint-end slope of the source luminosity function.

text: A population in statistics refers to the complete set of all elements, individuals, or objects that share a common characteristic and about which information is sought. It is the entire group that a researcher aims to study or draw conclusions about. For example, if a researcher wants to know the average height of students in a university, then the population would be all students enrolled at that university. Populations can be finite or infinite, depending on whether the total number of elements is countable or not. Populations are often too large or impractical to study in their entirety, which leads to the use of samples. A sample is a subset of the population that is selected for study, with the goal of making inferences about the entire population based on the data collected from the sample. The sample should ideally be representative of the population to ensure that the conclusions drawn are valid. Proper sampling techniques, such as random sampling, stratified sampling, or systematic sampling, are used to minimize bias and ensure the sample accurately reflects the population's characteristics. The importance of understanding the distinction between population and sample lies in the fact that statistical analysis is often performed on samples, and the results are then generalized to the population. This process relies heavily on the principles of probability and sampling theory to estimate parameters like mean, proportion, and variance of the population. When conducting research, clarity about whether data pertains to a population or a sample helps determine the appropriate statistical methods to apply. In summary, the population is the entire group of interest, while a sample is a subset of that group used to make inferences about the whole. Recognizing the difference is fundamental in designing studies, analyzing data, and drawing valid conclusions in statistics.

text: Lighting in cinematography is a critical tool that shapes a film’s mood, atmosphere, and narrative, guiding audience perception and enhancing storytelling in contexts like agricultural dramas or documentaries. It defines visual tone—bright, natural light might highlight the vibrancy of a wheat field, while low-key lighting could underscore the struggle against soil erosion or late blight. Techniques like three-point lighting (key, fill, back) create depth, emphasizing a character’s emotional state, such as a woman farmer’s resilience in managing hybrid seeds. Lighting also directs attention, using contrast to spotlight key elements, like a combine harvester in action, or soft diffusion to evoke hope in greenhouse scenes. It influences color palettes, ensuring authenticity in depicting rural life or pollination processes. A 2023 study by the American Society of Cinematographers notes that 70% of a film’s emotional impact stems from lighting choices. Challenges include balancing natural and artificial sources, especially in outdoor shoots, but advancements like LED panels offer flexibility. Intersectionally, lighting can challenge gender stereotypes by illuminating women’s leadership in agriculture, fostering equitable narratives. By manipulating shadows, highlights, and color, lighting transforms visuals, deepens conflict in drama, and supports media literacy in decoding gendered or cultural messages.

text: Jump cuts are a film editing technique where two sequential shots of the same subject are taken from slightly different camera positions or with a slight temporal gap, creating a noticeable and abrupt disruption in the continuity of time or space. Unlike traditional editing that aims to maintain smooth, seamless transitions, jump cuts deliberately draw attention to the editing process, often giving the appearance that time has “jumped” forward unexpectedly. This can result in a choppy, jarring effect that may seem like part of the scene is missing, as the subject appears to "leap" across the frame or rapidly change position while the background remains static. Originally considered a mistake or a breach of classical continuity editing rules, jump cuts became a defining stylistic device during the French New Wave cinema movement of the 1950s and 1960s, particularly in the work of directors like Jean-Luc Godard, who used them to challenge traditional storytelling and inject energy, spontaneity, and modernity into film. Jump cuts can serve various purposes: they can compress time efficiently, eliminate redundant or unnecessary action, or reflect a character’s mental state by creating a fragmented or disoriented sense of reality. In contemporary filmmaking and digital media—such as YouTube videos or vlogs—jump cuts are widely used for practical and stylistic reasons, including speeding up pacing, removing pauses or mistakes in speech, and maintaining viewer engagement. The technique is especially common in content that prioritizes energy, humor, or a conversational tone. While jump cuts can be effective in heightening tension, emphasizing urgency, or creating visual rhythm, their overuse or misuse can be distracting and may confuse the audience if not handled thoughtfully. Visually, jump cuts are often achieved by keeping the camera locked in the same position and cutting out segments of footage within a single take, although they can also occur across different takes. The key is the lack of a transitional device or change in angle that would normally bridge time or motion smoothly. In some cases, filmmakers use jump cuts intentionally to break the "invisible" nature of editing and remind viewers of the constructed nature of the film. Ultimately, jump cuts are a versatile editing technique that, when used creatively, can enhance storytelling by manipulating time, pace, and audience perception in bold and unconventional ways.

text: Geography and history are closely related disciplines and the physical environment is crucial to the course of history and how historical events lead to the exploitation of spaces. Geography—focused on spatial patterns of resources, climates, landscapes, and human activity—helps historians to understand why civilizations started in certain areas, how trade routes were established, why people fought over resources, and how the natural environment impacted human activity. For instance, the seasonal flooding of the Nile River allowed the rise of Ancient Egyptian civilization and blocked out a flat landscape, the mountainous geography of Greece spurred a population to become city states. Geography also affects migration, agrarian arrangements, economic development, and urbanization. It also deals with the relationships between nations - human settlements, borders, colonization, conquest, and the activities of human beings - how the world at large, has changed over recorded history. A related field, environmental history, studies the impact of human beings on their ecosystems and the way that environmental changes — for example, droughts, diseases or natural disasters — have shaped history. Climatic writ large — in the form of the Little Ice Age or famines caused by monsoon failures — had deep social and political impacts. Geography can help historians study how location and landforms influence strategic decisions, cultural interactions, and intellectual formations. The reverse value of the historical knowledge on geography is that it makes us understand geographic regions better by exposing the cultural and political significance invested in them. This interdisciplinarity is essential for conveying nuanced, contextual historical knowledge. In history and education, infusing the study of geography into history lessons pushes students to think spatially and systemically; that is, to connect people, places and time in a more dynamic way. Indeed, geography is more than a stage for history, a passive scene against which human drama unfolds.

text: Immersive theatre is a dynamic and innovative form of performance that breaks away from traditional theatrical conventions by actively engaging the audience in the storytelling process, often blurring the lines between performers and spectators. In immersive theatre, the audience is not merely passive observers; instead, they are invited to participate in the experience, moving through the performance space and interacting with the actors and the environment. This participatory approach creates a sense of immediacy and intimacy, allowing spectators to become integral to the narrative, influencing the direction of the story and their own experience of it. The settings for immersive theatre can vary widely, ranging from purpose-built environments to unconventional spaces such as warehouses, outdoor locations, or even private homes, each designed to enhance the thematic elements of the performance. The design of these spaces is often highly detailed and interactive, encouraging audience members to explore and engage with their surroundings, discovering hidden narratives and characters as they navigate the performance. This exploration fosters a deeper emotional connection to the story, as participants are not only witnessing the action but also experiencing it firsthand. Immersive theatre often incorporates elements of site-specific performance, utilizing the unique characteristics of the location to enhance the narrative and create a more profound sense of place. Additionally, the format allows for a diverse range of storytelling techniques, including non-linear narratives, multiple storylines, and varying perspectives, which can lead to a unique experience for each audience member. The flexibility of immersive theatre also encourages experimentation with different artistic mediums, such as visual art, music, and technology, further enriching the audience's experience. However, this form of theatre also presents challenges, as it requires careful consideration of audience safety, comfort, and engagement, ensuring that participants feel empowered to explore without feeling overwhelmed or lost. Ultimately, immersive theatre represents a bold and transformative approach to performance, inviting audiences to step beyond the confines of traditional theatre and engage with the art form in a more personal and meaningful way. By fostering active participation and exploration, immersive theatre creates memorable experiences that resonate long after the performance has ended, challenging audiences to reconsider their relationship with storytelling and the spaces they inhabit. This innovative approach not only enriches the theatrical landscape but also opens up new possibilities for artistic expression, making immersive theatre a vital and exciting aspect of contemporary performance art. Through its emphasis on interaction and engagement, immersive theatre invites audiences to become co-creators of the narrative, transforming the act of watching into an active and participatory experience that celebrates the power of storytelling in all its forms.

text: Earthing, also known as grounding, is the intentional connection of electrical equipment and circuits to the Earth, typically through a low-resistance path. This connection serves several crucial safety and operational functions. Primarily, earthing provides a safe path for fault currents to flow in the event of an insulation failure, allowing protective devices like circuit breakers and fuses to quickly operate and clear the fault, preventing electric shock and fire hazards. Without earthing, a fault could energize the metallic chassis of equipment, posing a significant danger to anyone who touches it. Earthing also stabilizes voltage levels, minimizing voltage fluctuations and reducing the risk of damage to sensitive electronic equipment. It aids in the effective operation of protective devices by providing a low-impedance path for fault currents. Different earthing systems exist – TT, TN, and IT – each with varying characteristics and suited for specific applications. Proper earthing is mandated by electrical safety regulations worldwide and is absolutely critical for ensuring the safety of personnel, protecting equipment from damage, and maintaining the reliable operation of electrical systems. Regular inspection and maintenance of earthing connections are essential to ensure its continued effectiveness.

text: Direct and indirect taxes differ primarily in how they are levied and collected, as well as their impact on individuals and businesses. **Direct taxes** are imposed directly on the income or wealth of individuals and businesses. Examples include **income tax**, which is levied on earnings, **corporate tax** on business profits, and **property tax** on the value of real estate. These taxes are typically progressive, meaning that the tax rate increases as the taxable amount increases, aiming to redistribute income from higher to lower earners. Direct taxes are paid directly to the government by the taxpayer and are often seen as more transparent and equitable. In contrast, **indirect taxes** are levied on the consumption of goods and services. Common examples include **sales tax** or **value-added tax (VAT)**, which are applied to the sale of goods and services, and **excise tax** on specific goods like tobacco, alcohol, and fuel. Indirect taxes are embedded in the price of the goods and services, meaning that the final consumer ultimately bears the tax burden, even though the tax is collected by the seller. Indirect taxes can be regressive, disproportionately affecting lower-income individuals who spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods and services. The choice between direct and indirect taxes depends on the government's fiscal goals, economic conditions, and social policies.

text: A Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) is a type of transistor that uses both electron and hole charge carriers, making it a bipolar device. BJTs are three-terminal semiconductor devices consisting of an emitter, a base, and a collector. The operation of a BJT involves the interaction between these three regions, where the base region controls the current flow between the emitter and collector. In an NPN BJT, a small current applied to the base terminal causes a much larger current to flow from the collector to the emitter, resulting in current amplification. Conversely, in a PNP BJT, the current flows from the emitter to the collector. The working principle of a BJT is based on the injection of minority carriers from the emitter into the base region, which then diffuse into the collector region, allowing for current amplification. BJTs can operate in different modes, such as active, saturation, and cutoff, depending on the biasing conditions. In the active mode, the BJT acts as an amplifier, where small changes in the base current result in larger changes in the collector current. BJTs are widely used in analog circuits, amplifiers, and switching applications, making them fundamental components in electronic devices and systems.

text: Ageing includes several biological, psychological and social processes that alter the potential and quality of individuals’ lives. A definitive hallmark of the aging process in biological systems is a systemic deterioration in strength, sensory apparatus including vision and hearing systems, and the function of organ systems, and a general experimentally induced progressive tissue dysfunction. Cognitive changes can be slower processing speed, mild forgetfulness or diminished executive function, with intelligence and learned knowledge generally preserved or enhanced. Psychosocial experiences (e.g., retirement, bereavement) and role changes (e.g., social-role transitions) may also affect mental and social health in older people. The effects of ageing also increase the risk for chronic diseases such as arthritis, cardiovascular disease and neurodegenerative disease. But, for many older adults, changing how they interact with the world, staying connected to family and friends and modifying lifestyles have allowed them to continue being human — to lead active, satisfying lives. The process of aging is highly individualized and the result may therefore be the consequence of the interaction of various genetic, environmental, and behavioural factors, further emphasizing the importance of healthy aging.

text: A thesaurus in library science and information science is a form of controlled vocabulary that seeks to dictate semantic manifestations of metadata in the indexing of content objects. .Establishment of relationships between concepts by means of synonyms and other similar words and their usage (equivalence), and through hierarchical relationships such as broader (/narrower) and related terms (associative). Created as a solution to problems of variability in natural language, such as synonyms, homonyms, and polysemy, a thesaurus enables a user who enters a search for something like “car” to also retrieve items indexed under “automobile.” Aligning with international norms such as ISO 25964, thesauri define best practice in structure (term lists, hierarchies, relationships), language consistency, and maintenance. Thesauri enhance precision within library catalogues, digital repositories, and discipline-specific databases by forcing indexers to use the same term and by helping users to determine how to input search terms—providing suggestions and related concepts. They are powerful enough to implement features, such as query expansion, in which a user’s input is expanded with synonyms and/or more general terms to enhance recall. For particular domains (e.g., medicine or education), domain-specific thesauri—such as the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) for medicine and ERIC Thesaurus for education—provide rich hierarchies, synonyms and vocabularies that support semantic search on the specialized literature. Maintenance of an thesaurus includes the tasks of the ongoing term maintanance, new concepts, depreceted terms, multilingual equivalences, adapting domain knowledge. Thesauri will play an ever?increasing part in ontologies and knowledge graphs, as linked data and the semantic web expand, together they will provide a shared terminology that will allow systems to work with one another. In short, a thesaurus organises information at the level of the word, makes retrieval better and faster, helps users to make sense of meanings everywhere, and helps diverse users to find things they can trust in complex search facilities.

text: Climate change and disasters share a complex, bidirectional relationship that continues to intensify as global temperatures rise. Climate change acts as a threat multiplier, increasing the frequency and severity of various natural disasters including heatwaves, droughts, wildfires, intense storms, and flooding events. Rising global temperatures accelerate evaporation, leading to more extreme precipitation in some regions while causing prolonged dry spells in others, thereby amplifying both flood and drought risks. Ocean warming and acidification contribute to stronger tropical cyclones and coral reef degradation, while melting glaciers and ice caps raise sea levels, exacerbating coastal flooding and erosion. Conversely, disasters themselves can worsen climate change impacts through feedback loops; for instance, wildfires release massive amounts of stored carbon into the atmosphere, further accelerating global warming. Similarly, widespread flooding can damage critical infrastructure, releasing hazardous materials and disrupting carbon sequestration processes. This vicious cycle creates cascading effects on ecosystems, human communities, and economic systems worldwide. As climate patterns become increasingly unpredictable, traditional disaster risk reduction approaches must evolve to incorporate climate adaptation strategies, building resilience against both sudden-onset disasters and slow-onset climate impacts. Addressing this interconnected relationship requires integrated approaches that simultaneously reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance adaptive capacity, and transform how societies prepare for and respond to disasters in an era of unprecedented environmental change.

text: Portrait photography is a genre of photography that focuses on capturing the likeness, personality, and mood of an individual or group of people. The primary goal of portrait photography is to create a compelling and evocative image that conveys the essence of the subject, whether through their expression, pose, or the surrounding environment. Portrait photography can take many forms, from formal studio portraits to candid street photography, and it can be used for a variety of purposes, including personal, commercial, and artistic applications. One of the key considerations in portrait photography is the use of lighting, which plays a crucial role in shaping the appearance and mood of the subject. Photographers often use a combination of natural and artificial light sources, such as softboxes, reflectors, and flash units, to create a flattering and dynamic illumination that highlights the subject's features and enhances their expression. Another important consideration is the choice of background and setting, which can provide context, depth, and visual interest to the image. Photographers often use simple and uncluttered backgrounds for studio portraits, while environmental portraits may incorporate elements of the subject's surroundings to tell a story or convey a sense of place. The pose and expression of the subject are also critical aspects of portrait photography, as they can convey a wide range of emotions, attitudes, and personalities. Photographers often work closely with their subjects to create a comfortable and collaborative atmosphere, using techniques such as guided posing, conversation, and humor to elicit natural and authentic expressions. Additionally, the use of composition, framing, and depth of field can help draw the viewer's attention to the subject and create a sense of intimacy and connection. By mastering the technical and artistic aspects of portrait photography, photographers can create powerful and memorable images that capture the unique and individual essence of their subjects.

text: A mix of cultural, chemical, biological, and genetic methods can be used to control plant diseases with the goals of limiting damage, preventing pathogen infection, and lowering pathogen populations.  Crop rotation, sanitation (removing diseased plant detritus), appropriate spacing for air circulation, efficient watering to prevent excessive moisture, and the use of disease-free seeds or planting materials are all examples of cultural management techniques.These measures reduce the favorable conditions for pathogens and disrupt their life cycles. Chemical control involves applying fungicides, bactericides, nematicides, or insecticides to protect plants from infection or to kill pathogens and vectors. However, chemical use must be managed carefully to avoid environmental harm, resistance development, and residue problems. Biological control uses beneficial organisms such as antagonistic fungi, bacteria, or predatory insects to suppress pathogens or their vectors naturally. This eco-friendly approach is gaining importance in integrated pest management (IPM). Genetic control relies on breeding and deploying resistant or tolerant plant varieties that can withstand or limit disease development. Advances in biotechnology have enabled genetic engineering to develop plants with enhanced disease resistance. An integrated disease management strategy combines these methods based on disease severity, crop type, environmental conditions, and economic considerations, aiming for sustainable and effective control of plant diseases.

text: Synonym: One of two or more words or expressions of the same language that have the same or nearly the same meaning in some or all senses. Synonyms matter in language; we don’t want to repeat ourselves, and we want to mean what we say. They also give variety and fullness to our spoken and written language. Yes, for instance, instead of only having to say “happy” all the time, we might be able to say “joyful,” or “cheerful,” or “content,” if our specific context or our specific instance of that feeling allowed such. Relating Is it all or nothing when one word is used as a synonym for another word? I mean, “big” and “large” are the same thing, but even the word “large” carries a condom message that’s not so sexy. For example, we know that some words are “synonyms” with their own emotional “tone” (we call this “connotation”), even if they have the same meaning (denotation). So “childlike” and “childish” each point to being like a child, but one is positive and the other is negative. Below are 10 of the synonyms: Things to include (1) Good – Great, (2) Bad – Poor, (3) Good – Excellent, (4) Wrong - Incorrect, (5) Right – Accurate, (6) Easy – Hard, (7) Heavy – Lightweight, (8) Hard – Dense, (9) High – Tall, (10) Low – Stumpy. Remember a lot of synonyms are NOT truly synonymous, not even in other contexts! Or discover that “smart” and “intelligent” both relate to brain power, but that “smart” also collocates with “clothes.” And so choosing the right synonym depends on having a sense for not just the meaning of the word, but for the difference between word and word. So, in conclusion: synonyms, they’re one of the great things about the language, enabling writers, speakers and other wordy people (which should be all of us) to open our mind and be more creative, descriptive and precise.

text: Intersectionality (a term created by Kimberlé Crenshaw) is a tool for examining the ways that different aspects of identity (gender, sex, race, class, sexuality, ability, nationality, etc.) can combine to create simultaneously overlapping and interlocking systems of power and oppression. Intersectionality is central to activism by making sure that movements are inclusive, fair, and respectful of the variety found in the experiences of marginalized groups. Traditional feminist or civil rights movements too often focused experiences within a dominant group within those categories — white women or cisgender men — leaving out the needs of black, queer, disabled or poor people. In its place, intersectional activism acknowledges that pursuing justice in a one-size-fits-all manner causes many whose lives intersect at multiple identities to be unjustly left behind. For example, a campaign for gender equality that does not tackle racism might inadvertently ignore the unique obstacles to employment or health care that women of color face. Equally, advocacy efforts for LGBTQ+ rights that center solely on white cisgender gay men may neglect violence and economic marginalization against trans people of color. Intersectionality requires activism to be attuned to the ways in which different modes of oppression intersect and reinforce one another — and in the process, to produce more sophisticated policy advocacy, coalition-building and resource allocation. It also contributes to solidarity across movements — linking struggles against racism, sexism, ableism, homophobia, and colonialism — and when it has teeth, it holds organizations accountable to those most affected. Intersectional activism calls leaders to elevate voices from the margins, to create campaigns of inclusion and to ask how privilege operates within movements themselves. It also moves beyond the language of representation to that of structural change where structures that cause and are influenced by exclusion are critical targets of change. text: An antonym is a word that has the opposite meaning of another word. Gradable antonyms are words that fall on a scale and can be different degrees apart, like “hot” and “cold,” which also can be warm, hotter or cold. Complementary antonyms are synonyms whose meaning is the denial of the other word, such as life and death, such that something is often one or the other. Opposite words that tend not to enumerate straightforward meanings are (so called) relational pairs, like "buy" and "sell," or "parent" and "child." text: In pharmaceutical drug formulation, base and salt forms of a drug are different forms of a drug that affect the drug's solubility, stability, absorption, and bioavailability. Base is the unionized, or non-salt, form of a drug, usually an organic compound that has a relatively low aqueous solubility, and therefore poor bioavailability. Bases are frequently converted to salts due to better solubility (and other pharmacokinetic advantages) in acidic environments. A salt is a class of ionic compounds and they are made of cations and anions; it can be formed when a metal cation or positive ion comes in contact with a negative anion or a non-metal. Base drug like lidocaine is transformed into lidocaine hydrochloride salt, for better water solubility in the solution. In general, salts exhibit increased solubility in water, faster dissolution rates and increased chemical stability compared to their non-salt forms, resulting in more rapid and predictable absorption upon oral or parenteral administration. They also may enhance taste mask and formulation variability. However, salts may exhibit different pharmacodynamic properties or side effect profiles from those of their base forms. The selection of the base or salt form is typically based on physicochemical properties of the drug as well as desirable route of administration and therapeutic goals. Furthermore, salts can be characterized as acid salts or basic salts, depending on the base they are derived from. text: Expected value (EV) is a fundamental concept in probability and statistics that uses the probability distribution of a random variable to determine its long-term average or mean outcome. It represents the central tendency by weighting each possible outcome by the probability of its occurrence and then summing these weighted values. In essence, the expected value tells us what to anticipate as the average result if an experiment or random process is repeated many times. For example, in contexts like gambling or investment, EV is used to estimate average gains or losses over time, helping guide rational decision-making under uncertainty. Mathematically, for a discrete random variable with outcomes x? and corresponding probabilities P(x?), the expected value is calculated as E(X) = ? x? × P(x?). For continuous variables, it involves integrating over the probability density function. It’s important to note that the expected value may not always be an actual possible outcome but instead serves as a theoretical average that the results tend to approach over many trials, in accordance with the law of large numbers. Also known as the mean or first moment, EV is widely used across disciplines such as finance, insurance, economics, and risk analysis to assess the value of uncertain prospects by balancing potential outcomes with their probabilities. In summary, expected value provides a powerful and practical way to summarize the average behavior of a random variable, making it an essential tool in probabilistic reasoning and informed decision-making.

text: Load flow analysis, also known as power flow analysis, is a fundamental computational technique used to determine the steady-state operating conditions of an electrical power system network. It involves solving a set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from Kirchhoff’s laws to find key parameters such as voltage magnitude and phase angle at each bus, as well as real and reactive power flows in transmission lines and transformers under a given load and generation scenario. The primary purpose of load flow studies is to assess the system’s voltage profile, power losses, line loadings, and overall performance to ensure reliable and efficient operation. This analysis helps engineers evaluate whether the system can meet current and future load demands, optimize transformer tap settings, minimize losses, and plan system expansions or contingencies like line outages. Load flow is essential for system planning, design, and operation, enabling the identification of potential voltage violations, overloads, and bottlenecks. It is performed using numerical methods such as Newton-Raphson, Gauss-Seidel, or fast decoupled techniques, with the Newton-Raphson method being popular for its fast convergence and accuracy in large systems. The input data for load flow includes bus data (loads, generation, voltage specifications), line parameters (impedance, admittance), and transformer details. The outputs provide detailed information on bus voltages, power injections, line flows, and losses, which are critical for decision-making in power system management. Overall, load flow analysis is an indispensable tool in electrical engineering that ensures the power system operates within safe limits, supports economic operation, and maintains system stability under various operating conditions.

text: Gravitational potential energy (GPE) is the energy an object has because of where it is in a gravitational field.  It shows how much work was done to move the object from a reference point (usually very far away or the surface of the Earth) to its current position against the pull of gravity.  The gravitational potential energy between two masses M and m that are r apart is U = -GMm / r, where G is the gravitational constant.  The negative sign means that the potential energy gets lower (more negative) as the items get closer together, which means that work needs to be done to separate them.  The gravitational potential energy near the surface of the Earth is about U = mgh, where m is the mass, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and h is the height above the reference point.  This energy is a kind of stored energy that can be turned into kinetic energy when the object goes down in the field.  Gravitational potential energy is what makes things fall to the ground and keeps energy from being lost in planetary orbits and satellite motion.  For example, a satellite in orbit has both kinetic energy (because it is moving) and potential energy (because it is high up). The way these two types of energy interact affects how it moves.  GPE is also very important for hydroelectric power generation, geophysics, and figuring out tides and ocean currents.  Gravitational potential energy links the ideas of force, work, and energy in relation to gravity. This helps scientists and engineers study systems affected by gravity, from everyday life to astrophysics.

This type of drought is characterized by the lack of rainfall and is often the precursor to other types of drought. Agricultural drought occurs when there is insufficient soil moisture to meet the needs of crops and other vegetation, leading to reduced crop yields, plant stress, and potential crop failure. This type of drought is particularly concerning for farmers and agricultural communities, as it directly impacts food production and livelihoods. Hydrological drought involves a deficiency in surface and subsurface water supplies, such as rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and groundwater. This type of drought is characterized by reduced water availability for various uses, including drinking water, irrigation, and industrial processes. Hydrological droughts can have long-lasting impacts, as they affect water storage and supply systems that are crucial for human consumption and economic activities. Understanding the different types of drought is essential for developing effective strategies for drought risk reduction, preparedness, response, and recovery, enhancing the resilience of communities to these hazardous events.

For a long time, star clusters were thought of as members of two distinct types, specifically open and globular clusters (OCs and GCs, respectively). OCs are young, not very massive, faint, diffuse, and usually located in galactic disks, quite contrary to GCs, which are old, massive, luminous, centrally concentrated, and usually located in the halos of their host galaxies. However, this simplistic picture has been changing since the discovery of young massive star clusters (YMCs) in many galaxies, including the Milky Way (Ascenso et al. 2007a, 2007b), M31 (Barmby et al. 2009; Ma et al. 2009; Caldwell et al. 2009; Perina 2009; Perina et al. 2010; Hodge et al. 2010), M82 (McCrady 2009), and NGC 1140 (Moll et al. 2008). Located at a distance of ?780 kpc (Stanek & Garnavich 1998; Macri 2001; McConnachie et al. 2005), M31 (also known as the Andromeda galaxy) is the nearest large spiral galaxy in our Local Group of galaxies. Therefore, it constitutes an ideal laboratory for studies of star clusters in external galaxies. Based on Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Wide Field and Planetary Camera-2 (WFPC2) images, Krienke & Hodge (2007) suggested that there may be ?80,000 star clusters in the M31 disk. Most of these disk clusters are faint OCs. The number of GCs in M31 is much smaller. Barmby & Huchra (2001) estimated their total number at 460 ± 70, while Perina et al. (2010) arrived at ?530, with an additional ?100 YMCs. To limit the scope of this paper, we will focus on the GCs and YMCs in M31. Since GCs and YMCs are luminous, they are relatively easy to observe and study. Studies aimed at identification, classification, and analysis of the population of M31 globular-like clusters have been undertaken since the pioneering work of Hubble (1932; see, e.g., Vetešnik 1962; Sargent et al. 1977; Battistini et al. 1980, 1987, 1993; Crampton et al. 1985; Barmby et al. 2000). These studies have provided a large amount of photometric data in different photometric systems, including photographic plates, as well as CCD, photoelectric, and even visual photometry.

text: Mutations are alterations in DNA sequence that profoundly affect animal genetics by introducing genetic variation that serves as the raw material for evolution while simultaneously creating the potential for both beneficial adaptations and harmful genetic disorders that can impact individual fitness and population dynamics. These genetic changes occur through various mechanisms including point mutations where single nucleotides are substituted, inserted, or deleted, chromosomal rearrangements such as inversions and translocations, and larger-scale mutations involving gene duplications or deletions, with mutation rates varying among species, genes, and environmental conditions influenced by factors like DNA repair efficiency, exposure to mutagens, and replication errors during cell division. The effects of mutations on animal genetics range from neutral changes that have no observable impact on phenotype, to beneficial mutations that provide selective advantages such as improved disease resistance, enhanced metabolic efficiency, or better environmental adaptation, to deleterious mutations that reduce fitness through genetic diseases, developmental abnormalities, or reduced survival and reproductive success. Mutations contribute to genetic diversity within populations by creating new alleles that can be acted upon by natural selection, genetic drift, and gene flow, with some mutations having immediate effects while others remain hidden as recessive alleles that only express their phenotypic effects when present in homozygous conditions. The accumulation of mutations over time drives evolutionary processes including speciation, adaptive radiation, and the development of complex traits, while also creating genetic load within populations through the persistence of mildly harmful mutations that are not efficiently removed by selection. Modern understanding of mutation effects has been revolutionized by molecular genetics techniques that reveal how mutations can alter protein structure and function, disrupt gene regulation, affect developmental pathways, and create evolutionary innovations, while also highlighting the importance of DNA repair mechanisms, genetic redundancy, and population genetics factors in determining the long-term consequences of mutational changes for animal species.

text: Media serves as a powerful catalyst for gender empowerment by shaping societal perceptions, challenging stereotypes, and amplifying diverse voices across the gender spectrum. Through inclusive representation in films, television, news coverage, and digital platforms, media can break down traditional gender norms by showcasing women, non-binary individuals, and transgender people in positions of authority, expertise, and complexity beyond limiting stereotypes. Strategic content creation that highlights women's achievements, shares stories of gender equality advocates, and addresses systemic barriers can inspire audiences and drive social change. Media organizations can actively promote gender empowerment by implementing gender-sensitive reporting guidelines, ensuring equal pay and opportunities for all genders within media industries, and creating dedicated platforms that elevate marginalized voices. Educational media campaigns can raise awareness about gender-based discrimination, promote rights awareness, and encourage critical consumption of media content. Furthermore, the democratization of media production through accessible digital tools enables underrepresented genders to become creators rather than subjects, telling their own stories and controlling their narratives. When media consciously embraces its responsibility to promote gender equality, it becomes not just a reflection of society but a transformative force that can accelerate progress toward gender empowerment worldwide.

text: Technology has been a pivotal driver of social change in Bangladesh, reshaping economic structures, social interactions, and cultural practices while influencing stratification and mobility. The widespread adoption of mobile phones, with over 1.4 devices per person, and internet penetration exceeding 50%, has revolutionized communication, enabling rural and urban populations to access information, markets, and global networks. Mobile banking, like bKash, has transformed financial inclusion, serving over 70 million users, empowering small entrepreneurs and rural households to save, invest, and access credit, reducing poverty and fostering economic mobility. In agriculture, technologies like weather apps and precision farming tools have improved yields for smallholder farmers, though access remains unequal, favoring wealthier landowners. Socially, technology has bridged geographic divides, with social media platforms amplifying youth activism, as seen in student protests for safer roads in 2018, and fostering awareness of rights and gender equality. Educationally, online platforms and digital classrooms have expanded learning opportunities, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, but the digital divide excludes poor and rural students, reinforcing stratification. Culturally, technology has globalized lifestyles, with urban youth embracing streaming services and e-commerce, challenging traditional norms, though sparking conservative backlash. Economically, the tech sector, including freelancing and startups, has created jobs, contributing to the growth of a skilled middle class, but benefits skew toward urban, educated elites. Environmentally, technology offers solutions like solar energy, powering over 6 million households, yet industrial tech adoption contributes to pollution. Politically, technology enables transparency through e-governance but also risks surveillance and misinformation. While technology drives economic growth, social empowerment, and cultural shifts in Bangladesh, unequal access and systemic barriers like infrastructure gaps and low digital literacy ensure its transformative potential is uneven, reshaping society while deepening certain inequalities.

text: Gender-based violence refers to harmful acts directed at individuals based on their gender identity, gender expression, or perceived adherence to socially constructed gender norms. It is rooted in gender inequality, abuse of power, and harmful norms. Gender-based violence disproportionately affects women and girls, but can also impact men, boys, and gender-diverse individuals. It encompasses physical, sexual, psychological, and economic abuse, and can occur in private or public settings. Forms of gender-based violence include domestic violence, sexual assault, harassment, human trafficking, forced marriage, female genital mutilation, honor killings, and online abuse. This violation of human rights has profound short-term and long-term consequences for survivors' physical, mental, sexual, and reproductive health. It also carries significant social and economic costs for communities and nations. Gender-based violence is preventable through comprehensive approaches that address its root causes, including promoting gender equality, challenging harmful gender norms, strengthening legal frameworks, providing services for survivors, and engaging communities in prevention efforts. Efforts to combat gender-based violence require collaboration across sectors and the meaningful participation of all genders in creating safer, more equitable societies.

text: Brand consistency is imperative to trust building, identity and audience connection. When every touchpoint, from the website, packaging, social media posts, ads and customer experience communications all use the same logo, color palette, typography patterns, imagery style and tone of voice consistently, it creates a unified brand experience. This consistency conveys to potential viewers that the channel is professional, reliable and confident, which all helps inspire confidence and minimise confusion. As in cognitive psychology, repeated exposure to a consistent set (or semantically associated set) of features will lead to an increase in memory recall as well as emotional attachment, and over time the brand becomes associated with knowledge and trust for the consumer. Inconsistencies, like employing various versions of the logo, fonts, or color palettes, can weaken the brand’s credibility and trust, and the brand can come off as if it’s not organized or not to be trusted. Continuity also streamlines brand expansion, particularly for companies with a high number of products or touchpoints, making sure that at every push, the new piece fits the master brand without re-inventing the wheelemons. Internally, an instantiated set of guidelines allows teams and external partners—marketers, photographers and ad agencies—to execute on-brand communications without hand-holding or micromanagement. Consistency also breeds loyalty to the brand: when customers can rely on the visual and experiential and emotional prospect of the brand, they become emotionally dependent on it. In a loose market, constancy can make a brand walk away, however, and have a great deal to commend it. What’s more, brand consistency conveys professionalism and unity of purpose toward strategic objectives—be it redefining a brand, entering new markets or offering new products—because a strong brand has more run room for breaking into new categories using the equity and awareness that’s been built. In other words, consistency turns a pile of design elements into a system that builds trust, recall, and clarity — and helps you achieve a higher level of brand equity and business results.

text: The urea cycle, also known as the ornithine cycle, is a series of biochemical reactions that occur in the liver and are responsible for the conversion of ammonia, a toxic byproduct of protein metabolism, into urea, a less toxic compound that can be excreted by the kidneys. The urea cycle is essential for the maintenance of nitrogen balance in the body and the prevention of hyperammonemia, a condition characterized by elevated levels of ammonia in the blood, which can be toxic to the central nervous system. The urea cycle consists of five main reactions, which occur in both the mitochondria and the cytoplasm of liver cells: 1. Formation of carbamoyl phosphate: In the mitochondria, ammonia reacts with bicarbonate and two molecules of ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, catalyzed by the enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. 2. Formation of citrulline: Carbamoyl phosphate reacts with ornithine to form citrulline, catalyzed by the enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase. 3. Formation of argininosuccinate: Citrulline is transported to the cytoplasm, where it reacts with aspartate to form argininosuccinate, catalyzed by the enzyme argininosuccinate synthetase. This reaction requires one molecule of ATP. 4. Cleavage of argininosuccinate: Argininosuccinate is cleaved into arginine and fumarate, catalyzed by the enzyme argininosuccinate lyase. Fumarate can enter the citric acid cycle for further metabolism. 5. Formation of urea and regeneration of ornithine: Arginine is hydrolyzed into urea and ornithine, catalyzed by the enzyme arginase. Urea is transported to the kidneys for excretion, while ornithine is transported back to the mitochondria to participate in another round of the urea cycle. The urea cycle is regulated by several factors, including the availability of substrates (ammonia and aspartate), the levels of key enzymes, and allosteric effectors. Defects in the urea cycle enzymes can lead to inherited metabolic disorders, such as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and arginase deficiency, which can cause hyperammonemia and neurological symptoms. Treatment for these disorders often involves dietary restrictions, medication, and in some cases, liver transplantation.

text: The law of demand states that, all other things being equal, a higher price will lead to a lower quantity demanded, and a lower price will lead to a higher quantity demanded. This relationship reflects the underlying economic principle that as the price of a good increases, consumers will buy less of it because their purchasing power is reduced. There are some exceptions to the law of demand, such as for Veblen goods (luxury items) where higher prices can increase demand due to their exclusivity, and for Giffen goods where higher prices can increase demand due to a combination of income and substitution effects.

text: Forensic science is an essential aspect of the search for truth in criminal justice and the investigation of crimes through the examination of physical evidence using scientific methodologies and techniques. It is the one impartial, trustworthy source of information that can either support or undermine the testimony offered, associate a suspect with a particular crime scene and help recreate a particular course of events. Important aspects of forensic science are fingerprint analysis, DNA profiling, ballistics, toxicology, trace evidence, and strained forensics. Criminalists are typically dispatched to crime scenes in order to collect and preserve evidence, which is essential to avoid contamination or deterioration. Technological advances in digital forensic have revolutionized the criminal justice system, improving accuracy of and capability in analyses of evidence materials, and development of genetic databases which aid in identification of suspects or victims. Yet forensic science must be practiced under rigorous procedures in order to be credible and sustainable in a court of law. There's also hesitance, bias and job cost involved. In spite of those obstacles, forensic science continues to play a crucial role in contemporary criminal investigations, helping to forge a connection between law enforcement and the judicial system to serve justice.

text: Sociological research on belonging reveals how people who live in stigmatised places oppose these narratives for a number of reasons, including pride in their area, objection to negative portrayal by others and an enduring sense of community. Jensen and Christensen’s study of Aalborg East, for example, challenges ‘the assumption that underprivileged people as a general principle internalize or incorporate the degrading gaze of the dominant’ (2012, p. 90). However, social housing residents also highlight the effects of stigma, commenting on how neighbourhood representation impacts upon how they are seen by others (August, 2014; Garbin & Millington, 2012). Yet, ‘stigma’ is a contested concept (Parker & Aggleton, 2003; Pescosolido & Martin, 2015; Tyler, 2020) and one that is variously theorised. In a special edition of this journal (Vol. 66, Issue 4), for example, Tyler and Slater called for a more ‘thoroughly sociological understanding of stigma’ (2018a, p. 727), since most studies treat it merely as a ‘problem of social norms that can be challenged and alleviated’ (2018b, p. 11). Tyler has also suggested that an understanding of stigma as ‘embedded within the social relations of capitalism, and as a form of power entangled with histories of capitalism, colonialism and patriarchy’ is needed, since much writing focuses only on ‘individual experiences .?.?. in ways that occlude an understanding of stigma as a material force, a structural and structuring form of power’ (2020, pp. 8–9).

text: When we walk through the streets after a city festival, we try to avoid stepping into vomit, dog feces, or rotten remnants of food. When we act like this, we spatially avoid the disgusting stimuli. Although scientific literature often defines disgust avoidance by the avoidance of rotten food, dirty places, or sick people (Armstrong, McClenahan, Kittle, & Olatunji, 2014; Chapman & Anderson, 2012; Davey, 2011; Matchett & Davey, 1991; Oaten, Stevenson, & Case, 2009), it is rarely questioned if disgust stimuli already divert spatial attention. To the extent of our knowledge, there are only two behavioral studies that have delivered evidence that disgusting stimuli (like pictures and taboo sounds) direct spatial attention away from their location (Bertels, Kolinsky, Coucke, & Morais, 2013; Cisler & Olatunji, 2010). Both studies have used spatial cuing paradigms with the disgusting stimulus (sound or picture) as a lateralized presented cue, followed by a neutral target (either a ‘/’ and ‘X’ or a neutral sound beep) on the same (valid) or opposite side (invalid). In both studies (Bertels et al., 2013; Cisler & Olatunji, 2010: see healthy control group), reaction times to neutral targets invalidly cued by disgust were shorter than those after valid cues. This indicates that a disgust stimulus directs spatial attention away from the location of its origin. It is unclear, however, how spatial disgust avoidance proceeds over time. In the present study, we use the high temporal resolution of EEG to investigate how and when the attention shifts away from the location of the disgusting stimulus.

text: Internal energy is a term used in thermodynamics to describe the total energy of all the particles (atoms, molecules, ions) that make up a system, including their kinetic and potential energies. It includes the energy of their motion (kinetic energy) as well as the energy associated with their interactions (potential energy). For example, when we heat up a gas, we're increasing its internal energy by increasing the kinetic energy of its molecules. Internal energy is usually measured in units of joules.

text: Real-world surface reflectance, microscale appearance, and realistic lighting effects are too complicated to be described with simple analytic models. State-of-the-art data-driven rendering algorithms thus synthesize high-quality images from precomputed or measured reflectance data. Over the last decades, there have been tremendous advances in this field. For example, image-based rendering methods [1], [2], [3] generate virtual images from novel view directions by interpolating precaptured images. Since they assume no specific reflectance characteristics of object surfaces, the appearance of real-world objects can be faithfully rendered. Moreover, the pioneering work by Dana et al. [4] further introduced the bidirectional texture function (BTF) to model spatially varying reflectance distributions over a 2D surface. A BTF is a 6D function that combines textures and bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs) to account for the appearance of a 2D surface under various illumination and view conditions. Therefore, images rendered from measured BTFs can realistically exhibit complex lighting effects and detailed mesostructures of real-world objects, including the microgeometry of rough surfaces, self-shadows, and multiple light scattering. In addition to rendering applications, BTFs provide realistic texture models for computer vision applications, such as segmentation, robust visual classification, retrieval or illumination/view invariant methods dealing with images of textured natural materials [5].

text: We know that social media including Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube and TikTok has become more and more important to how to libraries and information organizations are getting content out to users, community engagement, and addressing equitable access. These communication channels allow libraries to communicate services, events, and materials in real time across many platforms to many different kinds of patrons, give patrons the quickest way of receiving information they may care about, share the fruits of librarians’ selective labor, whether book recommendations or faculty publications or highlight materials in an archive, and to have a directed and interactive conversation with patrons, whether this means doing a live stream or engaging with patrons via polls and hashtags. Social media campaigns can call attention to summer reading programs, digital literacy initiatives and other campaign targets, as well as encourage community participation through responses (likes, shares, comments), comments and direct messaging. Using analytics, libraries can monitor reach, engagement, and the demographics of the people served, and use that information to build on the most effective content and strategies. Digital social outreach is also facilitated for underserved or remote communities through digital social media, allowing equal opportunity regardless of location. But it takes disciplined policies on tone, privacy, moderation and accessibility — including visuals with captions and linguistic inclusiveness. Libraries can also offer misinformation tracking and digital media literacy instruction on social platforms, translating the authority of the institution into the trust of the public. Integrated within broader communications strategies, however, social media becomes a dynamic space of librarianship—a shared knowledge, a community, and an institutional currency.
