text: Women’s gender is an increasingly “hot topic” in labour organisations and unions as they are trying to be more inclusive and responsive to the varied demands of their members. Labour unions have been directed by men in the past and union work has focussed on issues affecting male industrial workers. But with the workforce increasingly diverse, unions have had to also grapple with gender discrimination in how workers’ rights are interpreted, represented and on-the-job conditions. For instance, women have long had to fight wage inequality, sexual harassment, access to promotions and childcare support. In response, many unions have created women’s committees or gender equality sections to address the longstanding problems. And these constituencies are frequently among those advocating for family-supportive policies such as paid parental leave, flexible working time and measures against sex-based violence and harassment in the workplace. They are also planting seeds to boost the representation of women among union themselves as leaders. Unions are taking on the gender gap through collective bargaining as well. Take, for instance, a growing number of contracts that include provisions written specifically to ensure equal pay or provide protections against sexual harassment and accommodations for menstruation and menopause. This is an important development, since collective agreements may constitute powerful tools for institutionalizing gender equality at the workplace. Also, labor unions are getting intersectional too, understanding how issues like race, class and sexuality intersect with gender. More of the nation’s workers who identify as LGBTQ+, like those at Samuelson’s work site, are also being acknowledged and shielded by unions. They have also partnered with feminists and human rights organisations to push for broader change, including the ratification of international labour standards such as ILO Convention 190 - which addresses violence and harassment in the world of work. Despite this progress, challenges remain. There is still a lot of sexism within the unions, and women — particularly women of color — are not well represented in union leadership. In industries which have been male dominated there can still be resistance to gender being part of the union agenda. In summary, there have been many improvements in gender and unions. Real parity will come through systemic change, representation and constant pounding to create a work place that provides women — and workers of all types — a safe, fair and empowering place to work.

text: A 95% confidence interval is an estimate interval, calculated from sample data, that 95% of the time will contain the true parameter of the population if the same experiment is repeated many times or if you took a different sample. This does not imply that, from one sample, there is a.95 probability that the true parameter lies within the interval; rather, it means that in the long run, 95% of the confidence intervals generated this way would contain the true value of the parameter. For instance, let us say, that we carry out a study to predict the Mean weight of students in a college, and after the study we get the 95% Confidence Interval of 60 kg to 70 kg. We would interpret this as being 95% confident that the true average weight of all the students is between 60 and 70 kg. Confidence here is a reflection of the estimation method, not directly the interval. The middle of the interval is the point estimate (similar to a sample mean) and the margin of error is a measure of how far the interval extends from the point estimate, in consideration to the sample size, data variability, and confidence level. The higher the percentage of the confidence level (e.g., 99%) the larger interval will be due to the fact that the greater the degree of confidence, the wider the range. On the other hand, smaller sizes or large variability lead to higher intervals, meaning worse precision. Confidence intervals are important in any kind of decision that an individual would make under uncertainty, whether one is testing hypotheses, considering the effectiveness of a treatment, or estimating an unknown parameter in the population. They enable researchers as well as policymakers to consider the strength and validity of the findings. What a 95% confidence interval is really saying is not that you’re 95% certain the population mean is in your interval, but that you’re 95% certain that in the long run, if you took many random samples and computed a 95% confidence interval for each sample, 95% of those intervals would contain the actual population mean.

text: Diffusion of Innovations Theory, developed by Everett Rogers in his 1962 book, explains how, why, and at what rate new ideas, products, or practices (innovations) spread through social systems. The theory posits that the diffusion process is not random but follows a predictable pattern, influenced by the characteristics of the innovation itself, the communication channels used, the time over which diffusion occurs, and the characteristics of the individuals within the social system. Rogers identified five key characteristics of an innovation that influence its rate of adoption: Relative Advantage (how much better the innovation is perceived to be than the idea it supersedes); Compatibility (how consistent the innovation is with existing values, past experiences, and needs of potential adopters); Complexity (how difficult the innovation is to understand and use); Trialability (the degree to which an innovation can be experimented with on a limited basis); and Observability (the degree to which the results of an innovation are visible to others). Innovations perceived as having a high relative advantage, compatibility, trialability, and observability, and low complexity, are more likely to diffuse rapidly. The theory also categorizes adopters into five groups based on their innovativeness: Innovators (the first 2.5%, venturesome and willing to take risks); Early Adopters (the next 13.5%, opinion leaders who embrace change early and influence others); Early Majority (the next 34%, adopt new ideas just before the average person, deliberate); Late Majority (the next 34%, skeptical and adopt innovations only after the majority have tried them); and Laggards (the final 16%, tradition-bound and resistant to change, last to adopt). Communication channels, both mass media and interpersonal, play different roles at different stages of the diffusion process. Mass media is effective for creating awareness, while interpersonal channels, especially opinion leaders, are crucial for persuading individuals to adopt. The time factor refers to the rate of adoption and the amount of time it takes for an innovation to spread throughout a system. Finally, the social system refers to the interconnected individuals or units that adopt the innovation, with its norms, structures, and leadership influencing the diffusion process. Diffusion of Innovations Theory has been widely applied in fields ranging from public health and agriculture to marketing and technology adoption, providing a powerful framework for understanding how new ideas and behaviors spread through populations.

text: One of the general challenges in this context is the communication gap between the domain expert and the system analyst [3]. As business professionals often do not feel confident in understanding and interpreting process models, the validation of these models frequently has to rely on a discourse in natural language. For data modeling, verbalization techniques have been defined to provide for a direct mapping from model to natural language [4], [5]. This verbalization concept has been emphasized as an important advantage for the discourse between system analysts and domain experts in the context of requirements engineering [6]. In contrast to data modeling, there are no sophisticated verbalization techniques available for process models. While lists of elements and arcs could be easily transformed into statements like “Activity A is followed by Activity B”, this is hardly the way a domain expert would describe and think about a process. The technical challenge here is to create a textual description that captures the full meaning ofthe process, yet also to organize the text in a way that is intuitive to the reader. The reason why a proper process model verbalization technique is still missing might be a result of the difficulty to meet this challenge. A process model verbalization technique has to serialize the nonsequential structure of a process model into sequential, yet execution-order preserving, text. In addition, it must be capable of analyzing the short and grammatically varying labels of process model elements and of annotating them with their semantic components like action or business object. Furthermore, the verbalization technique needs to handle optionality of certain pieces of information.

text: The rule against perpetuity is a rule in the law against property becoming defunct, and prevents property from being indefinitely unfree (the binding of property, e.g. by entail), and the dead hand that limits marketability of goods (especially real property). As per the rule under Section 14 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, immovable property cannot be transferred to an unborn person beyond the life of any person who is living at the date of the transfer and 18 years thereafter. The purpose of this rule is to interrupt the indefinite retention of land by dead people and to open up the opportunity for future generations to use and dispose of it. For example, if a testator or transferor attempts to make a will or transfer which provides that the property will go to someone 100 years in the future, it will be invalid under this rule. The rule also promotes the availability to the owner of property else than by gift a retention of economic utility, as well as preventing the creation of trusts or interest that take away from property the right of alienation. It relates to both real and personal property and is primarily concerned with executory devises or future estates. But there are exceptions, for example, public charities or religious trusts, in which the perpetuity rule does not apply. Under the English common law, the period of perpetuity was 21 years after the death of the last living person at the time of the transfer. This rule strikes a balance between the individual’s right to control the distribution of his property and the public interest in preventing property from going off the market. Its rigorous application may lead to the invalidity of wills, deeds, or gifts that try to create fimtres as deep in the future as possible. Thus, in the drafting of legal instruments, a lawyer must ensure that the possibility for a future transfer is not confined beyond the allowable period of perpetuity.

text: Logistic regression is the type of analysis conducted when you have one or more independent variables (IVs) that predict an outcome. In contrast, where linear regression estimates the value that a dependent variable will take based on a set of independent variables, logistic regression models the log-odds (that is, the logarithm of the odds) that a dependent variable will take on a certain value. The logistic function transforms the linear function of \(x\) into a continuous probability value between 0 and 1 (which is exactly what we need for classifications). It can be stated as: log(1?pp)=?0+?1X1+?2X2+...+?kXkwhere p = is the probability of the event; and ?0,?1,…,?k are coefficients derived using the data itself. Logistic regression estimates parameters via maximum likelihood estimation, searching for the parameter values that will make the observed sample as likely as possible. It gives odds ratios for the predictors, which tell you how much the odds of the event change for a one-unit change in a predictor. For logistic regression, one does not have to know the exact functional form of the coefficient distribution, but the predictors must be independent and the model correctly specified. It is the workhorse here in soft drink industry, medical remainder, social science, marketing and machine learning to binary classification such as disease diagnosis, customer retention and credit card provision. Generalized forms, such as multinomial logistic and ordinal logistic regression are for outcomes which are respectively more than binary category and having ordered categories.

text: Soft skills are personal attributes and interpersonal abilities that enable individuals to interact effectively and harmoniously with others, complementing technical or hard skills in the workplace. They include qualities such as communication, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, time management, empathy, adaptability, and conflict resolution. For example, communication skills involve clearly expressing ideas and actively listening, which helps avoid misunderstandings and fosters collaboration. Teamwork reflects the ability to work well with colleagues towards common goals, sharing responsibilities and supporting each other. Leadership is the capacity to inspire and guide a team, while problem-solving and critical thinking involve analyzing situations and finding effective solutions. Time management helps prioritize tasks to meet deadlines efficiently. Employers highly value soft skills because they contribute to a positive work environment, enhance productivity, and improve relationships with clients and coworkers. Unlike hard skills, which are technical and often learned through formal education, soft skills are developed through experience and self-awareness. For instance, showing empathy means understanding others’ perspectives, which is crucial in conflict resolution and customer service. Adaptability allows employees to handle change smoothly, and a strong work ethic demonstrates reliability and dedication. text: Hate crime is a criminal offense committed against an individual or group that is motivated by bias, prejudice, or hostility based on the victim's actual or perceived membership in a protected category such as race, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, or other legally recognized characteristics, representing a particularly harmful form of criminal behavior that targets not only individual victims but also entire communities and groups. These crimes are distinguished from ordinary criminal offenses by their underlying motivation, which involves animus toward a specific group rather than purely personal or economic reasons, making them particularly damaging to social cohesion and community relations. Hate crimes can encompass a wide range of criminal acts including physical violence such as assault, battery, and murder; property crimes such as vandalism, arson, and destruction of religious or cultural symbols; intimidation and threats that create fear and psychological harm; and harassment through verbal abuse, graffiti, or other forms of targeted behavior designed to terrorize victims based on their group membership. The legal framework for hate crimes typically involves enhanced penalties for underlying criminal offenses when they are motivated by bias, with many jurisdictions requiring prosecutors to prove both that a crime occurred and that it was motivated by prejudice against a protected group. The impact of hate crimes extends far beyond individual victims to affect entire communities, creating climates of fear, reinforcing social divisions, and undermining the principles of equality and inclusion that democratic societies strive to uphold. Law enforcement agencies have developed specialized hate crime units and training programs to improve identification, investigation, and prosecution of these offenses, while also working with community organizations to build trust and encourage reporting. Prevention efforts include educational programs that promote tolerance and understanding, community outreach initiatives that build bridges between different groups, and legislative measures that strengthen hate crime laws and provide resources for victims, recognizing that hate crimes represent attacks on the fundamental values of diversity and human dignity that require comprehensive responses from criminal justice systems and society as a whole.

text: A classic problem for theories of language acquisition is how learners avoid overgeneralization in the face of an ability to generalize. An example is our knowledge of restrictions on novel combinations of verbs and argument structures, as in the use of “carry” in the double-object dative e.g., ?“Carry me that”. Children go through a stage of producing overgeneralizations, yet eventually learn that certain combinations of verbs and structures are restricted. This “paradox” (Baker, 1979) has received a good deal of attention in the literature. Broadly, two different classes of solution have been proposed, one emphasizing increasing knowledge of the semantics of words and constructions (e.g., Pinker, 1989) which eventually provide constraints that block overgeneralizations, and one emphasizing the use of distributional statistics to make inferences about which generalizations are permissible (e.g., Braine, 1971). There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that generalization is constrained by both types of information and that grammatical learning can be characterized as graded rather than absolute (e.g., Ambridge, Pine, Rowland, Freudenthal, & Chang, 2014).

text: Maxwell's equations represent a cornerstone of classical electromagnetism, comprising four fundamental partial differential equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields interact and propagate through space. Formulated by Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, these equations unified previously disparate concepts of electricity, magnetism, and light into a single elegant theoretical framework. The first equation, Gauss's law for electricity, establishes that electric charges generate electric fields, with the electric flux through a closed surface proportional to the enclosed charge. The second equation, Gauss's law for magnetism, states that magnetic monopoles do not exist, meaning magnetic field lines always form continuous loops without beginning or end. The third equation, Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, reveals that changing magnetic fields induce electric fields, forming the basis for electric generators and transformers. The fourth equation, the Ampère-Maxwell law, extends Ampère's original law by incorporating the concept that changing electric fields can generate magnetic fields, completing the symmetric relationship between electricity and magnetism. Together, these equations predict the existence of electromagnetic waves that travel at the speed of light, leading Maxwell to conclude that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. This profound insight laid the groundwork for modern physics, enabling technological advancements from radio communications to radar and forming a crucial bridge to Einstein's theory of special relativity.

text: The process of recombination, crucial for various cellular functions such as DNA repair and viral integration, occurs at Holliday junctions (HJs), which are key intermediate DNA structures [3]. This study aimed to characterize Holliday junctions and PRDM9 sequence motifs associated with recombination events and their associations with common Microdeletion and Microduplication Syndromes. Specifically, HJs were found to be dependent on a common trinucleotide motif in the sixth, seventh, and eighth positions of the 10-nt sequence d(CCnnnN6N7C8GG), while PRDM9, a recently identified regulator of meiotic recombination hotspots, appeared to be dependent on the 13-nt sequence d(CCNCCNTNNCCNC) [3, 4]. The association of HJ/PRDM9 sequence motifs with Microdeletion and Microduplication syndromes was characterized, leading to the identification of 32 sequence variations of Holliday Junctions and 363 sequence variations of PRDM9. These variations could potentially serve as prognostic biomarkers for Microdeletion and Microduplication Syndromes. Importantly, our findings revealed that these sequences are not randomly distributed in the genome but are predominantly present in most Microdeletion and Microduplication Syndromes, suggesting a potential mechanism for the generation and occurrence of these syndromes.

text: Edward B. Lewis discovered in 1978 that some genes (coined later Hox genes) located in sequence on the chromosome in the cell nucleus are expressed in the same order along the Anterior/Posterior (A/P) axis of the developing embryo [1]. This correlation is called spatial Hox gene collinearity and since then it is intensively studied. This collinearity is remarkable because it connects geometric entities differing by about four orders of magnitude: at the microscale the size of a Hox cluster is variable with minimum about 100 nm (See Section 4). At the macroscale the size of a multicellular early embryo is of the order 1 mm [2]. Lewis originally noticed the collinearity in the Drosophila embryo but it was later found that this property is observed in many other animal clades, e.g., vertebrates [3]. The evolution of Hox genes is investigated in depth and it is believed that an ancestral ur-Hox gene was in tandem duplicated and several Hox gene clusters were formed in different clades [4,5]. The structure of the different clusters varies from species to species and the vertebrates possess well organized and compacted clusters [3]. It is therefore the vertebrates, and in particular mice and chicks, that are extensively studied and several models are proposed to explain the accumulated experimental findings of Hox gene transcription.

text: Women's suffrage had a significant and wide-ranging impact, radically altering societal standards, political environments, and views on gender roles.  The protracted fight for gender equality reached a turning point when women were granted the right to vote, upending long-held assumptions about their skills and place in society.  The suffrage movement was a social and political upheaval that gained traction in many regions of the world in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.  Women were able to formally influence laws, regulations, and government choices by gaining the ability to vote, which raised awareness of issues impacting underprivileged groups, women, and children.  As the number of female voters increased, electoral politics changed, frequently resulting in the election of female legislators and the emphasis on gender-sensitive legislation.  By challenging conventional gender norms and promoting women's rights to education, employment, and the law, the suffrage movement also sparked larger social transformations.  It disproved cultural presumptions about women's alleged inferiority and showed that they were capable of leadership and civic engagement.  Beyond politics, women's suffrage had a profound impact on cultural views of gender and increased recognition of women's autonomy in both public and private domains.  Later generations of women's rights activists were also influenced by the movement, which helped sustain continuous fights for anti-discrimination legislation, equal pay, and reproductive rights.  Women's suffrage contributed to the democratization of political systems in many nations, increasing their inclusivity and representation.  Voting rights are just one facet of a larger social revolution, as evidenced by the ongoing fight for complete gender equality in spite of recent advancements.  Women's suffrage, however, continues to be a landmark in history, signifying advancements in gender equity and the acceptance of women as equal citizens.  Its success gave women the confidence to actively engage in democratic processes, influencing laws and cultures to better represent a range of viewpoints.  In addition, the movement emphasized the value of group activism and societal change, laying the groundwork for subsequent equality movements.  All things considered, women's suffrage sparked a global social revolution that upended patriarchal systems and increased the opportunities for women to participate in politics and society.

text: The accounting equation is the basic principle that is used throughout the entire accounting process, and shows the relationship between a business’s assets, liabilities and equity. It is also known as the accounting equation or balance sheet equation, and the equation is such that Assets = Liabilities + Equity, which means all business assets are either funded (liabilities) by borrowing or by the owner's investment and retained earnings (equity). Assets are items that the business owns and are used for the operation of the business, such as cash, inventory, equipment, receivable (payment owed to the business). Liabilities are obligations or money the company owes to outsiders (for example, loans, accounts payable and mortgages). Equity is that part of the owner’s interest left in the business after deducted total liabilities from total assets, includes the owner’s investment in the business and earnings not withdrawn. This equation should always be in equilibrium in a manner which accurately depicts the financial position of the company. One or more of these parameters are always affected by any trade, to ensure the balance remains. For instance, if a business takes a loan from a bank, both assets (cash) and liabilities (loan payable) rise by the same amount and that maintains the equality. If the company makes a profit, the equity grows from retained earnings. The equation is also the foundation of the double-entry bookkeeping system. It smoothes out the numbers, and provides other stakeholders with a clear signal about how the company pays for its assets, in terms of debt and equity. Understanding the accounting equation is vitally important to anyone who is learning accounting, as the basis of double entry accounting, it provides the structure for recording and reporting on all financial transactions, and also allows for simple analysis of a businesses health, by showing where the business stands in terms of assets and liabilities.

text: The sensitivity to small input changes is a vulnerability. In one famous experiment, a road-sign recognizer was confused by an image of a stop sign on which small squares of masking tape were applied at strategic locations; instead of saying “stop sign” the network said “speed limit sign.” In the current state of the art, it appears small changes in sensor outputs that feed a neural network can produce significantly wrong outputs. What looks to a human like a small continuous change to the input looks to the network as a discontinuous jump to a new state. Fragility can also be seen when comparing neural networks. Suppose two neural networks are each trained from a different training set taken as a sample from a larger population. By all standard measures the two training sets are fair representatives of the population. When this is tried in practice, the two networks can respond with different outputs when shown the same input. Statistically minor changes in the training data can result in major changes of the output.

text: The philosophy of science is a branch of philosophy concerned with examining the foundations, methods, and implications of scientific inquiry, asking not only how science works but also what it ultimately means as a human endeavor. It explores questions such as what distinguishes science from non-science (the demarcation problem), whether scientific theories describe reality or merely provide useful models, and how evidence, observation, and reasoning justify scientific claims. Central to this field are debates about induction—whether general laws can be reliably inferred from limited observations—and about the nature of scientific explanation, causality, and prediction. Thinkers like Karl Popper emphasized falsifiability as a criterion for scientific validity, while Thomas Kuhn argued that science progresses through paradigm shifts rather than steady accumulation of knowledge. The philosophy of science also addresses the role of values in research, the objectivity of scientific knowledge, and the extent to which science can uncover truths about unobservable entities like atoms or black holes. Beyond abstract theory, it engages with specific sciences—such as physics, biology, or psychology—examining how their methods shape their conclusions. Ultimately, the philosophy of science provides a reflective framework for understanding how scientific knowledge is constructed, why it is trusted, and what its limits may be, ensuring that science is not only a technical enterprise but also a deeply philosophical one that shapes our worldview.

text: International Relations (IR) is an academic discipline of political science that focuses on the study of the structures, processes, and dynamics of relationships between actors at the international level (states and/or non-state actors) -- such as international organizations, non-governmental organizations, individuals, multinational corporations, and social movements. The discipline of IR considers how power, interests and norms condition diplomacy, conflict, cooperation, trade, law, security and development among nations around the world. It focuses on the large-scale propositions of the international system, such as anarchy, power distribution and systemic change, and at the small-scale interactions, such as negotiations, treaty-making and crisis management. Informed by a variety of theoretical traditions—realism, liberalism, constructivism, Marxism, feminism, postcolonialism, and others—IR scholars examine topics including war and peace, the balance of power, human rights, and sovereignty, as well as globalization, international political economy, and environmental governance. IR uses qualitative, case-studies, statistical, and historical-comparative methods to explicate issues such as alliances, sanctions, peacekeeping, international law, global governance, and transnational networks. It enquires into what is normative in the areas of ethics, identity and justice in our globalising world. IR shapes foreign policy, the promotion of international development, military defense, and international cooperation. (4) It prepares the profession and citizens to address global challenges like pandemics, climate change, or mass migration by engaging such global systems with greater knowledge. In the end, IR gives us a way to theorize and empirically test how different sorts of actors are able to pursue goals, wield influence, and suffer restraint in a world without central authority, and so it shapes the particular ways in which we understand the current terrain of world politics.

text: Radioactive waste is classified according to its radioactivity, and the risk it presents for human health or the environment. The most deadly is high-level radioactive waste (HLW), which is mainly spent nuclear fuel and reprocessed waste. This waste is of very high radioactivity and high heat load necessitating sophisticated cooling and shielding. It is a toxic material which must be carefully stored for hundreds to thousands of years in secure above or below ground storage facilities. Intermediate-level radioactive waste (ILW) is waste that is not high-level waste, comprising reactor components, contaminated tools and other items which have been contaminated with radiation sources, which have intermediate-level if radioactivity, and some waste from reprocessing HLW. ILW doesn't produce as much heat as HLW, but still demands shielding, and is generally put in shielded containers for storage. Its management usually involves storage in surface facilities or underground vaults, with eventual plans for disposal in geological repositories. Low-level radioactive waste (LLW) is the least hazardous, consisting of items like protective clothing, contaminated equipment, and medical waste. LLW typically has lower levels of radioactivity and doesn't require the same level of shielding as higher-level waste. It is often disposed of in near-surface landfills or shallow burial sites, where its radiation hazards decrease over time. While LLW poses less risk, it still needs to be managed carefully to avoid contamination. These distinctions guide the methods of handling, storage, and disposal, with each category demanding different levels of regulatory oversight and technological solutions.

text: Embedded system design is about to create a special purpose computing system, to be included in a special system and to carry out certain special tasks within a preddetermined time limits. Unlike general-purpose computers, which are used in various environments, an embedded system is designed for a single specialized application, often dedicated to a specific task, model, or one application. The later process involves choosing microcontrollers or processors, and designing hardware circuits as well as software or firmware that executes the operation, captures and process the data from the sensors and connect to the communication interfaces. These embedded applications have requirements such as deterministic behavior, low latency and environmental robustness. The design also addresses memory management, power optimization, real-time operating system (RTOS), and safety standards. text: Secondary growth in plants refers to the lateral expansion of plant organs, resulting in increased thickness or girth, primarily occurring in woody perennials like trees and shrubs. This process is mediated by two lateral meristems: the vascular cambium and the cork cambium. The vascular cambium, located between the xylem and phloem, produces secondary xylem (wood) inward and secondary phloem outward, facilitating both structural support and efficient transport of water, nutrients, and photosynthates throughout the plant. Simultaneously, the cork cambium develops in the outer cortex, producing cork cells that form the protective outer bark, safeguarding the plant against physical damage, pathogens, and water loss. Secondary growth enables plants to achieve substantial size and longevity, allowing them to compete effectively for light and space in their environment. The annual rings visible in tree trunks represent the seasonal activity of the vascular cambium, with each ring typically corresponding to one year of growth. This remarkable adaptive mechanism has been crucial for the evolutionary success of woody plants, enabling them to dominate many terrestrial ecosystems and persist for centuries or even millennia in some cases.

text: Robotic perception, the process by which a robot interprets sensor data to construct a meaningful representation of its environment, faces several significant challenges. A primary issue is sensor noise and ambiguity, where imperfect data leads to inaccurate models or false positives, especially in dynamic or cluttered environments. Robustness to variation is another critical hurdle; a perception system must reliably function despite changes in lighting, perspective, texture, and partial occlusion, which often degrades performance. Furthermore, achieving real-time processing of large sensor datasets, such as high-resolution video streams and 3D point clouds, is computationally intensive and demands specialized hardware and efficient algorithms. Finally, the challenge of semantic understanding—going beyond simple geometric mapping to actually comprehend the function, purpose, and relationship of objects in a scene (e.g., distinguishing a chair from a table, not just a collection of points)—remains a complex area of ongoing research necessary for true robotic intelligence and autonomy.

text: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that investigates the nature, origin, scope, and limits of human knowledge. It addresses fundamental questions such as "What is knowledge? Central to epistemological inquiry is the analysis of concepts like truth, belief, justification, evidence, and rationality. The discipline examines various sources of knowledge, including perception, reason, memory, testimony, and intuition, while evaluating their reliability and limitations. Major epistemological debates include rationalism versus empiricism—where rationalists like Descartes emphasize reason as the primary source of knowledge, while empiricists like Locke argue that knowledge derives mainly from sensory experience. Other significant discussions involve internalism versus externalism about justification, and responses to skepticism regarding the possibility of certain knowledge. Epistemologists also explore the structure of knowledge systems, considering foundationalist, coherentist, and reliabilist models. Contemporary epistemology extends to social dimensions of knowledge, contextual factors in justification, and the relationship between knowledge and understanding. By critically examining how we form and justify beliefs, epistemology provides essential frameworks for evaluating claims across all domains of inquiry, from everyday reasoning to scientific investigation and philosophical discourse.

text: Slip in an induction motor is defined as a difference between the speed of the rotating magnetic field in the stator and the actual mechanical speed of the rotor. It is an important part of the operation of induction motors. At the best, should the rotor rotate at precisely the same speed as the magnetic field, there would be no relative movement between the conductors of the rotor and the magnetic field, hence no electro-magnetic induction would take place. But in practice, the rotor must slip with respect to the magnetic field to generate a relative motion, which in turn results in current being induced in the rotor conductors according to Faraday’s Law. This current interacts with the magnetic field, which creates torque and causes the rotor to rotate. This speed difference is necessary and is referred to as slip. Slip is generally stated in terms of percentage of synchronous speed and increases with load. When there is no load resistance the speed will be close to synchronous—there will only be a small difference between the rotation of the rotor and the synchronized field. As the load increase, the speed of the rotor to drop slightly, and that which increase the slip of the rotor allowing more current to be induced in order to produce the necessary torque. S2 slip is commonly in the range of 2-6% at full load in most industrial immiscible squirrel cage motor applications. Slip not only makes torque but is also an important diagnostic parameter; high slip may indicate an overloaded motor or other internal problems. So, slip is a vital factor in accessing, designing, and preserving the performance and reliability of the induction motor systems.

text: Bangladesh is a predominantly ganges delta in the South Asian region located in the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers. It has a physical geography and human geography, being the region of the largest rivers that empty in it, which have constructed one of the most fertile and most densely populated regions in the world due to the sediments. The country is largely flat, and with an average elevation of only 10 meters above the sea level makes the policy vulnerable to flooding. The south is characterized by the presence of extensive coastline along the Bay of Bengal with several estuaries and tidally active rivers and the world’s largest mangrove ecosystem, the Sundarbans. There are hill tracts in the eastern and the southeastern regions as well (e.g. the Chittagong Hill Tracts).These areas are characterized by rolling hills and chills, rise to significantly higher elevations, and are home to a non-Bengali tribal community. Bangladesh has a sub-tropical monsoon climate characterized by wide seasonal variations in rainfall, high temperatures and humidity. Its vast river system, with hundreds of tributaries and distributaries, sustains agriculture and transportation and the fisheries, but also brings devastating seasonal floods and riverbank erosion. The physical terrain also features numerous wetlands, oxbow lakes and flood depressions known as haors that are important to biodiversity and livelihoods. Bangladesh’s geographical condition has influenced the country differently in terms of cultural and economic aspects, thereby creating opportunities as well as constraints related to natural disasters such as floods, cyclones, and river erosion. These conditions require adjusting land use planning, resources sustainability and disaster risk reduction to ensure the environmental and socio-economic stability for the future of the country.

text: The concept of evolution played a central role during the formation of academic musicology in the late nineteenth century (Adler, 1885/1981; Rehding, 2000). During the twentieth century, theoretical and political implications of evolution were heavily debated, leading evolution to go out of favor in musicology and cultural anthropology (Carneiro, 2003). In the twenty first century, refined concepts of biological evolution were reintroduced to musicology through the work of psychologists of music to the extent that the biological evolution of the capacity to make and experience music ("evolution of musicality") has returned as an important topic of contemporary musicological research (Wallin et al., 2000; Huron, 2006; Patel, 2008; Lawson, 2012; Tomlinson, 2013, 2015; Honing, 2018). Yet the concept of cultural evolution of music itself ("musical evolution") remains largely undeveloped by musicologists, despite an explosion of recent research on cultural evolution in related fields such as linguistics. This absence has been especially prominent in ethnomusicology, but is also observable in historical musicology and other subfields of musicology

text: Mendelian inheritance The basic rules of genetic inheritance first described by Gregor Mendel in the 19th century based on his experiments with pea plants, and the basis for much of modern genetics. Mendel’s studies showed that characteristics are transferred as distinct units, now called genes, that are inherited from parents to their offspring in a predictable way. Mendelian genetics states that organisms have two forms of each gene (two alleles), one form inherited from each parent, and that those alleles can be dominant or recessive. Recessive alleles are only expressed if both alleles are recessive, and the observable trait or phenotype is determined by dominant alleles that mask the effect of recessive alleles in a heterozygous genotype. From his observations, Mendel established several important laws. The Law of Segregation The two alleles for a trait segregate during the formation of gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele for each trait. This is why children get one gene from each of their parents. The Law of Independent Assortment states that a gene or alleles of one trait do not affect another genes alleles during gamete formation (unless the genes are located very close on the chromosome or on the same chromosome and linked, then the alleles usually move together; known as linked genes). Mendelian inheritance is seen in traits that are determined by a single gene with no variation in the alleles of that gene, as seen in flower color of pea seeds. These regularities in patterns make it possible to use a Punnett square to predict the genotypes and phenotypes of offspring given an understanding of the allele combinations in the parent. But in real-life genetics is not so simple because you have incomplete dominance (1 allele is not completely dominant over another and heterozygotes show some degree of both genes), codominance (when 2 alleles are expressed in ~ equal amount), multiple alleles, polygenic inheritance (traits affected by multiple genes) and effects of the environment. Notwithstanding these complications, Mendelian inheritance still provides key vehicle by which the passage of traits from one generation to the next can be understood. It is important for research in sickle cell anemia, breeding programs, evolutionary biology. Mendel’s laws have become enriched from the discovery of DNA, chromosomes, and molecular genetics, but the original ideas concerning the separation of alleles and independent assortment continue to permeate genetic research and applications. Invisible individuals: The legacy of Mendelian inheritanceMendelian inheritance is the science of genes: the inheritance of discrete units that separate (segregate) and assort independently from generation to generation, which govern how inherited traits of an organism that can be considered the most fundamental discovery of classical genetics.

text: Broadcast journalism is evolving rapidly due to technological advancements, shifting audience preferences, and the rise of digital platforms. One major trend is the increasing dominance of mobile and social media consumption, with news organizations prioritizing short-form video content tailored for platforms like TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts to engage younger audiences. Live streaming has also gained prominence, enabling real-time reporting and audience interaction. Another significant shift is the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in news production, from automated transcription and editing tools to AI-generated news summaries, enhancing efficiency while raising ethical concerns about accuracy and bias. The rise of immersive journalism, including virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR), is transforming storytelling by offering interactive, 360-degree experiences. Additionally, there’s a growing emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion, with newsrooms striving to represent underrepresented communities both in coverage and staffing. Podcasting continues to surge as an alternative news medium, with many broadcasters expanding into on-demand audio content to reach niche audiences. Monetization challenges persist, leading to innovative revenue models like subscription-based services, branded content, and crowdfunding. Meanwhile, the decline of traditional TV viewership has pushed networks to adopt hybrid models, combining linear broadcasting with digital-first strategies. Trust and transparency have become critical, with fact-checking and anti-misinformation initiatives gaining traction amid growing public skepticism. Lastly, the globalization of news means broadcasters are increasingly collaborating across borders to cover transnational issues like climate change and political conflicts. These trends reflect a broader transformation in broadcast journalism, where adaptability, technological integration, and audience engagement are key to staying relevant in a fragmented media landscape.

text: The Industrial Revolution, which commenced in Britain in the late 18th century and then spread to Europe and North America in the 19th century, was rife with a sea-change from agrarian economies to production by machines or industry. Fueled by technological advances — including the steam engine pioneered by James Watt, mechanized textile machinery and iron smelting procedures — industrialization took productivity and efficiency to great new heights. Factories took over from home production, which facilitated the concentration of labor and the possibility of mass production. Advances in transportation — the railroads, canals, steamships — made goods and people move faster and farther, and spurred continental and global trade. This led to increased urbanization as rural workers abandoned their land for work in the city, and as a result, new social landscapes. The Revolution and unprecedented wealthThe Revolution itself brought unprecedented wealth, but also difficult working conditions, employment of children, and public health issues – crowding and pollution. These difficulties inspired labour movements, social reforms and trade unions fighting for workers’ rights. Industrialization also spurred fresh communication breakthroughs, such as the telegraph and postal reforms, altering citizen’s way of understanding and coordinated time. Internationally, this drove European imperialism as industrial powers felt the need to exploit foreign colonies, subjecting colonized places socially and economically. Developments in the industrial revolution and changes in mass production formed the basis for the appearance of the modern capitalist consumer society. It had economic effects, such as the factory system, the accumulation of capital, and financial organisations. It was culturally permeative, and affected new forms of social division of the working class and the bourgeoisie, and the overall social formation of traditional rural life. Government responses were varied : Laissez-faire capitalism prevailed in the early stages, although industrial inequalities led to policies such as factory regulations, social housing, and public education. Ultimately, life during the Revolution sparked market changes which led to significant increases in living standards, diet, health, and life expectancy. Its inheritance continues to be at the root of the organization of modern society, of economy and technology and labor.

text: International non-governmental organizations (NGOs) play a significant role in shaping global policies, advocating for human rights, and addressing social, environmental, and economic issues across borders. They often fill gaps left by governmental entities, particularly in areas such as humanitarian aid, development assistance, and advocacy for marginalized populations. By mobilizing resources and expertise from various countries, international NGOs can effectively respond to crises, such as natural disasters or conflicts, providing essential services like food, healthcare, and shelter. Their ability to operate independently of government agendas allows them to champion causes that may not receive adequate attention, such as gender equality, climate change, and poverty alleviation. NGOs often serve as a voice for the voiceless, bringing attention to human rights abuses and advocating for policy changes at both local and international levels. Through campaigns, research, and grassroots mobilization, they engage citizens and influence public opinion, thereby pressuring governments and institutions to adopt more progressive policies. Additionally, international NGOs often collaborate with local organizations to ensure that their initiatives are culturally relevant and sustainable, fostering community ownership and empowerment. This partnership approach enhances the effectiveness of their interventions and helps build local capacity for future challenges. Furthermore, by participating in international forums and policy-making processes, NGOs contribute to the development of global norms and standards, influencing treaties and agreements on issues such as environmental protection and human rights. Their advocacy can lead to significant changes in legislation and resource allocation, impacting millions of lives positively. However, the influence of international NGOs is not without criticism. Some argue that their presence can sometimes undermine local governance structures or that they may impose external values that do not align with local cultures. Additionally, the reliance on foreign funding can create tensions and lead to questions about accountability and transparency. Despite these challenges, the overall impact of international NGOs remains substantial, as they continue to play a crucial role in addressing complex global issues, fostering international cooperation, and promoting social justice. Their ability to adapt to changing circumstances and leverage technology for outreach and advocacy further enhances their influence, allowing them to mobilize support and resources more effectively. In an increasingly interconnected world, the significance of international NGOs in shaping policies and driving social change cannot be overstated, as they strive to create a more equitable and sustainable future for all.

text: Summit diplomacy refers to high-level meetings between heads of state or government, typically convened to address pressing bilateral or multilateral issues, forge agreements, and foster personal relationships that can influence international outcomes. Unlike traditional diplomatic channels that operate through professional diplomats and embassies, summit diplomacy emphasizes direct engagement among political leaders, often in carefully choreographed settings such as international summits, emergency conferences, or bilateral state visits. These encounters are valued for their ability to expedite decisions, reduce bureaucratic obstacles, and generate media attention that can shape domestic and international perceptions. Summit diplomacy can take the form of scheduled events like the G7, G20, or United Nations General Assembly, or ad hoc meetings during crises or transitions. Leaders may leverage summits to signal policy shifts, demonstrate solidarity, or reset strained relationships, as seen in historic examples such as the Yalta Conference, the Camp David Accords, or recent US-North Korea negotiations. The effectiveness of summit diplomacy depends on the personal rapport between leaders, their domestic political mandates, and the institutional structures that implement decisions post-summit. While it offers opportunities for breakthrough initiatives and symbolic gestures, it also carries risks of miscommunication, lack of follow-through, and overly personalized decision-making detached from broader institutional accountability. In addition, summit diplomacy often reflects power asymmetries, where stronger states set agendas and frame discussions, sometimes marginalizing less influential actors. It can serve both cooperative and competitive purposes, being used to resolve conflicts or consolidate strategic advantages. Technological advancements and global crises have increased the frequency of virtual summits, making summit diplomacy more accessible but also more fragmented and time-constrained. Overall, summit diplomacy is a vital instrument in contemporary International Relations, enabling direct interaction at the highest level of government to address complex challenges, shape global norms, and influence international negotiations across political, economic, and security domains.

text: Abstracting is the process of producing a short description of a document, often an article in a scholarly journal, a report, or a document such as a book, video, or audiovisual, in order to convey the most important and relevant information to the user in the least amount of text, and to reflect its primary content and intent. Unlike indexing, which is based on a fixed vocabulary of subject terms, abstracts are written in natural language and may range in length from 100 to 300 words, summarizing elements such as research questions, approach/method, results, and implications. Abstracts may be descriptive, indicating the type of the work, the overall scope, the methodology, and the general results without any detail; informative, indicating the type of the work, the scope, the main results, and the conclusions; or: critical, describing the type of the work, the scope, the main findings, conclusions, and evaluations of the relevance, accuracy, or quality of the work. Abstracting helps users quickly form an idea of the document and decide whether to read the full document. Abstracts are present in bibliographic databases, journals and conference proceedings and function as the main access points for scholars to search huge data repositories. ABSTRACTORS need to be brief, clear and accurate without biasing the interpretation. In the case of digital publication, abstracts may help the performance of search engines because an abstract that gives context is used by many search engines to rank and filter search results. They are also a tool to improve the metadata accuracy and facilitate cross-disciplinary research and information exchange. In general, abstracting reduces bulky documents full of concepts and factual details into succinct and accessible summaries, which helps users to make relevance judgments and to move through information that is dense.

text: Human rights in international law constitute fundamental entitlements and freedoms inherent to all human beings, regardless of nationality, ethnicity, gender, religion, or any other status, which are protected through a comprehensive framework of treaties, conventions, and customary international law. The foundation of this framework was established with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, followed by legally binding instruments such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, collectively known as the International Bill of Human Rights. Protection mechanisms operate through multiple channels, including treaty bodies that monitor state compliance, special procedures of the Human Rights Council that investigate specific violations, and international courts like the International Criminal Court that prosecute grave human rights abuses. Additionally, regional systems such as the European Court of Human Rights, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights provide supplementary layers of protection. Despite these robust structures, challenges persist in implementation due to issues of state sovereignty, limited enforcement mechanisms, resource constraints, and political obstacles that sometimes undermine the universal application of human rights standards.

text: The ALARA principle, which stands for "As Low As Reasonably Achievable," is a fundamental radiation safety concept used in medical, nuclear, and industrial settings to minimize ionizing radiation exposure to workers, patients, and the general public. This principle mandates that all reasonable efforts must be taken to maintain radiation exposures as far below regulatory limits as is practically achievable, considering both economic and societal factors. ALARA implementation relies on three key protective measures: reducing the time spent near radiation sources, maximizing distance from these sources, and utilizing appropriate shielding materials. Unlike absolute safety requirements, ALARA represents a risk-balancing approach that acknowledges some radiation exposure may be necessary for certain activities while requiring continuous evaluation of whether additional protective measures are warranted. The principle is legally enforced in many countries through radiation protection regulations and requires organizations to establish formal radiation protection programs, conduct regular risk assessments, and implement engineering controls and administrative procedures to ensure radiation doses are kept to the minimum practicable levels without compromising the benefits of radiation-related activities. ALARA exemplifies the philosophy that radiation exposure should be avoided when possible and minimized when necessary, reflecting a commitment to protecting human health and the environment from unnecessary radiation risks.

text: Due to its high prevalence, obesity is currently considered an epidemic. Owing multiple documented interactions between the brain, gut and adipose tissue, obesity is nowadays recognized as a neurological disease, rather than a simple metabolic disorder. Hypothalamus is a key region of the brain, responsible for homeostatic control of appetite. Hypothalamus integrates peripheral signaling from the gut, adipose tissue and other areas involved in energy metabolism, with information from the brainstem and higher cortical centers, such as reward-related regions (Benarroch, 2010). Reward-related limbic pathways are involved in non-homeostatic regulation of food intake, and may override normal satiety signals, which may result in hyperphagia and obesity. Corticolimbic pathways terminate in the striatum (STR), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and orbitofrontal cortex (PC). Information about the taste, appearance, smell and texture of foods is sent to orbitofrontal cortex, a somatosensory structure playing a role in reward-related feeding (Rolls, 2011). Limbic and paralimbic cortex (both responsible for regulation of emotions) are primarily activated during hunger, whereas activation of prefrontal cortex results in satiety (Tataranni et al., 1999). Cerebral mechanisms that underlie eating behaviors and may eventually result in pathological overeating and obesity, are still poorly understood. Dopamine, a neurotransmitter modulating rewarding properties of foods, especially those rich in sugars or fat, is likely to be involved.

text: Climate resilience refers to the ability of individuals, communities, systems, and ecosystems to anticipate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from the impacts of climate change and extreme weather events. It encompasses a range of strategies and actions aimed at reducing vulnerability to climate-related risks while enhancing adaptive capacity. The concept of climate resilience recognizes that climate change poses significant challenges, including increased frequency and intensity of natural disasters, rising sea levels, changing precipitation patterns, and shifts in temperature, all of which can have profound effects on livelihoods, health, infrastructure, and ecosystems. Building climate resilience involves several key components, starting with risk assessment and vulnerability analysis. Understanding the specific climate threats faced by a region or community is essential for developing targeted strategies to address those risks. This may involve mapping vulnerable areas, identifying at-risk populations, and evaluating the potential impacts of climate change on local resources and economies. Another critical aspect of climate resilience is promoting adaptive capacity, which refers to the ability of systems and communities to adjust to changing conditions. This can include investing in infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather, such as flood-resistant buildings and resilient transportation networks. Sustainable land-use practices, such as reforestation and sustainable agriculture, can also enhance resilience by maintaining ecosystem services that support human well-being. Community engagement and participation are vital for building climate resilience. Involving local stakeholders in decision-making processes ensures that strategies are culturally appropriate and reflect the needs and priorities of the affected populations. Education and awareness campaigns can empower communities to take proactive measures, fostering a sense of ownership and responsibility in addressing climate challenges. Furthermore, climate resilience often requires collaboration across sectors and levels of government. Integrating climate considerations into policies, planning, and development initiatives ensures that resilience is embedded in all aspects of governance and resource management. Financial mechanisms, such as insurance and funding for climate adaptation projects, also play a critical role in supporting resilience efforts. Ultimately, climate resilience is not just about adapting to the impacts of climate change; it is about transforming systems and practices to create more sustainable and equitable environments. By enhancing resilience, communities not only protect themselves from immediate climate threats but also lay the groundwork for long-term sustainability and prosperity. In summary, climate resilience encompasses the capacity to anticipate, prepare for, and respond to climate change impacts through risk assessment, adaptive capacity building, community engagement, and collaborative governance, all aimed at creating sustainable and thriving communities in the face of a changing climate.

text: Kelvin waves are equatorially trapped, eastward-propagating waves, believed to be largely forced by latent heat release associated with convection in the troposphere. Kelvin waves can be observed in atmospheric wind, temperature and pressure fields and are a source of eastward momentum in the middle atmosphere (e.g. Sato and Dunkerton, 1997). A distinguishing characteristic of Kelvin waves is that the wave perturbation velocities are confined to the zonal and vertical components and there are no meridional perturbation velocities. The horizontal perturbation wind field associated with a Kelvin wave is thus linearly polarised. Kelvin waves can be classified in three distinct period bands. The ‘slow’ band contains waves with periods between 15 and 20 days. Such waves were first observed in radiosonde temperature and zonal wind measurements in the troposphere/lower stratosphere (e.g. Wallace and Kousky, 1968). These waves generally cannot propagate into the mesosphere. A 6–10 day period band of ‘fast’ Kelvin waves was characterised by the LIMS and UARS missions. These observations also revealed the ‘ultra-fast’ Kelvin waves with periods around 3 days (e.g. Salby et al., 1984; Canziani et al., 1994).

text: Big Data refers to the vast, complex, and rapidly growing volume of digital information generated by various sources, including social media, sensors, transactions, and digital devices. Its defining features are often summarized by the three Vs: volume, velocity, and variety. Volume signifies the enormous amount of data being produced daily, ranging from terabytes to zettabytes. Velocity refers to the speed at which data is created, processed, and analyzed, requiring real-time or near-real-time handling in many cases. Variety indicates the wide range of data types and formats, such as structured data from databases, semi-structured data like XML or JSON, and unstructured data like videos, images, and text. Big Data is not merely about size but also about complexity, requiring advanced tools and techniques for storage, management, and analysis. Its significance lies in enabling organizations, including libraries and information centers, to uncover patterns, trends, and insights that were previously inaccessible. In the context of libraries, Big Data can help improve collection development, enhance user services, and support personalized recommendations by analyzing user behavior and preferences. It also plays a crucial role in data-driven decision-making, research, and policy formulation. Technologies such as distributed storage systems like Hadoop and Spark facilitate processing large datasets efficiently. Big Data analytics involves extracting meaningful information from massive datasets using machine learning, artificial intelligence, and data mining techniques. These insights can be used to optimize services, predict user needs, and develop innovative information products. However, managing Big Data also raises concerns about privacy, security, and ethical use of information. Libraries and information professionals are increasingly leveraging Big Data to stay competitive and relevant in an era characterized by information abundance. Overall, Big Data represents a transformative force across sectors, including information science, by offering unprecedented opportunities to understand, predict, and serve users more effectively.

text: Wireframes and mockups are essential tools in the design process, each serving distinct roles in transforming ideas into functional interfaces. Wireframes are low-fidelity, schematic renditions of a design layout that focus solely on structure and content hierarchy, using simple shapes, placeholders, and grayscale blocks to represent elements like headers, navigation, images, forms, and text. They help design teams and stakeholders align on information architecture, functionality, and user flow without getting distracted by colors or styling. This stage is about defining what goes where, how users navigate screens, and where primary actions should appear. Wireframes can be sketched on paper, drawn in digital tools like Balsamiq, or created as grayscale artboards in Figma or Sketch. Mockups, on the other hand, are mid-to-high fidelity visual designs that build on wireframes by incorporating actual typography, UI components, color palettes, imagery, and spacing. Wireframes are rough sketches that can be drawn on paper, or in a digital tool like Balsamiq (or as grayscale artboards on Figma / Sketch). Mockups are medium to high fidelity visuals that take wireframes a step further by adding real typography, actual UI elements, colors, images and sometimes even spacing. They are a fixed preview of the end interface and lack interactive behavior. Mockups are an essential way to iterate on visual balance, brand alignment, and aesthetic detail well before development begins — it also provides the flexibility for the client and stakeholders to imagine how everything looks once it is done. Design ? Designers produce mockups in tools like Adobe XD, Sketch, or Figma (where they use design systems/style libraries to maintain consistency). Whereas wireframes confirm the structure and interaction logic, mockups sweeten things up, disclosing the look and feel. They are both collaborative tools — wireframes for feedback on usability upfront, mockups to prep developers for styling and assets. The together depict a design progression from just functional (wireframe) to visual polish (mockup), ensuring that the user experience and brand identity are all taken care of before diving into development.

text: There is clear evidence that ethical considerations have a major influence on zoological research—how animals are studied, manipulated and looked after—reflecting internationally acknowledged principles that science should come at no cost to the animals involved. Scientists are now required to work under tight ethical regulations which focus on minimizing injury, distress, and suffering caused to the animals, be they wild or captive. This is, for example, the case for obtaining adequate permissions, using non-disruptive or less disruptive methods and only using invasive procedures when they are justified by clearly specified research questions. Research proposals are reviewed by oversight committees within the institution (e.g. IACUC) in order to meet the ethics and legal requirements of any study involving animals. Very importantly, the 3Rs– Replacement, Reduction and Refinement also determines the design of research. Researchers are required to use alternatives to animals where available, to minimize the number of animals used, and to refine procedures to minimize animal suffering. Animal welfare considerations also apply to conservation objectives, researchers having to weigh the value of data against potential disturbance to either habitats or animal populations42,43,44. In field research, ethical behavior includes respect for local communities, ecosystems, or species, often requiring the involvement of local knowledge and the collaboration with indigenous peoples. Some of the most invasive studies have been based here and abroad, where a tradition of wildlife tracking necessitated autopsies and surgeries of all shapes and sizes, from snakes to caracals, jackals to leopards (The Cut previously chronicled how animals killed in zoos are frequently embalmed for use in university dissection).“What had been viewed as traditional research has been evolving under the influence of technological advancement, in a way that hopefully reduces the requirement for direct interference with other animals,” said Paul O’Donoghue, a zoologist at the University of Wolverhampton in England, whose work with collars and camera traps in Africa has been cited as a beneficial substitute. Public awareness and attention for animal rights has also pushed towards institutions and researchers being more transparent and accountable in their activities. In the end, ethical issues are not challenges that must be overcome but fundamental aspects of sound zoological research that underpin a relationship of respect between humans and animals and that help to ensure that the scientific enterprise is always contributing to conservation and understanding.

text: Anywhere on or close to the Earth's surface, the Global Positioning System (GPS), a satellite-based navigation system, may offer exact location and time information.  GPS receivers that people or devices use to pinpoint their precise location through a process known as trilateration, a constellation of at least 24 satellites orbiting the Earth, and ground control stations that oversee and manage satellite operations make up this system.Each GPS satellite continuously transmits signals that contain its location and the exact time the signal was sent. A GPS receiver on the ground picks up signals from at least four satellites and calculates its own position by measuring the time it takes for each signal to arrive. The result is highly accurate geographic coordinates—latitude, longitude, and altitude—that can be used for navigation and mapping. GPS technology has revolutionized multiple fields: in transportation, it guides vehicles, airplanes, and ships, improving route planning and safety; in agriculture, it enables precision farming by helping farmers optimize planting, irrigation, and harvesting, thus increasing productivity while reducing resource waste. Environmental scientists use GPS to map terrain, track wildlife movements, and monitor changes in ecosystems. Disaster response teams rely on GPS for locating affected areas and coordinating relief operations efficiently. Surveyors and construction professionals use GPS to measure land parcels and guide infrastructure projects with high accuracy. Moreover, everyday technology such as smartphones and wearable devices use GPS for location-based services, including navigation apps, fitness tracking, and emergency assistance. Because GPS is so widely available and dependable, it has become an essential tool in today's world, assisting users in navigating challenging environments, increasing productivity, and enhancing safety in a variety of applications.

text: Graphs can be stored in memory generally by two primary data structures: adjacency matrix and adjacency list, possessing some advantages based on the form and density of the graph. An adjacency matrix is a 2D array of V x V vertices, where V is the number of vertices in the graph and the value of an entry Ai is 1 if there is an edge from vertex i to vertex j, otherwise 0. If the graph is undirected, then the adjacency matrix is a symmetric matrix, i.e., Ai = Aj. Such a representation supports O(1) time edge exist query between any two vertices, but occupies O(V²) space, where V is number of vertices, that may be infeasible to store when the graph is large and sparse with nonexistent edges. By contrast, an adjacency list is in some ways the complementary representation to an adjacency matrix expressed as an array or list of lists where the offsets are the starting point of each linked list, and the second element of the list points to the head of linked list and are used to maintain a list of "adjacent" pairs, it is space-efficient at O(V + E) (recall that V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges) but may be less time-efficient to a certain extent. This method is efficient for sparse graphs, being based on storing only present edges, but accessing given edge may require more than O(1) operations (typically O(k), where k is a number of neighbors of a vertex). In addition to these, graphs may be represented via the edge list; which is a listing of all edges or as a set of vertex pairs, but adjacency queries are less efficient. That's because the representation depends on applications: adjacency matrix is good for dense graph, fast edge looking up while adjacency list is good for sparse graph, efficient neighbors visiting. In-memory, adjacency lists are commonly represented using linked lists or dynamic arrays holding the corresponding vertices and adjacency matrices are represented as 2D arrays. In general, these representations allow graph algorithms such as BFS, DFS, shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms to access and modify the graph data structure in time proportional to the size and connectivity of the graph.

text: Since deciding whether or not to take a risk can have large consequences for personal and professional ventures, risk-taking propensity is examined in multiple scientific fields, such as neuroscience, psychology, criminology, economics, and management. For this purpose, several (computerized) behavioral tasks for measuring the construct have been developed. Well-known tasks include the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT; Bechara, Damasio, Damasio, & Anderson, 1994), the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART; Lejuez et al., 2002), the Cambridge Gambling Task (CGT; Rogers et al., 1999), and the Game of Dice Task (GDT; Brand et al., 2005). Recently, Figner, Mackinlay, Wilkening, and Weber (2009) introduced a new computer task to measure risk-taking propensity: the Columbia Card Task (CCT). In the CCT, participants turn virtual cards from a 32-card array. Most of these cards are win cards, which earn participants points. However, a small number of cards are loss cards, which make them lose points. In every trial, participants are given three information parameters to help them decide how many cards to turn: (1) the number of points they gain when turning a win card, (2) the number of points they lose when encountering a loss card, and (3) the number of loss cards present in the trial. The way in which cards are turned differs across task versions. In the so-called “hot” CCT, participants turn the cards one by one (thereby accumulating points) until they voluntarily stop and cash the points or until they turn a loss card, at which point the specified loss amount is subtracted from the points earned (and the remainder is cashed). In the “cold” CCT, however, participants indicate at the start of every trial how many cards they want to turn, after which the computer determines the trial's outcome, unseen by the participant.
