text: Enriched uranium is uranium with a higher percentage of isotope 235 than natural uranium (which consists mainly of isotope 238; about 99.3% of natural uranium is isotope 238, 0.7% is isotope 235). There are numerous enrichment techniques that include gaseous diffusion and gas centrifuge, with it being the latter being the most widely used. In gaseous diffusion, Uranium hexafluoride (UF6) gas travels through barriers with small holes, and since the U-235 molecules are lighter than the U-238 molecules, they can pass through the holes slightly faster, further separating the U-235 from the U-238 in stage after stage. This process, however, is energy-intensive. Gas centrifuge enrichment relies on quickly spinning canisters to segregate isotopes by a fraction of a mass unit; U-235 groups close to the middle, and U-238 near the outer parts. This method is more efficient and has largely replaced gaseous diffusion. Other methods include laser isotope separation and aerodynamic processes, though these are less widespread. Enrichment levels vary by application: commercial reactors typically require 3-5% U-235, research reactors sometimes higher, and weapons-grade uranium exceeds 90%. Enrichment technology requires careful control and international safeguards due to proliferation concerns. The process plays a critical role in the nuclear fuel cycle, enabling reactors to achieve a sustained chain reaction and efficient power generation.

text: Since its discovery in the early eighties AIDS, the clinical result of infection by HIV has caused over 25 million deaths worldwide [1]. The global reach and fatal prognosis of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection have emphasised the need for effective antiretroviral therapies. While several effective treatment regimens have been devised, involving inhibitors that target multiple viral proteins [2], the emergence of mutations in these proteins is a contributing factor to the eventual failure of treatment. Understanding the interactions of inhibitory drugs and viral proteins may in the future allow us to tailor treatment to individual patients and develop more effective therapies. The essential role played by reverse transcriptase (RT) in the replicative cycle of HIV has made it an attractive target for HIV/AIDS therapy. The enzyme uses the single stranded RNA viral genome as a template to create a single strand of DNA which is in turn used as a template to create a double stranded DNA (dsDNA) copy of the genome. The dsDNA copy is then suitable for integration into the chromosomes of human host cells. HIV-1 RT is a multifunctional enzyme with distinct polymerase and RNaseH active sites. At the polymerase active site incoming nucleotides matching the template RNA or DNA are incorporated into the growing complementary DNA chain. The RNaseH active site catalyses the breakdown of the RNA genome, freeing the DNA copy to act as a template for the creation of the final double stranded DNA genome. Inhibition of either enzymatic activity compromises viral replication. Two classes of inhibitor are currently in clinical use, called nucleotide analogue RT inhibitors (NRTIs) and non-nucleoside analogue RT inhibitors (NNRTIs).

text: Penicillin exerts its bactericidal effects through selective inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis by targeting peptidoglycan cross-linking enzymes, specifically binding to and inactivating penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that are essential for the final stages of bacterial cell wall construction in actively dividing bacteria. The mechanism begins with penicillin's beta-lactam ring forming a covalent bond with the serine residue in the active site of transpeptidase enzymes, which are responsible for cross-linking peptidoglycan chains through the formation of peptide bridges between adjacent glycan strands in the bacterial cell wall. This irreversible acylation of transpeptidases prevents the completion of peptidoglycan synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of linear peptidoglycan chains that cannot be properly cross-linked to form the rigid, protective cell wall structure required for bacterial survival. The structural similarity between penicillin and the natural substrate D-alanyl-D-alanine allows the antibiotic to act as a suicide inhibitor, mimicking the terminal dipeptide of peptidoglycan precursors and successfully competing for the enzyme's active site. Without proper cross-linking, the bacterial cell wall becomes structurally compromised and unable to withstand the high internal osmotic pressure of the bacterial cytoplasm, leading to cell lysis and death, particularly during active cell division when new cell wall synthesis is most critical. Penicillin's selectivity for bacterial cells stems from the fact that human cells lack peptidoglycan cell walls, instead possessing flexible plasma membranes that do not require the rigid structural support provided by cross-linked peptidoglycan networks. The antibiotic is most effective against actively growing bacteria because cell wall synthesis is most active during cell division, while dormant or slowly growing bacteria may be less susceptible due to reduced metabolic activity and minimal cell wall turnover. This mechanism explains why penicillin is particularly effective against gram-positive bacteria, which have thick peptidoglycan layers, and why resistance can develop through beta-lactamase production, altered PBPs, or reduced antibiotic penetration.

text: The standard error of an estimator quantifies the amount of variability or uncertainty associated with the estimate across different samples. It is essentially the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the estimator, providing a measure of how much the estimated value would vary if the sampling process were repeated multiple times under identical conditions. The standard error is important because it reflects the precision of the estimator: the smaller the standard error, the more stable and reliable the estimate; conversely, a larger standard error indicates greater variability and less confidence in the estimate. For example, if the sample mean is used to estimate the population mean, the standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as the standard deviation of the sample divided by the square root of the sample size. This relationship shows that increasing the sample size reduces the standard error, thereby increasing the precision of the estimate. The standard error plays a crucial role in constructing confidence intervals, where it is combined with the estimated parameter to determine a range within which the true parameter is likely to fall with a specified probability. It is also used in hypothesis testing to assess the significance of an observed effect by comparing the estimate to its standard error. In essence, the standard error acts as a gauge of the estimator’s accuracy, informing researchers about the confidence they can place in their estimates. It accounts for the inherent variability of data and the sample size, making it a vital component in the inferential process. The calculation of standard errors varies depending on the type of estimator and the underlying distribution but generally involves known formulas based on the data's variability and sample size. Accurate estimation of the standard error is essential for valid statistical inference, as underestimating or overestimating it can lead to incorrect conclusions. Overall, the standard error provides a meaningful summary of the uncertainty in an estimate, guiding analysts in assessing the reliability and precision of their results and supporting robust decision-making in research and applied statistics.

text: Giving a speech in English effectively involves careful preparation, clear and engaging delivery, and a strong connection with the audience. The first step in preparing an effective speech is to define the purpose and main message. This involves understanding the topic, the audience, and the desired outcome of the speech. Whether the goal is to inform, persuade, inspire, or entertain, having a clear purpose will guide the content and structure of the speech. Next, organize the speech into a coherent and logical structure, typically including an introduction, body, and conclusion. The introduction should capture the audience's attention, provide context for the topic, and present the main message or thesis. This can be achieved through a compelling anecdote, a surprising fact, a thought-provoking question, or a relevant quote. For example, "Imagine a world where technology and humanity coexist in perfect harmony. Today, I want to explore how we can achieve this balance and the benefits it can bring to our society." This introduction sets the stage for the speech, engages the audience, and outlines the main topic. The body of the speech should present the main points, evidence, and examples that support the thesis. Each main point should be clearly stated and elaborated with specific details, stories, or data. Using transitions between points helps to guide the audience through the speech and maintain a logical flow. For example, "Having discussed the potential of technology, let's now consider the ethical implications and how we can address them responsibly." This transition connects the previous point to the next, ensuring a smooth and coherent progression. The conclusion should summarize the main points, reinforce the thesis, and provide a memorable closing. This can involve a call to action, a thought-provoking statement, or a powerful quote. For example, "In conclusion, the balance between technology and humanity is not only possible but essential for our future. Let us embrace this challenge and work together to create a world where both can thrive. Thank you." text: An inflorescence, defined as the complete flower head of a plant including its stems, stalks, bracts, and flowers, is systematically categorized into distinct types based on its architectural pattern and the developmental sequence of its floral components. The primary classification distinguishes between racemose (indeterminate) and cymose (determinate) structures. In a racemose inflorescence, the main axis exhibits continuous growth, producing flowers laterally with the maturation gradient proceeding from the base towards the apex or from the periphery inwards in centripetal forms; common manifestations of this pattern include the simple raceme (e.g., lupine), the spike with sessile flowers (e.g., wheat), the corymb with a flat-topped appearance due to elongated lower pedicels (e.g., candytuft), and the umbel where all pedicels emanate from a single apex (e.g., onion). Conversely, a cymose inflorescence is characterized by the termination of the main axis in a flower, with subsequent flowering confined to lateral buds, resulting in a centrifugal blooming pattern; specific forms include the simple dichasium, which generates two lateral branches simultaneously (e.g., baby's breath), and the monochasium, which produces a single branch per node. Beyond these fundamental categories, specialized compound structures exist, such as the panicle, a branched raceme, and the highly complex composite head found in the Asteraceae family (e.g., sunflower), which comprises numerous small florets arranged on a receptacle, often mimicking a single flower to enhance pollinator attraction. This morphological diversity represents a critical evolutionary adaptation, directly influencing reproductive efficacy and ecological success.

text: Cell membrane, or plasma membrane, is an essential and dynamic structure surrounding all living cells, which presents a selective barrier and separates the cell's internal from its external environment, while at the same time controlling the traffic of particles into and out of the cell. The cell membrane consists mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with two layers of phospholipid molecules in which the tails are directed towards the interior of the cell and both faces are hydrophilic and point towards the inside and outside of the cell. Such arrangement gives mobility and pliability to the membrane, so that it can reseal itself and article accordingly. Scattered throughout this bilayer are a number of proteins, which have diverse functions- as channels and carriers to let ions and other molecules that cannot pass readily through the lipid bilayer, as receptors to sense chemical changes in the environment, as enzymes that can catalyse reactions, and as structural proteins that give the cell its shape. The membrane also has cholesterol, which increases its flow ability and stability - especially at various temperatures. Carbohydrate chains are also attached to proteins and lipids on the exterior surface of the cell membrane to make glycoproteins and glycolipids which are involved in cell recognition, communication and adhesion707. The cell membrane basically controls the balance of matter in the cell- it determines what comes in and what goes out, so that necessary nutrients can come in, and waste and potentially harmful substances can't. It becomes selectively permeable via only passive transport (including diffusion and osmosis, which don't require energy) and active transport (which does require energy). The receptors of the membrane can elicit a response to hormonal or environmental signals and this will trigger the intracellular pathways that will affect cell activities. The cell membrane is also capable of communicating with other cells, and the extracellular matrix, which allows for the formation of tissues, immune responses, and repair. Specialized structures such as microvilli in some cells that increase the surface available for absorption, while others form junctions for communication and for attachment. In the end, the composition of the cell membrane as a fluid three-tiered phospholipid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol, and carbohydrates, is the basis for its crucial roles in protection, communication, transport, as well as in maintenance of the cells´ internal environment, which makes it indispensable for the survival and function of all living cells.

text: X-ray spectra demonstrate that many compact sources are viewed through partially ionized gas. This gas manifests itself as a rich array of lines and bound–free features in the 0.1–10 keV energy range. The existence of this "warm absorber" gas and the fact that it often shows Doppler shifts indicating outflows, has potential implications for the mass and energy budgets of these sources. These features have been used to infer mass outflow rates for many accreting sources, notably those in bright, nearby active galactic nuclei (AGNs; Turner & Miller 2009; Crenshaw et al. 2003; Miller et al. 2009; Krongold et al. 2003; Kaastra et al. 2011; Kaspi et al. 2002). Intrinsic to the problem is the fact that the gas is not spherically distributed around the compact object. If it were, resonance lines would be absent or would have a P-Cygni character. P-Cygni profiles are observed in X-ray resonance lines from the X-ray binary Cir X-1 (Schulz et al. 2008); most AGNs do not show this behavior clearly. Understanding the quantity of warm absorber gas, its origin and fate, are key challenges. Interpretation of absorption spectra is often based on the assumption that the residual flux in the line trough is solely due to finite optical depth or spectral resolution. That is, the effect of filling in by emission is neglected.

text: Ethically, moral questions are central in criminology research to protect the rights, dignity, and well-being of research participants and to preserve the integrity of the research process epistemologically. Since some are themselves vulnerable members of the society that are being targeted, ethical standards will guard against the exploitation, the coercion or the harm. Informed consent is a basic ethical obligation of researchers to explain to participants the aims, methods, risks, and benefits of a study and of participants to make a voluntary decision to participate or not to participate. Promises of confidentiality and non-identification by law enforcement are a way to alleviate the fears or identification (and demonization) as lawbreakers or as objects of criminal activity, the latter of which may be threatened by stigma, retaliation or legal revenge. They should not deceive unless it is absolutely necessary, and only when it is “eminently defensible by its value” should they do so, followed by debriefing participants. Proposals are reviewed for ethical standards by such groups as ethical review boards or institutional review boards. And it is also the duty of researchers to report findings truthfully – not to be bias and culture-sensitive pecksniffs! The obedience of ethical principles contributes to trust, participation and the legitimacy and social significance of criminological research. Its stakes include harm and legal consequences along with reputational damage to the discipline such that requirements for ethical behavior are inescapable for the existence of sound and significant criminological investigation.

Addressing unemployment in Bangladesh is vital not only for enhancing individual livelihoods but also for ensuring social stability and fostering a resilient economy capable of adapting to global economic shifts. text: Curvature radiation (CR) arises when relativistic particles are constrained to move along curved orbits, for example, along magnetic field lines above a pulsar's stellar surface (e.g., Harding 1981). This mechanism has played a central role in explaining high-energy (HE) emission in all the standard pulsar models: the polar cap (PC) model (Daugherty & Harding 1982, 1996) where radiation occurs very close to the neutron star surface, the outer gap (OG) model (Cheng et al. 1986; Romani 1996) with radiation originating above the null charge surface, in a gap which develops close to the last open field lines, and the slot gap (SG) model (Arons 1983; Muslimov & Harding 2003) with radiation coming from narrow gaps close to the last open field lines, extending from the stellar surface almost up to the light cylinder. Additionally, synchrotron radiation (SR) may also be emitted by secondary electron–positron pairs created in the magnetosphere via magnetic pair production in the SG (Harding et al. 2008) or via photon–photon pair production in the OG (e.g., Hirotani 2005). Predictions of inverse Compton scattering (ICS) components are more uncertain, but are typically of much lower flux compared to the SR and CR components (Bulik et al. 2000). Lastly, cyclotron resonant absorption of radio photons by relativistic primaries, followed by spontaneous SR, has been invoked for millisecond pulsar (MSP) modeling (Harding et al. 2005) as well as for the Crab (Harding et al. 2008).

text: Fertilization is the process by which male and female gametes, such as sperm and egg cells, fuse to form a zygote, which is the first cell of a new organism. This process is a fundamental and essential aspect of sexual reproduction, enabling the exchange and combination of genetic information between parents and the production of offspring that are genetically distinct from themselves and each other. The process of fertilization can be described and categorized based on its mechanism, context, and implications:Gamete Production and Maturation: Fertilization begins with the production and maturation of gametes, which are specialized and haploid cells that contain half the number of chromosomes as the somatic cells of the organism. In animals, gametes are produced through a process called meiosis, which involves the replication and division of chromosomes and the separation of homologous pairs. This process generates genetic diversity and variation within gametes, as the chromosomes are shuffled and recombined during meiosis. The maturation of gametes involves their differentiation and preparation for fertilization, such as the acquisition of motility and the ability to recognize and fuse with gametes of the opposite sex.Gamete Recognition and Interaction: Fertilization requires the recognition and interaction of gametes, which is often mediated by specific molecules and receptors on the surface of the sperm and egg cells. These molecules and receptors enable the gametes to identify and bind to each other, initiating the process of fusion and the formation of a zygote. The recognition and interaction of gametes can be influenced by various factors, such as the compatibility and quality of the gametes, the presence of competitors or barriers, and the environmental conditions and context of fertilization.Gamete Fusion and Zygote Formation: Fertilization culminates in the fusion of gametes and the formation of a zygote, which is diploid and contains the full complement of chromosomes. This process involves the union of the genetic material of the sperm and egg cells, as well as the activation and initiation of the developmental program of the zygote. The fusion of gametes can be influenced by various factors, such as the timing and coordination of the fusion event, the compatibility and integration of the genetic material, and the environmental conditions and context of fertilization.Implications and Outcomes: Fertilization has significant implications and outcomes for the ecology and evolution of animals, as it shapes the genetic diversity and structure of populations and the adaptation and response of species to their environment. For example, fertilization can influence the distribution and abundance of species, the flow of energy and nutrients through ecosystems, and the coevolution of predators and prey, hosts and parasites, and males and females. Fertilization can also have significant implications and outcomes for the physiology and development of animals, as it initiates and coordinates the growth and differentiation of the zygote and the formation and function of the organism.The process of fertilization is a fascinating and essential aspect of the life cycle and diversity of animals, and it reflects the dynamic and interconnected nature of ecology and evolution. By studying the mechanisms and implications of fertilization, scientists can gain insights into the processes and strategies that shape the survival, reproduction, and adaptation of species and the incredible complexity of life on Earth.

text: In last two decades, language technologies developed for computational linguistics and natural language processing have contributed a great deal to other areas in social and formal sciences. Recently, word embeddings [1], where sequences of letters, words or phrases from a large body of texts are mapped to vectors of real numbers, allow us to more efficiently and effectively compute meaning. Embeddings are particularly useful when meaning depends on a domain or context, or in our case, when we don’t have manually crafted resources specific to a given time period, since the meaning of words can change over time. In section II, we estimate the validity and reliability of concreteness scores obtained from embeddings. Then, in section III, we apply our computations of concreteness to investigate the claim that reading a literary fiction story improves theory-of-mind (ToM) [2]. ToM refers to the ability to infer a person’s mental state from observable cues (i.e., facial expressions, tone of voice, and actions), and it is measured using the Reading the Mind in the Eyes task (RMET). We derive stories for our study from [2]. In this experiment, participants read short stories in 2013, but some of the stories were written as early as 1886. Although readers generally may not access earlier meanings of words, it is possible that in some cases, they might tailor their mental representations of the words to specific time periods. Consequently, for stories written before 2010, we provide a comparative evaluation of our results for computational and human estimates of concreteness.

text: Interlibrary loan (ILL) is a library service that enables users to access materials not available in their home library by borrowing from other institutions. It expands resource availability, connecting libraries regionally, nationally, or internationally. Users request items like books, journal articles, or microfilms through their library’s ILL system, often via online platforms like WorldCat or ILLiad. Librarians verify item availability, locate lending libraries, and facilitate borrowing or document delivery. Policies govern loan periods, renewals, and fees, which vary by institution. ILL supports research, education, and professional needs, particularly for rare or specialized materials unavailable locally. For example, a researcher needing a rare manuscript or a student requiring an out-of-print book benefits from ILL. Digital ILL systems deliver scanned articles or e-books, enhancing speed and accessibility. Libraries adhere to copyright laws, ensuring legal sharing of materials. ILL requires collaboration, with libraries maintaining reciprocal agreements to share resources equitably. Staff training ensures efficient processing, while user education clarifies request procedures. ILL services promote inclusivity by providing access to diverse materials for all users, including those in underserved areas. Usage data informs collection development, identifying gaps in local holdings. Challenges include costs, shipping delays, or restrictions on rare items, but digital advancements mitigate these. ILL strengthens library networks, fosters resource sharing, and enhances user satisfaction by ensuring access to critical materials, making libraries dynamic hubs for knowledge dissemination and supporting global research and learning communities effectively.

text: Climate change and natural disasters are intricately interrelated, as the ongoing shifts in climate patterns significantly influence the frequency, intensity, and nature of extreme weather events. As global temperatures rise due to increased greenhouse gas emissions, the atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to heavier rainfall and more severe storms. This phenomenon contributes to an increase in flooding events, which can devastate communities, disrupt infrastructure, and lead to loss of life. Additionally, warmer temperatures can exacerbate drought conditions, particularly in regions already vulnerable to water scarcity, resulting in crop failures, food insecurity, and heightened competition for resources. The increased intensity of heatwaves, another consequence of climate change, poses direct health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations, and can lead to wildfires that devastate ecosystems and communities alike. Furthermore, rising sea levels, driven by the melting of polar ice and thermal expansion of seawater, increase the risk of coastal flooding and storm surges, threatening coastal cities and ecosystems. These disasters not only cause immediate physical damage but also have long-term socio-economic impacts, including displacement of populations, increased poverty, and strain on public health systems. The interrelationship between climate change and disasters is further complicated by the fact that vulnerable communities, often with limited resources and adaptive capacity, are disproportionately affected by these events. This exacerbates existing inequalities and hinders recovery efforts, making it essential to integrate climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction strategies. Moreover, the increasing frequency of disasters can create a feedback loop, where the destruction of infrastructure and ecosystems due to extreme weather events contributes to further climate change, as deforestation and land degradation release additional carbon into the atmosphere. Addressing the interconnection between climate change and disasters requires a comprehensive approach that includes mitigation efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, adaptation strategies to enhance resilience, and policies that promote sustainable development and social equity. By understanding and addressing these interrelated challenges, societies can better prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change and natural disasters, ultimately fostering a more sustainable and resilient future.

text: The United Nations (UN) plays a pivotal role in the development, promotion, and enforcement of international law, serving as a central platform for dialogue and cooperation among its member states. Established in 1945, the UN aims to maintain international peace and security, promote human rights, and foster social and economic development, all of which are underpinned by a robust legal framework. One of the primary functions of the UN is to create and codify international law through its various organs and specialized agencies. The UN General Assembly, for instance, adopts resolutions and conventions that contribute to the development of international legal norms, while the International Law Commission (ILC) works to codify and progressively develop international law by drafting treaties and providing legal advice. The UN Security Council, responsible for maintaining peace and security, can also invoke international law when addressing threats to global stability, authorizing actions such as sanctions or peacekeeping missions based on legal principles. Additionally, the UN promotes the adherence to international law through its various treaties and conventions, such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which set standards for human rights and humanitarian law. The UN also plays a crucial role in dispute resolution, providing mechanisms for peaceful settlement of conflicts through negotiation, mediation, and adjudication, often involving the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the UN, which settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions on legal questions referred to it. Furthermore, the UN engages in capacity-building initiatives, assisting member states in strengthening their legal frameworks and institutions to ensure compliance with international law. The UN's role extends to addressing emerging global challenges, such as climate change and terrorism, by fostering international cooperation and establishing legal instruments to tackle these issues. Overall, the United Nations serves as a cornerstone of the international legal system, facilitating the creation, interpretation, and enforcement of international law, thereby promoting a rules-based international order that seeks to enhance global peace, security, and justice.

text: Information plays a fundamental and irreplaceable role in decision-making processes by providing the factual foundation, analytical insights, and contextual understanding necessary for individuals and organizations to evaluate alternatives, assess risks, and choose optimal courses of action in complex environments. Quality information reduces uncertainty by illuminating the current state of affairs, revealing patterns and trends that might otherwise remain hidden, and enabling decision-makers to understand the potential consequences of different choices through data-driven analysis rather than relying solely on intuition or past experience. The decision-making process begins with problem identification, where information helps clarify the nature, scope, and urgency of issues that require attention, followed by the generation of alternative solutions where comprehensive information about available options, resource requirements, and implementation challenges enables more creative and realistic planning. During the evaluation phase, information provides the criteria and metrics needed to assess the relative merits of different alternatives, including quantitative data such as costs, benefits, and performance indicators, as well as qualitative information about stakeholder preferences, organizational culture, and strategic alignment that influence the ultimate selection. Information also supports risk assessment by providing historical data about similar decisions, statistical analyses of potential outcomes, and scenario planning that helps decision-makers understand the range of possible consequences and their associated probabilities. The timing and accessibility of information critically influence decision quality, as delayed or incomplete information can force premature decisions or cause missed opportunities, while information overload can create paralysis and confusion that impedes effective choice-making. Different types of decisions require different information characteristics, with routine operational decisions typically relying on structured, quantitative data from internal systems, while strategic decisions demand broader environmental scanning, competitive intelligence, and long-term trend analysis that incorporates external information sources. Information systems and technologies have revolutionized decision-making by enabling real-time access to vast amounts of data, sophisticated analytical capabilities, and collaborative platforms that support group decision processes, though they have also created new challenges including information validity, data privacy, and the need for information literacy skills. The effectiveness of information in decision-making ultimately depends on the decision-maker's ability to interpret, synthesize, and apply information appropriately, recognizing that information alone cannot substitute for judgment, experience, and wisdom in navigating complex organizational and personal choices.

text: Pheromones are chemical signals secreted by animals that influence the behavior or physiology of other members of the same species, playing a crucial role in social interactions and reproductive behaviors. These chemical messengers are often released into the environment and detected by specialized receptors, triggering responses that can include mating behaviors, territory marking, alarm signaling, or social bonding. Pheromones are particularly important during reproductive periods; for example, female moths release sex pheromones to attract males from long distances, facilitating mate location and reproductive success. In mammals, female humans and other animals release pheromones that can influence male attraction and mating behaviors, though the extent and mechanisms in humans are still being studied. Many social insects, such as ants, bees, and termites, rely heavily on pheromones for colony organization, trail marking, and alarm signaling. For example, ants leave pheromone trails to guide others to food sources, while alarm pheromones alert colony members to danger. Pheromones also serve as territorial markers, signaling occupancy and deterring rivals, as seen in many mammals and insects. Beyond reproduction and territoriality, pheromones can influence social hierarchy and group cohesion—some species release specific chemical signals to establish dominance or facilitate cooperative behaviors. They are highly species-specific, ensuring that communication is effective only among members of the same species, which helps prevent cross-species confusion. Pheromonal communication is rapid and often effective over long distances, making it an essential tool for animals in complex environments. Understanding pheromones has important applications in pest control, wildlife management, and conservation, as synthetic pheromones can be used to manipulate animal behavior. Overall, pheromones are critical chemical mediators that regulate a wide range of animal behaviors, ensuring effective communication for reproductive success, social organization, and survival strategies.

text: Non-parametric tests are used when the assumptions of parametric tests—such as normality, homogeneity of variances, or interval/ratio data—are violated, making traditional methods like t-tests or ANOVA inappropriate. These tests are particularly valuable for analyzing ordinal data (e.g., Likert scales), small sample sizes (where normality cannot be assumed), or skewed distributions that resist transformation. They are also ideal for non-continuous data (e.g., counts or ranks) and datasets with outliers that could distort parametric results. For example, the Mann-Whitney U test replaces the independent t-test when comparing two independent groups with non-normal distributions, while the Wilcoxon signed-rank test substitutes the paired t-test for related samples. Similarly, the Kruskal-Wallis test serves as a non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA for comparing three or more independent groups, and the Friedman test replaces repeated measures ANOVA for dependent groups. Non-parametric methods are also preferred for categorical data (e.g., Chi-square tests for independence) or monotonic relationships (e.g., Spearman’s rank correlation instead of Pearson’s). While these tests are more flexible and robust to assumption violations, they generally have lower statistical power than parametric tests when data meet standard assumptions, potentially requiring larger samples to detect true effects. Fields like psychology (survey research), medicine (clinical trials with skewed outcomes), and ecology (species abundance rankings) frequently rely on non-parametric approaches due to the nature of their data. Researchers should choose non-parametric tests when diagnostic checks (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk for normality, Levene’s for homogeneity) indicate significant violations, ensuring valid inferences without relying on restrictive assumptions. However, if data can be transformed to meet parametric criteria, those tests are preferred for greater efficiency. Reporting non-parametric results typically involves medians, interquartile ranges, and rank-based statistics to accurately reflect the analysis. By providing a reliable alternative for imperfect data, non-parametric tests uphold rigorous statistical standards in diverse research contexts.

text: In recent years social scientists have become more engaged with the question how we develop the capacity to live with difference and reduce prejudice. The geography of encounter literature has critically acknowledged the varied forms which such contact takes, ranging from fleeting moments of connection between strangers at bus-stops, in cafés or at the school gate, to the more habitual co-existence of neighbours, and work colleagues (Amin, 2002, Hemming, 2011, Matejskova and Leitner, 2011, Valentine, 2008). Simultaneously, a rich social sciences literature emerged and investigated how ethnic diversity impacts social cohesion (Lancee and Dronkers, 2011, Laurence, 2014, Tolsma et al., 2009) and how inter-ethnic contact affects social relations between people living in more/less diverse communities (Vervoort et al., 2011, Stolle et al., 2013). More recent studies tested the effect of contextual diversity of other spaces, such as associations (Van der Meer, 2015) or schools (Janmaat, 2015), on outgroup attitudes. Yet, to our knowledge, the role of contact in different types of space has not been systematically investigated in one study.

text: A large portion of the Earth is cold: about 14% of the biosphere is polar and 90% (by volume) is cold ocean (less than 5 °C). About two thirds of global freshwater is contained in ice and roughly 20% of the soil ecosystem exists as permafrost [1]. The Arctic, a vast circumpolar area consisting mainly of seasonally ice-covered ocean surrounded by continental land masses and islands, is an important part of the cryosphere, which can be defined as the portion of the Earth where water is in solid form [2]. The Arctic lies above 60°N and is characterized by a harsh climate, unique ecosystems and highly resilient biota [3]. Four million human residents of which approximately 10% are indigenous peoples inhabit many communities in eight countries: Canada, the Kingdom of Denmark (including Greenland and the Faroe Islands), Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, and the United States of America (Alaska) [3]. Seasonal snow cover extends over a third of the Earth’s land surface, covering up to 47 million km2 [4] and is also an important feature of the Arctic. Snow cover can be considered as a dynamic habitat of limited duration [5] that acts as a medium and a mediator by transmitting and modifying interactions among microorganisms, plants, animals, nutrients, the atmosphere and soil [6]. Snow cover influences global energy and moisture budgets, thereby influencing climate [4]. The influence of seasonal snow cover on soil temperature, soil freeze-thaw processes, and permafrost has considerable impact on carbon exchange between the atmosphere and the ground and on the hydrological cycle in cold regions [7].

text: Dowry death is a specific, heinous criminal offense meticulously defined under the Penal Code (e.g., Section 304B) in Bangladesh, specifically legislated to vigorously combat the deeply entrenched and devastating social evil of dowry-related violence perpetrated against women. This provision directly addresses tragic instances where a married woman dies due to burns, other bodily injuries, or any other cause that is unnatural, provided such death occurs within seven years of her marriage, and it is conclusively shown that she was subjected to persistent cruelty or harassment by her husband or any of his relatives in direct connection with any explicit or implicit demand for dowry, immediately preceding her death. The essential elements that must be stringently established to secure a conviction for dowry death are: firstly, the death of the woman must have occurred within the initial seven-year period from the date of her marriage; secondly, the nature of the death must be unnatural, specifically caused by burns, bodily injuries, or other circumstances that are not considered normal; thirdly, it must be unequivocally demonstrated that the deceased woman was subjected to systematic cruelty or harassment by either her husband or any of his relatives; and crucially, such cruelty or harassment must be directly linked to, or in connection with, a demand for dowry; finally, the said cruelty or harassment must have occurred "soon before" her death, implying a proximate temporal connection between the abuse and the fatal event, though the exact timeframe for "soon before" is interpreted contextually by courts. If all these stringent conditions are met, the law creates a compelling legal presumption that the husband or his relatives caused the dowry death, effectively shifting the burden of proof onto the accused to refute this presumption. The severe punishment for dowry death, which is imprisonment for a term that shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, powerfully underscores the legislature's profound commitment to rigorously deter dowry-related violence and to protect vulnerable married women from the pervasive and often deadly cruelty and harassment driven by insatiable greed for dowry.

text: Iron (Fe) is an essential plant micronutrient and is essential in numerous physiological and biochemical processes of plant growth and development. Although needed in very small quantities compared to the macronutrients (such as nitrogen and phosphorus) and micronutrients (like zinc or copper), iron is necessary in the presence of adenosyltransferase due to its role in chlorophyll production, which is essential for photosynthesis. Iron is an integral part of various enzymatic systems of the chloroplasts and the mitochondria, which are involved in energy production and metabolism. The symptoms of iron deficiency in plants usually results from acids in the soil or high levels of salt that can interfere with the uptake of iron by the plant, leading to iron deficiency chlorosis. This lack could result in dramatic loss of crop quantity and quality. Availability of iron in soil is dependent on pH, texture, and organic matter; iron tends to form insoluble compounds in alkaline important soil. Farmers who apply iron directly to the plant (iron chelates or foliar sprays) do this in response to this. It also plays a role in the nitrogen-fixing process of leguminous plants and in the synthesis of some enzymes and proteins. The availability of certain micronutrients -- iron, zinc, manganese, copper, boron, and molybdenum -- in the correct quantities, even though required in very small amounts, are also necessary to reach the maximum health and potential of plants. Soil and plant tissue tests can help identify micronutrient deficiencies and guide fertility decisions. Besides the agronomic interest, the iron content is of nutritional interest for human because it enters the food chain through plants. text: Political science’s feminist challenge exposes that conventional theories and explanations, both in theory and practice, have obscured the ways in which gender is implicated in structures of power, political institutions, and policy. As feminist scholars have suggested, women’s experiences and men’s experiences of the world have been marginalized or erased in the discipline of political science, and by implication, our understandings of political phenomena have been incomplete or biased. Critique here has been intended to expose how patriarchy, the systematic rule of men in political, social and economic terms, undergirds governance, representation and policy. Feminists emphasize the importance of gender as an important analytic category to show how laws, policies, and social systems often play a role in perpetuating gender inequalities and limiting women’s rights and voice. What is more, they disrupt the public-private opposition (private, such as household work, care work, violence against women) by considering it is always already political, not something extruded from the political orders. Intersectionality is an important part of feminist political science, reflecting that gender interacts with race, class, sexuality, and other dimensions of oppression in ways that make a person’s political experience in the world different from others’. Expanding the analysis of politics, feminist scientists demand a diversity-friendly representation, gender(homework)- sensitivitly policies a'en reversal, moving the political culture to more equality and diversity. This criticism has led to specific positive measures such as affirmative action programmes in the form of gender quotas, acknowledgment of reproductive rights and of the need to address gender-specific violence. The feminist critique also serves as a challenge to get political scientist to be more reflexive, and to think about how they fill their role as scholars, and that their theory and work is inflected by their biases. Feminist political science at its best aims to democratize knowledge and political power, disrupting hierarchy, and fostering social justice.

text: Extreme Multi-label text Classification (XMC) is an essential task in natural language processing (NLP), which aims to recall multiple relevant labels and discriminate them from enormous numbers of irrelevant labels for a given text. text: ISO in photography describes how sensitive a camera sensor is to light. One of the three elements of the exposure triangle, which also includes aperture and shutter speed, ISO is responsible for deciding how dark or bright an exposure is going to be. A lower ISO, say ISO 100 or 200, refers to a less sensitive sensor which is better for the brighter environments to get cleaner images without noise or grain. At the opposite end of the scale, higher ISOs in the range of ISO 1600, 3200, or higher make the sensor more sensitive so a photographer can shoot in a low-light environment without having to use slower shutter speeds or wider apertures. But there’s a trade-off: Increasing the ISO both makes the camera sensor more sensitive to light and also adds more digital noise—graininess that degrades image quality and detail. If you have a modern digital camera with a larger sensor high ISO levels are better controlled and you can get usable results up to ISO 6400 or higher but still you will get some degree of noise. The correct ISO to use depends on the available light as well as the desired aperture and shutter speed, and the camera's noise-handling ability. For example, sports or action photographers may want higher-ISO settings to achieve fast shutter speeds in dark stadiums, while landscape photographers working in broad daylight will often use lower ISO to get the most detail. ISO also impacts dynamic range and color fidelity; you'll generally want to keep ISO as low as possible. Though it’s usually preferable to use the lowest possible ISO, knowing how and when to raise it properly gives photographers the ability to work with a range of lighting conditions in order to achieve a sharp, well-exposed photograph. Mastering ISO enables photographers to navigate the mix of brightness, sharpness and image quality of various shooting circumstances and artistic intentions.

text: The main areas of difference between synchronous and asynchronous (or induction) machines are their construction, applications, and working principles.  Synchronous speed is the steady speed at which synchronous machines run, precisely matching the frequency of the power source.  Their rotors are either cylindrical or salient poles, and in the case of synchronous generators, they are directly connected to the grid; in the case of synchronous motors, they are activated by a DC supply.  In order to precisely manage voltage and reactive power, these machines rely on magnetic locking between the rotor's magnetic field and the stator's revolving magnetic field.  Power generation, voltage regulation, and applications needing continuous speed operation are all handled by synchronous machines.  On the other hand, asynchronous or induction machines work on the electromagnetic induction principle, in which the stator's revolving magnetic field induces the rotor currents.  They rely on slip—the discrepancy between the synchronous and rotor speeds—to generate rotor currents rather than a DC source for excitation.  Induction machines usually have squirrel cage or wound rotors, and during regular operation, the rotor speed always stays below synchronous speed.  The primary distinction is that induction machines run at a speed that is somewhat slower than synchronous speed, contingent on load, whereas synchronous machines maintain a set speed dictated by the supply frequency.  Although synchronous machines are more costly and sophisticated, they provide superior voltage management and power quality control, which makes them appropriate for large-scale power plants.  Induction machines are the workhorses of industry for powering compressors, fans, and pumps because they are easier to use, more durable, and more affordable.  Induction machines rely on slip to produce torque, while synchronous machines rely on a magnetic lock to synchronize. This is the main difference between the two types of machines.  Both kinds are essential to electrical engineering and play complementary roles in industrial drives and power generation. The decision between them is determined by the demands of particular applications, control requirements, and financial considerations.

text: The mind–brain dualism is a common theme in the philosophy of mind, and is often addressed in debates on the human mind. There is a brain, and it is a matter-brain, made of neurons, and glial cells, and complex webs of interconnections among neurons in my skull that runs my body and processes sensory input and puts skin in and takes skin out of the game and does all sorts of other cognitive jobs. We empirically have it via neuroscience, neurobiology, medical imaging, and can map it piece by excruciating piece at an insane level of granularity. On the other hand, mind is often characterized as being the sum of mental phenomena or processes, those such as thoughts, feelings, beliefs, desires, intentions, etc., that come either from or are in some way related to the working of the brain. While the brain is physical and biological, the mind is the more intangible flow of lived experience, what you feel when you are conscious — what it is like to be inside your head and body. The relationship between mind and brain is the core of the well-known mind-body problem--what is the relationship between non-material mental experiences and material brain states? To a physicalist the mind is serious caged and no part of the mind can be no part is identical with a state of the nervous system or any part of it - see for example, brain),2 whereas to the dualist, the mind has an existence: DIFFERENT from the non-physical. Some intermediate positions, such as property dualism, claim that mental properties (or, more generally, properties had by conscious creatures) supervene on, but cannot be reduced to or identified with, properties of the brain. Higher brain functions such as reasoning, planning and selfhood are therefore also part of the mind, so it may be overly simplified to restrict the mind solely to what goes on in the brain. What we understand about the mind-brain relationship not only informs contemporary debates in philosophy, but bears on practical issues such as how to understand mental illness, to create artificial intelligence, and to determine if and when other animals are conscious.

text: Technological innovation is a “must” for sustainable development. It is not a nerdish focus on technology, but an attempt to create options. text: Pollution has severe and multifaceted impacts on plants, disrupting their growth, reproduction, and survival while destabilizing entire ecosystems. Air pollution, particularly from industrial emissions and vehicle exhaust, introduces harmful gases like sulfur dioxide (SO?), nitrogen oxides (NO?), and ozone (O?), which damage plant tissues, reduce photosynthesis, and stunt growth. Acid rain, formed when these pollutants mix with atmospheric moisture, leaches essential nutrients from soil and damages leaves, weakening plants over time. Heavy metals from industrial waste, such as lead and cadmium, accumulate in soil, inhibiting root development and enzyme function, while chemical pesticides and herbicides can cause mutations or death in non-target plant species. Water pollution from agricultural runoff introduces excess nitrogen and phosphorus, leading to algal blooms that deplete oxygen and block sunlight, suffocating aquatic plants. Plastic pollution in soil and waterways restricts root growth and reduces water infiltration, further stressing plant life. Noise pollution, though less obvious, disrupts pollination by deterring pollinators like bees and birds, while light pollution alters the photoperiods plants rely on for flowering and dormancy cycles. Climate change, driven by greenhouse gas pollution, exacerbates these effects by shifting temperature and precipitation patterns, forcing plants to adapt rapidly or face extinction. Collectively, pollution reduces biodiversity, diminishes crop yields, and weakens ecosystems' ability to sequester carbon or filter air and water. Urban plants, though often hardier, face compounded stresses from soil compaction and pollution, limiting their ability to mitigate urban heat islands. Without intervention, the cumulative effects of pollution will degrade food security, erode habitats, and accelerate species loss, underscoring the urgent need for sustainable practices, stricter regulations, and global cooperation to protect plant life—and by extension, all life dependent on it.

text: Resources can be broadly categorized into renewable and non-renewable based on their ability to regenerate or replenish over human timescales. Renewable resources are natural resources that can replenish themselves relatively quickly through natural processes, often within a human lifetime, or are practically inexhaustible. Examples include solar energy, which is continuously available from the sun; wind energy, generated by the Earth's atmospheric processes; hydroelectric power, derived from the flow of water; geothermal energy, from the Earth's internal heat; and biomass, derived from organic matter such as plants and animal waste, which can be regrown. While these resources are naturally replenishable, their sustainable use depends on the rate of consumption not exceeding their rate of regeneration. For instance, forests are renewable, but over-logging can lead to deforestation if trees are not replanted and allowed to mature. Renewable resources are crucial for transitioning to sustainable energy systems, reducing reliance on fossil fuels, and mitigating climate change. Non-renewable resources, on the other hand, are natural resources that exist in finite quantities and are consumed much faster than they can be naturally formed or replenished. Their formation typically takes millions of years, making them effectively non-replaceable within a human timescale. The primary examples are fossil fuels – coal, oil, and natural gas – which were formed from the anaerobic decomposition of buried dead organisms over geological eras. Once extracted and burned, they are gone forever. Other non-renewable resources include minerals and metals like iron, copper, gold, and aluminum, which are extracted from the Earth's crust. While these can be recycled to some extent, their original geological formation is a one-time process. The finite nature of non-renewable resources necessitates careful management, efficient use, and a global shift towards renewable alternatives to ensure long-term resource availability and minimize environmental impacts associated with their extraction and combustion.

text: Logistic regression is the type of analysis conducted when you have one or more independent variables (IVs) that predict an outcome. In contrast, where linear regression estimates the value that a dependent variable will take based on a set of independent variables, logistic regression models the log-odds (that is, the logarithm of the odds) that a dependent variable will take on a certain value. The logistic function transforms the linear function of \(x\) into a continuous probability value between 0 and 1 (which is exactly what we need for classifications). It can be stated as: log(1?pp)=?0+?1X1+?2X2+...+?kXkwhere p = is the probability of the event; and ?0,?1,…,?k are coefficients derived using the data itself. Logistic regression estimates parameters via maximum likelihood estimation, searching for the parameter values that will make the observed sample as likely as possible. It gives odds ratios for the predictors, which tell you how much the odds of the event change for a one-unit change in a predictor. For logistic regression, one does not have to know the exact functional form of the coefficient distribution, but the predictors must be independent and the model correctly specified. It is the workhorse here in soft drink industry, medical remainder, social science, marketing and machine learning to binary classification such as disease diagnosis, customer retention and credit card provision. Generalized forms, such as multinomial logistic and ordinal logistic regression are for outcomes which are respectively more than binary category and having ordered categories.

text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), often called the “World Court,” is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, established in 1945 by the UN Charter and seated in the Peace Palace at The Hague, Netherlands. It serves two main functions: settling legal disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on legal questions referred by authorized UN organs and specialized agencies. Unlike domestic courts, the ICJ only hears cases when states consent to its jurisdiction, either through treaties, special agreements, or declarations of acceptance. The Court is composed of 15 judges, elected for nine-year terms by both the UN General Assembly and the Security Council, with the requirement that no two judges may be from the same country and that the bench reflects the world’s major legal systems and civilizations. Its rulings in contentious cases are binding on the parties involved, though the Court lacks direct enforcement power, relying instead on the UN Security Council for implementation. The ICJ has adjudicated a wide range of disputes, including territorial boundaries, maritime rights, diplomatic relations, and treaty interpretations, and its advisory opinions have influenced the development of international law on issues such as decolonization, the legality of nuclear weapons, and the status of occupied territories. By providing a peaceful mechanism for resolving disputes and clarifying international legal principles, the ICJ plays a vital role in promoting global stability, the rule of law, and the peaceful settlement of conflicts among states.

text: Perfect competition is an idealized market structure characterized by a large number of buyers and sellers, where each firm sells a homogeneous or identical product, and no single buyer or seller can influence the market price. In this market, firms are price takers, meaning they must accept the prevailing market price determined solely by overall supply and demand. Key features of perfect competition include many sellers and buyers, free entry and exit of firms without any barriers, perfect information where all participants have complete knowledge about prices and products, and homogeneous products that are perfect substitutes. Additionally, resources such as labor and capital are perfectly mobile, and there are no transaction costs or externalities affecting the market. Because of these conditions, firms in perfect competition earn only normal profits in the long run, as any supernormal profits attract new entrants, increasing supply and driving prices down. The demand curve facing an individual firm is perfectly elastic, reflecting that even a slight increase in price would cause the firm to lose all customers to competitors. Perfect competition leads to allocative efficiency (price equals marginal cost) and productive efficiency (firms produce at the lowest point on their average cost curve), ensuring optimal resource allocation. Although perfect competition is a theoretical model rarely found in pure form in real markets, it serves as a benchmark to compare other market structures and understand how competitive pressures influence prices, output, and efficiency. Examples often cited include agricultural markets like wheat or corn, where many producers sell nearly identical products and have little control over market prices. In summary, perfect competition is a market structure with many small firms selling identical products, free market entry and exit, perfect information, and firms acting as price takers, resulting in efficient market outcomes.

text: Hormones play a crucial role in regulating reproduction across a wide range of animal species, orchestrating the complex processes involved in sexual development, mating behaviors, and reproductive cycles. In vertebrates, reproductive hormones are primarily produced by the endocrine glands and include key players such as gonadotropins, sex steroids, and peptide hormones. In mammals, the hypothalamus initiates the reproductive process by releasing gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which stimulates the pituitary gland to secrete luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). These hormones are essential for the functioning of the gonads; in females, FSH promotes the growth and maturation of ovarian follicles, while LH triggers ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone to prepare the uterus for potential implantation of a fertilized egg. In males, FSH stimulates spermatogenesis in the testes, while LH stimulates the production of testosterone, which is critical for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics and the maintenance of libido. In addition to these hormones, estrogen and progesterone play vital roles in regulating the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and parturition in females, influencing not only reproductive functions but also behaviors associated with mating and nurturing. Hormonal fluctuations throughout the reproductive cycle can affect physical and behavioral traits, such as estrus or heat cycles in females, which signal fertility and readiness for mating. In many species, environmental factors such as light, temperature, and social cues can influence hormone levels, thereby affecting reproductive timing and success. For instance, seasonal breeders rely on changes in day length to regulate their reproductive cycles, ensuring that offspring are born during optimal conditions for survival. In addition to their roles in sexual reproduction, hormones also influence parental behaviors, such as nesting, caring for young, and bonding, which are critical for the survival of offspring. In some species, hormones like oxytocin and prolactin are associated with maternal behaviors, promoting nurturing and protective instincts. Overall, the intricate interplay of hormones in reproduction highlights their essential role in coordinating physiological processes, influencing behaviors, and ensuring the continuation of species. Understanding the hormonal mechanisms underlying reproduction not only provides insights into animal biology but also has implications for human health, fertility treatments, and conservation efforts, as disruptions in hormonal balance can lead to reproductive challenges and affect population dynamics in wildlife.

text: The accelerator principle is an economic theory that investment levels are influenced by national income and the change in national income. This principle states that as the demand for products and services grows, businesses invest money in capital goods such as machinery and equipment to produce those goods and services. To the contrary, when demand is low, investment slows or even contracts. The point driving the accelerator is that a small increase in consumer demand can induce a much larger increase in investment (hence the name “accelerator”). The accelerator coefficient is a measure of the degree to which investment is sensitive to differences in output. For example, if firms anticipate higher future sales, they will ramp up their investment today to gear up for increased production, regardless of whether demand has surged. The accelerator principle is a supplement to the multiplier principle in macro-economic theory. If the multiplier tells us how larger investment brings a larger income, the accelerator tells us how larger income induces more investment. This interaction can amplify business cycles: as incomes rise, more investment is sparked (accelerator), which in turn boosts incomes (multiplier), producing a positive feedback loop. But it can also make downturns worse — falling incomes lead to less investment, which leads to even lower incomes. The theory implies a constant capital-output ratio, such that firms must invest more to produce more. Although it has proved to be a useful device in explaining how investment responds to changes in the level of economic activity, the accelerator principle has its constraints. It does not take into account such factors as interest rates, expectations, excess capacity or technological changes that also affect investment. It is, however, still a leading theory in accounting for the cyclical volatility of investment behavior.

text: Hearsay evidence is an out-of-court statement offered in court to prove the truth of the matter asserted. It’s generally inadmissible in court because the person who made the original statement wasn’t under oath and isn’t subject to cross-examination, raising concerns about its reliability and accuracy. For example, if a witness testifies, “John told me he saw the defendant commit the crime,” that’s hearsay because it’s an attempt to prove the defendant committed the crime based on John’s statement, not the witness’s direct observation. The core problem with hearsay is the inability to test the veracity of the original declarant (the person who made the statement). However, there are numerous exceptions to the hearsay rule, recognizing that some out-of-court statements are considered sufficiently reliable to be admitted. These exceptions include dying declarations (statements made by someone believing they are about to die), excited utterances (statements made spontaneously during a stressful event), business records, and statements against interest. The rationale behind these exceptions is that the circumstances surrounding the statement provide some assurance of its trustworthiness. Determining whether a statement constitutes hearsay and whether an exception applies can be complex and often requires careful legal analysis. The hearsay rule is a fundamental principle of evidence law designed to ensure fairness and reliability in legal proceedings.

text: Edward B. Lewis discovered in 1978 that some genes (coined later Hox genes) located in sequence on the chromosome in the cell nucleus are expressed in the same order along the Anterior/Posterior (A/P) axis of the developing embryo [1]. This correlation is called spatial Hox gene collinearity and since then it is intensively studied. This collinearity is remarkable because it connects geometric entities differing by about four orders of magnitude: at the microscale the size of a Hox cluster is variable with minimum about 100 nm (See Section 4). At the macroscale the size of a multicellular early embryo is of the order 1 mm [2]. Lewis originally noticed the collinearity in the Drosophila embryo but it was later found that this property is observed in many other animal clades, e.g., vertebrates [3]. The evolution of Hox genes is investigated in depth and it is believed that an ancestral ur-Hox gene was in tandem duplicated and several Hox gene clusters were formed in different clades [4,5]. The structure of the different clusters varies from species to species and the vertebrates possess well organized and compacted clusters [3]. text: Common networking protocols are standardized rules that define how data is formatted, transmitted, and processed across networks, ensuring reliable and interoperable communication between devices. At the core is the Internet Protocol (IP), responsible for addressing and routing packets to their destinations. Above IP, Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) ensures reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data, while User Datagram Protocol (UDP) provides fast, connectionless transmission suitable for time-sensitive applications. Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/HTTPS) governs web traffic, with HTTPS adding encryption for security. File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and its secure variant SFTP handle file transfers between hosts. Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), IMAP, and POP3 are used for sending and retrieving email. Domain Name System (DNS) resolves domain names to IP addresses, and Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) assigns IP addresses to devices on a network. Secure Shell (SSH) enables encrypted remote access to systems, while Telnet, now largely deprecated, performs similar tasks without encryption. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) monitors and manages network devices, and ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is used for diagnostics, such as through the ping and traceroute utilities. Ethernet defines standards for LAN communication at the data link layer. These protocols interact across different layers of the OSI model to ensure proper data handling, from physical transmission to user application. Understanding these protocols and how they collaborate is essential for network configuration, administration, and troubleshooting. Their standardized nature allows cross-platform, scalable communication across diverse network environments including enterprise, cloud, and consumer technologies.

Economic development, particularly the growth of the ready-made garment industry, has empowered women and fueled urbanization, while microfinance initiatives like Grameen Bank have uplifted rural communities. Education, bolstered by government policies offering free schooling and female stipends, has enhanced literacy and challenged traditional norms. Technology, especially widespread mobile and internet access, has transformed communication, education, and business, fostering digital inclusion. Political movements and democratization, rooted in Bangladesh’s independence struggle, continue to shape governance and civic participation. Environmental challenges, like frequent floods and cyclones, necessitate adaptive changes in livelihoods and infrastructure. Globalization and remittances from migrant workers have introduced new cultural influences and economic opportunities, while NGOs and civil society advocate for social justice and human rights. These factors collectively reshape societal dynamics, promoting progressive values but also creating tensions with traditional practices. Understanding these drivers is crucial for addressing Bangladesh’s evolving social landscape, balancing modernization with cultural heritage in a rapidly changing world.

text: A federal system is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units, such as states or provinces, with each level having distinct areas of authority and decision-making power. In a federal system, the central government typically has responsibility for matters such as national defense, foreign policy, and interstate commerce, while the constituent units have authority over issues such as education, healthcare, and local law enforcement. This division of power is often enshrined in a constitution, which outlines the respective powers and responsibilities of the central government and the constituent units. Federalism allows for a degree of autonomy and regional self-governance, while also providing a framework for cooperation and coordination between different levels of government. By dispersing power and promoting regional representation, federalism can help to promote diversity, innovation, and responsiveness to local needs, while also maintaining national unity and cohesion. Federal systems can be found in countries such as the United States, Canada, Australia, and Germany, and are often seen as a way to balance the needs of different regions and communities within a larger national framework. Overall, federalism provides a flexible and adaptable system of government that can accommodate diverse regional identities and interests, while also promoting national unity and cooperation.

text: The crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core are the four separate layers that make up the Earth's structure. Each layer has its own specific physical and chemical properties, with variations in thickness, composition, temperature, and pressure.  Less than 1% of the Earth's volume is made up of the crust, the thin, unyielding surface layer where people dwell. Continental crust, composed mainly of granitic rocks, averages about 35–40 km thick, while the denser basaltic oceanic crust is only around 6–7 km thick; this layer supports landmasses, oceans, and the ecosystems above it. Beneath the crust lies the mantle, extending to about 2,900 km depth and constituting roughly 84% of Earth’s volume. The upper mantle includes the lithosphere’s rigid part along with the crust; below this is the asthenosphere, a semi-fluid zone allowing slow convective motions that drive the movement of tectonic plates. The mantle is composed primarily of silicate minerals rich in magnesium and iron, and as depth increases, so do temperature and pressure, raising density and reducing mobility. Next is the outer core, a liquid layer about 2,200 km thick, made mostly of molten iron and nickel. Its fluid flow produces Earth’s magnetic field via dynamo action—a crucial shield protecting the planet from harmful solar and cosmic radiation. Temperatures here can reach 4,000–6,000°C, yet the iron-nickel alloy remains liquid due to extreme pressure. At the center lies the inner core, a solid iron-nickel sphere with a radius of about 1,220 km.Even at temperatures as high as 7,000°C or higher, the metals are forced into a solid state by the tremendous pressures at the center of the Earth.  As the Earth cools, the inner core expands gradually, releasing latent heat that fuels the geodynamo effect.  Through heat flow, convection, and electromagnetic processes, these layers—from the brittle crust to the dynamic mantle and core—interact to shape Earth's geology, create its magnetic field, propel plate tectonics, and sustain life.

text: Economic structures, way of living and social relationship have been changed through industrialization which has been proved as a change agent in Bangladesh. The leading force behind this change has been the Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector, employing more than 4 million workers, the majority of them being women. The implication is that people have moved en-masse away from the traditional agrarian lifestyle to urban wage employment. The fact that more women have joined the service sector has also challenged the old, stereotypical gender norms, as they have gained greater independence, both economical and in terms of power in the household. But it also has generated new modes of inequality by subjecting industrial workers to poor working conditions, minimal wages and a lack of labour rights. Industrial zones, like Dhaka, Gazipur, and Narayanganj have emerged as both sites of economic opportunity and of social strife. Environmental damage is also a significant side effect: of the textile factories that emit polluted water and air. And the woven texture of rural society, which has long stressed extended family and community reliance, is being replaced by the warp of more self-sufficient city ways. And while industrial-scale production brought many out of poverty and boosted GDP, it also brought stress, alienation and an identity crisis for many workers. If nothing else, industrialisation is necessary to modernise Bangladesh, to develop urban life, better communication, and to plug it into the world market, in this way to increase the rate and depth of social change.
