text: Mobile robots are autonomous or semi-autonomous machines designed to move through their environment, utilizing a combination of sensors, software, and advanced algorithms to navigate and perform tasks without direct human intervention. These robots can be classified into several categories based on their locomotion methods, including wheeled mobile robots (WMR), which are the most common and use wheels for efficient movement on flat surfaces; legged mobile robots (LMR), which mimic animal movement and can traverse uneven terrains; and tracked locomotion robots, which utilize tracks for stability on rough surfaces. Additionally, mobile robots can be aerial, such as drones, or aquatic, designed for specific tasks in the air or water. The applications of mobile robots are vast and varied, spanning multiple industries. In industrial settings, they are employed for material transport, inspection, and performing repetitive tasks, significantly enhancing efficiency and productivity. In healthcare, mobile robots assist in delivering medications, disinfecting areas, and even aiding in surgeries, thereby improving patient care and operational efficiency. In agriculture, these robots are utilized for planting, harvesting, and monitoring crops, allowing farmers to optimize their practices and increase yields. Furthermore, mobile robots play a crucial role in exploration and rescue missions, such as space rovers that navigate extraterrestrial terrains or robots deployed in disaster response scenarios to access hazardous environments. The technological advancements in mobile robotics have been remarkable, with the integration of sophisticated sensors, artificial intelligence, and machine learning enabling these robots to perceive their surroundings, make informed decisions, and adapt to dynamic conditions. Obstacle avoidance algorithms allow mobile robots to navigate around barriers and adjust their paths in real-time, enhancing their operational capabilities. Moreover, reconfigurable mobile robots can change their structure and locomotion methods to suit different tasks and terrains, increasing their versatility and effectiveness. As mobile robots continue to evolve, they are expected to play an increasingly significant role in various sectors, driving innovation and transforming how tasks are performed. The ongoing research and development in this field promise a future where mobile robots are integral to everyday life, enhancing productivity, safety, and efficiency across multiple domains.

text: The theory of intentionality, prominently revived by Franz Brentano and later developed by Edmund Husserl, posits that mental states are fundamentally "about something" or "directed towards an object." This "aboutness" is the hallmark of intentionality, distinguishing mental phenomena like beliefs, desires, perceptions, and thoughts from physical phenomena. When we perceive a tree, our perception is of the tree; when we believe it's raining, our belief is about the weather. This inherent directedness connects our minds to the world, providing the crucial link for how we understand and interact with reality. A key aspect of intentionality is that the "object" of a mental state doesn't necessarily have to exist in reality; one can imagine a unicorn or hope for world peace, even if these objects or states of affairs are non-existent or merely potential. Husserl further elaborated this, distinguishing between the "noesis" (the act of consciousness) and the "noema" (the content or object as it appears to consciousness), emphasizing that the way an object is presented to us (its "aspectual shape") is integral to our intentional experience of it. Thus, intentionality is not merely a relation between mind and world, but a constitutive feature of consciousness itself, shaping how we experience and make sense of everything we encounter.

text: Theatre in the round, also spelled theater in the round, also called arena stage, central stage, or island stage, form of theatrical staging in which the acting area, which may be raised or at floor level, is completely surrounded by the audience. Theatre in the round does not include a proscenium and therefore gives the audience a stronger and richer sense of theatrical immediacy and intimacy than do, for example, most thrust stages, in most spaces—in all but a few – especially when the usual fourth wall convention is dropped and the audience is set in literally closer, often at tables, as in some productions of the former Baseball Stadium setting of Bent or in The Spectator Sport FOB Essay Theatre in something like the style of old European spectator sport Rugby football; the fourth wall and ceiling are both absent; the heterotopia is a better metaphor or excuse than mimesis for the special-ness isolation of the audience home box seats area;[7] as well as needing to project less to even the furthest seat than in a smaller proscenium; of these things and at a minimum in optimal conditions the effect seems to make the ticket holder a spectator without an impulse or means to use much judgment, but rather merely an Usher of the whole event into being—not in a-any One act play per se but in the epic Form for this [sort of] event. This placement also means that actors must address themselves to the whole of the audience at all times, and it requires careful choreography and movement to ensure that no section feels left out and that everyone can see what is going on. Set There is usually no set in a typical theatre in the round, although what is seen in the background is usually simple but, more often than not, unobtrusive; designated as the playing area (the opposite of the auditorium) what is shown behind the stage can be as important as anything said, written or performed; if there is a script or Noh dance it can certainly can be no less important than what is designated as a set design. Lighting designers have to cut their lanterns very carefully to precisely the same criterion as sound, so they don’t create puddles of darkness that actors disappear into or cast distracting shadows or blind the audience, and sound designs bright, clear and well balanced sound across the theatre that reaches everyone. The concept of "theatre in the round" makes an intimacy very special, while the closeness of the public ca generate sensations and co-creation experiences, performances seem to happen right now and here, as they are: intimate. This type of stage plan is especially good for small, intimate dramas, plays involving lots of audience interaction or ones that are really trying to experiment with form. Theatre in the round has its origins in ancient Greek theatre, and is today a staging option for both some avant garde theatres and for its potential as a theatre in most modern large theatres; the picture frame stage, or proscenium stage, is at one end of the former and is limited to only some of the latter as of its common practice. While intimate, and immersive, and all that, it also poses technical challenges, like problematic blocking that will keep cast members from turning their backs on an audience for a moment too long, and how and where to make space behind and around patrons’ sightlines for set pieces, lights and sounds. Directors and designers have to collaborate very closely to make sure that the artistic vision can still be realized in these constraints, and are often forced to become inventive in their staging and technology, to be able to make an impact. Theatre in the round like this alters the media significantly and changes the nature of the theatrical experience – as they can see things that it is not possible for them to see from the traditional front-on seat – most significantly the reactions of the audience and also, because the set is not restricted to a single background, the set can (and often does) travel all the way around the audience. The in-the-round design celebrates theatre from the ground up - providing the most dynamic and immersive experience in contemporary theatre and all audiences can be part of the ground-breaking experience of how stories are told on stage.

text: The sources of the international law are the legal bases from which rules and obligations dominate relations between states and other international organkisations. The ICJ Statute lists the following sources of international law: (1) international treaties and conventions, (2) international custom, (3) general principles of law recognized by civilized nations, and (4) judicial decisions and teachings of academic writers as subsidiary means of determining the law. Treaties and conventions are written pacts concluded by, and resulting in binding obligations on, states or international entities. Examples are the UN Charter, the Geneva Conventions, and the Paris Agreement on climate change. States have to agree to them and ratify them of their own free will in order for them to be legally binding. Customary international law results from uniform state practice with the concomitant existence of opinio juris—belief that international practice is required by law. For example, diplomatic immunity and genocide are customary. General principles of law generally meant basic ideas that are common to all the major legal systems of the world, including the concept of justice, equity and good conscience. They are principles of lex gangionis to be applied as a gap-filler where no treaty or customary rule applies. Notable judicial decisions, specifically from the ICJ and other international courts, serve to interpret existing law and it can affect the development of law in the future, but are not binding precedence and are not used as such in common law jurisdictions. There is also a frequent resort to the writings of the most learned publicists as a subsidiary means for aid in informing the court of the scope of some complex legal overview. In reality these sources cross-fertilize and support one another. For example, a treaty may crystallize customary rules or courts decisions may articulate novel principles drawn from developing state practice. Taken together the sources of international law establish both the framework and authority to govern relations between states, create responsibility and support the peaceable resolution of conflict in the international sphere.

text: Glycosides are natural organic compounds consisting of two parts: a sugar moiety called the glycone and a non-sugar moiety known as the aglycone or genin, linked by a glycosidic bond. They are widely found in plants and serve various biological functions, including defense mechanisms and energy storage. The sugar part enhances the solubility and transport of the aglycone, which often possesses the pharmacological activity. Glycosides are hydrolyzed in the body to release the active aglycone, which exerts therapeutic effects. There are several types of glycosides based on the nature of the aglycone, including cardiac glycosides, saponins, flavonoid glycosides, cyanogenic glycosides, and iridoid glycosides. Cardiac glycosides, such as digoxin and digitoxin derived from Digitalis purpurea, are used to treat heart conditions like congestive heart failure and arrhythmias by increasing the force of cardiac contractions and regulating heart rate. Saponins, found in licorice and ginseng, have anti-inflammatory, expectorant, and immunomodulatory properties. Flavonoid glycosides like rutin exhibit antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Cyanogenic glycosides, present in plants like cassava, release toxic hydrogen cyanide as a defense mechanism but have limited medicinal use. Additionally, steviol glycosides from Stevia rebaudiana serve as natural sweeteners. Therapeutically, glycosides are valuable for their diverse biological activities, including cardiovascular benefits, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer effects. Their unique chemical structure allows targeted interactions with biological systems, making them important in both traditional and modern medicine.

text: In recent years, several newly emerging infectious diseases like Ebola, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) or avian influenza have suddenly appeared on the world stage. In spring 2009, a new strain of influenza, H1N1 (commonly known as “swine flu”) appeared. The first cases of H1N1 were discovered in April in Mexico and the United States. The disease rapidly spread to other regions of the world, leading the World Health Organization (WHO) to officially declare the first influenza pandemic of the 21st century in June 2009. In fall and winter of 2009, mass vaccination campaigns were implemented in many countries, with mixed success (12.9%–38.8% compliance rate depending on the state in the U.S., Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2010; 8%–30% depending on the canton in Switzerland, Bundesamt für Gesundheit, 2010). In August 2010, the pandemic was officially declared over. H1N1 thus appeared suddenly and quickly spread worldwide before abating. From the point of view of public consciousness, the H1N1 pandemic was thus a dynamically evolving event. An emerging infectious disease (EID) is a label attached to various newly emerging or re-emerging diseases like those caused by antibiotic multi-resistant bacteria, hemorrhagic fevers, HIV/AIDS, the West Nile Virus diseases, Lyme borreliosis, SARS, avian influenza or the H1N1 pandemic virus (Morens et al., 2004). The label has been popularized in books and television series, as well as the media in general and has thus become part of common sense (Washer, 2010). The novel and threatening character of EIDs makes them ideal vehicles to study how social representations emerge and spread, and substantial research has been conducted on the social representations of infectious diseases.

text: NITI Aayog, or the National Institution for Transforming India, is a policy think tank established by the Government of India in 2015 to replace the Planning Commission. It aims to foster cooperative federalism by involving states and union territories in the country’s development planning and policy formulation process. NITI Aayog’s primary role is to provide strategic and technical advice to the central and state governments, facilitating more decentralized and participative policymaking. Unlike the Planning Commission, which relied heavily on centralized planning, NITI Aayog emphasizes a bottom-up approach, encouraging states to identify their unique development needs and formulate tailored strategies. It promotes evidence-based policymaking, data collection, and innovative approaches to address complex socio-economic challenges. The organization also works on formulating long-term strategic visions, such as Vision India 2030, and supports sustainable development, infrastructure, health, education, and technology initiatives. NITI Aayog also fosters cooperative federalism by coordinating efforts between various levels of government and encouraging collaborative solutions rather than top-down directives. It functions through a system of governing bodies, including the Governing Council, comprising the Prime Minister and chief ministers of all states, which meets annually to review progress and set priorities. The organization emphasizes results-based governance, using data and analytics to measure outcomes and improve program implementation. It also promotes innovation, entrepreneurship, and inclusive development, aligning with India’s broader economic and social goals. NITI Aayog’s initiatives include promoting digital governance, climate action, and sustainable development goals. It also plays a role in designing policies for sectors like agriculture, industry, and urban development, with a focus on leveraging technology and innovation. Overall, NITI Aayog represents a significant shift towards a more participatory, data-driven, and collaborative approach to national development, moving away from the top-down planning model of the past to a more flexible and inclusive framework. Its success depends on fostering coordination among states, central agencies, and stakeholders to achieve India’s ambitious development objectives and ensure sustainable and inclusive growth across the country.

text: The key elements of Organizational Behavior (OB) operate at three primary levels: individual, group, and organizational. At the individual level, OB focuses on personality, perception, motivation, learning, and attitudes – understanding how individual characteristics influence job performance and satisfaction. This includes studying things like emotional intelligence, values, and stress management. Moving to the group level, OB examines dynamics like communication, leadership, power, conflict, and team development. It explores how individuals interact within teams, how decisions are made, and how to foster collaboration and cohesion. Finally, at the organizational level, OB investigates aspects like organizational culture, structure, change management, and human resource policies. This involves understanding how the overall organizational environment impacts employee behavior and performance, and how to design structures and processes that promote efficiency and effectiveness. Interwoven throughout these levels are foundational concepts like diversity, ethics, and globalization, recognizing the increasing complexity of modern workplaces. These elements aren’t isolated; they constantly interact and influence each other. For example, an individual’s personality (individual level) can impact their role within a team (group level), which in turn is shaped by the overall organizational culture (organizational level).

The Millennium Development Goals and subsequent Sustainable Development Goals frameworks have provided strategic direction for development cooperation, helping Bangladesh achieve remarkable progress in poverty reduction, maternal health, and primary education enrollment. However, the role of international organizations has also generated debates about dependency, conditionality attached to aid, and the imposition of external development models that may not align with local contexts. text: Speech communication is important in people's daily life. The missing of high-frequency components of speech signal usually leads to low naturalness and intelligibility, such as the difficulty of distinguishing fricatives and similar voices. Therefore, speech bandwidth extension (BWE), which aims to restore the missing high-frequency components of narrowband speech using the correlations that exist between the low and high-frequency components of the wideband speech signal, has attracted the attentions of many researchers. BWE methods can not only be applied to real-time voice communication, but also benefit other speech signal processing areas such as text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis [1], speech recognition [2], [3], and speech enhancement [4], [5]. Many researchers have made a lot of efforts in the field of BWE. Some early studies adopted the source-filter model of speech production and attempted to restore high-frequency residual signals and spectral envelopes respectively from input narrowband signals. The high-frequency residual signals were usually estimated from the narrowband residual signals by spectral folding [6]. text: Adverse drug reaction (ADR) monitoring is often challenging to implement in the developing world such as in Bangladesh, and challenges restrict the building of a productive ADR safety system, namely, pharmacovigilance. One of the main difficulties is that educating health professionals, including pharmacists, doctors and even nurses, on the significance and also on the process to report ADRs is scarce. In the absence of knowledge, under-reporting occurs frequently, resulting in insufficient safety information. Finally, lack of dedicated pharmacovigilance facilities and resources such as manpower, technology and funds, among other things, makes it unable to collect, analyse and act on safety signals in a timely manner. Insufficient laws and poor enforcement of pharmacovigilance requirements then tend to undermine the system. Moreover, the large amounts of self-medication, the sale of over the counter drugs without prescription and the presence of the counterfeit and poor quality drugs, render the accurate assessment of drug safety difficult. Patient education and knowledge related to adverse effect reporting is also scant and so is community participation. Speaking different languages, not-so-good communication and problems with the management of data prevent information to be rapidly passed along. Furthermore, collaboration between different parties (including healthcare practitioners, regulatory agencies, the pharmaceutical industry and international organisations) is commonly poor. To cater to these challenges, there is need for large-scale training programs, investment in infrastructures for pharmacovigilance, public awareness campaigns and development of strong regulatory policies in order to achieve a functioning and sustainable pharmacovigilance system in Bangladesh.

However, their use in biomedical applications has raised concerns regarding potential toxicity and inadequate biocompatibility, which may result in problems such as allergic reactions, tumor formation, teratogenicity, and inflammation [1], [5], [6], [7], [8]. The problem is often associated with the release of corrosion products and fretting debris, as well as the materials’ inadequate affinity for cells and tissues. Some cobalt–chromium alloys also contain a significant amount of nickel, despite being designated as metallic biomaterials for surgical implants by ASTM [2]. Ti–6Al–4V alloys, on the other hand, do not contain nickel as an alloy element, but nickel is included as a trace impurity. However, in Dulbecco's PBS(-) solution (i.e., phosphate-buffered saline without calcium and magnesium salts) recovered after fretting fatigue tests, a higher nickel content was detected than in the Ti–6Al–4V alloy itself. text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs (~22 nucleotides) that are typically encoded within the introns of other genes [1]. MiRNAs are synthesized as immature pro-miRNAs that are cleaved into pre-miRNA by Drosha ribonuclease type III. The pre-miRNA transcript is then further cleaved into its active form by Dicer 1 ribonuclease type III [2,3]. Mature miRNAs interact with Argonaute proteins to form an RNA silencing complex that interacts with the 3'-untranslated region (3' UTR) of target mRNA transcripts via approximate base pair matching to post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression [3,4]. Such miRNA–miRNA interactions either repress translation or promote cleavage of the mRNA transcript [1]. MiRNAs are unavoidably transcribed as a duplex, though often one strand is much less stable and therefore does not accumulate [3]. This less stable strand is called the passenger strand and is indicated by a-3p. Most passenger strands have minimal ability to interact with mRNA, though some are now being recognized as having regulatory capacities [5,6]. Recent research has identified a role of miRNAs in numerous processes, including growth and development [7], oncogenesis [8], and lipid metabolism [9]. Because of their small size and ability to interact with mRNA transcripts without exact base-pair matching, miRNAs are highly pleiotropic; they can target multiple genes while, conversely, many mRNAs are regulated by numerous miRNAs [10]. Therefore, the role of miRNAs is highly complex and only now beginning to be fully elucidated.

text: A seed drill is a device that sows the seeds for crops by metering out the seeds, positioning them in the soil, and covering them to a certain average depth. Manual broadcasting had led to irregular seed sowing, poor germination and low yield (Belavadi and Prakash, 1980). The seed drill transformed the way individual farmers worked, developed stronger strains of plants through selective breeding and helped make farming more efficient by reducing unnecessarily wasted seed. It is composed by some sections: the seed hopper, the tube and/or funnels to deliver the seeds in the field and the coulters/openers that make the furrows where the seeds are placed. Some of the newer seed drills even feature press wheels that help the seeds to be covered and lightly firmed up, while promoting better soil-seed contact. Seed drill has various advantages, including accurate sowing depth, proper spacing between rows, better germination rate, and which all together may enhance productivity and efficient utilization of resources. Modern seed drills can be modified to accommodate differing seed types and land conditions and are often used for sowing in conjunction with plant and fertilizer appliacators, potentially providing a fertilizing and sowing sevice in one pass. Seed drill machines can be manually-operated, ox-operated or horse-operated, and tractor-operated depending on the size of the farm and the available technology. The modern precision seed drills are GPS- and sensor-assisted, and calibrated to deliver seed in exact amounts, particularly important for high-value crops. Additionally, the employing of seed drills permits a better kill of weeds, due to the fact that the dense and uniform crop stand outcompetes the weeds more effectively. It also promotes conservation tillage as it reduces soil disturbance, helps conserve soil moisture, and improves organic matter. Seed drills are often marketed by governmental agencies and farmers' cooperatives who help farmers to pay for them or use them as extension tools to train farmers to use them in areas where they are less commonly used. text: Hardware-software co-design is a collaborative approach in mechatronic and embedded system development where hardware and software components are designed concurrently to optimize performance, efficiency, and functionality for specific applications, such as robotics or IoT devices. Unlike traditional sequential design, where hardware is developed before software, co-design ensures both are tailored together from the outset, balancing trade-offs like processing speed, power consumption, and cost. For example, in a robotic controller, the hardware (e.g., microcontroller, sensors) and software (e.g., control algorithms, firmware) are designed to complement each other, ensuring the processor’s architecture supports real-time tasks like sensor data processing. The process begins with defining system requirements, followed by partitioning tasks between hardware and software—computationally intensive tasks may be offloaded to dedicated hardware (e.g., FPGA for signal processing) to reduce software complexity. Tools like hardware description languages (HDL) and high-level programming (C, Python) facilitate simultaneous development. Co-design uses simulation and modeling to test interactions, identifying bottlenecks like memory constraints or latency early. It supports optimization techniques, such as hardware accelerators for machine learning or low-power modes for battery-driven systems. Challenges include managing design complexity, ensuring compatibility, and verifying system behavior under diverse conditions. Iterative prototyping, using tools like emulators or development boards, validates performance. In applications like autonomous vehicles, co-design ensures efficient integration of LiDAR processing (hardware) with navigation algorithms (software). It also enhances scalability, allowing systems to adapt to new requirements, and improves reliability by aligning hardware capabilities with software demands. By fostering synergy between components, hardware-software co-design delivers compact, efficient, and high-performance solutions, critical for complex mechatronic systems where seamless interaction between hardware and software is essential for tasks like real-time control, data processing, or user interaction in dynamic environments

text: The observational reports on the MLT region wind response to the geomagnetic storms provide quite contradictory results. Hook (1970), using meteor wind radar at College, Alaska, found evidence of enhanced southward wind at altitudes of 75–110 km, while Ma et al. (2001) reported enhanced eastward wind several days after the storm onset at midlatitude stations situated in Japan, with the magnitude of the enhancement depending on the season. Recently, Balan et al. (2004), using MU and MF radars located in Japan, found that the meridional MLT wind becomes more equatorward, while the zonal wind becomes more eastward. Price et al. (1991) have observed the neutral winds in the altitude region between 70 and 110 km at a high-latitude station (70°S) and found a tendency for equatorially directed wind in the early morning hours. Singer et al. (1994), using superposed-epoch analysis, demonstrated that there was enhanced westward zonal wind at middle latitudes and an eastward wind at higher latitudes and no reaction in the meridional wind. However, Fahrutdinova et al. (2001) reported a reduction in the mean zonal wind and appearance of the northward meridional wind. Nozawa and Brekke (1995), using the EISCAT measurements, found that the differences in the neutral wind patterns between disturbed and quiet days below 109 km are rather small and within the error bars of the experiments, which supported the earlier observations made by Kunitake and Schlegel (1991). Therefore, observations accumulated to date show that the neutral MLT winds could be enhanced, reduced or not affected during the geomagnetic storms and that the changes could be in different directions.

text: The fundamental difference between vertebrates and invertebrates lies in the presence or absence of a backbone or vertebral column. Vertebrates are animals that possess a well-developed internal skeleton made of bone or cartilage, which includes a backbone that encases the spinal cord. This backbone provides structural support, protection for the nervous system, and serves as an attachment point for muscles, enabling complex movements and agility. Examples of vertebrates include mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish. In contrast, invertebrates lack a vertebral column altogether. They do not have a backbone or spinal cord, and their structural support may come from an exoskeleton, a hydrostatic skeleton, or other supportive tissues. Invertebrates are far more numerous and diverse, comprising about 95% of all animal species, and include groups such as insects, arachnids, mollusks, crustaceans, worms, and cnidarians. The absence of a backbone in invertebrates allows for a wide range of body forms, sizes, and modes of life, from microscopic plankton to large, complex animals like octopuses. Invertebrates often have simpler body structures compared to vertebrates, but they have evolved a variety of sophisticated adaptations for survival in their respective environments. The presence of a backbone in vertebrates is associated with greater mobility, intelligence, and complex organ systems, which support advanced behaviors and physiological functions. Invertebrates, on the other hand, often exhibit remarkable diversity in body plans and reproductive strategies, allowing them to thrive in nearly every habitat on Earth, from deep oceans to deserts. Both groups play vital roles in ecosystems, with invertebrates often serving as pollinators, decomposers, and prey for other animals, while vertebrates are key predators, herbivores, and ecosystem engineers. The distinction between vertebrates and invertebrates is fundamental to understanding animal biology, classification, and evolutionary relationships, highlighting the incredible diversity and adaptability of the animal kingdom.

text: Climate refers to the long-term average patterns of atmospheric conditions in a specific region over extended periods, typically measured across 30 years or more, encompassing temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind patterns, and seasonal variations that characterize a particular area's typical environmental conditions. Weather, in contrast, describes the short-term, day-to-day atmospheric conditions at a specific location and time, including immediate factors like temperature, rainfall, cloud cover, wind speed, and barometric pressure that can change rapidly within hours or days. The fundamental difference lies in temporal scale: weather represents the immediate atmospheric state that people experience daily, while climate represents the statistical summary of weather patterns over decades, providing insight into what weather conditions are typical, expected, or normal for a region during specific seasons. Weather is highly variable and can fluctuate dramatically from one day to the next, with sudden storms, temperature swings, or unexpected sunshine, whereas climate is relatively stable and changes gradually over long periods, though it can shift due to factors like ocean current changes, volcanic eruptions, or human activities. For example, a particular day might be unusually cold in a typically warm climate region, representing weather variability rather than climate change. Climate determines what types of ecosystems, agriculture, and human activities are sustainable in a region, while weather influences daily decisions like clothing choices, travel plans, and outdoor activities. Understanding this distinction is crucial for comprehending environmental science, as climate change refers to long-term shifts in average conditions, while extreme weather events are individual occurrences that may or may not be related to broader climatic trends.

text: An oxymoron is a figure of speech that combines two contradictory or opposing words placed next to each other to create a paradoxical or thought-provoking effect. This rhetorical device highlights conflict, emphasizes contrast, or adds humor and depth to language by merging opposing ideas into a single phrase. For example, common oxymorons include “deafening silence,” “jumbo shrimp,” “bittersweet,” “original copy,” and “living dead.” These phrases seem self-contradictory at first but often reveal a deeper or nuanced meaning upon reflection. Oxymorons are frequently used in literature and everyday speech to express complex emotions or situations, such as Shakespeare’s famous lines in Romeo and Juliet: “Parting is such sweet sorrow” and “O brawling love! O loving hate!” The word “oxymoron” itself comes from Greek roots meaning “sharp” and “foolish,” which is fitting because the combination of contradictory terms can sharpen meaning through irony or paradox. Oxymorons can appear in various forms, often as adjective-noun pairs like “seriously funny” or “living dead,” but they may also take other grammatical forms. Their use encourages readers or listeners to pause and consider the layered meanings behind the words. Overall, oxymorons enrich language by capturing the complexity and contradictions inherent in human experience.

text: Binaural speech enhancement algorithms are used in various head-mounted communication devices, e.g., hearing aids (HAs). Modern HAs are equipped with multiple microphones and the left and right devices are connected through a wireless link. The spatial diversity provided by these multiple microphones enables the attenuation of the directional interfering signals such as competing speakers and are superior to single-channel approaches. Suppression of interfering signals can be grouped into two families of algorithms: 1- Blind source separation (BSS) algorithms that exploit the statistical characteristics of all involved sources. For instance, independent component analysis (ICA) based algorithms use second or higher order statistics of the signals [1], [2]. 2-Beamforming-based algorithms that rely on a known microphone configuration and a spatial model of the signal. In fact, beamformers are spatio-temporal filters that are steered towards the desired source and extract it in the presence of competing speakers and ambient noise [3], [4].

text: Film financing refers to the process of securing funds necessary to produce a film, encompassing a variety of methods and sources that filmmakers utilize to bring their projects to life. This crucial aspect of filmmaking involves budgeting, fundraising, and managing financial resources to cover various production costs, including pre-production, shooting, post-production, marketing, and distribution. Filmmakers often begin by creating a detailed budget that outlines all anticipated expenses, which serves as a roadmap for securing financing. There are several avenues for obtaining funds, including private investors, production companies, grants, crowdfunding, and pre-sales of distribution rights. Private investors may provide capital in exchange for a share of the profits, while production companies often have established networks and resources to facilitate financing. Grants from government bodies, arts organizations, and film commissions can also support independent filmmakers, particularly those focusing on culturally significant or innovative projects. Crowdfunding platforms have gained popularity in recent years, allowing filmmakers to raise small amounts of money from a large number of people, often in exchange for perks or early access to the film. Pre-sales involve selling distribution rights to a film before it is completed, providing upfront capital based on projected future earnings. Additionally, tax incentives and rebates offered by various regions can significantly reduce production costs, making certain locations more attractive for filming. Navigating the complexities of film financing requires a solid understanding of the industry, as well as strong negotiation skills to secure favorable terms. Filmmakers must also be prepared to present their projects compellingly, often creating pitch decks or sizzle reels to attract potential investors and partners. The landscape of film financing is continually evolving, influenced by technological advancements, changing audience behaviors, and the rise of streaming platforms, which have altered traditional distribution models. As a result, filmmakers must remain adaptable and innovative in their approach to securing funds. Ultimately, effective film financing is essential for transforming creative ideas into tangible cinematic experiences, enabling filmmakers to tell their stories and connect with audiences worldwide. By understanding the various financing options available and strategically leveraging them, filmmakers can enhance their chances of success in a competitive industry.

text: India’s Five-Year Plans, which were launched in 1951 with the creation of the Planning Commission, were overarching economic development plans intended to direct progress across multiple sectors in a centralized manner. The early plans focused on the rapid development of heavy industry — in steel, coal and machinery — in a bid to get the economy up on its feet. They emphasized public sector growth, infrastructure investment, and import substitution to become self-reliant. Agricultural development and land reform, along with poverty reduction, assumed greater importance in subsequent plans, particularly through the Green Revolution that aimed to increase agricultural output. Gradually, Education, Health, Rural Development, etc. defined the essentials of the plans. The plans also stressed regional balance to mitigate differences among states in regards to development. From the 8th Plan (1992) India began to integrate its economy with world markets and reoriented its economy towards a more market-driven approach and began to further liberalize its regulations since then. Some have criticised the plans, which fixed quantitative production, investment, employment, and social targets for each enterprise, as rigid and inefficient. The Planning Commission developed the Plan and represented it through while NITI Aayog after 2015 discontinued the Five-Year Plan regime. The Five-Year Plans, as we inherit them, are a legacy in form of providing and shaping institutional mechanisms of planned integrated development in India, and that also as an instrument of India’s socio-economic transformation during the span of a little over seven decades.

text: Salinity The condition where the solute composition of the soil or water is such that excessive amounts of soluble salts, usually sodium chloride, iron sulfide, and gypsum, impair the normal good growth of plants, soil characteristics, and general agricultural productivity. Soil salinization is a serious environmental problem in arid and semi-arid areas where strong evaporation (E a ) surpasses precipitation and its leaches, resulting in the accumulation of salts in the soil surface. These salts could be due to either natural sources, the use of saline water for irrigation, inadequate drainage, or encroachment of sea water. When the concentration of soluble salt in soil solutions becomes too high, it develops osmotic imbalance, water stress and limits water absorption in plants; hence plants are in physiological drought stress with available moisture. This crops poor germination, plant growth and nutrient uptake, as well as yield. Toxicity and other problems can also result from salinity by the accumulation of certain ions such as sodium and chloride to toxic concentrations. Symptoms of salinity stress manifest in the forms of leaf burn, reduced plant size, chlorosis, and wilting. Soil salinity is typically classified into salty, sodic, and salty-sodic groups depending on inherent salt composition and sodium level. Soil salinity management also includes actions designed to either increase the outflow (enhanced drainage, leaching with surplus irrigation water, application of gypsum to replace sodium ions in the cation exchange complex, use of salt-tolerant varieties, and correct irrigation scheduling). Routine monitoring of soil and water is necessary to monitor salinity levels and take appropriate management actions. Salinity is becoming an increasingly critical issue worldwide as a consequence of climate change, unsustainable irrigation, and land degradation, threatening food security and rural livelihoods. Scientists and extension workers are working on salt-tolerant crop varieties and sustainable land and water management in an effort to address some of the impacts of salinity. In short, salinity is the destructive accumulation of salts in soil or water that prevents plants from flourishing and undermines agricultural success if not controlled.

text: Protestant Reformation The Protestant Reformation, sparked by Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses, according to traditional historiography, stands as the most significant European fermentation of all centuries, from those of the first millennium to the fifty of the second. Responding to issues such as the swindling of the faithful (the “sale of indulgences”) by clerics and critique of papal power, Luther and his successors, including John Calvin and Huldrych Zwingli, emphasized direct access to scriptures, salvation though faith alone, and the value of individual conscience. They translated the Bible into vernacular languages, challenging the Church’s monopoly on religion interpretation and enfranchising common people. This religious revolution divided Western Christianity and spawned Protestant denominations — Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican — that rejected papal authority. A Reformation erupted in wars and conflicts—including the German Peasants’ War, the French Wars of Religion, and the Thirty Years’ War—that redrew Europe’s political map and would later help give birth to religious toleration and the separation of church and state. It also diminished the Holy Roman Empire and papal authority, and empowered secular rulers to control religious affairs. Protestant areas also tended to enjoy social and economic success, as reformers emphasized reading and hard work. Culturally, Reformation led to the development of a highly educated class of print readers which facilitated the spread of new ideas such as evangelicalism and resulted in the infrastructure of Protestant schooling, schools and universities. It also left its mark on art, music and ethics, establishing moral and ethical paradigms that have helped shape Western ideals and identity. Theologically, the Reformation spearheaded later religious movements, and reached even further forward into Enlightenment thought and liberal democratic individualism. It questioned the absolute authority of religion, advanced religious conscience and spread modernity. As such, it was the Protestant Reformation that effectively turned European society on its head; freeing the masses to think and believe what they wish and, it freed the state to rule as it desired.. For after the state, followed literacy, and then, the foundation stones for knowledge required to create modern civilization.

text: Determinism is the philosophical idea that every event or state of affairs, including every human decision and action, is the inevitable and necessary consequence of antecedent states of affairs. It is determined that, taking the state of the universe at any given time, only one future is possible, through the operation of cause and effect. Perhaps it's because any kind of determinism starts conversations about free will and moral accountability. Free will can be considered an illusion in a deterministic system if every decision has been determined by past causes. Causal determinism is commonly refuted on the grounds that (a) causal laws are only applicable to physical events and that (b) psychological determinism or even theological determinism is where human behaviour or divine predestination is determined in a psychological pathway. Compatibilists maintain that it is possible for free will and determinism to be compatible if freedom is construed as the ability to act in accordance with one’s own desires and without external pressure. According to incompatibilists, on the other hand, determinism is incompatible with true free will. Determinism informs morality, law, science, our notion of responsibility and accountability. The classical science instinct of scientific determinism – the notion of a clockwork universe – was challenged by the modern branch of quantum mechanics that opened a door to indeterminacies and to the randomness of events, thereby muddying the canvass. Still, determinism is widely regarded as an important topic in philosophy, sparking debates about the nature of causation, free will, and reality.

text: Environmental degradation is a significant problem in Bangladesh, impacting various aspects of the environment, including air, water, soil, and biodiversity. The causes of environmental degradation in Bangladesh are multifaceted, involving a combination of natural, economic, social, and institutional factors. Natural factors, such as climate change, natural disasters, and geological processes, contribute to environmental degradation by altering ecosystems, increasing the frequency and intensity of natural disasters, and leading to loss of biodiversity. Economically, the pursuit of rapid economic growth and industrialization, often at the expense of environmental protection, has led to pollution, deforestation, and the depletion of natural resources. Socially, population growth, urbanization, and the concentration of people in vulnerable areas contribute to environmental degradation by increasing pressure on natural resources and ecosystems. Institutionally, weak environmental governance, lack of effective environmental laws and policies, and limited public participation in decision-making processes allow environmental degradation to persist. The consequences of environmental degradation in Bangladesh are profound, impacting health, economy, and social well-being. Environmental degradation can lead to a range of health problems, including respiratory and waterborne diseases, and increase the risk of natural disasters and climate change impacts. Economically, environmental degradation can lead to loss of livelihoods, reduced productivity, and increased costs for adaptation and mitigation. Socially, environmental degradation can exacerbate social inequalities, as the poor and vulnerable are often the most affected by environmental problems. Moreover, environmental degradation can undermine social cohesion and stability, as communities face the consequences of environmental problems and compete for scarce resources. The problem of environmental degradation in Bangladesh thus requires comprehensive policies and interventions that address the root causes of degradation, promote sustainable development, and strengthen environmental governance and public participation in decision-making processes.

text: The User Experience (UX) designer is the individual responsible of creating value to users of a product interacting with it (the system), and the business providing the product or service. It is an approach that incorporates psychology, information architecture, interaction design, usability, and research to promote a holistic approach to solutions that satisfy both user needs and business goals. User Research The UX process frequently starts with user research—interviews, surveys, analytics, observations—to determine user goals, pain points, contexts, and behaviors. In this moment of truth, the value of artifacts such as the user personas and journey maps becomes evident to help you understand in a more empathic and goal-oriented design of your product. The second stage involves building structures of information in the form of sitemaps and wireframes, establishing content hierarchy and site navigation and verifying them through usability testing. Refinement next becomes active prototyping, where users can perform tasks in simulated worlds and giving designers something to iterate upon, the feedback being the real kind. Good UX design should also look at accessibility, performance, consistency, and cross-device responsiveness. UX is not just digital – every experience a user has, be it on a website, app, kiosk, or even physical product and service systems, adheres to the concept. From the start of the life cycle, UX designers work with developers, UI designers, and stakeholders to make sure the design decisions made are supportive of the business goals and technically realistic. They have metrics to measure and optimize like task success rate, time-on-task, error rates and subjective satisfaction. In the end, UX design is human-focused: It places the user at the heart of the design process so that every touchpoint is intuitive, useful, and in sync with user behaviors and accessibility guidelines.

text: Genre is a key storytelling mechanism to organize stories around shared conventions, themes, and emotional experiences, so that both creators and audiences understand the general sort of thing a story is. It provides a rough scaffold for the tone, plot structure, character types, settings and stylistic choices that constitute a film, novel or television show. For instance, a horror story will often take advantage of suspense, fear and locations of darkness, while a romantic comedy will often play on the sense of being in love, humor and happy endings. Genre serves a purpose, in that it makes a contract with the audience, building up the audience's expectations and giving them something to relate to, so that they can dive in emotionally even sooner. When moviegoers buy tickets to a movie that hails itself as “science fiction,” they expect to see either stunning new technology, fantastical ideas about the future or alternate worlds filled with strange characters. And this expectation colors the reception and perception of the story. Genres function here like a narrative tool-box offering writers a set of devices to play with, introducing and manipulating well-known archetypes, tropes and structures that work, but also introducing possibilities for experimentation through subverting or hybridising of established genres. Genres change over time, adapting to cultural trends, audience tastes and technological developments, and new hybrid genres — sci-fi romance, say, or horror-comedy — can be born out of creative play. Of course, genre inflects production decisions as well, costumes and sets, the music and cinematography. It assists marketers in placing and marketing the film. But when you rigidly apply the genre rules, it can get to be cliché, just like the best stories follow tradition but in a new way or with a fun twist. Genre As a final impact, genre acts as a language with which tales are made and received as well as how stories connect with their audience and meanings are exchanged.

text: The principle of conservation of charge is a basic law of physics that says that the total electric charge in an isolated system stays the same over time, even if things change or transform inside the system.  This means that electric charge can't be made or destroyed; it can only be moved from one portion of the system to another.  This principle is very important in electromagnetism and explains how electric currents, static electricity, and many other physical phenomena work.  It makes sure that the net charge stays the same when charged particles are separated or joined, keeping the balance between positive and negative charges.  To understand how electrical circuits work, how atoms and molecules interact, and how electromagnetic fields move, it's important to know that charge is conserved.  The continuity equation shows this quantitatively by linking the rate of change of charge density in a volume to the current flow across its border.  This idea is consistent with experimental findings, such as the flow of electrons via conductors and the emission of charged particles during radioactive decay.  If you break this law, it would mean that charge may appear or disappear on its own, which goes against a lot of experimental evidence and would make physical laws less consistent. Conservation of charge is integral to Maxwell’s equations, quantum electrodynamics, and particle physics, reinforcing the stability of matter and enabling technologies from electronics to communication. Understanding this principle allows scientists and engineers to predict and control electrical phenomena accurately and is essential in fields as diverse as chemistry, biology, and materials science.

text: Inverse dynamics are the joint force and torque calculations needed to generate a certain motion (e.g., joint positions, velocities, and accelerations) of a robot. Clearly the reverse of forward dynamics, which calculates the resulting movement from applied forces. Inverse dynamics employs the kinematic and dynamic models of the robot—usually obtained through the Newton-Euler or Lagrangian approach—to calculate the motor inputs that are required to follow a desired trajectory. This is particularly important for robot control where high precision, speed or force regulation is desired, such as manipulators grinding or polishing industrial parts, humanoid walking or surgical robotics. In other words, Inverse Dynamics calculates how much torque the motor of each joint must exert at each instant in order to move exactly along a given desired trajectory, taking into account the effects of its inertia, gravity, the Coriolis and centripetal forces. These are basic operations in a control model based control method such as a computed-torque control, a feed-forward control or an adaptive control, where a robot is moved stably and precisely even when its payload and/or an external force applied thereto are changed. Inverse dynamics have also been implemented in biomechanical research to analyze human motion, estimating joint forces from motion capture data. Computational costs are high in the case of more complex robots with many degrees of freedom, but efficient recursive algorithm such as Newton-Euler Recursive Algorithm come to reduce the computational tasks drastically. Inverse dynamics on the other hand is a technique used in simulations to achieve realistic animation of robots or assess the actuator specification in the design process. Inverse dynamics makes an essential contribution towards implementation of intelligent, safe, and efficient robotic behavior in the real world by connecting desired motion to the necessary physical inputs.

text: A Type II error, also known as a false negative, occurs in hypothesis testing when a researcher fails to reject the null hypothesis (H?) even though it is actually false. In other words, it is the mistake of concluding that there is no significant effect, difference, or relationship when, in reality, one does exist. The probability of committing a Type II error is denoted by ? (beta), and its complement, 1 – ?, is called the power of the test, which represents the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. For example, suppose a medical researcher is testing a new drug to determine whether it is more effective than an existing treatment. If the drug truly works better but the statistical test fails to detect this improvement, the researcher has made a Type II error—overlooking a real effect. Such errors can have serious consequences, such as missing effective treatments, underestimating risks, or failing to identify meaningful patterns in data. The likelihood of a Type II error depends on factors such as sample size, effect size, variability in the data, and the chosen significance level (?). Larger sample sizes and stronger effects reduce the risk of this error, while small samples or subtle effects increase it. text: The mammalian placenta is a vital organ that develops during pregnancy, serving as the critical interface between the mother and the developing fetus, and performing multiple essential functions that support fetal growth and development. Primarily, the placenta facilitates the exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste products between maternal and fetal blood supplies without allowing the two bloodstreams to mix directly. Oxygen and essential nutrients such as glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids are transferred from the mother’s blood to the fetus, providing the energy and building blocks necessary for cellular growth and organ formation. At the same time, metabolic wastes produced by the fetus, including carbon dioxide and urea, are transferred back to the mother’s circulation for elimination. The placenta also acts as an endocrine organ by producing important hormones like human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), progesterone, and estrogen, which help maintain pregnancy, regulate the maternal immune response, and prepare the mother’s body for childbirth and lactation. Additionally, the placenta provides a protective barrier against certain pathogens and harmful substances, though it is not impermeable, and some viruses or chemicals can cross this barrier. The placenta is an organ that consists of fetal tissues (chorionic villi) and maternal tissues (decidua), structurally composed to provide a large surface area for efficient exchange. It has a rich blood supply to provide enough blood flow to keep up with the high metabolic requirements of a rapidly growing fetfetus. The placenta induces immune tolerance by dampening local immune responses and protecting the fetus from being rejected by the maternal immune system which would otherwise recognise the genetically different fetus as foreign. This complicated immunological dialogue is what allows pregnancy to persist. While the specifics of placental development and function are diverse between mammalian species, the general role of a functional placenta in maintaining reproductive success is universal. The placenta acts as both an endocrine gland and a homeostatic regulator, mediating nutrient and gas exchange between the mother and fetus as well as monitoring the fetal environment by controlling levels of hormones responsible for feedback signaling functions in contralateral maternal or developmental compartments during fetal development and initiation of birth. The placenta is delivered as the afterbirth after birth. Abnormal placental function during pregnancy can prevent the fetus from developing, which in turn leads to problems like low birth weight, preterm birth or miscarriage. Therefore, the presence of a functional placenta is essential to nurture the fetus during post-implantation development in utero by providing nutrients and an immune barrier for fetal growth (Kaufmann et al., 2003; Pijnenborg et al., 2011), as well as allowing adaptation of both mother and offspring to successful delivery of birth with minimal consequences on postnatal survival.

text: The kinked demand curve model is an economic theory developed to explain the observed phenomenon of price rigidity, or stability, in certain oligopolistic markets. Proposed by Paul Sweezy, it posits that an oligopolistic firm faces a demand curve that is "kinked" at the prevailing market price (P0), due to asymmetric assumptions about how rival firms will react to price changes. Specifically, the model assumes two distinct responses from competitors: First, if an oligopolist raises its price above P0, its competitors are assumed not to follow the price increase. Instead, they will keep their prices unchanged, hoping to capture market share from the firm that initiated the price hike. Consequently, the segment of the demand curve above the kink is relatively elastic, meaning a small price increase will lead to a disproportionately large decrease in quantity demanded for that firm's product, as customers readily switch to cheaper rivals. Second, if an oligopolist lowers its price below P0, its competitors are assumed to immediately match the price reduction. They will lower their own prices to prevent losing their market share. As a result, the firm that cut its price will only experience a relatively small increase in sales, as it primarily retains its existing customers and gains only marginal new ones. Thus, the segment of the demand curve below the kink is relatively inelastic. This asymmetric response creates a sharp "kink" in the demand curve at the current market price and output level. The crucial implication for the firm's marginal revenue (MR) curve is that it exhibits a vertical discontinuity or gap precisely at the output level corresponding to the kink. This means that if the marginal cost (MC) curve fluctuates within this vertical gap, the profit-maximizing output and price (where MR=MC) will remain unchanged. Therefore, the kinked demand curve model helps to explain why prices in an oligopoly tend to be stable and resistant to moderate changes in production costs or demand conditions, as firms have little incentive to either raise or lower prices from the prevailing level. While it explains rigidity, a limitation of the model is that it does not explain how the initial price P0 itself is determined, only why it might remain stable once established.

text: Media effects cover a wide variety of the effects that exposure to mass media or social media can have on individuals’ knowledge, attitudes, emotions or behavior; on users’ social norms; and on political and social institutions. The nature of these effects can be immediate and/or delayed, direct, or indirect, consciously or subconsciously intended and the magnitude of it can depend on factors related to the audience, the media content and the social network. As concerns about media effects focus primarily on the power of media messages, they center on the ways media messages shape political attitudes, public health behaviors, cultural values, and social norms. Early theories like the hypodermic needle model assumed powerful, uniform effects, but later studies revealed a more complex picture, acknowledging audience agency, selective exposure, and mediated influence. Contemporary media effects research includes models such as agenda-setting, framing, cultivation, social learning, and uses and gratifications, each highlighting different mechanisms of influence. For example, agenda-setting shows how media influence what topics people think about; framing shapes how they think about those topics; and cultivation theory explains how repeated media exposure molds their worldview. Media effects can also be negative, such as promoting stereotypes, misinformation, or desensitization, as well as positive, such as raising awareness or promoting social change. Understanding media effects is essential for policymakers, educators, and communicators to harness media’s power responsibly and mitigate potential harms in an increasingly media-saturated world.

text: One kind of performance that uses digital technologies in its planning, creation, and delivery is called "digital theatre."  It expands the possibilities of live theatre and reimagines how audiences engage with the art form by combining virtual and real elements.   Live-streamed stage shows, on-demand recordings, fully virtual productions for online platforms, interactive web-based experiences, and performances utilising multimedia tools such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and projection mapping are all included. Although digital theatre first appeared as a reaction to audience preferences and technological advancements, it really took off during major world crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, which compelled performers and organisations to adjust to remote and online formats in order to stay in touch with their audiences.  People who might be restricted by location, financial constraints, or physical mobility can now enjoy performances from around the globe thanks to digital theater's ability to transcend geographical boundaries.It also enables new forms of storytelling that play with time, space, and perspective in ways that traditional staging cannot, incorporating live chat, branching narratives, and audience interactivity to create immersive and participatory experiences. Artists use digital tools to experiment with hybrid forms that mix live acting with pre-recorded media, animation, motion capture, and real-time audience feedback, expanding both the aesthetic language and the collaborative process of theatre-making. Digital theatre also raises questions about liveness, presence, and intimacy—central concerns of the stage—by challenging the boundaries between performer and viewer, stage and screen, real and virtual. While some critics argue that digital formats risk losing the unique communal energy of in-person performance, others see them as opportunities to democratize and diversify theatre by reaching broader, younger, and more global audiences. Digital theatre is not limited to large, well-funded institutions; independent artists and grassroots groups also use accessible digital tools to create, share, and archive their work, fostering cross-cultural exchange and innovation. It also opens possibilities for sustainable practices, reducing the need for travel and physical resources. However, it brings challenges such as digital inequality, copyright concerns, and questions about fair compensation for artists working in online spaces. Ultimately, digital theatre represents both a continuation of theatre’s long history of technological adaptation and a bold reimagining of what performance can be in the 21st century, using digital means not only to replicate the stage but to expand its reach, deepen its impact, and transform how stories are told and shared in an increasingly interconnected world.

text: The nervous system in animals functions as a highly organized communication and control network that enables them to sense, process, and respond to internal and external stimuli, ensuring survival and coordination of body activities. It is composed of specialized cells called neurons, which transmit electrical impulses rapidly across the body, and supporting cells that maintain and protect them. The system is broadly divided into the central nervous system (CNS)—consisting of the brain and spinal cord, which process and integrate information—and the peripheral nervous system (PNS), which connects the CNS to the rest of the body through sensory and motor pathways. Sensory receptors detect changes in the environment, such as light, sound, touch, or chemical signals, and relay this information to the CNS, where it is interpreted and appropriate responses are generated. Motor neurons then carry signals from the CNS to muscles or glands, producing actions ranging from simple reflexes to complex behaviors. In simple animals like cnidarians, the nervous system may exist as a nerve net, while in more advanced animals, it becomes centralized and highly specialized, allowing for learning, memory, and complex decision-making. The nervous system also regulates involuntary processes such as heartbeat, digestion, and respiration through the autonomic division, while the somatic division controls voluntary movements. By integrating sensory input, coordinating motor output, and maintaining homeostasis, the nervous system allows animals to interact effectively with their environment, adapt to challenges, and perform the wide range of behaviors necessary for growth, reproduction, and survival.

text: An open-loop control system in robotics is a control mechanism where the output is generated based on a predefined input command without using feedback to monitor or adjust the system’s performance. In this system, the controller sends signals to actuators, such as motors or valves, to execute tasks like moving a robotic arm or driving a wheel, assuming the system behaves as expected. For example, a stepper motor in a 3D printer moves a set number of steps based on input pulses without verifying the actual position. Open-loop systems are simple, cost-effective, and fast, making them suitable for predictable, repetitive tasks where external disturbances are minimal, such as in conveyor belts or basic robotic grippers. They rely on accurate system modeling and calibration to ensure desired outcomes, as there is no mechanism to correct errors caused by factors like friction, load changes, or environmental variations. Common applications include irrigation systems or simple robotic toys. Advantages include low complexity and reduced hardware costs, as no sensors are needed. However, their lack of feedback makes them less robust, leading to inaccuracies if conditions deviate from expectations. For instance, a robot using open-loop control may overshoot its target if unexpected resistance occurs. Advances in actuator precision and system design mitigate some limitations, but open-loop systems are unsuitable for dynamic environments requiring adaptability. Challenges include handling uncertainties and ensuring reliability without real-time adjustments. In robotics, open-loop control is often used in initial designs or low-cost systems, but it is frequently paired with closed-loop systems for tasks demanding higher accuracy and robustness, such as autonomous navigation or precise manipulation in industrial settings.

text: In the machine learning technique known as reinforcement learning, agents interact with their surroundings and receive feedback in the form of incentives or penalties, which helps them learn how to make decisions.  Robots or agents use trial-and-error exploration in reinforcement learning, modifying their actions to maximize cumulative rewards over time, in contrast to supervised learning, which depends on labeled datasets.  The fundamental idea is that the agent chooses actions according to a policy, monitors the state and reward that result, and updates the policy to make better choices in the future.  This method is similar to how both humans and animals learn by doing, gradually figuring out the most effective ways to accomplish objectives.  Robots may learn complicated behaviors like object handling, navigation, and game play without explicit programming thanks to reinforcement learning algorithms like Q-learning and deep Q-networks (DQN).  In order to gradually improve its control strategy, a robot learning to balance on a beam, for instance, will experiment with various motions. It will receive positive reinforcement for successful balancing and negative feedback for falls.  Because reinforcement learning allows for autonomous adaptation, it is especially well-suited for situations in which the best course of action is unclear or constantly shifting.  For jobs like autonomous driving, where the robot learns to maneuver through traffic, or robotic control systems, where it learns to optimize actuator commands for fluid and effective motion, it is frequently utilized in robotics.  Multi-agent systems, in which several robots cooperate to accomplish common goals, are also supported by reinforcement learning.  Researchers strive to improve algorithms for faster learning, better generalization, and safety in real-world deployments. Despite its advantages, reinforcement learning has drawbacks, such as high sample complexity, requiring numerous interactions to learn effective policies, and stability issues, particularly in high-dimensional or continuous action spaces.  All things considered, reinforcement learning enables robots to independently acquire complicated behaviors through ongoing contact with their surroundings, increasing their intelligence, adaptability, and capacity to manage challenging tasks in uncertain situations.

text: Consideration is an essential part of contract law and is the value that passes between the parties that want to enter into a contract. It can be money or goods or services or a promise to do something and a promise not to do something. The consideration must be lawful, real and sufficient, though it need not be adequate (in other words, the courts don’t get involved in whether or not the deal was economically fair; it just matters that something of value was given). For instance, if A agrees to sell a computer to B for $500, $500 is the consideration from B and the computer is the consideration from A A fundamental rule is that consideration must be provided by the promisee, and the promisee must have given something in exchange. Consideration also shouldn’t be past — something already done before the promise (though there are exceptions (like under Indian law, which permits past consideration in certain situations)). It is the evidence that the contract is a bargain and not merely some unilateral act of kindness. A contract not supported by consideration is usually void, except in the case of a deed (a type of written and signed agreement). Currie v. Misa (1875) defined consideration to be a right, interest, profit, benefit or forbearance, detriment, loss, responsibility, given, suffered or undertaken by the other. Hence, consideration is necessary for the validity of a contract as it represents something given in return for something else and an agreement to pay compensation is a willingness to be subjected to the liability.

text: In film, continuity is the degree to which the details, style, characters, and other attributes of a scene, episode, or film adhere to or to lead to a logical sequence and aesthetic structure. It’s a matter of preserving coherence in everything that is visible in the frame — actors’ spatial positions, their costumes, makeup, the objects in the set, lighting, weather, dialogue — so that one shot joins undetectably to the next, even if scenes are shot out of order. Effective continuity helps keep audiences in the story, rather than noticing the clumsy jolts of discontinuity — when an actor’s drink, for example, is suddenly full after they’ve picked it up and taken half the contents away, or an actor’s haircut has changed between shots. There are different types of continuity, with visual continuity maintaining consistency of the places, props and costumes among takes; spatial continuity prevents confusing the directions of subjects and objects; and interframe continuity, the decisión of the result of the sequence and the sequence of time, they must be linear with a peculiarity: when shooting at different times, the lateness can cause apparent solapamientos. Continuity of dialogue and action also comes into play, ensuring that lines and movements remain in perfect sync across takes. The job of making sure everything fits together belongs mostly to the script supervisor, the person who keeps track of everything that happens on the set, and who absolutely must know what’s been filmed at any given time. Editors contribute during post, though, piecing together matching takes and using invisible cuts to maintain the illusion of nonstop action. This becomes even more of a problem when we are dealing with a complex scene, with multiple camera angles, stunts, those long shooting hours, and then even the slightest mistake becomes obvious. Here and there, filmmakers might even want to break or resist continuity for aesthetic or narrative reasons (think of surreal or avant-garde works), but in general, if we are to remain immersed in watching a movie (its own little world), continuity is everything. When these goofs happen, they distract audience members and detract from the overall quality of the movie, no matter how small they may be. So a true attention to detail is necessary from pre-production planning (storyboarding shots) through on-set supervision and post production editing in order for there to be a consistent visual language. Continuity is like the ticker tape of the cinema; it’s what makes watching a movie seem effortless, it forms that unmistakably seamless cinematic feel which prevents the viewer from having to rethink or re-emotion their way through a film because an image or performance just doesn’t connect with what they’ve seen before.

text: The V-I (voltage-current) characteristics of a thyristor, also known as a silicon controlled rectifier (SCR), describe how the current through the device varies with the applied voltage under different conditions. A thyristor has three terminals: the anode, cathode, and gate. The V-I characteristics can be divided into several regions based on the state of the thyristor and the applied voltage and current. In the forward blocking region, the anode is positive with respect to the cathode, but no current flows until a sufficient positive current is applied to the gate terminal. This triggers the thyristor into the forward conduction region, where it allows a large current to flow from the anode to the cathode. The thyristor remains in this conducting state as long as the anode-cathode voltage remains positive and the current exceeds the holding current. In the reverse blocking region, the cathode is positive with respect to the anode, and the thyristor acts as an open circuit, preventing current flow. The reverse breakdown region occurs when the reverse voltage exceeds a certain threshold, causing the thyristor to conduct in the reverse direction, which can lead to damage if not properly managed. The V-I characteristics of a thyristor are crucial for understanding its operation in various applications, such as power control, motor control, and phase control circuits. The thyristor's ability to handle high currents and voltages, combined with its fast switching capabilities, makes it a versatile component in modern electronic systems.
