text: Germination is the initial stage in a plant's life, as a seed develops into a seedling. It starts when the seed imbibes water, swells, its coat breaks and enzymes are released. The re-hydration induces the seed metabolism, in that the stored food in the endosperm or the cotyledons is broken down (with proteins into their amino acid components, starch into sugar, fats into fatty acids, etc.) and used for growth or for energy. The nutrients are used by the embryo as it grows. After imbibition and activation of enzymes the radicle (young root of embryo) is the first structure to come out of the seed. [60] This it enables the seedling to establish itself in the soil and begin to absorb water. The plumule (embryo shoot) then appears. There are two types of germination: epigeal, when cotyledons are over the soil surface (e.g. beans) and hypogeal when cotyledons are underground (maize). Germination is the result of a combination of environmental conditions as well as the availability of the proper seed in the proper conditions. It is due to these factors that germination of the seed also takes place and the greater the number of favourable conditions available, germination can occur. These key ingredients are water, oxygen, and a proper temperature. Assemblies, like cell division and growth, that rely on aerobic respiration require oxygen. Enzyme activity is a function of temperature; light sensitivity varies among species: some require light to germinate; others need darkness. Dormancy, marked by lack of growth, can also prevent germination, if the conditions for growth have been brought to optimal. Dormancy may be artificially or naturally overcome, such as scarifying (abrading) the seed coat or stratifying (cold treating) the seed. After the seedling breaks through and photosynthesis begins, one no longer needs the reserve food in the seed. Germination is a critical life history stage of plants, therefore knowledge of germination is important for agriculture, forestry, and conservation, as adequate germination is fundamental to the establishment, growth and productivity of crop species.

On the other hand, transparent and accountable journalism fosters greater civic engagement, encourages ethical media behavior, and supports a more informed society. text: This paper addresses the statistical properties of the Riemann zeta function zeros. The study of this topic began in 1944 when Selberg [26] demonstrated that the number of zeros in a sufficiently long interval on the critical line follows a Gaussian distribution (see also [7], [10], [11], [24]). In the 1970s, Montgomery and Dyson discovered that the spacings between the zeta zeros bear a striking resemblance to the spacings between eigenvalues of random Hermitian Gaussian matrices. This similarity was analytically substantiated by Montgomery [19] and numerically supported by Odlyzko [21] (see also [3], [23]). The connection between zeta zeros and random matrix eigenvalues has attracted considerable attention, as evidenced by review papers such as [18]. Recently, Bourgade [1] reinforced this connection by demonstrating that at the mesoscopic level, Riemann’s zeros exhibit correlations similar to those previously identified by Diaconis and Evans [5] for eigenvalues of unitary random matrices (see also [2]).

text: There are several factors that contribute to vignetting. Some arise from the optical properties of camera lenses, the most prominent of which is off-axis illumination falloff or the cos4 law. Here, vignetting is a result of foreshortening of the lens when viewed at increasing angles from the optical axis [13]. Other sources of vignetting are geometric in nature—light arriving at oblique angles to the optical axis may be partially obstructed by the field stop or lens rim. To determine the vignetting effects in an image, the most straightforward approach involves capturing an image completely spanned by a uniform scene region, such that brightness variations can solely be attributed to vignetting [1], [11], [20], [28], [29]. In such a calibration image, ratios of intensity with respect to the pixel on the optical axis describe the vignetting function. Suitable imaging conditions for this approach, however, can be challenging to produce due to uneven illumination and camera tilt, and the vignetting measurements are valid only for images captured by the camera under the same camera settings. Moreover, a calibration image can be recorded only if the camera is at hand; consequently, this approach cannot be used to correct images captured by unknown cameras, such as images downloaded from the Web.

text: The development of efficient and accurate numerical algorithms for astrophysical flow has become of great interest to the astrophysical community. Variable resolution approaches have provided an avenue for efficient simulation of hydrodynamical flow including multiphysical effects which involve substantial variation in length scale. Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) has been recognized as one of the most versatile and efficient approaches to enable the simulation of multiscale phenomena for which fixed-resolution simulation is either impractical or impossible. AMR discretizations employ a hierarchy of grids at different levels. High resolution is applied only to those regions of the flow which would otherwise be subject to unacceptably large truncation error. The utility of the AMR approach is underscored by the extensive list of codes that are targeted toward astrophysical research which utilize AMR. The list includes AstroBEAR, Enzo (O'Shea et al. 2004), Flash (Fryxell et al. 2000), Orion (Truelove et al. 1998; Klein 1999; Crockett et al. 2005), Nirvana (Ziegler 2005a), Ramses (Fromang et al. 2006), RIEMANN (Balsara 2001), and AMRVAC (Keppens et al. 2003), and the list of codes for which the development AMR capability is in progress including Athena (Gardiner & Stone 2005) and Pluto (Mignone et al. 2007).

text: John Locke, an English philosopher who lived in the 17th century, is often hailed as the father of liberal political thought; his views about the relationship between government and the governed have endured as the foundation of modern democracy and constitutional theory. In his most important work, Two Treatises of Government, Locke claimed that the only legitimate form of government is one based on the consent of the governed and that such a government has as its first priority the protection of the natural rights of individuals — specifically the rights to life, liberty, and property. And he opposed the idea of the divine right of kings, supporting instead that of the social contract: in which, as individuals, we ourselves create a government for the purpose of advancing peace and security. For Locke, political rulers do not have an unlimited or absolute power. When a government enslaves and does not perform the job of protecting the rights of its people, they may legitimately rebel and set up a new government in its place. He stressed the rule of law, the divide of power and the system of checks and balances to prevent tyranny. Locke also helped develop the notion of religious tolerance, and believed that the state must not dictate religion to the individual. His thoughts inspired the American Declaration of independence, the French Revolution, and the liberal constitution of the globe. For Locke, property was one of the preconditions of freedom, and labor was the basis of ownership. On human nature he was inclined to optimism, believing that men can reason and rule themselves. While Hobbes had seen men as brutish in the absence of an overriding authority, Locke saw civil society as a rational cooperation in which the parties engage positively. To sum up, Locke’s concept of the government—defined in terms of a rights bearers, with restricted powers, requiring popular consent—lies at the foundation of liberal democracies and enlightenment notion of the constitution.

Unlike previous philosophers, who laid ideal forms of government, he made the quest for power the central quest of politics and described it in terms laws), the means whereby power is, and may be acquired.” He’s best known for his view that a ruler doesn’t necessarily need to adhere to traditional moral or ethical guidelines instead he should be guided by those principles, and only when those principles endanger the security or wellbeing of the state then he need not. His guiding principle is "the end justifies the means" – that leaders should be willing to use any means of manipulation, deceit or cruelty in order to maintain their power and secure the state. Machiavelli dissected the distinction between politics and morality, opining that a person of authority could only achieve power if he or she could masquerade as both a lion (strong and fierce) and a fox (cunning and sly). Machiavelli also promoted the notion that fortune and skill (virtù) work hand in hand, whereby fortune caused need changes people's skills, and that a prince can shape fortune to fit his needs. His opinions mirror the instability that characterized Italian city-states at the time as they were subject to wars, treachery, and foreign interference. The book is frequently seen as a manual for tyrants; it can also be read as a call for strong, competent leadership in a time of chaos. Machiavelli’s works laid the groundwork for the study of modern political science by examining power, statecraft, and the practicality of governance. His lasting importance is that his ideas are highly illustrative of both authoritarian and democratic politics, thus he becomes a key figure in understanding the politics of power.

text: A cash crop is a crop that is grown primarily for sale and profit rather than for direct consumption by the farmer or local community. Unlike subsistence crops that are cultivated to meet the food needs of the farmer’s household, cash crops are intended to be sold in local, national, or international markets. Examples of cash crops include cotton, tobacco, sugarcane, coffee, cocoa, tea, oilseeds (like mustard and sunflower), rubber, and various horticultural products such as fruits and flowers. The cultivation of cash crops plays a vital role in the economies of many developing and developed countries, generating employment, foreign exchange earnings, and boosting the income of farmers. Cash crops are often more profitable than food crops but usually require higher inputs in terms of seeds, fertilizers, irrigation, pesticides, and labor. They also demand efficient market access, transport, and storage infrastructure. While cash crops can uplift rural livelihoods, they can also lead to monoculture, land degradation, overuse of water, and reduced biodiversity if not managed sustainably. Additionally, over-dependence on cash crops may increase vulnerability to price volatility and climate risks. For example, a sudden drop in global coffee prices or an outbreak of a disease affecting cotton can devastate farmers’ incomes. Governments and agricultural extension agencies provide support through market regulation, minimum support prices, export incentives, and crop insurance to reduce these risks. In recent years, organic and fair-trade cash crops have gained popularity, offering premium prices and encouraging ethical and environmentally friendly production practices. In conclusion, cash crops are central to agricultural commercialization, income diversification, and rural development, but they require careful planning and risk management to ensure long-term sustainability and farmer well-being.

text: The problem of induction, first systematically formulated by philosopher David Hume in the 18th century, challenges the logical foundation of inductive reasoning—the process of drawing general conclusions from specific observations. This fundamental philosophical dilemma questions how we can justify the assumption that the future will resemble the past or that unobserved instances will resemble observed ones, which underlies virtually all scientific inquiry and everyday expectations. For instance, while we may have observed the sun rising countless times, there is no logically necessary reason it must rise tomorrow; we simply extrapolate from past experiences to future expectations. Unlike deductive reasoning, where conclusions necessarily follow from premises, inductive inferences cannot be conclusively validated through experience alone without circular reasoning—using induction to justify induction itself. This creates an unsettling skeptical challenge: if our scientific methods and empirical knowledge rely on induction, and induction cannot be rationally justified, then much of what we consider knowledge lacks a secure foundation. Philosophers have proposed various responses, including pragmatic justifications, probabilistic approaches, and Popper's falsificationism, yet none have fully resolved Hume's insight that we cannot logically bridge the gap between observed regularities and future occurrences without appealing to the principle of uniformity of nature—which itself must be assumed rather than proven.

text: International Political Economy (IPE) is an interdisciplinary field that examines the complex interactions between politics and economics on a global scale. It focuses on how political institutions, processes, and power dynamics shape economic policies and outcomes, as well as how economic factors influence political behavior and international relations. IPE explores a range of topics, including trade, finance, development, globalization, and the role of international organizations, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Trade Organization (WTO). Scholars in this field analyze the effects of economic policies on state behavior, the role of non-state actors, and the implications of global economic trends for domestic politics. IPE also addresses issues of inequality, environmental sustainability, and the impact of economic globalization on national sovereignty. By integrating insights from political science, economics, sociology, and history, IPE provides a comprehensive understanding of how global economic systems function and the political forces that drive change. This field is particularly relevant in addressing contemporary challenges, such as trade disputes, financial crises, and the responses to global issues like climate change and pandemics, highlighting the interconnectedness of political and economic phenomena in shaping the world order.

text: Fiscal policy refers to the use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy, aiming to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as economic growth, full employment, price stability, and a sustainable balance of payments. The primary objectives of fiscal policy include promoting economic stability, reducing unemployment, controlling inflation, and fostering long-term economic growth. To achieve these objectives, governments use various tools, including changes in tax rates, government spending, and the management of public debt. Expansionary fiscal policy involves increasing government spending, reducing taxes, or a combination of both to stimulate economic activity, boost aggregate demand, and reduce unemployment. This approach is typically used during periods of economic downturn or recession. Conversely, contractionary fiscal policy involves decreasing government spending, increasing taxes, or both to cool down an overheating economy, reduce aggregate demand, and control inflation. This approach is usually employed during periods of high inflation or strong economic growth. Fiscal policy can also include automatic stabilizers, such as unemployment benefits and progressive taxation, which automatically adjust to economic conditions to stabilize economic fluctuations. Effective fiscal policy requires careful consideration of the economic context, the potential impacts on different sectors of the economy, and the coordination with monetary policy to achieve the desired macroeconomic outcomes.

text: Ontology, the philosophical study of being, examines the nature, sorts, and structures of reality. It poses such basic questions as: What does being mean? What kinds of entities exist? How are these entities related? Ontology classifies entities under such types as physical objects, minds, properties and events and abstract entities. It differentiates between (kinds of) being, and investigates the nature of identity, change, and sameness. Ontology studies the question of what there is and what can be grouped into kinds or classes, and how these groupings can be structured, and particularly about how universals, which are abstractions such as qualia and values, can exist and how they relate to particulars. It also considers questions about existence itself — whether existence is a property and how it contrasts with non-existence. Ontological investigation is the essential work of metaphysics, and it affects questions in all areas of philosophy by clarifying what it is what we are talking about when we discus what sorts of things can be talked about and how they are related. Various ontological positions are realism, which takes the position that there is independent existence of some objects even despite our cognition, and nominalism, which denies independent existence to universals. Today, the logical, linguistic, and scientific evidence, the developments since his time, and a variety of categories help to sharpen the articulation of the classification and the status of such things as possible worlds or fictional objects in general ontology. At the end of the day, Ontology just offers a general schema for making sense of the sheer complexity and diversity of reality out there and it serves as the basis for a lot of philosophical reflection.

text: Linkage describes the common inheritance of the in wasted highly genes (i.e. gene's location is common with genes on the same chromosome) due to their physical proximity on the same chromosome and consequent reduced chance of recombination separating them during meiosis. Linked genes do not segregate independently as Mendel's law of independent assortment predicts. The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the stronger is their linkage; that is, the less likely they are to be separated and the more likely it is that they will be transmitted as a unit to the next generation. This idea is word-bank in genetics because it explains non-Mendelian proportions in transmissions from ancestors to descendants. Linked may be tight, in which genes are very close, or loose, when some recombination between genes is possible. Linkage analysis allows scientists to create genetic maps by counting recombination events, because 1% recombination = 1 map unit or centimorgan. Binary genotype information is used to identify gene loci controlling traits, disease status or to identify markers of significance to breeding and evolution studies. In plants, linkage analysis assists breeders in the selection of two or more desirable characteristics simultaneously and prevent the drag of undesirable genes along with the desirable genes. Linkage is one of the key concepts in the field of genetics and therefore is crucial to the understanding of molecular biology and biotechnology.

text: A typical tracking system consists of three components: 1) an appearance model, which can evaluate the likelihood that the object of interest is at some particular location, 2) a motion model, which relates the locations of the object over time, and 3) a search strategy for finding the most likely location in the current frame. The contributions of this paper deal with the first of these three components; we refer the reader to [5] for a thorough review of the other components. Although many tracking methods employ static appearance models that are either defined manually or trained using only the first frame [2], [4], [6], [7], [8], [9], these methods are often unable to cope with significant appearance changes. Such challenges are particularly difficult when there is limited a priori knowledge about the object of interest. In this scenario, it has been shown that an adaptive appearance model, which evolves during the tracking process as the appearance of the object changes, is the key to good performance [10], [11], [12]. Training adaptive appearance models, however, is itself a difficult task, with many questions yet to be answered. Such models often involve many parameters that must be tuned to get good performance (e.g., “forgetting factors” that control how fast the appearance model can change), and can suffer from drift problems when an object undergoes partial occlusion.

text: The structured facts in knowledge graphs (KGs) have become fundamental resources for many intelligent applications (Ji et al., 2002). A fact is represented in the form of a relational triple (head entity, relation, tail entity) such as (Washington, D.C., capitalOf, United States). Learning embeddings for KGs is a typical way of applying such structured knowledge to downstream tasks. Hence, extensive research efforts have been devoted to developing powerful KG embedding models (Rossi et al., 2020). A recent study (Zhang et al., 2019a) indicates that the embedding models usually rely on a large number of relations and triples to capture semantic patterns for knowledge reasoning. However, a KG is incomplete by nature and contains a limited number of observed facts (Galárraga et al., 2017), resulting in insufficient expressiveness of the learned embeddings. Intuitively, augmenting the relational triples and semantic patterns can improve KG embeddings and thereby benefit downstream tasks. Previous work to resolve the incompleteness issue of KGs is through the task of KG completion (a.k.a. link prediction). It seeks to fill in the missing relational triples in KGs. Typically, there are two different solutions. One is to complete KGs by harvesting additional information from the Web (Shi et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2020). But it usually suffers from the noisy data of the Web and the errors in knowledge fusion. The other is to train an embedding model based on observed triples and then use the embeddings for KG completion (Bordes et al., 2013). To precisely capture the semantic patterns hidden in observed triples, many fully-expressive models have been proposed (Kazemi and Poole, 2018; Balazevic et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019).

text: Molecular genetic markers describe genetic variations and provide a link between observed phenotypes and the underlying genotype [1,2,3]. The development of high-throughput methods for the detection of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) has led to a revolution in their use as molecular markers [4,5,6,7]. SNPs may be considered the ultimate genetic marker as they represent the finest resolution of a DNA sequence, are generally abundant in populations and have a low mutation rate [8]. The principal challenge in SNP discovery remains the discrimination between true genetic polymorphisms and the often more abundant sequence or mapping errors. SNP discovery is further confounded in polyploid species where multiple related genomes are present within each nucleus. The identification of sequence errors can be based on three methods: sequence quality score, redundancy of the polymorphism in a sequence alignment and presence of multiple haplotypes at a locus [9,10]. SNP redundancy provides an effective means for estimating confidence in the validity of SNPs independently of sequence quality scores and has been demonstrated to be an accurate method for SNP discovery in a range of species [11,12,13]. Many plant genomes are large and complex. The bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) genome is 17 Gbp in size, around 6 times larger than the human genome [14], consists of 75%–90% repeats [15,16] and is hexaploid, containing of the A, B and D genomes, each with 7 homoeologous chromosomes. The presence of multiple genomes, large size and abundant repeats make any genetic and genomic analysis a challenge [17]. The recent shotgun sequence assembly of isolated chromosome arms for the group 7 chromosomes provides a reference for SNP discovery across these chromosomes [18,19,20]. When combined with the recently produced whole genome shotgun sequence data for several wheat cultivars [21], there is a potential to identify large numbers of cultivar specific SNPs.

text: Animal behavior encompasses a wide array of actions and responses that animals exhibit in their daily lives, driven by instincts, learning, and environmental stimuli. Behaviors can be classified into several categories, including innate or instinctive behaviors, which are genetically programmed and performed in response to specific stimuli without prior experience. Examples include reflexes, mating rituals, and parental care. Learned behaviors are acquired through experience and observation, allowing animals to adapt to new situations or improve existing skills. For instance, birds learning to forage effectively or predators honing hunting techniques exemplify learned behaviors. Social behaviors involve interactions among individuals within a species, such as cooperation, communication, territoriality, and dominance hierarchies. These behaviors facilitate group living, mating, and resource sharing, increasing survival chances. For example, wolves hunting in packs or bees communicating through dances demonstrate complex social behaviors. Foraging behaviors relate to how animals find and acquire food, which can involve exploration, problem-solving, and tool use in some species. Mating behaviors include courtship displays, vocalizations, and rituals that attract mates and ensure reproductive success. Parental behaviors involve caring for offspring, protecting them from predators, and teaching survival skills. Defensive behaviors are responses to threats, such as fleeing, hiding, or fighting to escape predation. Migration, a specialized behavior, involves seasonal or periodic movement from one area to another to access resources, breeding sites, or more favorable climates. It is driven by environmental cues like temperature, food availability, and daylight. Migration helps animals avoid harsh conditions, find mates, and access abundant resources, contributing to population stability and species survival. Animal behavior is often shaped by evolutionary pressures, ensuring that actions increase reproductive success and survival in specific environments. Studying behaviors provides insights into animal ecology, social dynamics, and evolutionary history, highlighting how organisms interact with their surroundings and each other. Understanding animal behavior is essential for conservation, managing wildlife populations, and mitigating human-wildlife conflicts. It also reveals the complexity of animal minds and social structures, demonstrating intelligence, communication, and adaptive strategies that have evolved over millions of years. Overall, animal behavior reflects the intricate relationship between an organism and its environment, showcasing the diversity of strategies animals use to survive, reproduce, and thrive.

text: Fluency is the ability to express oneself effortlessly, accurately, and naturally in a language, whether speaking or writing, with smooth flow, appropriate vocabulary, and minimal hesitation, enabling effective communication. In spoken language, fluency involves clear pronunciation, natural rhythm, and the ability to convey ideas without frequent pauses or errors; in writing, it reflects coherent, polished expression with varied sentence structures. Improving fluency requires consistent practice and strategic approaches. Regular immersion in the language, such as conversing with native speakers or engaging in language exchange programs, builds confidence and natural phrasing; for example, joining a conversation club can enhance spoken fluency. Reading extensivelyâ€”books, articles, or essaysâ€”exposes one to diverse vocabulary and sentence patterns, which can be applied in writing or speech. Listening to podcasts, audiobooks, or speeches helps internalize natural rhythms and intonation, particularly for non-native speakers. Practicing speaking aloud, such as by narrating daily activities or recording oneself, improves articulation and reduces hesitation. Writing regularly, like journaling or drafting essays, refines written fluency, especially when paired with feedback from peers or tools like Grammarly to correct errors. Learning common phrases, idioms, and collocations enhances natural expression, while expanding vocabulary through flashcards or apps like Anki strengthens word choice. Mimicking native speakersâ€™ speech patterns or writing styles, such as shadowing a TED Talk, builds fluency by emulating authentic language use. Consistent practice in real-life contexts, like ordering food or emailing professionally, reinforces practical application. Seeking constructive feedback from teachers or mentors identifies weaknesses, such as overused words or awkward phrasing, for targeted improvement. Finally, maintaining patience and persistence is crucial, as fluency develops gradually through regular exposure, practice, and reflection, enabling communicators to express ideas with clarity, confidence, and ease across diverse settings.

text: Sensory memory is the initial stage of memory processing that briefly holds vast amounts of incoming sensory information for a fraction of a second, serving as a temporary buffer that allows the nervous system to register and process environmental stimuli before they either fade away or move into more permanent memory systems. This memory stage operates automatically and unconsciously, capturing detailed impressions of sensory experiences across all modalities without requiring attention or conscious effort, though the information retained is extremely fragile and disappears rapidly unless further processed. The two most extensively studied forms of sensory memory are iconic memory, which holds visual information for approximately 250-500 milliseconds, and echoic memory, which retains auditory information for roughly 2-4 seconds, with the longer duration of echoic memory reflecting the temporal nature of sound and the need to integrate sequential auditory information into meaningful patterns. Iconic memory allows us to perceive smooth motion in movies despite viewing a series of static images, while echoic memory enables us to understand spoken language by briefly holding the sounds of words and sentences long enough for linguistic processing to occur. The capacity of sensory memory is enormous, potentially storing complete sensory scenes, but this information decays rapidly through a process of automatic forgetting unless attention is directed toward specific elements that then move into short-term memory for further processing. Research using techniques like partial report procedures has revealed that sensory memory contains much more information than we can consciously access, with studies showing that people can report only a small fraction of briefly presented stimuli even though the complete sensory impression was initially registered. Sensory memory plays a crucial role in perception by providing continuity between discrete sensory inputs, allowing us to experience the world as stable and coherent rather than as a series of disconnected sensory fragments, and serving as the foundation for all subsequent memory processing and conscious awareness of our environment.

text: A construction due to Arratia [1,2] shows that it is possible to make rigorous sense of the informal notion of starting an independent Brownian motion at each point of the real line and letting particles coalesce when they collide. Arratia proved that the set of particles remaining at any positive time is locally finite almost surely. Arratia’s argument is based on the simple observation that at the time two particles collide, one or the other must have already collided with each particle that was initially between them. The same argument shows that if we start an independent circular Brownian motion at each point of the circle and let particles coalesce when they collide, then, almost surely, there are only finitely many particles remaining at any positive time.

text: About 30 years ago, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren reported the isolation and culture of a spiral bacterial species from the human stomach [1]. Helicobacter pylori previously named Campylobacter pyloridis is a curved microaerophilic Gram-negative bacterium, 2 to 4 ?m long with a diameter of 0.5 to 1 ?m. This spiral-shaped bacillus is highly motile due to its unipolar bundle of two to six sheathed flagella and it colonizes the mucus layer of the gastric epithelium of humans. The bacterium migrated out of Africa along with our ancestors and has been intertwined with our species for at least two hundred thousand years [2]. While not as deadly as some bacteria, H. pylori is the most successful pathogen in human history since it infects up to half of the world’s population. The prevalence of H. pylori infection is the highest in developing countries (up to 100%) where risk factors are mainly low socioeconomic conditions including large family size, while decreasing in Western countries (10%–60%). The most common routes of H. pylori transmission are oral-to-oral and fecal-to-oral contact. Parents and siblings seem to play a major role in transmission. Acquisition of H. pylori infection occurs predominantly in childhood, with more severe gastroduodenal diseases appearing mostly during adulthood. Although H. pylori infection always causes a chronic active gastritis, the majority of infected individuals (~85%) remain asymptomatic throughout life. In some cases, this gastric inflammation may evolve toward more severe diseases such as duodenal or gastric ulcers, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma or non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma. H. pylori infection was classified as a type I carcinogen in 1994 by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (World Health Organization) [3].

text: Molecular techniques have provided new tools for species identification and thus a more precise assignment to species, because they are identifying the organisms at their genetic composition level, rather than based on morphological characters which can be misleading due to phenotypic plasticity or developmental stage (e.g., even cryptic) species. Character-based DNA-sequencing approaches such as DNA-barcoding, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and sequencing of predetermined genes (e.g., the mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase subunit I or ribosomal RNA genes) provide scientists with the opportunity to compare genetic sequences across taxa and find those minimal differences that allow an inference about separate species. These methods may be particularly valuable where morphological characters are insufficient or when species are microscopic, degraded or represented only in fragments (as with forensic evidence, environmental DNA [eDNA] from water or soil and processed food articles). DNA barcoding, for instance, uses a short section of the genetic sequence as compared to reference databases in order to determine identification at various taxonomic levels. Molecular methodologies also assist in the discovery of cryptic species -taxa that are genetically distinct but morphologically similar-relative to our overall knowledge of biodiversity and conservation demands. In addition, they can be applied to track invasive species and illicit wildlife trade as well as authenticate labelled biological products. Molecular tools in ecological research are now able to assess species diversity among a complex community, and metabarcoding is the method that analyses the DNA extracted from mixed environmental samples allowing for simultaneous detection of multiple species. This non-invasive but scalable approach enhances biodiversity monitoring and eco-system health assessment. Furthermore, molecular phylogenetics establishes species relations from sequences of DNA; it becomes the model of speciation, genetic distances and the evolution story of life. These strategies can also be a powerful tool in taxonomy, explaining relationships between classification schemes and resolving debates about species limits. It also would be another mold to feature these, since molecular methods have reproducibility and standardization that ensures their integrity for scientific and regulatory purposes. These methods do require special instrumentation, technical competency and bioinformatics support; however their increasing accessibility and lower cost make them more key than ever in modern biological research. Molecular tools, with their novel informational resource of biodiversity at the gene level, have been widely applied in species conservation and ecology studies [106], public health [107], sustainable management of resources. They are indeed only the next step in the process of species identification that takes us far forward into our search for a more exact, time-and labor saving and an exhaustive knowledge of the organic world.

text: Kinematics in robotics refers to the study of motion without considering the forces that cause it. It focuses on the relationships between the positions, velocities, and accelerations of a robot's components, particularly its joints and end effector, as they move through space. Kinematics is divided into two main areas: forward kinematics, which involves calculating the position and orientation of the end effector based on given joint parameters (such as angles for rotary joints or distances for linear joints), and inverse kinematics, which determines the required joint parameters to achieve a desired position and orientation of the end effector. Understanding kinematics is essential for controlling robotic systems, as it enables the precise movement of robots in various applications, from industrial automation to robotic surgery. By applying kinematic principles, engineers can design algorithms that guide the robot's movements, ensuring they follow specified trajectories and perform tasks accurately. Additionally, kinematics plays a crucial role in simulation and modeling, allowing for the prediction of a robot's behavior in different scenarios before actual implementation. Overall, kinematics is a foundational aspect of robotics that aids in the design, programming, and operation of robotic systems, facilitating their ability to perform complex tasks in dynamic environments.

text: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) and CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) are two distinct CPU design philosophies that influence how processors handle instructions. RISC architecture emphasizes simplicity and efficiency, using a reduced set of highly optimized instructions that can be executed within a single clock cycle. This approach allows for simpler and faster hardware design, as each instruction performs a basic operation, reducing the complexity of the decoder and control units. RISC processors typically use a load-store architecture, where only simple load and store instructions access memory, and all other instructions operate on registers. This design often results in higher performance and lower power consumption, making RISC architectures popular in mobile devices and embedded systems.In contrast, CISC architecture employs a larger and more complex set of instructions that can perform multi-step operations or access memory directly. This allows a single instruction to accomplish more complex tasks, potentially reducing the number of instructions needed for a program. However, this complexity can lead to slower execution times and more intricate hardware design. CISC processors often include microcode to translate complex instructions into simpler micro-operations. While CISC architectures can simplify compiler design and potentially reduce the size of programs, they may not perform as efficiently as RISC processors for certain tasks. The choice between RISC and CISC often depends on the specific requirements of the application, balancing factors such as performance, power consumption, and complexity.

text: Hash tables are a data structure that maps keys to values using a hash function, which computes an index into an array of buckets or slots, allowing for efficient lookup, insertion, and deletion of elements. The hash function takes a key as input and generates a hash code, which is used to determine the index at which the corresponding value is stored. However, when two different keys hash to the same index, a collision occurs. To resolve collisions, hash tables employ various techniques, such as chaining, where colliding elements are stored in a linked list at the hashed index, or open addressing, where the hash table searches for an empty slot to store the colliding element, using techniques like linear probing or quadratic probing. Some hash tables also use a combination of these techniques, such as using chaining with a limited chain length, and then switching to open addressing when the chain length exceeds a certain threshold. Additionally, some hash tables use techniques like rehashing, where the hash table is resized and the elements are rehashed to reduce the likelihood of collisions. By resolving collisions effectively, hash tables can maintain an average time complexity of O(1) for lookup, insertion, and deletion operations, making them a fundamental data structure in many applications, including caching, indexing, and database query optimization.

text: Mise-en-scène, a French term meaning "placement in the scene" or "putting into the scene," refers to everything that appears within the frame of a film shot and its arrangement. It encompasses all the elements that the audience sees and hears (to some extent, as sound design can be considered part of the overall "world" created) and how these elements are deliberately composed by the director and their team to convey meaning, mood, and narrative information. The core components of mise-en-scène include setting and décor, costume and makeup, lighting, and blocking of actors. Setting and décor involves the choice of locations, sets, and props, which establish the historical period, geographical location, social status of characters, and overall atmosphere. A dilapidated room, for example, might suggest poverty or neglect, while a meticulously organized office could convey order or control. Costume and makeup reveal character traits, social roles, emotional states, and even contribute to the visual appeal or symbolism of a scene. A character's worn clothing might indicate a struggle, while elaborate makeup could signify a specific persona. Lighting is a crucial element, shaping the mood, highlighting key elements, creating shadows, and defining three-dimensionality. High-key lighting often suggests brightness and happiness, while low-key lighting can evoke mystery or danger. The direction, intensity, and color of light are all meticulously controlled. Finally, blocking of actors refers to their arrangement and movement within the frame, which can convey relationships, power dynamics, and emotional states. The distance between characters, their proximity to objects, and their movement patterns all contribute to the narrative. Together, these elements of mise-en-scène are not merely decorative but are carefully crafted artistic choices that contribute significantly to the film's storytelling, character development, thematic depth, and overall aesthetic impact, guiding the audience's interpretation without explicit dialogue.

text: DC motors are classified into several types based on how their field windings are connected to the armature circuit, each offering distinct characteristics and applications. Series DC motors have the field winding connected in series with the armature, causing the same current to flow through both, resulting in high starting torque that decreases as speed increases, making them ideal for applications requiring high initial torque like electric trains, cranes, and automotive starters, though they have poor speed regulation and can reach dangerously high speeds under light loads. Shunt DC motors have the field winding connected in parallel with the armature, maintaining relatively constant field current and providing excellent speed regulation with moderate starting torque, making them suitable for applications requiring constant speed like machine tools, fans, and centrifugal pumps. Compound DC motors combine both series and shunt field windings, offering characteristics between series and shunt motors; cumulative compound motors have additive field effects providing good starting torque with better speed regulation than series motors, ideal for applications like elevators, rolling mills, and heavy-duty machinery, while differential compound motors have opposing field effects but are rarely used due to unstable operation. Separately excited DC motors have field windings powered by an independent DC source, providing the best speed control and allowing field weakening for speeds above rated values, commonly used in variable-speed industrial drives and precision applications. Permanent magnet DC motors (PMDC) use permanent magnets instead of electromagnets for the field, offering compact size, high efficiency, and good speed regulation, making them popular in small appliances, automotive accessories, and portable devices. Brushless DC motors (BLDC) eliminate mechanical commutators and brushes by using electronic switching with permanent magnet rotors, providing higher efficiency, longer life, quieter operation, and better speed control, making them increasingly popular in computer fans, electric vehicles, drones, and high-performance applications despite higher initial cost and control complexity.

text: Sustainable tourism transport is confronted with various interconnected problems: environmental, infrastructural, financial and social. From an environmental point of view, tourism transport – especially air travel and cruise shipping – is one of the largest CO? emitters, which cause both climate change and local air and noise pollution. This adds urgency to the question of decarbonization strategies and the adoption of clean energy. Logistically, airports, roads, rail systems and cruise berths are overwhelmed, resulting in delays, danger and a poor experience for visitors. They require significant investment and planning, which is itself a slow process. Economically, the finance of transport infrastructure is commonly based on public–private partnership, route subsidies or tourism levies–challenging to design and politically sensitive. From a social perspective, increased transportation access can disrupt localities, increase property values and change neighborhood dynamics, with some residents pushing back. In addition, access is not always equitable, with far-off or rural destinations left behind, and the benefits of tourism may be confined to its less exposed destinations. Complex regulation — from international air routes to maritime laws, cross-border rail and urban transit — needs to cohere across jurisdictions. Not to mention safety, security, and health protocols (pandemic controls, for example) also add layers. Some solutions (e.g., EV fleets, smart traffic systems) require technology adoption, but financial and knowhow barriers hinder this as well. Finally, people’s comfort, speed and price expectations place pressure on operators to find innovative and sustainable solutions. Tackling these challenges requires joined-up stakeholder engagement across tourism, transport, urban planning, technology and environment.

text: Sponge species, or Porifera, are distinguished by their absence of genuine tissues and organs and their simple, porous body structure.  They are multicellular animals with a stiff, frequently asymmetrical body made up of loose cell aggregates encased in a gelatinous matrix called mesohyl.  Numerous microscopic pores called ostia are scattered throughout their bodies, allowing water to pass through and aiding in respiration, waste elimination, and filter feeding.  Choanocytes are specialized cells with flagella that generate currents, which power the water flow system.  Spicules, which are small, needle-like structures consisting of silica or calcium carbonate, or spongin fibers, which are a type of collagen, make up the skeleton of porifera.  They have specialized cells that carry out a variety of tasks, but they lack genuine tissues and a nervous system, giving them a basic level of order.  The majority of creatures are hermaphroditic, indicating they possess the capability to reproduce both asexually and sexually.   Although their adults are often sessile and firmly attached to substrates such as rocks or coral reefs, their larvae are motile, facilitating dispersal.   Porifera, as filter feeders, extract food particles from the water that flows through their bodies.  Being among the first multicellular organisms, they offer valuable insights into the evolution of more complex species, which makes them significant from an evolutionary standpoint.  They are resilient in a variety of settings because of their extraordinary capacity for regeneration and repair.  They are ecologically significant as filter feeders that contribute to the preservation of water quality and purity because of their straightforward body plan, which includes a porous structure and a canal system that allow them to effectively filter vast quantities of water.  They differ from more developed animals in that they lack genuine tissues and organs, but they exhibit a high degree of biological structure in their cellular specialization and structural complexity.  All things considered, Porifera are crucial to comprehending the beginnings of multicellularity, and for hundreds of millions of years, their straightforward yet efficient body shape has enabled them to flourish in oceanic habitats.  They are an intriguing group to research the evolution of multicellular life and ecological interactions in aquatic habitats because of their distinctive characteristics and evolutionary background.

text: Biodiversity, representing the vast variety of life on Earth at all scales—from the genetic variations within a single species to the multitude of different species inhabiting an ecosystem and the vast array of ecosystems across the globe—is fundamentally important because it forms the bedrock of planetary health and resilience, directly underpinning the essential services that sustain all life, including human civilization. A rich and diverse array of species and ecosystems ensures greater ecological stability and adaptability, meaning that complex natural systems are better equipped to withstand environmental disturbances such as climate shifts, disease outbreaks, or natural disasters. Each species, no matter how seemingly insignificant, plays a unique and often crucial role in the intricate web of life; for instance, pollinators like bees and butterflies are vital for agricultural productivity, microorganisms decompose waste and cycle nutrients, and various plants and animals contribute to soil formation and climate regulation. These "ecosystem services" are invaluable and largely irreplaceable, providing humanity with clean air and water, fertile soil for food production, regulation of water cycles, pest control, and raw materials for medicines and industries. Beyond these practical benefits, biodiversity holds immense intrinsic value, possessing inherent worth independent of human utility, and offers profound aesthetic, cultural, and spiritual significance, inspiring art, providing recreational opportunities, and enriching human experiences. It also serves as an irreplaceable genetic library, holding the potential for new medicines, crops, and technological innovations yet undiscovered. The irreversible loss of biodiversity, driven by human activities, diminishes the planet's capacity to support life, reduces its resilience to environmental change, and ultimately threatens human well-being, making its preservation not just an environmental imperative but a crucial component of sustainable development for current and future generations. Therefore, understanding and protecting biodiversity is paramount for the health of our planet and the future of humanity.

text: 2D-3D pose tracking or pose estimation is concerned with relating the spatial coordinates of an object in the 3D world (with respect to a calibrated camera) to that of a 2D scene [22], [27]. Although the complete literature review is beyond the scope of this paper, most methodologies can be described as follows: First, one chooses a local geometric descriptor (e.g., points [33], lines [18], [28], or curves [19], [39]) or image intensity [4] that can best quantify features on the image to its corresponding 3D counterpart. Then, explicit point correspondences are established in order to solve for the pose transformation. As with most correspondence-based algorithms which rely on local features, it can be readily seen that these techniques may suffer from the existence of homologies (due to noise, clutter, or occlusions). Aside from the nontrivial task of establishing correspondences, many 2D-3D pose estimation techniques make certain (sometimes rather restrictive) assumptions on the class of shapes that they can handle. Recently, the authors of [39] have proposed relaxing such restrictions by focusing on free-form objects. However, even for this type of algebraic approach it may become increasingly difficult to estimate the pose for an arbitrary or complex shape.

text: Motile cilia (flagella) arose in the eukaryotic lineage in single-celled protists, where they took on signaling capacities, and it was only with the emergence of the multicellular animal kingdom that their non-motile cousins (primary cilia) appeared. Motile cilia in multi-ciliated organisms beat in coordinated waves and are found in various tissues, where they perform a variety of functions. For example, motile cilia in the trachea function in sweeping mucus and particulates out of the lungs and in the fallopian tubes they assist in moving the ovum from the fallopian tube to the uterus. Primary cilia, on the other hand, have a role in sensory detection. In worms, for example, they are present exclusively in a handful of neurons used to detect food. Although there are some cells with motile and primary cilia in vertebrates, most cells have primary cilia whereas only a handful of cells have motile cilia. Cilia maintain separate cytoplasmic and membrane compartments, but are completely lacking vesicles. Instead cilia rely on specialized modes of transportation called intraflagellar transport (IFT) to deliver cargo proteins and lipids along the axoneme. IFT can operate in the anterograde direction (towards the ciliary tip) using complex B factors, or in the retrograde direction (towards the ciliary base) using complex A factors; together these factors regulate the transport speed and net cargo flux. An important, recently emerged aspect of cilia is the gatekeeper role of the septin family of proteins, regulating initial entry and exit of ciliary factors at the base of the cilium [1]. The transition zone, where the gatekeeper functions, is an adjacent structure at the base of the cilium, forming the linkers between microtubule and ciliary membrane; it is probably required for unloading ciliary-directed cargo and sorting ciliary-based signaling mechanisms [2] so that the cell can interpret their context.

text: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) are two fundamental protocols in computer networking, each designed for different purposes. TCP is a connection-oriented protocol, ensuring reliable data transmission by establishing a connection between sender and receiver before data transfer. It guarantees delivery through mechanisms like error checking, flow control, and retransmission of lost packets, making it ideal for applications where accuracy is critical, such as email, web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS), and file transfers (FTP). However, this reliability comes at the cost of speed, as TCP's overhead for managing connections and ensuring order slows down transmission. On the other hand, UDP is a connectionless protocol that prioritizes speed over reliability. It sends data packets without establishing a connection or verifying delivery, resulting in lower latency but potential packet loss. This makes UDP suitable for real-time applications like video streaming, online gaming, and VoIP, where speed is more important than occasional data loss. Unlike TCP, UDP does not handle packet sequencing or retransmission, leaving error handling to the application layer if needed. In terms of structure, TCP headers are larger due to additional fields for reliability features, while UDP headers are simpler and smaller, contributing to its efficiency. Security-wise, TCP is more robust due to its handshake process, whereas UDP is more vulnerable to attacks like spoofing. Ultimately, the choice between TCP and UDP depends on the specific needs of an applicationâ€”TCP for reliability and UDP for speedâ€”highlighting their complementary roles in networking.

text: Political culture refers to the widely shared beliefs, values, attitudes, norms, and symbols that define the relationship between citizens and the government, and among citizens in relation to politics within a given society. It represents the collective subjective dimension of politics, shaping how individuals perceive political authority, legitimate governance, and their own role in the political process. Political culture is not static; it is learned through processes of political socialization and evolves over time, influenced by historical experiences, economic conditions, social changes, and the performance of political institutions. Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba, in their seminal work "The Civic Culture," categorized political cultures into three ideal types: parochial, where citizens have little awareness of or engagement with the political system beyond their local community; subject, where citizens are aware of government and its authority but primarily as subjects who obey laws rather than active participants; and participant (or civic) culture, where citizens are actively engaged in the political process, expect to influence outcomes, and possess a strong sense of civic duty and efficacy, balanced with respect for authority. The components of political culture are diverse. They include attitudes towards authority (e.g., trust, deference, skepticism), beliefs about the legitimacy of political institutions (e.g., parliament, judiciary), values concerning democratic principles (e.g., freedom, equality, rule of law), expectations regarding government performance and responsibilities (e.g., provision of welfare, economic management), and norms of political behavior (e.g., voting, protesting, respecting minority rights). Political culture significantly influences political stability, the effectiveness of governance, and the nature of democratic transitions. A civic or participant culture, for instance, is often seen as conducive to stable democracy, as it fosters both engagement and acceptance of rules. Conversely, a fragmented or highly polarized political culture can lead to instability and make consensus-building difficult. Differences in political culture can also explain variations in how similar political institutions function across different countries. While political culture provides a broad framework for understanding political behavior, it is not deterministic; individual actions and specific events can still shape political outcomes. Nonetheless, understanding the dominant political culture of a society is crucial for analyzing its political dynamics, predicting how citizens might react to policy changes, and comprehending the unique character of its political system.

text: Volatile oils, also known as essential oils, are extracted from aromatic plants through several established methods, each selected based on the plant material's characteristics, oil location, and desired quality of the final product. Steam distillation represents the most widely used method, where plant material is placed in a distillation apparatus with water, heated to generate steam that carries volatile compounds through a condenser where the steam-oil mixture is cooled and separated, with the oil floating on the water surface due to its lower density. Water distillation involves directly boiling plant material in water, suitable for delicate flowers and leaves that might be damaged by direct steam contact, though this method may result in some hydrolysis of sensitive compounds. Hydro-distillation combines both water and steam, where plant material is submerged in water and heated, creating both direct water contact and steam extraction simultaneously. Solvent extraction using organic solvents like hexane, petroleum ether, or ethanol dissolves both volatile and non-volatile compounds, followed by solvent removal through evaporation, though this method may leave solvent residues and extract unwanted compounds. Supercritical fluid extraction employs carbon dioxide under high pressure and controlled temperature, providing a clean, efficient method that preserves heat-sensitive compounds and leaves no toxic residues, making it ideal for pharmaceutical and food-grade applications. Cold pressing or expression mechanically presses oil-rich plant materials, particularly citrus peels, without heat application, preserving thermolabile compounds but limiting applicability to oil-rich tissues. Enfleurage, a traditional method using animal or vegetable fats to absorb volatile compounds from fresh flowers, followed by alcohol extraction, though rarely used commercially today due to time and cost constraints. The choice of extraction method significantly influences the chemical composition, yield, and quality of volatile oils, with steam distillation providing the highest purity for most applications while supercritical extraction offers superior quality for premium products despite higher operational costs.

text: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor, widely regarded as one of the greatest writers in the English language and the world’s preeminent dramatist. He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and became an iconic figure in literature through his extraordinary ability to capture the human experience with depth, complexity, and poetic grace. Shakespeare’s works explore universal themes such as love, power, jealousy, betrayal, ambition, and mortality, presented with remarkable psychological insight and mastery of language. He wrote 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and several narrative poems, and his contributions continue to influence literature, theatre, and the English language. His major tragedies, such as *Hamlet*, *Macbeth*, *Othello*, and *King Lear*, delve into the darker aspects of human nature and explore internal conflict, moral ambiguity, and the consequences of ambition. His comedies, including *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, *As You Like It*, *Much Ado About Nothing*, and *Twelfth Night*, are known for their wit, humor, mistaken identities, and reflections on love and society. In his historical plays like *Henry IV*, *Henry V*, and *Richard III*, Shakespeare dramatizes the lives and reigns of English monarchs, blending fact with dramatic fiction to explore national identity and political legitimacy. His narrative poems, *Venus and Adonis* and *The Rape of Lucrece*, showcase his lyrical ability and interest in mythological themes. Shakespeare’s influence extends beyond his literary contributions; his phrases, characters, and plots have permeated global culture, education, and discourse. The emotional range and philosophical depth found in soliloquies like “To be, or not to be” reveal his unparalleled understanding of human consciousness. He died in 1616, but his legacy endures in countless adaptations, scholarly interpretations, and ongoing performances, making him a timeless figure whose works continue to resonate with audiences across cultures and generations.

text: Requirement analysis is a critical early stage in the software development process such as the collection and detailed representation of the needs of the stakeholders for a new or modified system. This process includes the determination of functional (what the system should do) and non – functional requirements (how the system should behave such as security, usability, availability). It means interviewing users, examining existing systems, observing workflow, analyzing business processes to design new system and define project scope and goals. Output typically consists of detailed requirements, or user stories which can serve as the basis for system design, development, and testing. Good rquirements analysis helps reduce ambiguities, creep, & rework - b/c people develop a mutual understanding of what is and isn't in scope between devs, customers, and users. It also aids in identifying features, evaluating feasibility, and setting acceptance criteria. Communication and validation are supported through use-case modeling, prototyping, and requirement workshops. Incorrect requirements analysis is the major cause of failure of IT projects. This is due to the fact that the requirements of the stakeholders are not clearly understood or defined. For this reason, the needs of the organisation must be thoroughly analyzed to be able to match the right software solution to the right business needs, so that the provided system actually serves the users and operates as expected.

text: Big data techniques are targeted toward solving system-level problems that cannot be solved by conventional methods and technologies. With the emergence of new networked sensor technologies including large scale wireless sensor networks (WSNs), body sensor networks, Internet/network/vehicle/Web-of-Things, the next generation of big data systems will need to deal with machine-generated data from these forms of networked sensor systems. text: A fundamental aspect of the approach to memory delineated here is its foundation on goal-directed cognition, asserting that memory processes are inherently motivated. This perspective is encapsulated within a conceptual framework known as the Self-Memory System (SMS) (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Conway, Singer et al., 2004), which aims primarily to elucidate the structure and rationale of the SMS. While various findings from disparate domains are employed to exemplify facets of the SMS, a comprehensive review of the complete spectrum of findings is not undertaken in this context (for exhaustive reviews, refer to Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Conway, Singer et al., 2004; McAdams, 2001, as well as edited volumes by Bluck, 2003; Hackmann & Holmes, 2004; Beike et al., 2004; Skowronski, 2004). The SMS comprises two principal components: the working self and the autobiographical memory knowledge base. When these components intertwine during acts of remembering, specific autobiographical memories are formulated. However, each component can function independently and may potentially engage in processing sequences beyond those governing memory. This article delves into a detailed examination of both components and their interplay during the process of remembering. Initially, the article outlines two fundamental distinctions underpinning the SMS framework. These include distinguishing between the self-coherence of autobiographical knowledge and its alignment or misalignment with experiential reality, and discerning between very recent memories and long-term retention.

text: The English language, with its global reach and diverse history, encompasses a wide range of dialects that reflect the unique cultural, social, and historical contexts of their speakers. These dialects can be broadly categorized into several main groups, each with its own distinct characteristics and variations. One of the primary categories is British English, which includes the dialects spoken in England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland. British English is often characterized by its non-rhotic accent, where the "r" sound is not pronounced unless it is followed by a vowel, and its rich and diverse vocabulary, influenced by the various languages and cultures that have shaped the British Isles. Another significant category is American English, which encompasses the dialects spoken in the United States and Canada. American English is typically rhotic, with the "r" sound pronounced in all positions, and it has a more standardized and homogeneous vocabulary and pronunciation compared to British English. The dialects of the English-speaking Caribbean, including Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, and Barbados, form another distinct category. These dialects are often influenced by the African languages and cultures brought to the region through the transatlantic slave trade, as well as the indigenous languages and cultures of the Caribbean. They are characterized by their unique vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammatical structures, reflecting the rich and diverse cultural heritage of the region. The dialects of English spoken in Africa, such as those in South Africa, Nigeria, and Kenya, form another significant category. These dialects are often influenced by the indigenous African languages and cultures, as well as the colonial and historical contexts of the continent. They are characterized by their unique vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammatical structures, reflecting the complex and multifaceted nature of African societies and cultures. The dialects of English spoken in Asia, including India, Pakistan, and the Philippines, form another distinct category. These dialects are often influenced by the indigenous languages and cultures of the region, as well as the colonial and historical contexts of the continent. They are characterized by their unique vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammatical structures, reflecting the rich and diverse cultural heritage of Asia. Finally, the dialects of English spoken in Australia and New Zealand form another significant category. These dialects are often influenced by the indigenous languages and cultures of the region, as well as the colonial and historical contexts of the continent. They are characterized by their unique vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammatical structures, reflecting the complex and multifaceted nature of Australian and New Zealand societies and cultures. By understanding the main dialects of English and their distinct characteristics and variations, language learners and non-native speakers can improve their comprehension and communication skills, as well as their appreciation of the rich and diverse nature of the English language.

text: Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of cultural reproduction offers an influential explanation of the mechanisms that generate intergenerational inequalities in educational outcomes. Bourdieu famously argued that parents transmit cultural capital to children, children convert their acquired cultural capital into academic success and, as a consequence, families who possess cultural capital have a comparative advantage which helps them to reproduce their privileged socioeconomic position (Bourdieu, 1977, Bourdieu, 1984, Bourdieu and Passeron, 1990). The theory of cultural reproduction has motivated much empirical research, most of which documents positive correlations between cultural capital and educational success (Aschaffenburg and Maas, 1997, Cheadle, 2008, De Graaf et al., 2000, DiMaggio, 1982, DiMaggio and Mohr, 1985, Dumais, 2002, Jæger, 2009, Roscigno and Ainsworth-Darnell, 1999, Sullivan, 2001, van de Werfhorst and Hofstede, 2007, Xu and Hampden-Thompson, 2012, Yamamoto and Brinton, 2010). Although previous research documents positive correlations between cultural capital and educational success, we know surprisingly little about the institutional contexts that generate these correlations. Bourdieu argued that the educational system comprises a field within society: an institutional setting governed by a particular set of rules and inhabited by agents with varying levels and compositions of economic, cultural, and social capital (Bourdieu, 1977, Bourdieu, 1986).

text: Governance refers to the processes, structures, and mechanisms through which public institutions conduct affairs, exercise authority, make decisions, and manage resources to fulfill societal objectives with accountability, transparency, and participation. It encompasses both formal and informal arrangements, including legal frameworks, administrative systems, policy implementation, civil society engagement, and inter-institutional relations that shape how power is distributed and exercised within a state or organization. Governance extends beyond the activities of government to include the roles of citizens, the private sector, non-governmental organizations, and international bodies in influencing decision-making and public outcomes. Good governance is characterized by principles such as rule of law, equity, inclusivity, responsiveness, consensus orientation, efficiency, and strategic vision, contributing to stability, development, and democratic legitimacy. It operates at multiple levels—local, national, regional, and global—each with distinct responsibilities, actors, and challenges. Effective governance ensures the delivery of public goods and services, protection of rights, conflict resolution, and alignment of policy with public interest. It adapts to changing societal contexts, technological advancements, and global dynamics by fostering innovation, participatory mechanisms, and inter-sectoral collaboration. Governance involves the coordination of institutions such as legislatures, executives, judiciaries, regulatory agencies, and oversight bodies to ensure coherent and accountable administration. It also includes mechanisms for monitoring performance, evaluating policy impact, and promoting continuous improvement through feedback and learning. In democracies, governance is rooted in legitimacy derived from public consent, institutional transparency, and civic engagement, enabling citizens to influence policies and hold leaders accountable. In other contexts, governance may rely more heavily on hierarchical control, tradition, or informal networks, affecting its effectiveness and legitimacy. The quality of governance significantly influences economic performance, social cohesion, human development, and environmental sustainability. Challenges such as corruption, inefficiency, political instability, and exclusion can undermine governance and erode public trust. International organizations promote standards of good governance through development assistance, technical cooperation, and monitoring initiatives that assess indicators like public sector integrity, rule of law, and government effectiveness. As global interdependence grows, governance increasingly involves multilevel coordination and adaptation to transnational issues that transcend borders and sectors. Ultimately, governance represents the collective capacity to steer society toward shared goals through ethical leadership, institutional integrity, inclusive participation, and effective management of public affairs.

text: There are a vast number of pattern selection methods that have been developed for different classifiers and applications [32], [38], [39]. For example, great efforts have been put into selecting patterns for instance-based classifiers (see, e.g., [13], [29], [34], [41], [46], [55], [56], [57], [71]) and support vector machines (see, e.g., [28], [62]). These methods can be categorized using a range of different taxonomies [31]. However, in this work, the authors prefer to describe pattern selection methods from two perspectives: geometrical and statistical. Those methods in the geometrical category consider the location of a pattern in the input space; patterns with certain geometrical properties are then selected. Exemplar geometry-based methods include those using hit miss networks [40] and Voronoi cells [4]. Geometrical information is used in pattern selection as it is the geometry that counts most for classification accuracy [30]. In contrast, methods in the statistical category analyze the statistical information of a pattern; a pattern is then selected if it can statistically represent a group of patterns around it [16]. A number of comprehensive review papers are available in the literature for further background in this area [8], [19], [31], [70].

text: The importance of gene regulation cannot be overstated; the evolution of complex multicellular organisms whose cells possess identical genomes, yet exhibit phenotypic and functional diversity, coincides with the evolution of complex gene regulatory systems capable of controlling differential gene expression [1,2]. Further, multicellular life must have the ability to regulate its transcriptome in response to extracellular signals from the environment, and surrounding cells if it is to develop, adapt and survive. To this end eukaryotes have evolved a repertoire of extracellular signals and receptors which activate diverse signal transduction pathways ultimately resulting in the regulation of specific genes through recruitment of transcription factor (TF) complexes [3]. Central to this process in many genes is the involvement of cis-regulatory sequences (CRSs); non-coding functional regions of DNA which mediate TF binding and regulate transcription [4]. Interest in cis-regulatory sequences has intensified since the human genome sequence was first mapped [5,6] and subsequently shown to only contain 20,000–25,000 protein coding genes [7]; far fewer than was previously anticipated, leaving ~97% of the genome with no predicted coding function. Consequently, comparative genomics [8,9] has been used to demonstrate that conservation of non-coding DNA regions between evolutionarily divergent species is a powerful tool for the prediction of cis-regulatory sequences [10,11,12,13] including promoter and enhancer regions, insulators and locus control regions (reviewed; [14]). More recently, the international consortium ENCODE published a series of papers highlighting that 80.4% of the human genome functions in some form of biological process, and conservative estimates suggest that there may be 4.5 times more functional information within the genome than that which encodes proteins [15].
