text: Structuralism and functionalism are two foundational schools of thought in psychology that differ in their focus, methodology, and philosophical orientation regarding the study of mental processes and behavior. Structuralism, primarily associated with Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener, aimed to analyze the structure of conscious experience by breaking it down into its most basic elements—sensations, feelings, and images—using introspection as its primary research method. The goal of structuralism was to identify the components of the mind and understand how they combined to form conscious experience, akin to how chemists study molecules by examining their atomic parts. In contrast, functionalism, influenced by William James and rooted in Darwinian principles, sought to understand the purpose and adaptive functions of mental processes and behavior. Rather than dissecting the contents of consciousness, functionalism explored how mental activities such as thinking, perception, and emotion help individuals adapt to their environments and fulfill practical needs. It emphasized the fluid, dynamic nature of the mind and was more concerned with the "why" and "how" of psychological phenomena than with their static elements. Methodologically, structuralism relied heavily on controlled lab experiments and introspective reports, while functionalism embraced broader methods including direct observation, comparative psychology, and the study of children and animals. Structuralism was more rigid and reductionist in its approach, often criticized for its reliance on subjective data and limited applicability. Functionalism, on the other hand, paved the way for applied psychology, education, and behavioral research by aligning mental functions with everyday life. It also laid the foundation for subsequent movements such as behaviorism and cognitive psychology. While structuralism contributed to the formalization of psychology as a scientific discipline, its influence waned due to methodological limitations, whereas functionalism’s emphasis on utility and adaptation remains central to modern psychological inquiry. In essence, structuralism asked what the mind is made of, while functionalism asked what the mind does, marking a critical shift in psychology from a focus on mental content to a focus on mental activity and function within a broader biological and social context.

text: Forgetting, which refers to the inability of retrieving or identifying previously encoded information, is a result of diverse factors and their multiple underlying mechanisms influencing different memory stages. One of the main reasons is that of decay theory, which suggests that memory trace disintegrate over time if not brought to mind or actively passed over in some way (Eysenk and Keane 2000), bringing about loss of information, particularly within working Memory. The other major reason is interference, in which a background of conflicting information makes it hard to pull out the memory you’re looking for; this can either be proactive (old memories prevent new learning) or retroactive (new learning gets in the way of old). Retrieval failure also contributes to forgetting when cues necessary to access stored information are absent or insufficient, even though the memory is intact. Additionally, encoding failure occurs when information never fully enters long-term memory due to lack of attention or shallow processing. Psychological factors such as stress, trauma, or repression can cause motivated forgetting, where unpleasant memories are unconsciously blocked. Organic causes like brain injury, neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer’s), or damage to memory-related structures such as the hippocampus can lead to amnesia or permanent forgetting. Ultimately, forgetting is a natural and adaptive process, preventing information overload and enabling the brain to prioritize relevant memories.

text: Max Weber's idea of Verstehen stresses the importance of placing oneself in the shoes of the people being researched in order to understand their social behaviour. It means "interpretive understanding," which includes not only watching what individuals do, but also figuring out what their acts signify and why they do them. Verstehen is essential for comprehending the intricacies of social behaviour in Bangladesh that cannot be entirely elucidated through statistics or legislation alone. For instance, customs like dowry, child marriage, or not letting women go to school are frequently considered as old-fashioned. Verstehen helps academics figure out why these customs still happen by looking at the cultural, economic, and psychological factors that keep them going. In a lot of rural places, families can think that offering a dowry will keep their daughter safe or that marrying her off early will keep her from being ashamed in public. From the outside, these activities look oppressive, but Verstehen helps you understand what the people involved were trying to do, which was driven by poverty, social pressure, and cultural values. Likewise, religious practices in Bangladesh—such as public prayers, fasting, or the donning of Islamic clothing—are richer when understood through Verstehen because they are not just rituals, but are inseparable from identity, piety, and community membership. You can also understand, with Weber’s approach, how people experience political corruption — not just as a crime, but a strategy for survival in a system in which favoritism is king. Verstehen thus helps in a better- understanding of Bangladesh society, so that the gap between life worlds and academic analysis can be bridged.

text: Consumer Equilibrium: A consumer is said to be in equilibrium when he is at the point of maximum satisfaction such that he has the means to buy them, and the goods are at given prices. That is, the level at which the consumer spends his income (any rearrangement of spending involves lower utility). At that point of tangency between the budget line and an indifference line exist the equilibrium. At this point of tangency, the slope of the indifference curve (the marginal rate of substitution, MRS) is equal to the slope of the budget line (the ratio of the prices of the two goods, P?/P?). Formally speaking, the consumer is in equilibrium when MRS = P?/P?, i.e., when the consumer is willing to make trades between the two goods at the same rate they are being made in the market. If these conditions are met, the consumer is in equilibrium and will have no incentive to change their consumption pattern. In either direction movement would contradict the budget constraint, or place the consumer on a lower indifference curve (yielding less satisfaction). If anything happens with income or prices, the budget line will move, and now have a new equilibrium. This framework is crucial for causal inference of consumer behavior, and to understand how actual circumstances such as price changes, taxes, or subsidies affect individual behavior.

text: The Memorandum of Association (MOA) is a foundational document in the formation of a company, outlining its constitution and defining its relationship with the outside world. The MOA includes several key clauses that provide essential information about the company. The name clause specifies the company's name, which must be unique and not resemble any existing company. The registered office clause states the location of the company's registered office, providing a legal address for official communications. The object clause outlines the company's objectives and the scope of its operations, defining the purpose for which the company is established. The liability clause specifies the nature of the members' liability, whether it is limited by shares, guarantee, or unlimited. The capital clause states the company's authorized share capital, providing information on the financial structure of the company. Lastly, the association clause expresses the intention of the subscribers to form the company and their agreement to abide by its rules. The MOA serves as a charter of the company, providing a clear and comprehensive framework for its operations and governance, ensuring that the company's activities are aligned with its stated objectives and legal requirements.

text: An ultrasonic sensor in robotics operates by emitting high-frequency sound waves (typically 20–200 kHz, beyond human hearing) and measuring the time it takes for the reflected waves, or echoes, to return after bouncing off an object, enabling distance measurement or object detection. The sensor consists of a transmitter, which generates ultrasonic pulses, and a receiver, which detects the reflected waves. The working principle relies on the time-of-flight method: the sensor calculates distance by multiplying the time taken for the echo to return by the speed of sound (approximately 343 m/s in air) and dividing by two, accounting for the round trip. For example, if the echo returns in 0.01 seconds, the object is about 1.7 meters away. Ultrasonic sensors are widely used in robotics for tasks like obstacle avoidance in mobile robots, level sensing in industrial automation, or parking assistance in vehicles. They are effective in various lighting conditions and can detect most surfaces, but performance may degrade with soft, sound-absorbing materials or in noisy environments. The sensor’s microcontroller processes the time-of-flight data, outputting distance measurements to the robot’s control system for navigation or task execution. Advances in signal processing improve accuracy and reduce interference, while multi-sensor arrays enhance coverage. Challenges include limited range (typically a few meters), sensitivity to temperature or humidity (which affect sound speed), and potential interference from other ultrasonic sources. Despite these, ultrasonic sensors are cost-effective, reliable, and versatile, making them integral to robotics applications requiring non-contact distance sensing in dynamic environments like warehouses or autonomous exploration.

text: Enzymatic reactions exhibit a high degree of chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, making them highly valuable for biotechnological applications. However, many enzymes require specific cofactors to facilitate catalytic reactions. These cofactors are categorized into prosthetic groups and coenzymes/co-substrates, and can be classified as inorganic (e.g., metal ions), organic (e.g., flavin, pterin), or organometallic (e.g., heme, cobalamin) [1]. Enzymes utilize a diverse array of organic cofactors, including vitamins and their derivatives, sugars, small peptides, and lipids, such as adenosine triphosphate (ATP), nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (phosphate) (NAD(P)), coenzyme A, pyridoxal phosphate, flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), flavin mononucleotide (FMN), vitamin K, and glutathione [2]. These cofactors facilitate the transfer of chemical groups and electrons in redox reactions, and together with the protein, they contribute to the formation of a three-dimensional catalytic site that enhances substrate binding and conversion [3]. Among the most versatile cofactors are the riboflavin (vitamin B2) derivatives, specifically flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) [4]. These cofactors can be found in flavoproteins in both covalently bound (approximately 10%) and dissociable forms [5], enabling them to perform one- and two-electron transfer reactions. This versatility supports a wide range of catalytic reactions and biological processes [6]. The key catalytic component of these cofactors is the isoalloxazine ring (Figure 1), which can adopt multiple redox states [7].

The most important idea in parametric minimum distance inference is the quantification of the degree of closeness between the sample data and parametric model as a function of an unknown set of parameters through a suitable distance-like measure. text: Normalisation is the database design process by which data structures are designed in the way that ensures minimal redundancy as well as a reduction of dependency to make sure there´s more than one related table on a node. Any data will be stored only in one location and hence the data integrity (and efficiency) increases. Each step is called a normal form, starting with the First Normal Form (1NF) which stipulates that every cell in a table must contain at most one value and that each record should be unique to eliminate repeating groups,OCUMENT}'. The Second Normal Form (2NF) builds on 1NF by removing partial dependencies, ensuring that all non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key, particularly in tables with composite keys. This prevents data duplication caused by attributes depending on only part of a composite key. The Third Normal Form (3NF) requires that all non-key attributes are not only fully functionally dependent on the primary key but also free from transitive dependencies, meaning no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. This further reduces redundancy and improves data consistency. By applying normalization from 1NF through 3NF, databases become more scalable and easier to maintain, reducing update anomalies and improving query performance. However, over-normalization can lead to complex joins, so designers balance normalization with practical performance needs.

text: Diversion programs in the criminal justice system are alternative interventions designed to steer individuals, typically those accused of minor offenses or first-time offenders, away from traditional formal prosecution and incarceration. Instead of proceeding through the standard court process that could lead to a criminal record and potential imprisonment, participants in diversion programs are offered an opportunity to address the underlying issues that contributed to their behavior and avoid the full consequences of a criminal conviction. These programs are often implemented at the pre-charge or pre-trial stage, meaning they can occur before formal charges are filed or before a trial begins. The primary goals of diversion programs are multifaceted: to reduce the burden on overcrowded courts and correctional facilities, to provide more effective and rehabilitative outcomes for certain offenders, and to minimize the negative long-term impacts of a criminal record, particularly on young people. Common types of diversion programs include substance abuse treatment programs, mental health counseling, anger management courses, educational or vocational training, community service, and restitution to victims. Successful completion of a diversion program typically results in the charges being dropped, dismissed, or never formally filed, allowing the individual to avoid a criminal conviction. This can have significant benefits for participants, including maintaining employment, housing, and educational opportunities that might otherwise be jeopardized by a criminal record. For the justice system, diversion programs can be more cost-effective than traditional prosecution and incarceration. They also promote restorative justice by focusing on rehabilitation and addressing the root causes of crime rather than simply imposing punishment. However, participation is usually voluntary, and failure to comply with program requirements typically results in the individual being referred back to the traditional criminal justice system for prosecution. Diversion programs represent a progressive approach to justice, emphasizing prevention, rehabilitation, and the potential for positive change within communities.

text: Planck’s hypothesis, proposed by Max Planck in 1900 to explain blackbody radiation, revolutionized physics by introducing the idea that energy is quantized rather than continuous. Planck suggested that electromagnetic energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta, with each quantum’s energy (EE) proportional to its frequency (??), expressed as E=h?E=h?, where hh is Planck’s constant (6.626×10?34 J?s6.626×10?34J?s). This hypothesis resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe, a discrepancy in classical physics where Rayleigh-Jeans law predicted infinite energy at high frequencies, by showing that energy quantization limits high-frequency radiation. Planck’s work assumed that oscillators in a blackbody’s walls could only possess energy in integer multiples of h?h?, a radical departure from classical wave theory. Although Planck initially viewed quantization as a mathematical trick, Einstein later extended the idea to light particles (photons) in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect, cementing quantum theory. Planck’s hypothesis laid the groundwork for quantum mechanics, influencing concepts like wave-particle duality, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and Schrödinger’s equation. Applications include lasers, semiconductors, and quantum computing, where discrete energy levels are fundamental. The hypothesis also underpins spectroscopy (analyzing atomic transitions) and cosmology (modeling the early universe’s radiation). Despite its success, Planck’s quantization initially faced skepticism, as it challenged Newtonian continuity, but experimental validation (e.g., atomic spectra, electron diffraction) confirmed its validity. Planck’s constant (hh) became a cornerstone of modern physics, linking energy and frequency across quantum phenomena. By bridging classical and quantum realms, Planck’s hypothesis not only solved a specific thermal radiation problem but also reshaped our understanding of energy, matter, and light, paving the way for technologies from LEDs to MRI machines and redefining the boundaries of physical theory.

text: Linked Data is a method of publishing and interlinking structured data on the web, enabling machines to understand and process information more effectively. By following these principles, Linked Data facilitates the creation of a global data space where information from disparate sources can be connected, queried, and analyzed in novel ways. This approach enhances the discoverability and reusability of data, fostering innovation and collaboration across various domains, from scientific research to business analytics.

text: The burden of proof is a legal principle that determines which party in a legal proceeding is responsible for providing evidence to support their claims or defenses, ensuring a fair and just resolution. In criminal cases, the burden typically rests on the prosecution to prove the defendantâ€™s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, a high standard requiring evidence so convincing that no reasonable person would question it. This aligns with the presumption of innocence, protecting individuals from wrongful conviction by demanding robust evidence, such as witness testimony, physical evidence, or digital records, to establish guilt. In civil cases, the burden usually falls on the plaintiff to prove their case by a preponderance of the evidence, meaning it is more likely than not that their claims are trueâ€”a lower threshold than in criminal law. The burden of proof can shift in specific circumstances; for example, in affirmative defenses like self-defense, the defendant may need to provide evidence supporting their claim, though the ultimate burden often remains with the prosecution. Originating in common law traditions and codified in legal systems globally, the burden of proof ensures that the party making an assertion bears the responsibility of substantiating it, preventing baseless accusations from prevailing. It also shapes trial dynamics, guiding how evidence is presented and evaluated. Challenges arise when evidence is ambiguous or when systemic issues, like limited access to legal resources, hinder a partyâ€™s ability to meet the burden. In some jurisdictions, statutory exceptions, such as in certain regulatory or administrative cases, may place the burden on the defendant, altering traditional dynamics. The burden of proof is thus a critical mechanism for balancing fairness, accountability, and truth-seeking, ensuring that legal outcomes are grounded in evidence rather than speculation or bias.

text: A Gas-cooled Reactor is a nuclear reactor design that uses gases, typically carbon dioxide or helium, as the primary coolant to remove heat from the reactor core, offering unique advantages in terms of high-temperature operation and inherent safety characteristics. The original gas-cooled reactor designs, developed primarily in the United Kingdom and France during the 1950s and 1960s, used carbon dioxide as coolant and graphite as neutron moderator, with natural uranium metal fuel clad in magnesium alloy arranged in a graphite lattice structure. The carbon dioxide coolant circulates through the reactor core under pressure, typically around 20 to 40 atmospheres, absorbing heat from the fuel elements and carrying it to steam generators where the thermal energy is transferred to water to produce steam for electricity generation. The graphite moderator not only slows down neutrons to thermal energies for efficient fission in natural uranium but also provides structural support for the fuel elements and helps maintain reactor geometry during operation. More advanced gas-cooled reactor designs, such as the Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor and High-Temperature Gas-cooled Reactor, use helium as coolant and can achieve much higher operating temperatures than water-cooled reactors, potentially reaching 750 to 950 degrees Celsius. These high temperatures enable greater thermodynamic efficiency for electricity generation and open possibilities for high-temperature industrial applications such as hydrogen production, synthetic fuel manufacturing, and process heat for chemical industries. The High-Temperature Gas-cooled Reactor utilizes TRISO fuel particles, which are tiny uranium kernels coated with multiple layers of carbon and silicon carbide that can withstand extremely high temperatures without releasing fission products. Gas-cooled reactors offer several safety advantages including the chemical inertness of helium coolant, which cannot cause corrosion or chemical reactions, and the ability to maintain cooling even with significant coolant leakage due to the low density of gases compared to water. The modular design of some modern gas-cooled reactors allows for factory fabrication and simplified construction, though the technology faces challenges including higher capital costs and the need for specialized materials capable of withstanding high-temperature, high-radiation environments.

In the philosophy of science, a persistent topic of debate is the question of scientific realism versus anti-realism, or whether scientific theories provide true descriptions of the natural world or if they exist only as predictive models. Philosophers of science explore what experimentation and observation can achieve, as well as the impossible, pursued from the standpoint of the ethical and the political. Philosophy of science questions the very belief in the principles upon which science as a human activity is based, and offers a model of the development of scientific knowledge. It considers the nature of evidence, the status of theory, and the source of observation, and presents a set of reflections that offer valuable insights into the reliability, ambition, promise, and potential pitfalls of scientific inquiry.

text: An encoder is a combinational circuit that converts multiple input signals into a binary code output, essentially performing the inverse operation of a decoder. It takes active input signals, such as switches, sensors, or data lines, and encodes their position or identity into a binary number for efficient data representation and transmission. For example, an 8-to-3 encoder accepts 8 input lines and produces a 3-bit binary output indicating which input is active. Encoders are used in various applications, such as keyboard encoding, where key presses are converted into binary signals for processing, or in data compression systems, where signals are encoded to reduce bandwidth. The primary function of an encoder is to reduce multiple input lines to a smaller number of output lines, facilitating efficient data handling, storage, and communication. Conversely, a decoder performs the reverse operation: it takes a binary code and activates one among many output lines corresponding to that code, enabling specific device control or data retrieval. Decoders are widely used in memory addressing, digital displays, and communication systems. Both encoders and decoders involve logic gate networks that generate the correct outputs based on inputs, ensuring accuracy and reliability. They are essential in reducing wiring complexity and enabling scalable digital systems. Their design is based on Boolean logic, with priority encoders handling multiple simultaneous inputs, and their operation is crucial for address decoding, data routing, and device selection. Encoders and decoders underpin many digital systems, microprocessors, and communication protocols, providing efficient means for data encoding, decoding, and signal management. Their proper functioning is vital for system integrity, speed, and scalability, supporting complex digital architectures and high-speed data transmission in modern electronics and computing.

text: A play's theme serves a basic purpose by expressing the main idea, underlying message, or universal truth that the author wishes to convey to the audience. It gives the story depth and significance and directs the character, plot, and dialogue development. They serve as the backbone of the play, connecting various elements and events to convey a cohesive and purposeful story rather than just a sequence of actions. By presenting a theme, the play engages the audience intellectually and emotionally, often challenging prevailing ideas or highlighting contradictions within human nature and social structures. Themes can be explicit, clearly stated through dialogue and action, or implicit, subtly woven into the play’s fabric through symbolism, motifs, and character interactions. Common themes include love, power, identity, justice, freedom, betrayal, and the struggle between good and evil, though plays can address any subject matter relevant to the human condition. The theme influences the tone and style of the play, shaping how the audience perceives the narrative and the moral or emotional responses it elicits. It also provides a framework for interpreting the characters’ motivations and conflicts, as their decisions and transformations often reflect thematic concerns. Additionally, themes allow plays to transcend their specific settings and time periods, resonating with diverse audiences across cultures and generations by touching on universal truths. Through thematic exploration, playwrights can provoke discussion, inspire change, and foster empathy by revealing different perspectives and experiences. The theme thus elevates a play from mere entertainment to art that speaks to enduring questions and societal issues. In conclusion, a play's theme serves to bring the dramatic components together into a cohesive whole, shedding light on the intricacies of human nature and life while encouraging audiences to think critically outside of the theatre.

text: Labeling theory in criminology is based on the social response a person may receive after committing a crime and the effect of that past on one’s future behavior and self-concept. Introduced in the 1960s by thinkers like Howard Becker, Edwin Lemert and others, the theory is based on the idea that deviance does not lie in an act but in the societal response to an act. When one "gets caught" committing a deviant act and is accordingly labeled - for example as a "criminal", as a "thief", as a "delinquent" – the individual internalizes the label and conforms to the norms and values of the label. This will cause more people to commit acts of deviance as well (secondary deviance). The act itself (primary deviance) may be of a minor nature or even an accident, but societal reactions – stigmatisation, exclusion, and response-with-punishment – may push the individual to the margin and a narrower range of legitimate opportunities. The labeled person may begin to internalize the label and behave in a deviant manner, making it a self fulfilling prophecy. The criminal justice system itself is criticized during this time in the form of labelling theory for perpetuating deviance through applied punishment, discrimination, social and legal control, reinforcement of labels, stereotyping, and stigma that facilitates deviant behavior. It focuses on power in the definition of deviance, and argues that those who have power (eg the law, police, media) label a specific wrongdoing and the people who engage in it, unfairly stigmatizing them and creating stigma for them. Although the theory is useful in describing the process by which social constructions of deviance and stigmatization have long-term consequences, it is not entirely adequate in explaining why people commit an initial act of deviance. Nonetheless, labeling theory has had a major impact on criminal justice reform, especially as it supports diversion programs, restorative justice, and rehabilitation over the marking of individuals, including youth, as having something wrong with them and thus stigmatising them and making it harder for them to reintegrate themselves into normal life.

text: The title of this mini-review is a paraphrase of Dobzhansky’s famous dictum, “Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution” [1,2]. The reason for this paraphrase is to emphasize how, since Dobzhansky’s day, genetics and evolution science have moved into the era of a revolutionary new technology, DNA sequencing. Whenever such a technological revolution occurs, science must always ask itself what impact data from the new methods has on the validity of prevailing concepts. Our current ideas of heredity center on DNA replication and transmission [3]. Although cell and organismal heredity involves transmission of all cellular molecules, we conventionally view RNAs, proteins, lipids, polysaccharides and other biomolecules as derivative products resulting from biochemical activities determined by genomic DNA sequences [4]. According to this DNA-centered perspective, stable inherited changes in organismal properties result primarily from alterations in the genome. New DNA sequences can encode new biochemical capabilities that lead to novel traits. If evolution is the acquisition of new characters over time [5], the most basic causal events should emerge from the processes that generate new DNA sequences. Those events are traceable in genome sequences, which today serve as the ultimate empirical data to test evolutionary hypotheses.

text: Confucius, a Chinese philosopher who lived from 551 to 479 BCE, made profound contributions to Chinese culture and philosophy, significantly shaping moral thought, social relationships, and political theory in East Asia. His teachings, encapsulated in texts such as the "Analects," emphasized the importance of virtue, ethics, and proper conduct in both personal and public life. Central to Confucian thought is the concept of "ren," often translated as "benevolence" or "humaneness," which advocates for compassion and empathy in human interactions. Confucius believed that cultivating "ren" was essential for achieving a harmonious society, encouraging individuals to act with kindness and respect towards others. Another key aspect of his philosophy is the idea of "li," which refers to the proper rituals and norms governing behavior in various social contexts. Confucius argued that adherence to these rituals fosters respect and order, reinforcing the social fabric necessary for a stable society. His focus on familial relationships, particularly the importance of filial piety, emphasized the duty of children to honor and respect their parents and ancestors, thereby promoting a sense of duty and responsibility that extended to the broader community. Confucianism also advocated for the idea of the "gentleman" or "junzi," representing an ideal moral character who exemplifies virtue, self-discipline, and leadership. This notion influenced not only personal conduct but also the expectation of ethical governance, asserting that rulers should embody moral integrity and lead by example. Confucius's ideas on governance were revolutionary for their time, advocating for meritocracy in the selection of officials rather than hereditary privilege, thus laying the groundwork for the civil service examination system that became a hallmark of imperial China. His teachings encouraged rulers to prioritize the welfare of their subjects, fostering a government that is just and benevolent. The impact of Confucius extended beyond his lifetime; his ideas were systematized into Confucianism by later scholars, influencing dynastic policies, educational systems, and social norms throughout Chinese history. Confucian thought played a crucial role in shaping East Asian cultures, including Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, where his principles were integrated into local traditions and governance. Even in contemporary society, Confucian values continue to resonate, promoting respect for authority, emphasis on education, and the importance of community and family ties. The enduring legacy of Confucius is reflected in the ethical and moral frameworks that guide interpersonal relationships and social conduct, illustrating his profound influence on the development of East Asian civilizations and the broader philosophical discourse on ethics and governance. His contributions not only defined a cultural identity for China but also established a philosophical foundation that continues to inform discussions on morality, ethics, and social harmony in modern times.

text: General models of communication conceptualize how information is shared between people (or groups), identifying the primary components and how information is transmitted (message flow). The original and most basic model, linear model, was developed by Claude Shannon [13] and Warren Weaver, and describes communication as a linear process in which a message is sent by a sender (or transmitter) to a receiver via a channel. There is also room in this model for “noise,” or disturbance that can interfere with communicating a message. But it does not take into account the two-way process of communication. To account for this, the interactive model includes feedback from the receiver to the sender, thus allowing communication to become a two way process, while also showing respect for the way in which context influences meaning. The transactional model extends our understanding of communication by highlighting how communication is simultaneous, continuous, and dynamic, where a sender and a receiver exchange messages in a long-lasting way and, being in a continuous feedback interaction, they are mutually shaping each other, and are being shaped by personal, social and environmental contexts. These communication models are basic to the understanding and learning of how communication succeeds and fails, and how to traverse the space between everyday interpersonal language use, organizational communication, and mass communication in both directions, how meanings and errors are made, and how feedback keeps misunderstandings at bay.

text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs, miRs) are a class of evolutionary conserved small (18–22 nt) non-coding RNAs. MiRs, discovered in 1993 in C. elegans, play a pivotal role in biological processes in normal development and disease in both plants and animals [1,2,3,4]. MiRs accomplish their functions by guiding the interaction of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) to complementary or partially complementary sequences in target mRNAs, thereby regulating gene expression through translation inhibition or degradation of transcripts [5,6]. A miR can regulate multiple transcripts depending on the cell type, function and differentiation stage, and a single transcript can be regulated by more than one miR [7,8,9]. Inference of microRNA function usually cannot be derived exclusively through the prediction of their candidate targets. Even with the compilation of predicted targets and pathways the targets regulate, the functions of miRs need to be determined experimentally [10]. To identify function, expression levels or activity of miRs are modulated to observe the effects on cells. A preferred approach is to inhibit miR activity rather than up-regulate miR expression, since the former may reveal the function of the miR at physiological levels in cells. As miRNA activity is dependent on the relative concentration of the miR and its targets, up regulating a miR at levels higher than physiological may result in repression of target mRNAs that normally would not be targeted in normal conditions [11].

text: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation is a fundamental principle in physics that describes the gravitational force between two objects with mass. According to this law, every point mass attracts every other point mass by a force acting along the line intersecting both points. The magnitude of this force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. Mathematically, the law is expressed as F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2, where F is the gravitational force, G is the gravitational constant, m1 and m2 are the masses of the two objects, and r is the distance between the centers of the two objects. The gravitational constant G is a fundamental physical constant that has been experimentally determined to be approximately 6.67430(15)×10^?11 N·(m/kg)^2. Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation has significant implications for understanding the behavior and interactions of objects and systems in various contexts, from the motion of planets and stars to the dynamics of galaxies and the universe. By applying this law, scientists and astronomers can predict and analyze the gravitational forces and motions of celestial bodies, leading to advancements in numerous fields and applications, such as astrophysics, cosmology, and space exploration.

Hence our use of the term “pedestrian” in the remainder of the paper, rather than the more general “people” or “person.” We do not consider more detailed perception tasks such as human pose recovery or activity recognition. Pedestrian detection is a difficult task from a machine vision perspective. The lack of explicit models leads to the use of machine learning techniques, where an implicit representation is learned from examples. As such, it is an instantiation of the multiclass object categorization problem (e.g., [79]). Yet the pedestrian detection task has some of its own characteristics, which can influence the methods of choice. Foremost, there is the wide range of possible pedestrian appearance, due to changing articulated pose, clothing, lighting, and background. The detection component is typically part of a system situated in a physical environment, which means that prior scene knowledge (camera calibration, ground plane constraint) is often available to improve performance.

text: Memory is a complex cognitive process that involves three key stages: encoding, storage, and retrieval, which together explain how information is processed, maintained, and accessed by the brain. Once encoded, the information moves to the storage phase, where it is held for a short or extended period depending on its nature and importance. Storage occurs in different memory systems: sensory memory, short-term memory (or working memory), and long-term memory. Finally, retrieval is the process of accessing and bringing stored information back into conscious awareness for use, such as recalling a friend’s phone number or remembering facts for an exam. Successful retrieval depends on how well the information was encoded and stored, and it may be influenced by cues, context, or emotional states. The efficiency of these three stages determines memory performance and is essential for learning, problem-solving, and decision-making. Failures in any of the stages can result in forgetting or misremembering information.

text: Data can be broadly classified into several types based on its nature, format, and the way it is measured or collected. The two primary categories of data are qualitative (categorical) and quantitative (numerical) data. Qualitative data describes characteristics or attributes and is often divided into nominal and ordinal types. Nominal data represents categories without any inherent order, such as gender, nationality, or colors, where the values are labels without a numerical meaning. Ordinal data, however, involves categories with a meaningful order or ranking, such as survey ratings (e.g., poor, average, excellent) or class levels, but the intervals between ranks are not necessarily equal. Quantitative data, on the other hand, represents measurable quantities and is further divided into discrete and continuous data. Discrete data consists of countable values, often integers, such as the number of students in a class or the number of defective items in a batch. Continuous data can take any value within a range and includes measurements like height, weight, temperature, or time, where values can be fractional or decimal. Additionally, data can be classified based on its source or format, such as structured data, which is organized and easily searchable in databases (e.g., spreadsheets, tables), and unstructured data, which lacks a predefined format, including text, images, videos, and social media posts. Another important distinction is between time-series data, which is collected over time intervals to observe trends, and cross-sectional data, which captures information at a single point in time. Understanding the types of data is crucial because it determines the appropriate methods for analysis, visualization, and interpretation. For example, statistical tests and machine learning algorithms vary depending on whether the data is categorical or numerical. In summary, data types encompass qualitative and quantitative categories, each with subtypes like nominal, ordinal, discrete, and continuous, and recognizing these distinctions is essential for effective data handling and analysis.

The war also contributed to the decline of serfdom, as peasants were often conscripted or had opportunities for paid military service, giving them more leverage and mobility. For England, the loss of its continental possessions (except Calais) forced its focus inwards, leading to increased maritime development and eventual overseas expansion. For France, the expulsion of the English allowed for greater political unification and the consolidation of royal power, setting the stage for its emergence as a major European power. In essence, the Hundred Years' War was a catalyst for fundamental changes in warfare, national identity, and state-building, marking a crucial transition in the political and social landscape of Western Europe.

text: The torque-slip characteristic of an induction motor describes the relationship between the motor's developed torque and the slip (the difference between synchronous speed and actual rotor speed). This characteristic is crucial in understanding motor behavior under different load conditions. At zero slip, which corresponds to synchronous speed, the rotor does not experience any relative motion with respect to the rotating magnetic field, so no current is induced, and consequently, no torque is generated. As slip increases slightly—such as during light load—some torque is developed. As the load on the motor increases, slip increases, and the rotor current increases accordingly, which increases torque output. This continues until a certain point where the motor produces its maximum torque, known as breakdown torque or pull-out torque. This is typically two to three times the full-load torque. If the load is increased further beyond this point, the rotor cannot sustain the required torque, and the motor will slow down sharply or stall. This point marks the unstable operating region of the motor. The characteristic curve has three distinct regions: low-slip (stable region) where torque increases nearly linearly with slip, breakdown region where torque peaks, and high-slip (unstable region) where torque drops as slip continues to increase. At starting, slip is 100%, and torque is non-zero—referred to as starting torque—which is a key performance indicator in selecting motors for high-load applications. These characteristics vary depending on rotor design; for example, deep-bar or double-cage rotors are optimized for high starting torque. Understanding the torque-slip characteristic helps engineers select motors appropriate for specific mechanical loads and ensure reliable startup and operational performance.

text: The barriers to women's economic empowerment are numerous and deeply entrenched, spanning legal, social, cultural, and structural dimensions, preventing women from achieving their full economic potential and contributing equally to economies. Gender inequality in education also plays a critical role, as lower literacy rates and limited access to higher education for girls and women constrain their employment opportunities and earning potential. The disproportionate burden of unpaid care work (childcare, elder care, household chores) is a major structural barrier, as it consumes women's time and energy, limiting their availability for paid employment, career progression, and skill development. This often leads to occupational segregation, where women are concentrated in lower-paying, often informal sectors, or in jobs that offer less security and fewer benefits. The gender pay gap, resulting from direct discrimination, occupational segregation, and the undervaluation of "women's work," further reduces women's economic returns. Lack of access to affordable and quality childcare, as well as rigid workplace policies that do not support work-life balance, also push women out of the workforce or into precarious employment. Social and cultural norms, including harmful stereotypes about women's roles and capabilities, can restrict women's mobility, decision-making power, and participation in the public sphere, making it difficult for them to pursue certain careers or leadership positions. Furthermore, gender-based violence, including sexual harassment in the workplace, creates unsafe environments that impede women's economic participation and stability. Overcoming these barriers requires a multi-pronged approach that includes legal reforms, investment in education and skills training for women, promoting shared caregiving responsibilities, implementing family-friendly workplace policies, ensuring equal pay, and challenging discriminatory social norms and practices.

text: Mycorrhiza refers to a symbiotic association between fungi and the roots of most terrestrial plants. This relationship is mutually beneficial, with the fungi aiding plants in nutrient and water absorption, while the plants provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced through photosynthesis. Mycorrhizae significantly enhance plant growth and health, especially in nutrient-poor soils, by increasing the surface area for absorption and facilitating the uptake of essential nutrients like phosphorus, nitrogen, and micronutrients. There are two main types of mycorrhizae: ectomycorrhizae, which form a sheath around the root tips and penetrate between root cells, and endomycorrhizae, where fungal hyphae invade the root cells themselves, forming structures called vesicles and arbuscules. These hyphal networks extend far into the soil, beyond the reach of roots alone, enabling plants to access nutrients that would otherwise be unavailable. Mycorrhizae also improve soil structure by promoting soil aggregation and increasing water retention, which enhances drought resistance. The fungi involved in mycorrhizal associations belong mainly to the phyla Glomeromycota, Ascomycota, and Basidiomycota. Besides improving nutrient uptake, mycorrhizae can also protect plants against soil-borne pathogens by outcompeting harmful microbes or inducing plant defense mechanisms. They play a crucial role in ecological succession, forest regeneration, and habitat stability by promoting plant diversity and resilience. In agriculture, mycorrhizal inoculants are used to improve crop yields, reduce fertilizer dependency, and promote sustainable farming practices. Mycorrhizal relationships are ancient and widespread, dating back hundreds of millions of years, and are considered essential for the health of most terrestrial ecosystems. They support plant adaptation to stressful conditions, such as high salinity or heavy metal contamination, by aiding in detoxification and nutrient management. Overall, mycorrhizae are vital for plant nutrition, soil health, and ecosystem sustainability, making them one of the most important symbiotic relationships in nature. Their study and application hold promise for enhancing agricultural productivity, restoring degraded lands, and conserving biodiversity in the face of environmental challenges.

text: In graphic design, margins, gutters, and bleeds are essential layout components that ensure visual clarity, structural integrity, and professional output, particularly in print and digital design. Margins are the empty spaces surrounding the content area, typically along the edges of a page or screen, providing breathing room and preventing elements from feeling cramped. For example, a book’s margins ensure text doesn’t crowd the page edges, enhancing readability. Gutters are the spaces between columns or content blocks within a grid system, maintaining separation and guiding the viewer’s eye through the layout. In multi-column designs, like magazines, gutters prevent text or images from overlapping, ensuring clarity. Bleeds refer to artwork or elements that extend beyond the page’s trim edge, typically by 3-5mm, to account for slight cutting inaccuracies during printing, ensuring no white edges appear in the final product. For instance, a poster with a full-color background requires bleed to achieve a seamless edge. These elements work together to create balanced, functional layouts; margins and gutters organize content, while bleeds ensure polished print results. In digital design, margins and gutters adapt to responsive layouts, maintaining consistency across screen sizes. Misusing these can lead to cluttered or unprofessional designs, like text cut off in print. By defining these parameters early, designers align with project goals, enhance user experience, and ensure technical precision, making margins, gutters, and bleeds critical for cohesive, visually appealing outcomes across various design applications.

text: 1.2 Types of actuators there are three major types of actuators: hydraulic, pneumatic, and electric actuators having different characteristic features that are appropriate for various application purposes. Hydraulic movables work by directing pressurized fluids in the creation of force and motion. Their high power density is popular with heavy load applications, such as construction robots or industrial machines. But they are heavy, need elaborate upkeep and can spring leaks. Pneumatic actuators generate movement with compressed air. They are also faster, cleaner and lighter than hydraulics, which are often used in factory automation and pick-and-place robots. Pneumatics are too quick to respond and lack the fine control of force that hydraulic or electrical systems deliver. Electric actuators such as DC, servo and stepper motors have used electric power to provide mechanical motion, in which they are highly accurate, efficient and can easily be interfaced to digital control systems. Good enough for anything that demands high accuracy control, such as robotic arms and space rovers. Electric actuators don’t need the fluid systems and compressors used with hydraulic and pneumatic systems, simplifying design and maintenance. But they don't necessarily compare with hydraulics for force. The one to choose depends on the application — hydraulics when power is the priority, pneumatics when speed and simplicity are, and electrical when precision and control are.

text: Effective emotion regulation is critical to adaptive functioning in clinical and nonclinical populations alike. Emotional responses can be modulated through several methods involving dynamic cognition-emotion interactions, and this is an active area of study with regard to the cognitive and affective dysregulation characteristic of various psychological disorders (e.g., depression, Johnstone, van Reekum, Urry, Kalin, & Davidson, 2007; phobias, Larson et al., 2006). This work suggests that, just as emotional states can impair or facilitate behavioral responses on cognitive tasks (e.g., Gray, 2001), cognitive processes impact affect. For example, attention and reappraisal have been found to modulate subjective ratings of negatively valenced pictures (Ochsner, Bunge, Gross, & Gabrieli, 2002), autonomic responses to stressors (Butler et al., 2003; Gross, 2002), and activation in affect-relevant subcortical regions such as the amygdala (Ochsner et al., 2004; Pessoa, 2005). Further, areas of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) known to play an important role in cognitive processing, including the dorsolateral and medial PFC and the orbitofrontal cortex, are recruited to modulate fear responding (Ochsner et al., 2002; Ochsner & Gross, 2005). Indeed, PTSD is believed to be characterized by medial PFC hypoactivity, as top-down inhibition of limbic system hyperactivity is impaired in this disorder (Maier, 2015).

text: Inference is when readers figure something out from the information in the text, even though it is not explicitly stated. Drawing inferences is a critical reading skill, as writers typically don't spell everything out explicitly and readers need to read between the lines to make meaning. For example, if a passage reads, “He walked into the room with his fists clenched and his face red,” the reader can tell that the character is angry, even though the word “angry” is never used. To interpret a text, readers need to use context clues and prior knowledge. That involves reading the text closely, recording key details and considering what those details imply. For example, a character could be presumed shy or nervous if they refuse look someone in the eye or speak quietly. Inference questions on the exams often look like “What can be concluded?” or “What does this statement mean?” To be entirely correct students must eliminate personal opinions, hunches, and only rely on text-based evidence. Inference also requires practice, particularly when reading literature, news articles, or persuasive text in which authors imply things without stating them directly. Strong inferences make sense and answer the question based on what is stated in the passage. In the next functional level, inferring, readers relate textual information to prior knowledge to comprehend character actions, anticipate story events, and understand the ideological messages in complex or abstract texts (Dale et al. It also adds a layer of engagement and cerebral wrangling to reading, as readers literally join the dots to decode the author’s actual meaning.

text: A proximity sensor is a vital device in robotics and automation that detects the presence or absence of nearby objects without requiring physical contact. These sensors are essential for enabling robots to navigate their environments safely, avoid obstacles, and interact with objects and humans effectively. Proximity sensors operate based on various principles, with the most common types being infrared (IR) sensors, ultrasonic sensors, capacitive sensors, and inductive sensors. Infrared sensors emit infrared light and measure the reflection from nearby objects to determine their presence and distance. They are widely used in applications such as obstacle detection and object tracking. Ultrasonic sensors, on the other hand, utilize high-frequency sound waves to measure the distance to an object by calculating the time it takes for the sound waves to bounce back. This type of sensor is particularly effective in various environments, including outdoor settings, and is commonly employed in robotic navigation systems. Capacitive sensors detect changes in capacitance caused by the presence of an object, making them suitable for detecting non-metallic materials, while inductive sensors are designed to sense metal objects by measuring changes in inductance. Proximity sensors have numerous applications in robotics, including obstacle avoidance, where they enable robots to detect and navigate around obstacles, ensuring safe movement in dynamic environments. They also play a crucial role in object manipulation, assisting robots in accurately detecting and handling items during tasks such as assembly, packaging, and sorting. Furthermore, proximity sensors enhance human-robot interaction by allowing robots to sense the presence of humans, which is essential for collaborative work environments where safety is paramount. In material handling systems, these sensors are used to detect the presence of items on conveyor belts, ensuring efficient operation and flow of materials. The advantages of proximity sensors include their non-contact detection capabilities, which reduce wear and tear, and their quick response times, enabling real-time interaction with the environment. However, they also have limitations, such as range constraints, with some sensors only effective within short distances, and sensitivity to environmental factors, which can affect their performance. Overall, proximity sensors are indispensable components in modern robotic systems, providing the necessary feedback and information that allow robots to perceive and interact with their surroundings, ultimately enhancing their functionality and versatility across various applications in industries such as manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare.

text: Reporting and editing are separate yet mutually reliant processes in journalism--each serving a significant function in bringing news to readers. Their job isn’t to endorse candidates or persuade you to vote for them, but to find the truth, to add meaning, to tell you what is important in terms you can understand and believe. Reporters are the narrators who transform raw data received in the field into news in the newsroom. And then there’s the edit: The work that comes after the reporting, and that’s done by assigning editors themselves — the winnowing and refining and shaping that goes into making raw material into what’s publishable or what’s on the air. Editors review the work of the reporter to ensure it is accurate, coherent, grammatically correct, is in the proper style and meets ethical standards. They make sure the story is consistent with the media outlet’s practices and policies. Editors may rearrange material, change headlines and leads, and excise irrelevant or potentially harmful material. Where reporters are concerned with getting and writing down facts, editors are concentrating on making facts available and guiding them into a package that has meaning for readers. Reporting is about investigation and creativity and editing about analysis and correction. Editors and news reporters have to collaborate and communicate together, after all, as editors need to work through with reporters their reactions to a story to make the final story better. Reporting and editing, the two are provocatively twinned, are the practice by which news is not just true and current but also clear, balanced and responsible.

text: The performance of machine learning methods is heavily dependent on the choice of data representation (or features) on which they are applied. text: The half-life of a drug is the time it takes for its plasma concentration to fall to half its original value after a single dose. It is an important pharmacokinetic parameter that determines the duration in which the drug remains in the body and hence the dosing interval. For example, drugs with a short half-life may need to be taken more than once a day, while those with a long half-life only require a once daily or less frequent dosing. Half-life varies depending on the volume of the drug's distribution and body clearance. It is also useful in establishing the time required to achieve steady state concentrations on repeated dosing as well as when a drug is eliminated following the cessation of treatment. TI The measure of safety for a drug in which the toxicity as measured by the toxic dose (TD50) and the effective dose (ED50) are compared and expressed as the TI. A high therapeutic index signifies a great margin of safety under which the drug can be used (i.e., a low risk of adverse effects). Some drugs, such as penicillin have a high therapeutic index, while others such as warfarin have a low therapeutic index and need to be closely monitored. TI assists doctors in knowing how low or high a drug can be prescribed, particularly among long-term treatments or in high doses. It also guides drug selection in populations with altered sensitivity (elderly, children, or patients with organ failure). To recap, half-life is about duration of action or how long the drug continues to exert an effect and tells you dosing frequency while therapeutic index is about safety, or the amount of time or material between what helps and what hurts.

text: The Denavit-Hartenberg (D-H) parameters are a standardized method for modeling the kinematic structure of robotic manipulators by defining the spatial relationships between consecutive joints and links using four geometric parameters. Introduced by Jacques Denavit and Richard Hartenberg in 1955, this convention simplifies the representation of robotic arms by assigning a coordinate frame to each joint and describing their relative positions and orientations through four variables: 1) Link length (a?): The distance along the common normal (perpendicular axis) between the joint axes of two consecutive links; 2) Link twist (??): The angle between the joint axes, measured around the common normal; 3) Joint offset (d?): The linear displacement along the joint axis between adjacent links; and 4) Joint angle (??): The rotational angle about the joint axis connecting two links. These parameters are used to construct homogeneous transformation matrices, which mathematically describe how each joint’s movement affects the end-effector’s position and orientation. The D-H convention is particularly useful for serial-chain robots (e.g., industrial robotic arms) because it reduces complex 3D kinematics into a systematic, recursive framework, enabling efficient forward and inverse kinematics calculations. However, it assumes specific geometric constraints (e.g., perpendicular or parallel joint axes) and may require modifications (like modified D-H parameters) for certain configurations. Despite limitations, D-H parameters remain foundational in robotics for motion planning, simulation, and control system design, bridging the gap between mechanical design and algorithmic motion control in applications ranging from manufacturing to surgical robotics. Advances in parallel and soft robotics have spurred alternative modeling approaches, but D-H parameters continue to be a cornerstone in teaching and industrial robotics due to their clarity and adaptability.

text: Diegetic sound refers to any sound that originates from within the world of the film and can be heard by both the characters and the audience. This includes sounds like characters’ dialogue, footsteps, ambient noises such as rain or traffic, and music that is part of the scene, like a radio playing or a character singing. Diegetic sound helps create a sense of realism and immerses the audience in the story’s environment because it exists naturally within the film’s narrative world. It can be either on-screen (visible source) or off-screen (sound coming from something not shown but understood to be present in the scene) .In contrast, non-diegetic sound is sound that does not originate from the story world and is only heard by the audience, not by the characters. This type of sound is added during post-production to enhance the emotional or dramatic effect of a scene. Common examples include the musical score or soundtrack, voice-over narration that explains or comments on the story, and sound effects used for emphasis or mood rather than realism. Non-diegetic sound guides the audience’s emotional response, builds tension, or provides narrative information that characters themselves are unaware of .In summary, the key difference is that diegetic sound exists within the film’s reality and is audible to characters, while non-diegetic sound is external to the story world and intended solely for the audience’s experience. Both types of sound are essential tools in filmmaking, often used together to enrich storytelling and audience engagement .

text: The nuclear fuel cycle encompasses all the stages involved in the production, use, and disposal of nuclear fuel for energy generation. The cycle begins with the mining and milling of uranium ore, where uranium is extracted from the earth and processed into a concentrated form known as yellowcake. The next stage is conversion, where yellowcake is converted into uranium hexafluoride (UF6), a gaseous compound suitable for enrichment. Enrichment is the process of increasing the proportion of uranium-235, the fissile isotope used in most nuclear reactors, from its natural abundance of about 0.7% to the levels required for reactor fuel, typically around 3-5% for light water reactors. The enriched UF6 is then fabricated into fuel pellets, which are assembled into fuel rods and loaded into fuel assemblies for use in the reactor. Once the fuel has been used in the reactor and has reached the end of its service life, it is considered spent nuclear fuel (SNF) and must be managed. The back-end of the fuel cycle involves the storage, reprocessing, or disposal of SNF. Storage can be either short-term, where SNF is stored in spent fuel pools at the reactor site, or long-term, where it is stored in dry casks. Reprocessing involves the separation of valuable materials, such as plutonium and uranium, from the SNF, which can then be recycled into new fuel. Disposal involves the permanent storage of SNF in a geological repository, ensuring that it is isolated from the biosphere. The nuclear fuel cycle is a complex and multifaceted process that requires careful management to ensure the safe and efficient use of nuclear energy.

text: Selective attention is the cognitive process by which individuals focus their awareness on a specific stimulus or task while ignoring other irrelevant or distracting information in the environment. For example, when reading a book in a noisy café, selective attention allows you to concentrate on the words while tuning out background chatter. This process is influenced by factors such as the intensity or novelty of stimuli, personal interests, goals, and emotional significance. Selective attention can be voluntary (goal-directed) or involuntary (stimulus-driven), and it is governed by both top-down and bottom-up mechanisms. Neuropsychological research has identified key brain regions involved in selective attention, such as the prefrontal cortex and parietal lobes, which help modulate the focus of perception and action. Experiments like the “cocktail party effect,” where people can hear their name in a noisy environment, and the “inattentional blindness” paradigm, where unexpected objects go unnoticed, demonstrate the limitations and power of selective attention. While selective attention helps improve efficiency and task performance, it can also lead to missing important information that falls outside the focus of attention, showing how perception is not a perfect reflection of reality but a filtered, prioritized experience.

text: Process scheduling algorithms determine the order in which processes are executed by the CPU, optimizing system performance and resource utilization. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) is the simplest approach, executing processes in the order they arrive, but it suffers from the "convoy effect," where short processes wait behind long ones, leading to poor average waiting time. Shortest Job First (SJF) prioritizes processes with the smallest burst time, minimizing average waiting time, but requires accurate predictions of process duration and can cause starvation for longer jobs if not implemented with aging. Round Robin (RR) allocates a fixed time slice (quantum) to each process in a cyclic order, ensuring fairness and responsiveness, especially in time-sharing systems; however, performance depends heavily on the quantum size—too large mimics FCFS, while too small increases context-switching overhead. Priority Scheduling assigns priorities to processes, executing higher-priority ones first, but risks starvation for low-priority processes unless combined with aging techniques. Multilevel Queue Scheduling categorizes processes into separate queues (e.g., foreground for interactive tasks, background for batch jobs), each with its own scheduling policy, balancing responsiveness and throughput. Multilevel Feedback Queue dynamically adjusts process priorities and queues based on behavior (e.g., CPU-bound vs. I/O-bound), offering flexibility for diverse workloads. These algorithms address trade-offs between throughput, latency, fairness, and starvation, with FCFS favoring simplicity, SJF optimizing turnaround time, and RR ensuring equitable CPU sharing. Modern operating systems often combine these strategies (e.g., Linux’s Completely Fair Scheduler) to adapt to varying workloads while maintaining efficiency and user responsiveness.

text:
The Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453) was a protracted series of conflicts between the Kingdom of England and the House of Valois (France), primarily over territorial claims, feudal rights, and the French throne, which profoundly reshaped medieval Europe’s political, military, and cultural landscapes. Significance includes:
National Identity Formation: The war accelerated the consolidation of French and English national identities. Joan of Arc’s (1412–1431) leadership and the French monarchy’s eventual victory under Charles VII fostered French unity, while England’s defeat precipitated internal strife (e.g., the Wars of the Roses, 1455–1487), shifting its focus inward. Military Revolution: The conflict introduced game-changing innovations—longbows (e.g., Battle of Crécy, 1346), gunpowder artillery (e.g., Battle of Castillon, 1453), and professional standing armies—rendering traditional feudal levies obsolete and transforming European warfare. Feudal Decline: The war’s financial and logistical demands eroded feudalism, as monarchs centralized power by taxing populations directly (e.g., English Parliament’s role) and bypassing noble intermediaries, laying groundwork for modern nation-states. Economic Disruption: Prolonged warfare devastated trade, agriculture, and populations (e.g., the Black Death, 1347–1351, exacerbated by conflict), reshaping labor systems and accelerating the decline of serfdom as labor shortages empowered peasants.
Dynastic and Territorial Shifts: England lost nearly all French territories except Calais, ending its continental ambitions and refocusing on maritime expansion. France emerged as a centralized monarchy, paving the way for its Renaissance-era dominance.
Cultural Legacy: The war inspired chivalric literature (e.g., Froissart’s Chronicles) and later romanticized nationalism, while its brutality (e.g., chevauchée tactics) exposed the dark side of medieval warfare, influencing modern perceptions of just war and sovereignty. Ultimately, the Hundred Years’ War marked the transition from medieval to early modern Europe, redefining governance, warfare, and collective identity.

text: The formation of caves and stalactites is a fascinating geological process that involves the dissolution and deposition of minerals, primarily calcium carbonate, in limestone and other soluble rocks. Caves, also known as cavern systems, form through the process of chemical weathering, where acidic water dissolves and erodes the rock, creating underground voids and passageways. The primary agent of cave formation is water, which becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and the soil. This acidic water, known as carbonic acid, reacts with the calcium carbonate in limestone, dissolving it and creating a solution of calcium bicarbonate. Over time, this process enlarges cracks and fissures in the rock, forming underground channels and cavities that eventually develop into cave systems. The formation of caves is influenced by several factors, including the composition and structure of the rock, the flow and chemistry of the water, and the climate and environmental conditions. Caves can form in a variety of geological settings, from horizontal bedding planes to vertical joints and faults, and can range in size from small cavities to vast, interconnected systems. The most common type of cave is the limestone cave, which forms in regions with extensive limestone deposits and abundant groundwater. However, caves can also form in other types of soluble rocks, such as gypsum, salt, and quartzite, through similar processes of dissolution and erosion. Once a cave system is formed, the deposition of minerals can create a variety of speleothems, or cave formations, including stalactites, stalagmites, and columns. Stalactites are icicle-shaped formations that hang from the ceiling of a cave and form through the deposition of calcium carbonate. As water containing dissolved calcium bicarbonate drips from the ceiling of the cave, it loses carbon dioxide to the cave atmosphere, causing the calcium carbonate to precipitate and form a small ring or tube. Over time, as more water drips and deposits calcium carbonate, the stalactite grows downward, elongating and thickening into its characteristic shape. The growth rate of stalactites can vary depending on the flow and chemistry of the water, as well as the environmental conditions within the cave. In some cases, stalactites can grow several centimeters per year, while in others, they may grow only a few millimeters per century. The formation of stalactites is often accompanied by the formation of stalagmites, which are upward-growing formations that form on the floor of the cave. Stalagmites form through the same process of calcium carbonate deposition, as water drips from the ceiling and deposits minerals on the cave floor. Over time, as more water drips and deposits calcium carbonate, the stalagmite grows upward, eventually meeting and fusing with a stalactite to form a column. The formation of caves and stalactites is a slow and ongoing process that can take thousands or even millions of years. These geological features are not only scientifically significant but also culturally and aesthetically valuable, providing insights into the Earth's history and offering breathtaking landscapes for exploration and appreciation. Understanding the processes and mechanisms of cave and stalactite formation is essential for preserving and protecting these unique and fragile environments, as well as for advancing our knowledge of the Earth's dynamic systems.

text: Bandwidth and latency are two distinct but related concepts in networking that are often confused with each other. Bandwidth refers to the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a network connection in a given amount of time, typically measured in bits per second (bps). It represents the capacity of the network to handle data transfer, with higher bandwidth indicating a greater ability to transfer data quickly. Latency, on the other hand, refers to the time it takes for data to travel from the sender to the receiver, typically measured in milliseconds (ms). It represents the delay or lag in the communication, with lower latency indicating a more responsive and real-time interaction. To illustrate the difference, consider a highway analogy: bandwidth is like the number of lanes on the highway, determining how much traffic can flow simultaneously, while latency is like the speed limit, determining how quickly the traffic moves. A network can have high bandwidth but still experience high latency if the data is delayed in transit, and conversely, a network with low bandwidth can have low latency if the data is transmitted quickly, but the amount of data is limited. Understanding the distinction between bandwidth and latency is crucial for optimizing network performance and ensuring that applications receive the necessary resources to function effectively.

text: Viruses of plants are minute pathogenic particles, consisting of either RNA or DNA enclosed in a protein coat, known as a capsid, which lack a cellular structure and depend on the host plant for reproduction and dissemination. Plant viruses can cause a variety of diseases which can significantly reduce the health, yield and quality of plants. They are delivered into plant cells through wounds, grafting, or are inoculated by vectors, including insects (for example, aphids, whiteflies), nematodes, and fungi during feeding or vegetative travel over the plant. Once inside, viruses reprogram the host cell’s metabolism in order to make more of their own viral particles, which then travel both locally through plasmodesmata connecting cells and systemically through the vascular network. Many infected plants show symptoms of mosaic (light and dark green splotchy areas on leaves), leaf curl, chlorosis (yellowing), stunting and/or deformed leaves or fruits with some plants dying. Viruses lack cell metabolism, and the chemical pesticides for fungi or bacteria cannot control them. Management primarily lies in prevention by planting material free from virus infection, vector control, crop rotation, and planting of resistant cultivars. Plant viruses cause substantial threats to worldwide food security, and the studies in plant virology have greatly contributed to the development of new strategies for virus control for lessening financial loses and securing sustainable provision of crops.

text: The retina is the thin light-sensitive layer of the eye where the light signal is transformed into a neural signal. The cornea and lens forms an image at the retina when light passes through the eye. The retina contains the two most important types of photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) for light-intensity and colour vision. Rods greatly outnumber cones and are more sensitive to light and function in low light vision (but they do not provide image color).
